concepts.mech: He argued that suffering is positive and felt directly, while satisfaction is merely the absence of a want, so life swings between pain and boredom. Relief comes briefly in aesthetic contemplation, when the will goes quiet, in compassion, and in ascetic renunciation.
concepts.lim: The argument assumes all pleasure is relief from lack, which is questionable: curiosity, play and absorption don't obviously start from deficit. Hedonic adaptation research supports part of the picture, but adaptation is partial and varies by event.

concepts.dek: People can endure almost any how if they have a why. But Frankl insisted meaning is found, not invented.
concepts.kw: purpose meaning of life suffering logotherapy concentration camp why live existentialism existential
concepts.idea: Viktor Frankl, a psychiatrist who survived the Nazi camps, reported that people with something to live for seemed better able to bear extreme deprivation. From this he developed logotherapy. The primary drive is meaning, he held, rather than pleasure as in Freud or power as in Adler. Meaning comes through work, love, and the stance taken toward unavoidable suffering.
concepts.insight: When nothing can be changed, your attitude still can. And happiness can't be pursued directly. It follows from devotion to something beyond yourself.
concepts.why: A direct counter to existentialists who say meaning is invented. For Frankl it's discovered, almost perceived.
life: A caregiver for whom the exhausting work is what holds life together.
Finding a purpose in an illness that you didn't choose.
Chasing happiness and finding it recedes.

sides: Meaning is objective and found in each situation.
There's no meaning to find. You create it by choosing.
Looking for meaning at all is where the trouble starts.
tension.note: If meaning is found rather than made, what separates a true meaning from a sincere mistake?

concepts.mech: Frankl held that meaning is specific to a person and a moment, and is discovered, not invented. When circumstances can't be changed, the attitude taken toward them still can, and happiness follows from devotion to something beyond oneself instead of being pursued directly.
concepts.lim: Much of the evidence is his own observation and clinical experience, and those who lost all sense of meaning in the camps didn't write about it. Research on meaning in life links it to well-being but can't settle whether meaning is objective.

concepts.dek: We can explain everything the brain does and still not explain why any of it is experienced.
concepts.kw: consciousness qualia what is it like experience mind body physicalism bat
concepts.idea: Explaining how the brain discriminates stimuli, integrates information and reports on itself is difficult but looks like ordinary science. Chalmers (1995) argued this leaves something out: why any of it is accompanied by experience. Nagel pressed a related point in 1974 with the bat: knowing its sonar physiology wouldn't tell you what it's like to be one.
concepts.insight: Physical explanations describe structure and function. Experience seems to be neither. There may be a gap that more data can't close.
concepts.why: What you know most certainly, that you're experiencing something, is what science can least explain.
life: Wondering whether your red looks like someone else's red.
Pain that has no visible cause and is still the most real thing in the room.

sides: Consciousness can't be reduced to physical processes as currently understood.
There's no hard problem. The sense that there's something extra is itself a product of the brain.
If everyone has a private "beetle" no one else can see, it drops out of language. Maybe "qualia" is a grammatical confusion.
tension.note: Whether the gap lies in the world or in our concepts is exactly what neither side has yet shown.

rel: The self as a story the brain tells
deeper: Facing up to the problem of consciousness
What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
concepts.mech: The argument is that physical explanation works by describing structure and function, and experience doesn't follow from any such description. Thought experiments such as philosophical zombies, creatures functionally identical to us but without experience, are offered to show the gap is conceptual, not just missing data.
concepts.lim: It leans on intuitions about conceivability that other philosophers reject, and it hasn't yet produced a research programme of its own. Illusionists reply that the datum itself is mistaken.

concepts.dek: Your brain doesn't detect anger. It guesses anger, based on body signals, context and concepts you've learned.
concepts.kw: feelings emotions universal facial expressions anxiety vs excitement interoception
concepts.idea: Agreement about which emotion a face shows varies across cultures and tasks. Barrett draws on this, and on reviews of physiological and neuroimaging studies, to argue that no emotion has a consistent bodily or neural signature. In her theory the brain predicts what bodily sensations mean, using concepts learned in a culture, and the result is the emotion.
concepts.insight: If so, a racing heart can be anxiety, excitement or attraction, depending on how it's categorized. More precise emotion words should help regulation, and some research suggests they do.
concepts.why: Emotions don't just happen to you. They're partly a skill of interpretation.
life: Calling nerves "excitement" before a talk and feeling different.
Being hungry and deciding your partner is irritating.
A language with a word for a feeling you'd never isolated before.

sides: Emotions are constructed predictions, varying by person and culture.
Core emotions have evolved circuits. Variation is real but sits on top of a universal base.
tension.note: Even if the theory is wrong, the practical question stands: does renaming a feeling change it, or only change how you describe it?

rel: What feeling is, at the bottom
concepts.mech: On this account, interoceptive signals are ambiguous and the brain categorizes them using context and prior experience. The same racing heart can become anxiety, excitement or attraction. Emotional granularity, the ability to make finer distinctions, is proposed to help regulation because it gives the brain more options for prediction.
concepts.lim: Basic emotion theorists point to recognition of expressions above chance in many cultures and to conserved circuits in other animals, and they dispute Barrett's reading of the meta-analyses. Evidence that finer emotion words improve regulation is mostly correlational.

concepts.dek: The famous experiment that "disproved free will" may have been measuring noise.
concepts.kw: free will determinism libet decision brain decides before you
concepts.idea: In Libet's 1983 experiment, people flicked a wrist whenever they chose and noted when they felt the urge. Brain activity began building a few hundred milliseconds before that reported urge, and many concluded the brain decides before we do. In 2012 Schurger and colleagues showed that a similar ramp can emerge from random neural fluctuations crossing a threshold, which would make it no marker of a decision.
concepts.insight: In 2012, Schurger and colleagues reproduced that buildup with random neural noise drifting toward a threshold. It may not be a decision at all. The famous blow to free will may barely land.
concepts.why: A striking result can outrun its evidence, and the free will debate stays philosophical even when it looks empirical.
life: Feeling you decided, when you might have just acted.
Pop articles announcing that science has ended free will.

sides: Conscious will comes too late to cause action.
The readiness potential reflects random fluctuations, not an unconscious decision.
Even full determinism wouldn't remove free will, if free will means acting from your own reasons.
tension.note: Even a clean result would test only a narrow idea of free will: a snap decision to flick a wrist.

deeper: An accumulator model for spontaneous neural activity prior to self-initiated movement
concepts.mech: The readiness potential is found by averaging brain recordings aligned to the movement. Schurger's model treats spontaneous fluctuations as noise that looks like a slow ramp when the moment of crossing a threshold is used to align the data. Libet's timing also relies on participants' reports of a clock reading, which is itself imprecise.
concepts.lim: Showing the ramp isn't an early decision doesn't show that conscious intention causes action. Libet's task, an arbitrary wrist flick, is also far from deliberate choices, and other decoding studies are limited in their own ways.

concepts.dek: Loneliness makes you more alert to rejection, which makes you act in ways that get you more of it.
concepts.kw: lonely isolated why can't i make friends social anxiety withdraw
concepts.idea: Lonely people tend to notice social threats faster and to read ambiguous cues as negative. Cacioppo treated loneliness as an aversive signal, like hunger, that pushes toward reconnection but also puts the person on guard. The guardedness can look like coldness to others, so the rejection expected becomes more likely.
concepts.insight: That vigilance backfires. Expecting rejection, people turn guarded, others read it as coldness, and the fear is confirmed. It's why "just put yourself out there" rarely works.
concepts.why: How many people are around you doesn't settle loneliness. It's a lens that distorts what they seem to be doing.
life: Reading a short reply as hostility.
Leaving a party early to avoid being left out.
Feeling lonelier in a crowd than alone.

sides: Loneliness is an evolved alarm, and the fix targets perception, not just contact.
The rise of loneliness is also structural: work, cities, the decline of institutions. A cognitive fix doesn't touch that.
tension.note: If loneliness is partly a distorted lens, who is responsible for correcting it, the person wearing it or the social world that made it?

concepts.mech: The model describes a feedback loop: perceived isolation heightens attention to threat, which biases interpretation, which changes behaviour, which reduces warmth from others and confirms the expectation. Reviews of interventions have found that those targeting maladaptive social thinking tend to do relatively well compared with simply increasing contact.
concepts.lim: Much of the evidence is correlational or cross-sectional, so it's hard to separate cause from consequence. A perception-focused account also leaves aside material conditions: loneliness has structural roots in work, housing and the decline of shared institutions.

concepts.dek: The problem with work isn't only the pay. You can do it all day with nothing of you in it.
concepts.kw: job meaningless work burnout sunday scaries purpose career bullshit jobs
concepts.idea: A worker can be fed, housed and respected and still feel absent from the hours that fill the day. In the 1844 manuscripts Marx described four estrangements under wage labour: from the product, from the activity of working, from one's capacities as a being who makes and creates, and from other people, who become competitors.
concepts.insight: Work, for Marx, is how we express ourselves. When it's fully external, people feel human only outside it and like machines inside it. Call the complaint estrangement, not laziness.
concepts.why: It names a feeling well-paid people can't justify: secure, comfortable, and absent from their own days.
life: Doing excellent work you'd never mention to anyone.
Feeling most yourself on Saturday morning.
The relief of making something with your hands after a week of meetings.

sides: Alienation is structural, rooted in how production is owned.
It's psychological too, and it extends to consumption and relationships.
Pre-modern labour was hardly unalienated. Some argue meaning at work depends more on autonomy and craft than on ownership.
tension.note: Can work be self-expression for most people in a large modern economy, or only for some?

rel: The role that replaces the self
What money can and can't fix
concepts.mech: Marx argued that the product belongs to someone else, the activity is compelled as a means of survival, and work, which should express the self, becomes something endured. People then feel themselves only in leisure and like instruments at work.
concepts.lim: The account assumes a human essence expressed through labour, which Marx himself and many readers later questioned. Empirical work on what makes a job worthwhile stresses autonomy, skill and a sense of impact, which can be present or missing with no change in ownership.

concepts.dek: Older people aren't happier because they're old. They're happier because they know time is limited.
concepts.kw: aging older happier priorities friends time running out mortality
concepts.idea: Older adults tend to favour emotionally close relationships over new contacts and report more stable emotions than the young. Carstensen's socioemotional selectivity theory attributes this to time horizon, not age: when the future feels open, people collect information and novelty, and when it feels limited, they invest in meaning and closeness.
concepts.insight: It isn't age. Young people facing short horizons (illness, a move, the 1997 Hong Kong handover) chose like the old. Older people imagining extra years chose like the young.
concepts.why: Much of what we call wisdom may just be a different sense of time.
life: Last weeks before leaving a city, when every dinner matters.
Grandparents who don't care about meeting new people.
Clarity after a health scare that fades once the scare is over.

sides: Perceived time, not age, drives the shift.
The "positivity effect" in older adults is smaller and less consistent than early studies suggested.
tension.note: If a shorter horizon clarifies what matters, why wait for it? Whether the shift can be reproduced outside the lab is less clear.

rel: How to think about the end
Heidegger on facing your own death
What you overrate when time feels endless
concepts.mech: The evidence is largely experimental manipulation of perceived time. Young people facing short horizons, such as serious illness or the 1997 Hong Kong handover, chose companions the way older adults do, and older adults asked to imagine extra years chose more like the young.
concepts.lim: The positivity effect the theory predicts is smaller and less consistent than early studies suggested. Later-life priorities also reflect shrinking networks, health and money, which a time-horizon account doesn't separate out.

concepts.dek: Bronze medallists often look happier than silver medallists. It depends what you compare yourself to.
concepts.kw: regret almost won counterfactual comparison second place disappointment
concepts.idea: Observers watching footage of the 1992 Olympics rated bronze medallists as happier than silver medallists. Medvec, Madey and Gilovich (1995) explained it with counterfactual thinking: the silver medallist's nearest alternative is gold, the bronze medallist's is no medal at all. Satisfaction seems to track the closest imaginable alternative more than the outcome.
concepts.insight: Satisfaction depends less on the outcome than on the nearest imaginable alternative. Being close to better can feel worse than being far from it.
concepts.why: It's why near misses sting more than clear losses, and why the most ambitious are rarely the most satisfied.
life: Missing a train by one minute versus thirty.
Feeling worse about a 2nd-choice university than about a backup you never expected.

sides: What we imagine shapes what we feel.
Expectations matter too. A silver medallist who expected bronze is happy. Replications have been mostly supportive, though not uniformly.
tension.note: Is it proximity to the better outcome that hurts, or only that expectations were set by what the athlete hoped for?

rel: What we fix our attention on
concepts.mech: Upward counterfactuals (what almost happened better) lower satisfaction, and downward counterfactuals (what almost happened worse) raise it. The effect is strongest when the alternative feels one step away, as it does between second and first, and between third and fourth.
concepts.lim: The data are observers' ratings of facial expression, not athletes' own reports of satisfaction, and the original samples were small. Follow-up studies have been broadly supportive but vary with the setting and with whether the moment is the result or the podium.

concepts.dek: Nothing in life is as important as you think it is while you're thinking about it.
concepts.kw: overestimate happiness move to california lottery would i be happier if decisions
concepts.idea: Midwestern and Californian students both predicted that Californians would be happier because of the weather, and they were not, in life satisfaction at least. Schkade and Kahneman (1998) argued that whatever is salient when you consider a question gets weighted far above its share of actual daily experience. In Kahneman's phrasing, nothing is as important as you think it is while you are thinking about it.
concepts.insight: It cuts both ways. We overrate what a promotion or new city will do for us, and how badly a setback will hurt. In life, attention moves on. In imagination, it doesn't.
concepts.why: For any big decision: the thing you're fixated on will fill far less of your days than your thoughts.
life: Believing a bigger flat will change your mood.
Dreading a change that you barely notice six months later.

sides: Life satisfaction judgments are distorted by attention.
Some things, such as long commutes, chronic pain or unemployment, keep hurting. Not every effect is illusory.
tension.note: The difficulty is telling in advance which fixations will fade and which will not.

rel: What matters when time is short
deeper: Does living in California make people happy?
concepts.mech: When we judge how a change would affect our lives, attention goes to the obvious difference, such as climate or income, and we imagine it filling our days. In ordinary life attention moves elsewhere and we adapt, so the imagined effect overshoots.
concepts.lim: The weather study is one study, and adaptation is uneven: chronic pain, long commutes, unemployment and some bereavements keep hurting. The framework says we overweight things but not which things will fade.

concepts.dek: For a decade, the answer was "happiness plateaus at $75,000". Then an adversarial collaboration complicated it.
concepts.kw: does money make you happy salary income rich wealth plateau
concepts.idea: The claim that happiness stops rising after $75,000 was repeated for a decade. It came from Kahneman and Deaton (2010), who found emotional well-being levelled off near that income. Killingsworth (2021), using experience sampling, found no plateau. The two then ran an adversarial collaboration with Mellers (2023), and each turned out to have part of it.
concepts.insight: Result: for most people, well-being keeps rising with income. The plateau appears only for the unhappiest 20 percent. Money relieves unhappiness up to a point, and does little for misery with other causes.
concepts.why: A model of good scientific disagreement: rivals sharing data to find out who was right.
life: A raise that changes a lot, if money was the stressor.
A raise that changes nothing, if it wasn't.

sides: Both partly right: it depends where you start.
tension.note: Income is tied to so much else that even a clean curve would not say what extra money does for any one person.

deeper: Income and emotional well-being: a conflict resolved
concepts.mech: Averages across a population can hide different slopes for different people. In the joint analysis, well-being generally kept rising with income, but among the unhappiest fifth it flattened, which suggests money helps with some sources of unhappiness and not with others.
concepts.lim: These are associations. Higher income comes with many other advantages, and reverse causation is possible, so the curve does not show what extra money would do for a particular person. Samples are mostly American adults, and measures of well-being differ between datasets.

concepts.dek: The traits that win people power are often the first things power erodes.
concepts.kw: powerful people detached arrogant leaders boss lose empathy corrupt status entitlement
concepts.idea: People tend to be given influence for being attuned and generous, and then to lose some of that attunement once they hold it. Keltner calls this the power paradox. In a well-known experiment, people reminded of a time they had power were more likely to draw an E on their forehead so that it read correctly to themselves and backwards to anyone else, which he reads as reduced perspective-taking.
concepts.insight: In one study, people primed to feel powerful who were asked to draw an E on their forehead were more likely to draw it readable to themselves and backwards for everyone else. Power seems to narrow perspective-taking.
concepts.why: It explains how decent people become detached from those they lead, without ever deciding to.
life: The friendly colleague who changes after a promotion.
Leaders who stop noticing how meetings feel to everyone else.
Feeling oddly entitled after a small win.

sides: Power reliably erodes empathy, so it needs active checks.
Effects in priming studies are small and some failed to replicate. Power may amplify existing traits rather than change them.
tension.note: The everyday pattern is easier to see than the lab evidence is to trust.

rel: When power protects a fragile self
concepts.mech: Keltner's approach and inhibition account says power frees people from social constraint and raises attention to rewards and goals, which diminishes attention to others' states. Experiments typically prime a sense of power and then measure empathy or perspective-taking in small tasks.
concepts.lim: Priming effects of this kind are small and some have failed to replicate, and power may amplify existing dispositions instead of changing people. The premise that power is won through empathy is also contested, since aggressive and self-promoting people rise too.

concepts.dek: Almost nobody is watching you as closely as you think.
concepts.kw: care what strangers think self conscious embarrassed everyone looking judged noticed
concepts.idea: Wear an embarrassing T-shirt into a room and you'll feel stared at. In Gilovich's 2000 study, wearers guessed about half the room had noticed it. Under a quarter had. We start from our own vivid sense of ourselves and adjust too little for how busy everyone else's attention is.
concepts.insight: We anchor on our own vivid experience of ourselves and don't adjust for how little attention others have to spare. Everyone else is busy at the centre of their own spotlight.
concepts.why: A lot of social anxiety is a forecasting error about how others see you.
life: Replaying a stumble in a meeting nobody else remembers.
Skipping the gym because people will judge you, when they're all watching themselves.
Assuming your bad hair day is the main topic of the evening.

sides: We overestimate how much others notice us.
Even if few people look, the possibility of being seen is enough to change how you carry yourself.
tension.note: The numbers say relax. The feeling of being seen doesn't listen to numbers.

rel: Why being seen feels so heavy
What we're afraid the look will cost
deeper: The spotlight effect in social judgment
concepts.mech: Your own appearance and slips fill your awareness, so they become the anchor for your guess about what others see. You do correct for other people's competing concerns, but not enough, and the estimate stays inflated.
concepts.lim: The core result comes from low-stakes lab and campus settings. It doesn't show that others never judge, and in high-stakes or close-knit settings, being watched can be accurate.

concepts.dek: Some people sabotage their own effort so failure won't say anything about them.
concepts.kw: sabotage what we want procrastinate self sabotage fear of failure excuses ruin chances
concepts.idea: Some people who doubt their ability will arrange to perform worse, and seem to prefer it. In Berglas and Jones's 1978 study, participants given success they couldn't explain more often chose a drug expected to impair performance. A handicap turns failure into an excuse and success into a bigger achievement.
concepts.insight: What gets feared is what failure would prove. Not trying protects the belief that you could have.
concepts.why: It explains procrastination before things that matter most: the bigger the verdict, the more tempting the excuse.
life: Not studying, then saying you didn't really try.
Arriving late and exhausted to the interview you cared about.
Sending the application at 11:58 pm.

sides: Handicapping guards a fragile self-image, at the cost of the outcome.
It's mostly for an audience: people handicap more when others are watching.
tension.note: Both may be true at once. The open question is whether an excuse nobody hears still works.

rel: When not trying hardens into habit
Patterns of undoing what you want
deeper: Control of attributions about the self through self-handicapping strategies
concepts.mech: The handicap moves the blame for a bad result from ability to circumstance, so the self-image survives a failure. If the person succeeds anyway, the handicap makes the success look larger. The price is a worse real outcome.
concepts.lim: The original drug study was small and its sample narrow. Most everyday handicapping is behavioural (less practice, late starts), which is harder to separate from ordinary procrastination. Whether it protects the self or mainly manages impressions is still argued.

concepts.dek: In a graded hierarchy, almost everyone has someone to look down on, which is why it lasts.
concepts.kw: caste hierarchy inequality discrimination class status oppression rank privilege ambedkar society
concepts.idea: Caste rarely looks like one group ruling the rest. Ambedkar described a ladder in which nearly everyone has someone beneath them, so contempt flows downward more easily than anger flows up. In Annihilation of Caste (1936) he argued this is why the order lasts: most of its victims also hold a stake in it.
concepts.insight: In Annihilation of Caste (1936) he observed that a system where most people hold some rank is harder to overturn than one with a single dominant group, because even the people at the bottom of the middle still have a stake in the order.
concepts.why: It explains why unfair arrangements get defended by the people they disadvantage, and why solidarity between the lower ranks is rare.
life: A group looked down on by the one above it, and looking down on the one below.
Insisting on a small distinction of rank that outsiders can't even see.
Opposing a change that would help you because it would also lift someone you rank over.

sides: Hierarchy sustains itself through graded rank, so reform has to dismantle the ranking itself, not just improve conditions inside it.
Class division is the root. Other hierarchies follow from economic position and fall with it.
Social attitudes change slowly, and legal reform plus education can move them without confrontation.
tension.note: The argument is about structure. Whether the fix is legal, economic or cultural is still debated.

rel: Where resentment goes in a ladder
Power and the people beneath it
deeper: A different account of how rank and exclusion harden
What rank does to people lower in it
concepts.mech: If every rank is superior to some other, dismantling the hierarchy costs almost everyone something, and the groups best placed to unite are set against each other. Ambedkar called it an ascending scale of reverence and a descending scale of contempt.
concepts.lim: This is a structural argument, not a measured finding, and it can understate cross-caste solidarity in anti-caste movements. Marxists would add that land, labour and property relations do more of the work than the ranking itself.

concepts.dek: Two people with the same income can have very different freedom.
concepts.kw: capability approach freedom wellbeing development justice income poverty flourishing opportunity sen nussbaum
concepts.idea: Two people with the same income can have very different freedom. A wheelchair user and a runner need different things to move through a city. Sen and Nussbaum argue that justice should be judged by what people are actually able to do and be, their capabilities, not by what they own.
concepts.insight: Sen made the point that famines usually trace to people's lack of entitlement to food, and rarely to too little of it. Nussbaum later proposed a list of central capabilities, from health to affiliation to play, that any decent society should secure.
concepts.why: It moves the question from 'how much do you have?' to 'what are you free to do with it?', and that changes what counts as a good life and a just society.
life: A salary that looks fine but doesn't cover childcare, so one parent can't take the job.
A park that exists but can't be reached safely after dark.
A legal right that nobody has the time or money to use.

sides: Compare actual situations to see which change reduces injustice. No complete theory of the perfect society is needed.
A short list of central capabilities should be guaranteed to everyone as a threshold of justice.
Fairness is best secured through primary goods, such as rights and income, that are useful to anyone.
tension.note: Sen and Nussbaum disagree on whether to fix a list. The shared point is to look at lives, not just resources.

rel: What money buys, and what it does not
Why income looks more important than it is
Freedom as something you can use or not
deeper: The list and the case for it
concepts.mech: Resources are only a means. What counts is how they convert into real options, which depends on health, social rules and surroundings. Sen applied this to famines, which often occur where people lack entitlement to food, not where food is absent. Nussbaum added a list of central capabilities as a minimum threshold.
concepts.lim: Capabilities are hard to measure and compare, and which ones matter, or whether to list them at all, is itself contested. Critics also ask whether the approach can guide policy better than income or primary goods.

concepts.dek: Before choosing, you have to see, and most of the work is in the seeing.
concepts.kw: attention morality ethics seeing unselfing perception goodness love other people murdoch weil selfish
concepts.idea: Moral life may happen mostly before any decision. In Murdoch's example, a mother-in-law who sees her son's wife as vulgar looks again and finds her spirited, and nothing outside her has changed. Murdoch argued that goodness is largely a matter of how we attend to others, a task she called unselfing, and that choices follow from what we've already seen.
concepts.insight: Murdoch called this unselfing: loosening the grip of our own fears and wishes so we can see someone as they are. Simone Weil, whom she admired, called attention the rarest and purest form of generosity.
concepts.why: Goodness becomes a daily practice of perception, and less a performance at moments of crisis.
life: Noticing that your irritation with someone says more about your day than about them.
Listening without preparing your answer.
Looking at a hurried colleague and asking what they might be carrying.

sides: The moral life is mostly continuous work on how you see, not choosing between options.
Morality lies in free choices; what matters is what you commit to when it counts.
Attention has limits; people who are tired or stressed see others less generously, whatever their ideals.
tension.note: The idea is hard to test. It is easy to recognise.

rel: What we mistake for the other person
What we cannot see in ourselves
deeper: Her essay on attention and school study
concepts.mech: Fear, envy and self-regard colour perception before reasoning begins. Sustained, honest attention to a particular person loosens those distortions. Weil, whom Murdoch admired, called attention a rare form of generosity. On this view, good action follows from clear seeing.
concepts.lim: It's hard to test, and it leaves open how to tell a more accurate view from a merely kinder one. Attention also needs time, rest and security, which not everyone has equally.

concepts.t: One is not born, but becomes
concepts.dek: Much of what we call natural is something we keep doing.
concepts.kw: gender identity performativity social construction becoming woman beauvoir butler role expectations
concepts.idea: Some things that feel like nature may be things we keep doing. Beauvoir wrote in The Second Sex that one is not born, but becomes, a woman. Butler built on this to argue that gender is a set of repeated acts under social norms rather than an inner core, and that the repetition produces the look of a nature.
concepts.insight: Beauvoir described how girls are taught to see themselves as the Other, defined in relation to men. Butler proposed that gender is produced through repetition within a framework of norms, so it can be shifted at the edges.
concepts.why: It asks which parts of who you are were chosen and which were taught.
life: Doing something because it's what someone like you does.
Noticing that you behave differently in a work meeting and at home.
A person who feels more themselves after changing a role everyone expected them to keep.

sides: Woman is made by situation and expectation, which can be changed. Freedom is the task.
Identity is produced by repeated acts under norms, and its stability is an effect, not a source.
Social construction goes only so far; biology, development and temperament leave their own marks.
tension.note: The argument is about how much of identity is made, and how. It does not say identity is fake.

rel: The gaze that fixes who we are
deeper: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
concepts.mech: For Beauvoir, a girl learns to see herself as the Other, defined in relation to men, through situation and expectation. For Butler, identity is an effect of norms enacted again and again, so it holds steady only as long as the repetition does, and it can slip at the edges.
concepts.lim: These are theoretical claims, not measured findings, and they are often misread as saying gender is a free choice, which Butler rejects. Critics argue the account says too little about biology, development and material constraints.

concepts.t: Care as a way of reasoning
concepts.dek: Is knowing what is right the same as being responsible for someone?
concepts.kw: care ethics morality relationships responsibility justice rights moral development gilligan women different voice
concepts.idea: A well-known model of moral development ranked abstract, rule-based reasoning as the mature end point. Gilligan noticed it had been built mostly on boys, and described another starting point: relationships and responsibility, and the question of who needs what. Her book In a Different Voice (1982) shaped ethics more lastingly than it shaped the psychology.
concepts.insight: In In a Different Voice (1982) she argued that the earlier research had studied mostly boys. Later research found that the difference is smaller than first thought, and that men and women use both ways. The care perspective itself has held its place in ethics.
concepts.why: Attentiveness to particular people counts as a form of moral intelligence, and not as a lapse from principle.
life: Deciding whether to tell a friend something hard by asking what she can bear, not what's fair.
Staying late to help a colleague, not because a rule says to.
Hesitating over a strict policy because of the person in front of you.

sides: Moral maturity is reasoning from impartial principles that apply to everyone alike.
Care and responsibility are an equally mature starting point, and the two views need each other.
The two styles are used by everyone; where they differ by gender, the gap is modest.
tension.note: The original gender claim is contested. The ethical point survives it.

deeper: A philosophical account of care ethics
concepts.mech: Care ethics treats moral problems as situations among particular people who owe each other something, and doesn't try to settle them with impartial rules. Attentiveness to need counts as part of the reasoning. Gilligan argued that justice and care are both mature, and each corrects the other.
concepts.lim: The empirical claim of a gender difference in moral reasoning hasn't held up well. Later work finds modest differences and wide overlap. The ethical case for care stands apart from that claim.

concepts.t: The work of feeling on demand
concepts.dek: When warmth is part of the job, you're paid for what you feel.
concepts.kw: emotional labor work job service smile customer burnout surface acting authenticity hochschild flight attendant
concepts.idea: When warmth is part of the job, you're paid for what you show, and sometimes for what you feel. Hochschild's study of airline flight attendants in The Managed Heart (1983) described emotional labor as managing feeling to fit the role. She separated surface acting, displaying a feeling you don't have, from deep acting, trying to feel it.
concepts.insight: In The Managed Heart (1983) she distinguished surface acting, where you show a feeling you do not have, from deep acting, where you try to feel it. Studies since have linked long stretches of surface acting with exhaustion.
concepts.why: It names a hidden cost of jobs built on warmth, and why being kind at work can leave you with less for yourself.
life: The nurse who is composed with every family and then cries in the car.
A customer service voice that can't be turned off at the end of a shift.
Being cheerful for a manager who doesn't ask how you are.

sides: When feeling is sold, people can lose track of what they feel, and workers pay for it.
Managing impressions is a normal skill, and not by itself a cost.
Some people find emotional work rewarding, and its effects depend on control and support.
tension.note: The cost depends on how much control a person has over the job.

rel: Work that does not feel like ours
deeper: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
Her later work on the felt story behind politics
concepts.mech: The role sets feeling rules, and the worker closes the gap between what she feels and what's required by faking the display or by working on the feeling itself. Hochschild argued that when this is done for a wage, workers can lose their sense of what is theirs. Later studies link long stretches of surface acting with exhaustion.
concepts.lim: Hochschild's evidence was ethnographic and focused on one industry. Later research on exhaustion is mostly self-reported and correlational, so it can't show that surface acting causes burnout. Autonomy and support seem to change the effect substantially.

concepts.dek: Relations may come first, and the self second.
concepts.kw: betweenness aidagara relational self individual society japan china guanxi ripples obligation community watsuji fei xiaotong
concepts.idea: Western accounts often begin with a self who then enters relationships. Watsuji argued that a person exists between others, as both an individual and a member of a web. Fei Xiaotong described rural Chinese society as ripples spreading from each person, with obligations that thin out with distance. Both start from the relation, not the self.
concepts.insight: Watsuji criticised Heidegger for describing existence as time lived alone. Fei contrasted the 'differential mode of association' with societies that arrange people like sticks in bundles, each with the same standing in the group.
concepts.why: It offers a different starting picture of the self, in which relationships are part of what a person is.
life: Feeling different depending on who is in the room, and being all of those people.
Owing more to a cousin than to a stranger, without thinking about it.
Not being able to describe yourself without mentioning the people around you.

sides: Human existence is relational by nature. Ethics is the study of what happens between people.
Social structure can be read as networks that radiate from each person.
Persons have standing before relations, and rights that no group can override.
tension.note: These are ways of describing, not proofs. The question is which one describes your life.

rel: What happens when the web thins
concepts.mech: Watsuji's term ningen joins 'person' and 'between', and he criticised Heidegger for describing existence as time lived alone. Fei contrasted the differential mode of association, radiating from each person, with societies arranged like bundles of sticks, where everyone holds the same standing in a group.
concepts.lim: Both are broad descriptions of cultures, and they risk flattening variety inside them. They're interpretations, not tested claims, and they don't settle whether individual rights should override group obligations.

concepts.dek: What you call dependence may be what keeps a relationship warm.
concepts.kw: amae dependence indulgence closeness intimacy attachment japan culture sulking indulge doi kakar
concepts.idea: There is a feeling many people know and few languages name: the wish to be indulged by someone close, to be a bit unreasonable and still forgiven. Takeo Doi called it amae and argued it is central to Japanese relationships. He also held that the feeling is universal, even if the vocabulary is not.
concepts.insight: In The Anatomy of Dependence (1971) he noted that English has no everyday word for the feeling. His work has been criticised for turning a feeling into national character. Sudhir Kakar's studies of Indian childhood make a related case that mother-child closeness and extended family shape adult expectations of intimacy.
concepts.why: It gives a name to the comfort of being unguarded with someone, and asks whether independence is the only ideal.
life: Sulking until someone close notices.
Asking a friend for a favour you'd never ask a stranger, and feeling more cared for when they agree.
A relationship in which each person can be a little unreasonable.

sides: Depending on someone close is a basic and healthy need, not a defect of adulthood.
Secure attachment supports independence. The two grow together.
Reducing a culture to one feeling hides variety within it.
tension.note: It names a feeling many people recognise, in many languages.

rel: When wanting closeness collides with fear of it
concepts.mech: Doi took the word from the child's expectation of the mother's indulgence and traced it into adult life, in how employees and friends lean on each other without asking. In The Anatomy of Dependence (1971) he argued that the lack of an everyday English word is itself a clue. Kakar's work on Indian childhood makes a related case.
concepts.lim: Doi's account has been criticised for turning a feeling into national character, and cross-cultural evidence for amae as a distinct, central emotion is mixed. Attachment research also suggests that closeness and independence grow together, not in tension.

concepts.dek: When nobody forces you to work, the pressure is yours.
concepts.kw: burnout achievement productivity exhaustion self-exploitation hustle depression performance work fatigue society han
concepts.idea: When nobody forces you to work, the pressure can feel like your own. Byung-Chul Han argues that the old disciplinary society, which said 'you must', gave way to an achievement society that says 'you can'. People then exploit themselves and call it freedom, so exhaustion looks like personal failure.
concepts.insight: In The Burnout Society (2010) he links the rise of exhaustion and depression to a world where the only limit is the self. It's an essay, not an empirical study, and the connection between a cultural mood and clinical illness is not proven.
concepts.why: It offers a reading of why exhaustion can feel like a personal failing even when the demands are built in.
life: Feeling guilty for resting on a day off.
Turning a hobby into a side income and then dreading it.
Measuring yourself against a standard that nobody set.

sides: Self-imposed performance pressure is the typical form of control now, and it is harder to resist because it feels like freedom.
Power has become a matter of discipline and self-management for a long time already.
Burnout depends on workload and support. Cultural readings add little to measurement.
tension.note: It works as a diagnosis of a mood, not as a proof.

concepts.mech: In The Burnout Society (2010) he argues that when the only limit is the self, the pressure to perform meets no resistance from outside, so there is no one to push back against. He links the rise of exhaustion and depression to this positivity.
concepts.lim: It is an essay, not a study, and the link between a cultural mood and clinical depression or burnout is not shown. Workload, job control and pay explain much of measured burnout, and Han says little about people who have no option to refuse.

concepts.dek: Domination changes the dominator as well.
concepts.kw: colonialism colony empire psychology identity power stereotype orientalism lazy native internalised nandy said fanon alatas
concepts.idea: Colonial rule is usually described as something done to the ruled. Ashis Nandy argued that it was also a psychological project that pulled both sides into one hierarchy, in which the 'manly' and 'mature' ruled the 'childlike'. It damaged the rulers as well, and he thought both could take part in undoing it.
concepts.insight: Syed Hussein Alatas traced how the stereotype of the 'lazy native' justified rule and long outlived it. Edward Said showed how descriptions of others became instruments of power.
concepts.why: It shows how a story about other people becomes a story about yourself, and why ending a system can leave its habits behind.
life: A stereotype that survives the conditions that produced it.
Seeing yourself through the eyes of someone who looked down on your community.
A culture judging its own habits backward by an inherited standard.

sides: Colonialism worked on minds, and recovering self-respect means questioning its categories.
Freedom requires a decisive break from the colonial mind, sometimes by force.
Economic exploitation is the heart of it. The psychology follows from the interests.
tension.note: Where psychology ends and economics begins is still argued.

rel: Becoming what you are seen as
deeper: The Myth of the Lazy Native
The role of description in rule
concepts.mech: The hierarchy of ruler and ruled borrowed the language of gender and age, and made domination look like care. Alatas traced how the stereotype of the 'lazy native' justified rule long after it ended, and Said showed how descriptions of others served power. Habits of mind outlast the institutions.
concepts.lim: These readings rest on history, literature and interpretation, not on psychological evidence. Critics argue that they underplay economic extraction, and that recovering 'tradition' as a remedy can romanticise it.

concepts.dek: You will never meet most of the people you feel bound to.
concepts.kw: nation nationalism belonging identity community print flag patriotism imagined anderson tagore chatterjee
concepts.idea: Most of the people you feel bound to, you'll never meet. Benedict Anderson argued that a nation is an imagined community: each member carries an image of belonging together with strangers. 'Imagined' doesn't mean false. It describes how something so large holds together at all.
concepts.insight: He pointed to newspapers and novels, read by millions at the same time, as the technology that made it possible. Partha Chatterjee asked what is left to imagine when the model comes from the colonisers, and Tagore warned that nationalism makes people efficient and morally smaller.
concepts.why: It helps explain why people will give so much for a group they can't see, and what is gained and lost by it.
life: Feeling something when a stranger from your country wins.
A flag that moves you before you know why.
Being proud or ashamed on behalf of people you have never met.

sides: Nations are made through shared media and a sense of simultaneity. The feeling is real.
Nationalism asks people to trade conscience for the success of a machine.
Colonised societies were handed ready-made models, and made their own space within them.
tension.note: They agree that national feeling is made. They differ on whether it is worth what it costs.

rel: Group identity as protection against death
deeper: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World
concepts.mech: Newspapers and novels, read by many people at the same moment, gave readers a sense of shared, simultaneous time. Anderson thought print capitalism made that sense possible at scale. Chatterjee asked what is left to imagine when models come from the colonisers, and Tagore feared what nationalism does to conscience.
concepts.lim: Anderson's emphasis on print is rooted in a particular history, and critics say it underplays older ethnic and religious ties that nations built on. The claim is about origins, not about whether national feeling is good.

concepts.t: Who gets to speak for others
concepts.dek: Even sympathetic descriptions can silence the person described.
concepts.kw: subaltern voice representation speaking for others postcolonial listening power marginalised spivak chakrabarty
concepts.idea: A sympathetic description can still leave the person described unable to speak. Spivak asked whether the oppressed can be heard when the terms of hearing are set by others. When an intellectual speaks on someone's behalf, she asked, do they speak, or are they replaced? The question applies most when the speaker is generous.
concepts.insight: In 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988) she argued that well-meaning observers can't simply let the voiceless speak for themselves. Dipesh Chakrabarty similarly asked whose history is treated as universal, and whose as a local variation.
concepts.why: It questions the comfort of speaking for others, and asks what listening would require.
life: A report about a community written without anyone from it.
Being asked to represent your whole group.
Receiving help that comes with a description of you.

sides: The conditions for being heard are not neutral, and speaking for others can repeat the silencing.
Intellectuals should step back and let those affected speak for themselves.
Imperfect representation is better than silence, if it is open to correction.
tension.note: It is a question to keep asking, and has no tidy answer.

concepts.mech: In 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988) she argued that well-meaning observers can't simply let the voiceless speak. Representation always happens in someone's categories. Chakrabarty makes a related point about whose history counts as universal and whose as a local variation.
concepts.lim: The essay is dense and often read as saying the subaltern literally cannot speak, which Spivak later said was not her point. It also gives little practical guidance and can be taken as a reason to stay silent.

concepts.dek: You are looking at yourself with eyes that are not friendly.
concepts.kw: double consciousness identity race belonging outsider borderlands mestiza minority self-perception du bois anzaldua
concepts.idea: There is a particular strain in watching yourself being watched by people who think little of you. Du Bois described a 'two-ness' in one body, looking at oneself through the eyes of others. In The Souls of Black Folk (1903) he treated it as both a burden and a vantage point on the society that produces it.
concepts.insight: Du Bois set this out in The Souls of Black Folk (1903). Anzaldúa, in Borderlands (1987), proposed that holding contradiction without resolving it can be a strength. Both ideas have been taken up well beyond their original settings.
concepts.why: It names a familiar experience, of watching yourself being watched, and asks what can come from it.
life: Adjusting your accent without deciding to.
Feeling that you are representing a group whenever you speak.
Being comfortable in two worlds and fully at home in neither.

sides: The divided self is a burden, and also a vantage point on the society that divides it.
Tolerating ambiguity creates a new way of being, not merely a split.
Stereotype threat and identity management have been studied, with mixed results for some effects.
tension.note: It describes an experience. How to resolve it is a personal and political question.

rel: Feeling watched more than we are
concepts.mech: The self takes in an outside gaze that is hostile, and has to hold it alongside its own view. Anzaldúa, in Borderlands (1987), described living between cultures and languages, and proposed that tolerating contradiction without resolving it can become a way of seeing, not only a split.
concepts.lim: Both are interpretive and literary accounts, not measured findings. Related psychological ideas such as stereotype threat have had mixed replication, so the concrete effects are less settled than the experience described.

concepts.dek: The self-deception that turns every defeat into a win.
concepts.kw: self-deception humiliation face-saving ah q lu xun rationalisation pride defeat consolation denial china
concepts.idea: Ah Q is beaten and mocked, and each time he finds a way to feel he has won. They are only 'sons' hitting 'father', or he is the one being cheated. Lu Xun named this 'spiritual victory' and wrote it in 1921 as satire. The comedy works because the mechanism is recognisably general.
concepts.insight: Lu Xun wrote it in 1921 as a satire of a national habit, and its comic force lies in recognising the mechanism as a general human one. Psychology calls neighbouring things rationalisation and cognitive dissonance.
concepts.why: It shows how pride can protect us from facts by turning each loss into a story where we come out ahead.
life: Explaining a rejection as the other person’s loss.
Telling a story where being passed over proved your principles.
Winning arguments only inside your head.

sides: A society that cannot face its defeats trains people to console themselves, and stays where it is.
Defences protect against anxiety, and are neither simply good nor bad.
Some defences, such as humour and sublimation, are mature and useful.
tension.note: The line between a healthy consolation and a self-deception is hard to draw.

deeper: Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me)
concepts.mech: The mind rewrites the loss into a story where one comes out ahead, so the loss never has to be faced. Psychology has neighbouring ideas, rationalisation and cognitive dissonance. Lu Xun's further claim is social: a society that cannot admit defeat trains people to console themselves, and stays where it is.
concepts.lim: It is a satire read as a national diagnosis, and that reading can slide into stereotype. A consoling story is also sometimes a reasonable response when the defeat can't be changed, which the concept doesn't separate from self-deception.

concepts.dek: You can be certain, and wrong.
concepts.kw: memory false memory eyewitness misinformation suggestion recall certainty remembering reconstructed loftus
concepts.idea: Ask people how fast two cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other, as Loftus and Palmer did in their classic study, and the estimates run higher than for people given a milder verb. Some later reported broken glass that wasn't there. Memory is partly rebuilt each time it's recalled, and later information can shape it.
concepts.insight: In later work she showed that false memories of events that never happened can be implanted by suggestion. Confidence turns out to be a poor guide to accuracy, which has changed how courts treat eyewitnesses.
concepts.why: It means that the story of your past is partly rebuilt each time you tell it, and certainty is not proof.
life: Two siblings with different, equally vivid memories of the same day.
A story of your childhood that has been told so often it feels like a film.
Being sure about a detail that a photograph contradicts.

sides: Memory is malleable, and sincere certainty can coexist with error.
Real traumatic memories exist, and doubt about memory should not be used to dismiss survivors.
Most everyday memories are accurate in their gist, even when details drift.
tension.note: Memory is neither a record nor a fiction. It is a reconstruction that is usually, not always, reliable.

rel: The part of us that fills in the story
When the rebuilt memory is convenient
concepts.mech: Recall draws on fragments and expectation to assemble an account, and suggestion can supply details or even whole events that feel remembered. Confidence tracks the vividness of the memory more than its accuracy. This has changed how courts weigh eyewitness evidence.
concepts.lim: Misinformation effects are well established for details, but how often fully false memories arise, and how they compare to real ones, is debated. It also doesn't show that traumatic memories are generally unreliable.

concepts.t: The five stages are not a schedule
concepts.dek: Grief has no required order.
concepts.kw: grief stages denial anger bargaining depression acceptance mourning dying loss bereavement kubler-ross
concepts.idea: Popular culture turned five responses into a schedule for grief. Kübler-Ross described denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance as reactions she heard from dying patients. She didn't present them as stages everyone passes through in order, and later said as much.
concepts.insight: She said later that the stages were not a fixed order, and later studies of bereaved people have not found a standard pattern. Most people show resilience, and some show prolonged difficulty.
concepts.why: It lifts the worry that you're grieving wrongly, and keeps what was useful: people at the end of life want to be asked and heard.
life: Feeling fine for weeks and then undone by a smell.
Being told you are ‘in the anger stage’.
Going straight to acceptance, and being worried about it.

sides: Dying people share recognisable responses, and naming them makes it easier to talk.
Grief follows many paths. Resilience is the most common, and a fixed sequence is a myth.
Labels help only if they open conversation, not if they prescribe it.
tension.note: Her contribution was to ask and listen, and that is untouched by the criticism of the stages.

rel: How the end changes what matters
deeper: A different account of death and culture
concepts.mech: Her model came from listening to terminally ill people, and its main effect was to make a taboo subject easier to talk about. Studies of bereaved people have not found a standard sequence. Many show resilience, and a smaller group has prolonged difficulty.
concepts.lim: The stages weren't derived from a systematic sample, and they were applied far beyond the dying, where they have little support. The risk is that a mourner measures themselves against a script.

concepts.dek: Talent does not appear without conditions.
concepts.kw: woolf room of ones own money independence writing creativity freedom women conditions privacy time income
concepts.idea: Talent does not appear without conditions. Woolf argued in 1929 that a woman who wants to write needs money and a room with a lock on the door. She imagined Shakespeare's equally gifted sister, refused schooling and driven to despair. Asking who is talented misses the question of who is given the means.
concepts.insight: She imagined Shakespeare's equally gifted sister, who would have been refused schooling and driven to despair. Asking who is talented misses the question of who is given the means.
concepts.why: It makes creativity a matter of circumstance as much as character, and asks what you would do with a quiet room.
life: Doing your best thinking when someone else handles the other things.
Assuming people have no ideas when they have no time.
Needing a door to close.

sides: Creative work depends on material freedom; talent without a room goes unnoticed.
Genius finds its way regardless of conditions.
What matters is what people can do with what they have, not just what they have.
tension.note: The question has outlived its first answer: whose room, and who pays for it?

rel: What people are actually able to do
concepts.mech: The argument links creative output to material freedom: time, privacy, income and the absence of obligation. Work that looks like individual genius rests on conditions that were distributed unequally. Her example is a thought experiment about what those conditions allow.
concepts.lim: It is an essay with a narrow frame, mostly middle-class English women, and other writers have pointed out that many who lacked far more still made art. The conditions it names are plausibly necessary for a lot of work, but not sufficient for any.

concepts.dek: What you hope for can be what holds you back.
concepts.kw: optimism hope attachment fantasy good life precarity disappointment stuck career dream berlant
concepts.idea: Hope can be the trap. Berlant called it cruel optimism: an attachment to something that blocks the very thing you want, such as a promise of security or upward mobility that conditions no longer support. The hoping itself keeps you in those conditions.
concepts.insight: She developed the idea in Cruel Optimism (2011) from studying how people kept trusting in promises of security and upward mobility when conditions no longer supported them. It's a theory, not a measurement.
concepts.why: It gives a name to the hard feeling of hanging on to something that is making things worse, without calling it foolish.
life: Staying in a field because of how it was promised to feel.
A long pursuit of a standard that keeps moving.
A hope that is also the reason you are tired.

sides: Attachments to a promised life can be rational and still harm; the loss of the fantasy is also a loss.
The sunk-cost fallacy explains persistence without a special theory.
The honest response is to see the situation and choose again.
tension.note: The attachment is the point. Letting it go is a loss, not just a correction.

deeper: Related research on hope and striving
Why we mispredict what will satisfy us
concepts.mech: The object of desire, a job or a picture of the good life, organises how a person gets through the day. Giving it up means losing that whole structure, so persistence can be reasonable even while it hurts. Berlant developed this in Cruel Optimism (2011).
concepts.lim: It is an interpretive theory and hard to test, and it risks reading any persistence as pathology. When exits are blocked by money or law, staying may simply be the constrained choice, which is not the same as optimism.

concepts.dek: The moment before you separate the knower from the known.
concepts.kw: pure experience consciousness subject object absorption flow nishida kyoto school immediate experience
concepts.idea: Hearing a melody or seeing a colour, there is a moment before you say that 'I' am hearing 'it'. Nishida began there, with what he called pure experience. In An Inquiry into the Good (1911) he argued that the split into knowing subject and known object comes later, as a division of something already whole.
concepts.insight: He drew on William James's idea of a stream of experience and on his own practice of Zen sitting. He wrote An Inquiry into the Good (1911) in Japan, and later developed it into a philosophy of place, 'the logic of basho'.
concepts.why: It questions whether the self is the starting point of experience, or something drawn out of it.
life: Being so absorbed in a task that you stop noticing yourself.
The moment of hearing music before you think about it.
A walk where you are not narrating it.

sides: Experience comes first, and the self and the world are carved from it.
The thinking self is the one certain thing.
Experience arises from brain processes and can be studied from outside.
tension.note: A way of describing, not a result. It changes where the question starts.

rel: Why there is experience at all
The self as a story told afterward
concepts.mech: Nishida drew on William James's idea of a stream of experience and on his own Zen practice. If experience comes first, then the self and the world are carved from it, not assembled by a self that stands outside it. He later developed this into the logic of basho, or place.
concepts.lim: The claim is phenomenological and rests on introspection, and critics ask whether any experience can be described as pre-reflective without already being reflected on. Cognitive science can study experience from outside, which this approach sets aside.

concepts.t: Rules that depend on who you are
concepts.dek: The right answer may depend on who you are, and who you are with.
concepts.kw: context ethics duty relationships rules universal particular culture who depends ramanujan indian thought
concepts.idea: Asked what you should do, an Indian text, proverb or folktale will often say 'it depends'. Ramanujan suggested that Indian thought leans context-sensitive: rules are stated for kinds of people in kinds of situations, whereas Western ethics often looks for rules that hold for anyone. He called it a tendency, not an essence.
concepts.insight: In 'Is There an Indian Way of Thinking?' (written in 1989) he drew on proverbs, folktales and texts to show that the answer to 'what should I do?' is frequently 'it depends'. Carol Gilligan reached a similar point from psychology.
concepts.why: It asks whether fairness means treating everyone the same, or treating each person as they need.
life: Judging an act differently when you know the person.
A parent who has different rules for different children.
A contract that works only because everyone knows who is who.

sides: Rules attach to context and role, and no universal rule is final.
Moral rules must hold for anyone in the same position, or they are not moral.
Responsibility in relationships is a form of moral reasoning, not an exception to it.
tension.note: Context can be wisdom or favouritism. The difference is the hard part.

deeper: The Collected Essays of A. K. Ramanujan
Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
concepts.mech: He drew on proverbs, folktales and texts in 'Is There an Indian Way of Thinking?' (written in 1989) to show that obligations attach to role, stage of life and circumstance. A rule is a judgement about a case, not a statement that holds for everyone. Gilligan reached a similar point from psychology.
concepts.lim: The contrast is a broad generalisation, and it is overdrawn: Indian traditions also contain universal norms, and Western ethics contains strong particularist strands. Ramanujan himself hedged it.

concepts.dek: What happens in the first relationships becomes part of what a society is.
concepts.kw: mothering parenting family gender object relations infancy mother child caregiving chodorow reproduction
concepts.idea: If women do most of the early care of children, children may learn to feel self and other differently, depending on who cared for them. Chodorow argued that this arrangement reproduces itself: daughters and sons come away with different inner capacities, and those shape who does the caring next.
concepts.insight: In The Reproduction of Mothering (1978) she used object-relations psychoanalysis, the view that early relationships shape the inner world. Critics say her account generalises from one kind of family and gives too little weight to other forces.
concepts.why: It treats parenting arrangements as something that works on the mind, and asks what would change if they changed.
life: Assuming that the person who did the early care is the one who knows how to do it.
A child whose idea of closeness comes from who held them.
Noticing patterns in a family that no one chose.

sides: Social arrangements are inherited through early relationships, and change when who does the caring changes.
The drama is in the child’s wishes toward each parent, and in the father’s place.
Many other influences, including culture, temperament and peers, shape development.
tension.note: The argument is about how much a family arrangement shapes a mind. It is contested.

concepts.mech: In The Reproduction of Mothering (1978) she used object-relations psychoanalysis, the view that early relationships shape the inner world. Girls remain closely identified with the mother, boys must separate, and the difference carries into how each later relates to others and to parenting.
concepts.lim: The mechanism is psychoanalytic and hard to test, and the account generalises from one kind of family, the Western middle-class home. Critics say it gives too little weight to culture, temperament, peers and economic pressure.

concepts.dek: What disgusts us marks where our categories end.
concepts.kw: purity pollution disgust dirt taboo boundaries abjection categories outsiders cleanliness douglas kristeva
concepts.idea: Shoes are fine on the floor and not on the table. Mary Douglas argued that dirt is matter out of place rather than a physical fact, and that purity rules show where a group draws its lines. What feels disgusting is often what threatens to blur a category.
concepts.insight: Julia Kristeva proposed a psychological version, abjection: the revulsion at what threatens the boundary between self and not-self, such as a corpse or a wound. Both say that disgust is about order, not just hygiene.
concepts.why: It helps explain why groups treat outsiders as unclean, and why a violated boundary can feel like a threat.
life: A reaction of disgust to something harmless that is in the wrong place.
Social rules about who may share a table.
A sudden feeling of unease at something that blurs a category.

sides: Pollution rules are a map of a society’s classifications, and a way of defending them.
The abject is what a self must expel to be a self, and it never fully leaves.
Disgust evolved to avoid disease, and its social uses were built on top.
tension.note: Both are interpretations. They shift the question from 'what is disgusting?' to 'what is it protecting?'

rel: What we push out of sight
concepts.mech: Douglas, in Purity and Danger (1966), read pollution rules as a map of a society's classifications and a way of defending them. Kristeva added a psychological version, abjection: revulsion at what threatens the boundary between self and not-self, such as a corpse or a wound.
concepts.lim: Both are interpretations. Research on disgust shows a strong pathogen-avoidance component that this account does not need, and it does not explain why some boundary violations disgust while others do not.

jung.line: Broke with Freud over what the unconscious is. Freud saw a basement of repressed wishes. Jung saw a layer shared by all humans, and a psyche trying to become whole. His methods are interpretive rather than experimental, which is both their power and their problem.
jung.vs: Freud said libido was sexual at root. Jung said it was general psychic energy. The split got personal too.
jung.tag: Drew the unconscious as a map of the self.

freud.line: Argued that much of mental life is unconscious and defended against. Many of his specific theories failed, but his core picture, that we often don't know why we act, has largely held up.
freud.vs: Sartre denied there's an unconscious hiding things from consciousness. Experimental psychology kept the unconscious and dropped most of the drama.
freud.tag: We often don't know why we do what we do.

nietzsche.line: Asked where values come from, and the answer was uncomfortable psychology: morality often disguises power, resentment and fear. He wanted values that affirm life instead of punishing it.
nietzsche.vs: He argued against Schopenhauer's pessimism and Christianity's ethic of pity. People often read him as a nihilist. He saw nihilism as the problem to overcome.
nietzsche.tag: Wanted to know what our values are hiding.

kierkegaard.line: Thought philosophy had forgotten the person who actually exists. He wrote about anxiety, despair and choosing a self, often under pseudonyms so each life-view could be shown from inside.
kierkegaard.vs: Camus said his leap of faith amounted to "philosophical suicide".
kierkegaard.tag: Anxiety is what it costs to become yourself.

sartre.line: Existence precedes essence. We have no fixed nature, so we are what we make of ourselves. Freedom is total, and most of us spend our lives hiding from it.
sartre.vs: Beauvoir pushed him to see how situations limit freedom. Camus broke with him over communism and political violence.
sartre.tag: We're free, and most of us run from it.

camus.line: Started with one question: if life has no ultimate meaning, why not suicide? His answer was revolt. Live lucidly and fully, without hoping for a final explanation.
camus.vs: Refused the label "existentialist", and refused the leap of faith too.
camus.tag: Live fully and stop waiting for an answer.

heidegger.line: Asked what it means to be, and started from everyday existence instead of abstract minds. Introduced being-toward-death and the They. His 1933 Nazi membership hangs over his work.
heidegger.vs: Adorno attacked his "jargon of authenticity". Sartre built on him, and he rejected Sartre's reading.
heidegger.tag: Asked what it means to be, beginning with daily life.

foucault.line: Studied how prisons, clinics and schools produce the kinds of people they claim to describe. For him, power runs through knowledge and norms as well as rulers.
foucault.vs: Habermas and Fraser argued that his account leaves nothing to base a critique on.
foucault.tag: Institutions make the people they claim to describe.

fromm.line: Put Freud and Marx together. Societies produce typical personalities, and freedom without connection pushes people toward submission and conformity.
fromm.vs: Broke with the Frankfurt School, who thought he was too optimistic and too humanist.
fromm.tag: Freedom without connection ends up as submission.

frankl.line: Founded logotherapy, which treats meaning as the primary human motive. His account of the camps is among the most widely read books of the 20th century.
frankl.vs: He argued against Freud's pleasure principle and Adler's will to power, and implicitly against Sartre's claim that meaning is invented.
frankl.tag: Meaning is the deepest human drive.

arendt.line: Wrote about totalitarianism, action and what it means to think. "The banality of evil" provoked fury, and it still does.
arendt.vs: Stangneth's research points to an Eichmann more ideological than Arendt allowed.
arendt.tag: Thought hard about evil, action and thinking itself.

beauvoir.line: Argued that freedom is always situated in bodies, histories and relations. "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." The Ethics of Ambiguity is existentialism's clearest ethics.
beauvoir.vs: Corrected Sartre's individualism. My freedom needs other people to be free too.
beauvoir.tag: Freedom always comes with a body and a history.

schopenhauer.line: The great pessimist. Beneath appearances he saw a blind, striving Will, and a life that is mostly suffering. He shaped Nietzsche, Freud, Wittgenstein and Tolstoy.
schopenhauer.vs: Nietzsche started out as his disciple and ended up his opponent.
schopenhauer.tag: Life is blind striving, and mostly suffering.

dostoevsky.line: Put ideas into characters and let them fight. Philosophers still mine his novels on freedom, guilt, spite and faith.
dostoevsky.vs: His novels push back against the rational egoism of Russian radicals.

kahneman.line: With Amos Tversky, he showed that judgment strays from rationality in predictable ways. He won the Nobel in economics without being an economist.
kahneman.vs: Admitted publicly that parts of his popular book rested on priming studies that failed to replicate.
kahneman.tag: Judgment goes wrong in predictable ways.

bowlby.line: Founded attachment theory. Infants are wired to stay close to caregivers, and those bonds shape how we later approach intimacy and threat.
bowlby.vs: Broke with Kleinian analysis by insisting that real experiences, and not only fantasies, shape development.
bowlby.tag: Early bonds shape how we love and how we fear.

girard.line: Desire is imitative. Imitation breeds rivalry, and societies manage the rivalry with scapegoats. He built a theory of culture out of close readings of novels.
girard.vs: Critics say his theory is too total to test.
girard.tag: We want what other people want.

becker.line: Argued that our awareness of death drives much of culture. The Denial of Death won the Pulitzer two months after he died.
becker.tag: Culture is a way of denying death.

kohut.line: Founded self psychology. He saw narcissism as a normal line of development that can stall when a child's needs for mirroring go unmet.
kohut.vs: His long dispute with Kernberg over narcissism has never been settled.
kohut.tag: Narcissism is a need for mirroring that went unmet.

kernberg.line: Described borderline and narcissistic personality organisation as resting on splitting and primitive defenses.
kernberg.vs: Thought Kohut's empathic approach was too soft for pathological narcissism.

klein.line: Was among the first to analyse children, and argued that our earliest relationships are with "objects" split into good and bad.
klein.vs: Fought Anna Freud over the direction of British psychoanalysis.
klein.tag: Our first relationships are with good objects and bad objects.

tangney.line: Spent decades separating shame from guilt and tracing their opposite effects on behaviour.
tangney.tag: Shame and guilt push us in opposite directions.

berridge.line: Showed that wanting and liking are separate brain processes, which changed how we understand addiction and desire.
berridge.tag: Wanting and liking use different circuits.

perel.line: Writes about the pull between security and desire in long relationships, and about infidelity.
perel.tag: Security and desire tend to pull apart.

tennov.line: Coined "limerence" based on hundreds of first-person accounts.

skinner.line: A radical behaviourist who worked out how schedules of reinforcement shape behaviour.
skinner.vs: Chomsky's review of his theory of language helped bring behaviourism's dominance to an end.

festinger.line: Proposed cognitive dissonance theory, one of the big ideas in social psychology.
festinger.vs: Daryl Bem proposed self-perception as a rival explanation.
festinger.tag: We bend our beliefs to fit what we've done.

lucretius.line: Wrote Epicurean philosophy as verse, including the argument that death is nothing to fear.
lucretius.tag: He argued in verse that death is nothing to fear.

nagel.line: Wrote two of philosophy's most cited short papers: one on what it is like to be a bat, one on why death is bad.
nagel.tag: What is it like to be a bat? And why is death bad?

aristotle.line: His analysis of the emotions in the Rhetoric is still among the sharpest.
aristotle.tag: Still among the sharpest early accounts of emotion.

marmot.line: Led the Whitehall studies, which showed that social rank predicts health.

milgram.line: Ran the obedience experiments that put situationism on the map.
milgram.vs: Haslam, Reicher and Perry have given his findings a different reading.

seligman.line: Co-discovered learned helplessness, then co-reversed its explanation. Founded positive psychology.

eisenberger.line: Researches the neural basis of social pain and of connection.

gazzaniga.line: His split-brain research turned up the left-hemisphere "interpreter".

mcadams.line: Built up the field of narrative identity research.
mcadams.vs: Galen Strawson rejects the idea that a self has to be a story.
