The book is known for its difficulty. Lacan writes in an allusive, sometimes playful style and takes for granted a lot of learning. The main strands are the mirror stage, the claim that the unconscious is structured like a language, and the interplay of what he calls the Imaginary, the Symbolic and the Real. Admirers see a deep rereading of psychoanalysis, while critics accuse him of obscurity. It is best approached with a guide, and with patience.
ideas: The mirror stage says an uncoordinated infant sees a whole image of itself and greets it with delight. The first sense of an I rests on an outside image, partly a misrecognition.
Lacan argues that the unconscious is structured like a language. Symptoms and slips work like words that stand for other words, and so they can be read.
The signifier, a term he takes from linguistics, matters more than what it signifies. Meaning arises from the chain of signifiers, and not from a direct link to things.
He sorts experience into three orders, the Imaginary, the Symbolic and the Real. The Symbolic is the world of language and law that structures a person's place among others.
The opening seminar on Poe's story The Purloined Letter uses the story to show how a signifier steers the people who handle it, whatever they intend.
Desire, for Lacan, is the desire of the Other. We want what we think others want, and we want to be wanted, so desire never settles on a final object.
Lacan criticises the ego psychology of his time, which aimed to strengthen the ego. He holds that the ego is an imaginary construct and not a reliable ally.

In the Rome Discourse Lacan separates empty speech from full speech. Empty speech circles round what the patient says, while full speech is where a patient first hears something true about their own desire.
The Name-of-the-Father is the signifier that gives a child a place in the symbolic order and sets limits on desire. Lacan argues that when it is foreclosed, psychosis can result.

Critics such as Sokal and Bricmont object to Lacan's use of mathematical terms and topology, saying the borrowings are loose and the style hides weak arguments. His defenders reply that the difficulty is part of how the texts ask to be read.

books.thesis: What if madness is an understandable strategy for a self that feels unsafe in the world?
books.summary:
R. D. Laing, a Scottish psychiatrist, wrote this book as an attempt to understand people diagnosed with schizophrenia from the inside. Its question is what madness looks like if we assume it makes sense. Laing proposes that a person who lacks a basic sense of being safe in the world may withdraw and divide, and that the resulting behaviour is a strategy for survival.

He uses an existential and phenomenological approach, describing how a person experiences their own body, other people and their own identity. Case descriptions are used throughout to show how a patient's speech and behaviour become intelligible once one takes them seriously. Later readers have criticised Laing for downplaying the biology of psychosis, and he himself moved further from conventional psychiatry. The book remains a landmark in its attempt to listen.
ideas: Laing starts from the idea that psychotic speech and behaviour can be understood as meaningful. He thinks the clinician's task is to grasp how the world looks to the patient.
Ontological security is a firm sense of oneself as real and continuous. Someone who lacks it experiences ordinary life as a threat to their existence.
A person can live as an embodied self, at home in their body, or as an unembodied self, watching life from a detached position. Laing links the second to schizoid experience.
Laing describes a false-self system in which the person presents a compliant outside while the real self stays hidden and untouched. The strategy protects but also isolates.
He names three dreads of the insecure person, engulfment, implosion and petrification. Each is a fear that closeness or being seen will destroy the self.
The schizoid person often keeps others at a distance in order to protect the self. Laing says this protection can leave the self depleted and unreal.
Laing is critical of purely clinical language, which tends to describe the patient as a collection of symptoms and not as a person in a situation.

Laing uses an existential-phenomenological method, drawing on thinkers such as Kierkegaard, Sartre and Binswanger. The aim is to describe the patient's way of being in the world from the inside, before any diagnosis.
For the insecure person, being seen or understood can feel like a threat. Concealment therefore feels like safety, and relationships are a matter of defending the self.
Later critics say Laing paid too little attention to biology and came close to romanticising madness. The book itself is more careful, but this was the direction his later work took.

books.thesis: Identity is built across eight life stages, each with its own crisis.
books.summary:
Erik Erikson was an analyst trained in Vienna who spent his career in America. This book asks how a person acquires a sense of who they are, and how that sense depends on both the inner life and the society around them. He takes Freud's interest in childhood and widens it to include culture and history.

The central proposal is a scheme of eight stages across the whole life, each organised around a crisis between two outcomes. Erikson supports the ideas with studies of two Native American peoples, with case material, and with an essay on how young people in Germany came to follow Hitler. Critics find the stages too neat and too tied to his own society, but the idea of an identity crisis has become part of everyday language.
ideas: Erikson describes eight stages of life, from infancy to old age. Each stage poses a crisis, and the way it is handled shapes the later ones.
In infancy the crisis is trust against mistrust. A baby who is reliably cared for gets a basic confidence that the world and other people can be depended on.
Toddlers face autonomy against shame and doubt, as they begin to do things for themselves. Harsh handling can leave a lasting sense of shame about their own wishes.
School age brings industry against inferiority. A child wants to make things and master skills, and failing at this can lead to a feeling of being inadequate.
Adolescence centres on identity against role confusion. Young people try out roles and loyalties, and Erikson uses the term identity crisis to describe the strain of this search.
Erikson draws on his work with the Sioux and the Yurok to argue that child-rearing practices fit the demands of each culture, and that psychology must take culture seriously.
Later stages include generativity against stagnation in adulthood and integrity against despair in old age. The final crisis is whether a person can accept the life they had.

Erikson's epigenetic principle holds that development follows a ground plan in which each part has its time of special ascendancy. Each stage builds on the one before, and a missed stage can be partly repaired later.

The book includes studies of Hitler's imagery and German youth, and of Maxim Gorky's early life. Erikson uses them to show how a leader's story can speak to a society's unresolved childhood conflicts.

He describes how children aged ten to twelve arranged toy scenes in a play study, and found regular differences in how boys and girls used space. He read these as reflecting their bodily sense of themselves, an interpretation later critics have found dated.

books.thesis: People act in pursuit of goals, above all overcoming felt inferiority and finding a place among others.
books.summary:
Alfred Adler worked with Freud early on and then broke away to build his own school. This book is a set of lectures given to a general audience. It asks why people act as they do, and it answers by looking forward. For Adler, behaviour makes sense once we see the goal toward which a person is moving, even if they would not name it.

He argues that all children begin with a feeling of inferiority because they are small and dependent. They compensate by striving for competence, and the way each person does it becomes a style of life. A healthy style includes concern for others, which Adler calls community feeling. Critics say his ideas can be vague and hard to test. His influence is wide, however, and many later therapies carry traces of his thinking.
ideas: Adler explains behaviour by the goal it serves, not only by its past causes. A person's actions fit together once you see what they are aiming at.
All children feel inferior because they are small in a world of larger people. Adler treats this feeling as a normal spur to development and not as a sickness.
An inferiority complex arises when the feeling becomes too heavy to handle. The person may then seek superiority by showing off or by retreating into symptoms.
Each person forms a style of life in early childhood, a pattern of how they approach tasks and other people. Adler says it stays fairly consistent through adult life.
Community feeling is the sense of belonging with others and wanting to contribute. Adler treats it as the main mark of a healthy person.
Character traits such as vanity, envy and shyness are tools used to pursue a goal, not fixed givens. Adler says they can be understood by asking what the person gains.
Adler distinguishes between pampered and neglected children. Both can develop a distorted style of life, because both have missed the experience of cooperating with others.

Adler sees a striving for superiority, or perfection, as the basic movement of mental life. It is a drive to rise from a felt minus to a felt plus, and it can be healthy or damaging depending on its direction.

Common sense and private intelligence are set against each other. A person who follows private intelligence uses a logic that only makes sense to themselves, and Adler sees this as the mark of a troubled style of life.
Adler rejects a sharp split between conscious and unconscious and treats the person as an undivided whole. This is the meaning of the name Individual Psychology.

books.thesis: Adlerian psychology told as a dialogue. Freedom means accepting that some people won't like you.
books.summary:
This Japanese bestseller presents the ideas of Alfred Adler as a conversation between a philosopher and a sceptical young man over several nights. The question is whether people can really change, and what freedom costs. The philosopher says that we can, and that most of what holds us back is our own choice, even though it does not feel that way.

The dialogue form lets the young man push back on each claim. They go through the denial of trauma as a cause, the separation of tasks, and the role of community feeling. Readers either find the argument bracing or think it blames people too much for their own suffering. The book is a popular rendering and not a scholarly study, so it simplifies Adler, and it also has its own distinct emphasis.
ideas: The philosopher rejects the idea that past trauma determines the present. He argues that we use past events to serve our current goals, an approach Adler called teleology.
All problems, on this view, are interpersonal. Feeling inferior or ashamed always involves a comparison with other people.
The separation of tasks says that whose task a matter is depends on who bears its final consequences. Interfering with another person's task, or letting others interfere with yours, causes conflict.
Praise and rebuke are both seen as ways of ranking people, which creates dependence. The book prefers encouragement that treats others as equals.
Being disliked by some people is a sign that you are living according to your own views. The authors say seeking everyone's approval costs you your freedom.
Community feeling means seeing others as companions, not competitors. The book says it is reached by contribution, not by getting recognition.
The book urges people to live earnestly in the present moment, and not treat life as a path toward a future goal. Each moment is meant to be lived in full.

The book is written as a dialogue between a philosopher and a sceptical youth over five nights. The youth voices the reader's objections, and the form lets Adler's ideas be tested against ordinary doubts.

Relationships are described as horizontal and not vertical, meaning people are equal though not the same. The authors argue that treating others as above or below us lies behind much anxiety and resentment.
The book names three steps: self-acceptance, trust in others and contribution to others. Self-acceptance means working with what one has, and not wishing to be someone else.

books.thesis: Much of who we are lives in an adaptive unconscious, out of reach of introspection.
books.summary:
Timothy Wilson is a social psychologist, and this book asks how well we can know our own minds. He argues that much of mental life goes on outside of consciousness, in a system he calls the adaptive unconscious. It judges, evaluates and sets goals very quickly, and it does so without telling us.

The evidence comes from decades of experiments showing that people often cannot report the real causes of their choices. They give reasons that sound sensible but are guesses. Wilson's view of the unconscious is more practical than Freud's, since it is a useful system and not a store of hidden wishes. He also argues that to know ourselves we may need to watch our behaviour as we would watch a stranger's. Some of the research cited has been challenged in later replication efforts.
ideas: Wilson proposes an adaptive unconscious, a set of mental processes that work fast and outside awareness. It handles much of what we perceive, judge and decide.
This is a different unconscious from Freud's. It is not a place for repressed wishes. It is more like an efficient set of tools that we cannot inspect.
People are often wrong about why they did something. In experiments, they offer reasons that sound plausible but do not match what actually influenced them.
Introspection gives us a story about ourselves, not direct access. We build the story from what seems reasonable and from our theories about how people work.
Explicit and implicit attitudes can differ. A person can sincerely say they hold one view while their quick reactions show another.
Wilson argues that we construct a self-narrative that we find believable and flattering. The story shapes how we see ourselves, even if it is not accurate.
Wilson suggests that to learn about ourselves, we may do better to watch what we do and how others react to us than to look inward.

Self-perception theory holds that we often work out our own attitudes by observing what we do, much as an outsider would. Wilson uses it to show that feelings we take as direct sometimes come from watching ourselves.

In a well-known study, people asked to list reasons for liking posters chose ones they later liked less. Wilson takes this as evidence that analysing our reasons can lead us away from our real preferences.

People are also poor at predicting how they will feel in future, tending to overstate how strongly and how long events will affect them. Wilson treats this as another sign that we know our own minds less well than we think.

books.thesis: We deceive ourselves so we can deceive others better, and we pay for it in bad decisions.
books.summary:
Robert Trivers is an evolutionary biologist, and here he asks why people lie to themselves when the truth would serve them better. His proposal is that self-deception exists because it helps us deceive other people. A person who believes their own story gives off fewer signs of lying, and so is more convincing.

The book ranges across biology, psychology and history. Trivers looks at deception among animals, at the way people inflate their own virtues, and at the costs of biased thinking in marriage, organisations and war. He also considers how the mind keeps the truth available somewhere while hiding it from awareness. Critics say the evolutionary logic is neat but hard to test, and some accuse the book of stretching the idea to cover too much.
ideas: Trivers argues that self-deception evolved to help us deceive others. If you believe your own claim, you show fewer cues of lying, and the claim becomes more persuasive.
Deception is widespread in nature, from animals that mimic others to organisms that hide their true condition. Trivers uses this to argue that deceiving is an ordinary strategy.
People tend to see themselves as better than average and as more in control than they are. Trivers treats these inflated views as typical self-deception.
We are quick to find faults in others while overlooking the same faults in ourselves. He argues that this bias shapes conflicts between individuals and between groups.
Self-deception has costs. A mind that does not see the truth can make bad decisions, and Trivers discusses how it contributes to errors in organisations and in war.
In close relationships, such as marriage, each partner may keep up a flattering picture of themselves and a critical picture of the other, which fuels conflict.
The mind may store accurate information in one place while the conscious self holds a different version. Trivers suggests this split lets us act on the truth without admitting it.
Trivers describes biased information flow, in which self-deception can arise at several stages. We may avoid information, encode it in a slanted way, remember it selectively or reason badly about it.

He gives organisational examples such as the Challenger and Columbia shuttle disasters. In these cases, he argues, warnings were played down because accepting them would have been costly for those in charge.

Trivers also looks at false national and historical narratives, which let groups think well of themselves. He argues that these accounts spread in much the same way as individual self-deception, and can have serious consequences.

books.thesis: Plenty of behaviour, from charity to education, runs on hidden status motives we don't admit.
books.summary:
Kevin Simler and Robin Hanson ask why so much human behaviour comes with a noble explanation that does not quite fit. People say they give to charity to help others, go to school to learn, and see doctors to get better. The authors suggest that other motives, often about status and impressing others, do part of the work, and that we are built not to notice.

They build the case across a range of everyday activities, using ideas from evolutionary psychology and economics. The brain, on their account, works like an organisation with a press secretary who gives the public story while other parts pursue other goals. Critics say the book explains too much with one mechanism and that its evidence is uneven. It is best read as a provocation about hidden motives, and not as settled science.
ideas: The elephant in the title is the set of motives we do not discuss. The authors say we hide them from ourselves because that helps us hide them from others.
The mind has a press secretary. It produces flattering reasons for our actions, while other parts of the brain pursue less admirable aims we are not told about.
People often show off by being useful and generous. The authors argue that visible charity, for example, is shaped by how it looks to others and not only by effects.
Education may serve to signal qualities such as intelligence and conformity to employers, as well as to teach. The authors point to how many people want the credential more than the lessons.
In medicine, they argue, much spending shows care for the patient and not actual benefit. People want to be seen to care, and so they favour the visible effort.
Conversation, laughter and art are seen as ways of displaying quality to others. The authors suggest we enjoy them partly because they make us look good.
The authors stress that hidden motives are not necessarily bad. They suggest that seeing them clearly could help us design institutions that work better.

The authors argue that political behaviour is largely about showing loyalty to a group. Voting and arguing serve as signals of belonging, which would explain why people care more about taking a side than about policy results.
Norms are enforced in public but are often broken in private. The authors argue that we are good at hiding our own violations from ourselves, and at noticing other people's.

Critics say the argument is sweeping and hard to test, since almost any behaviour can be given a signalling explanation after the fact. The authors accept that motives are mixed and that the stated reason is often partly true.

books.thesis: Split-brain research and the interpreter point to this: the self is a story the brain tells after the fact.
books.summary:
Michael Gazzaniga is a neuroscientist who helped found the study of split-brain patients. His question is whether we are in charge of our own actions, or whether the brain works things out and tells us afterward. He answers that the sense of a single controlling self is something the brain constructs from many parts working at once.

The argument rests on his experiments with patients whose brain hemispheres had been surgically separated. In these cases, the left hemisphere invents explanations for actions it did not originate, and he calls this the interpreter. Gazzaniga then turns to free will and law. He holds that the brain is deterministic, but that people remain responsible, because responsibility arises in social interaction and not within one skull. Philosophers still dispute whether this answer works.
ideas: In split-brain patients, the two hemispheres can act on different information. Gazzaniga uses this to show that a single unified mind is not as basic as it feels.
The interpreter is a system in the left hemisphere that generates explanations for our behaviour. It will produce a plausible story even when it has no access to the real cause.
In his experiments, a patient would do something prompted to the right hemisphere, and the left would invent a reason. The patient believed the reason, with no sense of making it up.
The brain is made of many specialised modules working in parallel. Gazzaniga argues that the feeling of one self in charge is built on top of that.
He accepts that the brain is a physical system and that its workings are determined. He argues that this does not make free will meaningless.
Responsibility, he says, is a social matter. It exists in the interactions between people and not inside any single brain, so it survives even if the brain is deterministic.
In law, Gazzaniga argues that brain science should be used with care. Knowing about a person's brain does not by itself tell us whether to excuse them.

Gazzaniga argues for emergence, in which a higher level of organisation has properties that cannot be read off from the parts. He compares it to traffic, which cannot be understood by studying one car, and uses it to say that mind and brain are best explained at different levels.
Patients with certain brain injuries deny or explain away problems such as paralysis. Gazzaniga sees the same explanation-making at work as in his split-brain studies.

He discusses experiments in which brain activity precedes the report of a decision. He argues that these show the brain working before the interpreter speaks, and do not show that people are not responsible.

books.thesis: Identity is an internal life story, and the plot shapes how we live.
books.summary:
Dan McAdams is a personality psychologist, and this book asks what it means to have an identity. His proposal is that, from late adolescence on, people build an internal story of their lives that gives them a sense of unity and purpose. He calls this a personal myth, and he suggests that its plot and tone shape how people live.

McAdams draws on Erikson's theory of identity and on research in personality. He describes the parts a life story has, including imagery, theme, tone, characters and turning points. He also notes that stories are shaped by culture and by the needs of different life stages. Critics ask how much of a person is captured by the story they tell, and whether stories are accurate. McAdams treats them as meaningful whether or not they are strictly true.
ideas: McAdams holds that identity is an internalised and evolving life story. The story gives a person a sense of unity and purpose over time.
He calls the story a personal myth. The word does not mean false. It means a story that carries meaning and shapes a life.
The story typically begins to form in adolescence, when people first have the ability to think about their lives as a whole and to ask who they are.
A life story has recognisable features, such as an overall tone, recurring images, a theme and an ideological setting of beliefs and values.
Certain events stand out as nuclear episodes. These are key scenes, such as peaks, turning points and low points, that give the story its shape.
McAdams describes imagoes, idealised personifications of the self such as the healer or the warrior, and says they organise how a person plays roles.
Two broad themes, agency and communion, recur in life stories. One is about power and achievement, and the other about love and connection.
McAdams builds on Erikson, treating identity as the task of adolescence and early adulthood. In his view the life story is the form identity takes once a person can place themselves in time.
A personal myth draws on the stories a culture makes available, such as familiar plots and figures. This makes identity both personal and shared, since no one invents a story from nothing.
McAdams proposes ways to judge a life story, including coherence, openness, credibility, differentiation and reconciliation. A good story hangs together but still has room to change.

books.thesis: Most of what your brain does happens without you. "You" are a small part of it.
books.summary:
David Eagleman is a neuroscientist, and in this book he asks how much of what goes on in the brain is available to the person it belongs to. His answer is very little. Most processing happens without awareness, and consciousness sees only a small part. The conscious self, he says, is more like a press officer than a chief executive.

He supports the point with examples from perception, from illusions, from sport and from brain damage. He also proposes that the brain is a team of rivals, with different systems competing and cooperating. This has consequences for blame and punishment, since a person's choices rest on factors they did not choose. Eagleman argues for a more forward-looking approach in law. Critics say the practical conclusions are broader than the science supports.
ideas: Most of what the brain does is out of reach of awareness. Eagleman compares consciousness to the tip of an iceberg, with most of the activity out of sight.
Perception is built by the brain and not a direct view of the world. Visual illusions are used as evidence that what we see is a construction.
He describes the brain as a team of rivals, with different systems that disagree. A person's behaviour comes out of these competing drives and not a single will.
Skilled actions, such as catching a ball or hitting in baseball, happen faster than conscious thought. We are mostly told about them afterward.
Brain damage and disease can change a person's behaviour and character. Eagleman discusses a man with a tumour who committed violence, to ask what this means for responsibility.
A Ulysses contract is a commitment made in a calm state to bind one's later self. Eagleman uses it to show how the rational and impulsive parts of us can cooperate.
In law, Eagleman argues that we should focus less on blame and more on predicting and reducing future harm, since people's choices rest on factors outside their control.
Eagleman cites chicken sexers, who learn to sort chicks by sex without being able to say how they do it. The example shows that expert skill can run on knowledge that its owner cannot report.
Some Parkinson's patients who took certain dopamine drugs developed compulsive gambling. Eagleman uses such cases to show that character and choice are sensitive to brain chemistry.
He describes in-group bias as built into the brain, shaping how strongly we respond to other people. His point is that prejudice does not need conscious endorsement to operate.

books.thesis: The unified self is something the brain constructs. It's useful, but it isn't what it seems.
books.summary:
Bruce Hood is a developmental psychologist, and this book asks whether the sense of being one continuous self is accurate. He argues that it is not. The feeling of a unified I is constructed by the brain from many processes, memories and social influences, and it can be taken apart under certain conditions.

Hood goes through evidence from psychology, neuroscience and philosophy, including Hume's remark that he could find no self when he looked inward. He emphasises that the self is shaped by other people, and by the stories we tell. Calling it an illusion does not mean it has no use. Hood says it is a helpful construction that we need in order to live. Critics point out that an illusion needs someone to be fooled, and the argument leaves that puzzle only partly addressed.
ideas: Hood argues that the self is a construction of the brain. There is no single place where the self sits, and the feeling of unity is built from many processes.
He recalls Hume's report that when he looked inward he found only particular perceptions and never a self. Hood treats this as an early version of his view.
The self is shaped by other people. Our beliefs, habits and sense of who we are come in large part from the groups we belong to.
Memory is reconstructive. The past that supports our sense of continuity is rebuilt each time we recall it, and so it is open to error.
The sense of choosing is not direct evidence of being in control. Hood draws on studies suggesting we often act first and construct a reason afterward.
We tell stories about ourselves to hold the pieces together. Hood says these narratives give coherence to a self that would otherwise feel scattered.
Hood says the illusion is a useful one, and that knowing it is constructed may change how we think about blame, ambition and personal identity.

Hood describes the rouge test, in which a mark is put on a child's face and the child is watched for whether they touch it in a mirror. Passing it at around eighteen months is taken to show an early sense of a bodily self.

He notes that people in different cultures describe themselves in different ways. Western ideas of an independent, bounded self are not universal, which supports his claim that the self is built from experience.

Disorders and injuries, such as split-brain cases or dissociative states, show how the self can break apart. Hood treats them as clues that unity is something the brain makes and not something it starts with.

books.thesis: First volume of Attachment and Loss. The bond to a caregiver is a biological system, and no mere by-product of feeding.
books.summary:
John Bowlby was a British psychiatrist trained in psychoanalysis, and this first volume of his trilogy Attachment and Loss lays out the basic theory. His question is why infants cling to their caregivers and become distressed on separation. The prevailing view held that babies attach because they are fed. Bowlby argued that the bond is its own biological system, with survival value.

He draws on ethology, on studies of animals and on observations of children separated from their parents. Attachment behaviour, such as crying, following and clinging, is seen as an instinctive system that keeps the young close to protection. The theory has been refined and extended since, and some critics note that it can underplay cultural variation. The book is dense and technical, but it set out ideas that shaped later work on childhood and love.
ideas: Bowlby rejects the idea that babies become attached merely because the caregiver feeds them. He argues that the bond serves protection and comes from its own system.
Attachment behaviour includes crying, smiling, clinging and following. These behaviours work to keep the infant close to a caregiver, especially when frightened or tired.
He drew on ethology, including studies of imprinting in animals, to argue that attachment has an evolutionary basis and should be studied as behaviour in its natural setting.
Attachment works like a control system. The child monitors the caregiver's nearness and acts to restore it when the distance grows too great.
A secure bond lets a child explore. Bowlby describes exploration and attachment as linked, with the child venturing out and then returning for comfort.
Separation from the caregiver causes protest, then despair, then detachment. Bowlby argues that this sequence shows how strong and how real the bond is.
The bond develops in phases over the first years, moving from general responsiveness to people toward a preference for particular figures.
Bowlby uses the term monotropy for the infant's tendency to attach most strongly to one main figure. He does not mean that other attachments are absent, only that one usually stands first.

He introduces the environment of evolutionary adaptedness, the setting in which human behaviour took its shape. Attachment is explained as a response to the dangers of that setting, above all being left alone and exposed.
He draws on James Robertson's filmed observations of young children in hospital to show the stages of protest and despair. These made the effects of separation hard to dismiss.

books.thesis: Late lectures that sum up attachment theory for clinicians and parents.
books.summary:
This volume gathers lectures Bowlby gave late in his career, and it presents attachment theory in a form meant for clinicians and parents. The question behind it is how early relationships shape later life, and how that knowledge can help in therapy and in raising children. The central image is of a parent who acts as a secure base from which a child explores.

Bowlby describes patterns of attachment, links them to how parents behave, and argues that these patterns tend to persist into adult relationships. He applies the ideas to family problems and to the work of therapists, who can offer a similar base to their patients. Critics say that the evidence for long-term continuity is more mixed than the lectures suggest. The tone is plain and the book is far easier to read than his first volumes.
ideas: A secure base is a figure the child can go out from and return to. Bowlby says a child with this base is better able to explore and learn.
Therapy, he argues, works when the therapist acts as a secure base. The patient can then explore painful memories and feelings that felt too risky before.
Parents who are sensitive and responsive to a child's signals tend to have secure children. Bowlby treats this as a main influence on later well-being.
He describes anxious and avoidant patterns of attachment, drawing on the research of Mary Ainsworth. Children in these patterns have learned different ways of coping with an unreliable caregiver.
Bowlby suggests that early experiences form internal working models of self and others, which shape expectations in later relationships.
He discusses how a parent's own childhood affects how they treat their children, so that patterns of care can repeat across generations.
Bowlby argues that attachment needs continue through life and are not something adults outgrow. He sees the wish for close bonds as normal at every age.

Bowlby describes compulsive self-reliance and compulsive care-giving as two disordered patterns. In the first, a person insists on needing no one, and in the second, they care for others as a way of getting care.

He argues that real events in childhood, such as threats of abandonment, matter more than fantasy in the causes of later disturbance. This was a deliberate break with psychoanalytic views that stressed inner fantasy.
School refusal is read as often arising from anxiety about leaving the parent, or about what may happen at home while the child is away. Bowlby points to the parent's own anxiety as a common factor.

books.thesis: It names and describes the obsessive, uncertain state of being in love.
books.summary:
Dorothy Tennov, a psychologist, coined the term limerence for the state most people call being in love, in the sense of being obsessed with another person. She asks what this state is like from the inside and how common it is. Her description is plain and unromantic, and it centres on intrusive thinking about the person, a craving to be loved back and a mix of hope and dread.

The book draws on interviews and questionnaires she collected, and she lets people speak in their own words. She distinguishes limerence from sexual attraction and from the calmer affection of a long relationship. Not everyone, she found, experiences it, which she saw as a real difference between people. Critics note that her methods were informal. Still, many readers recognise her portrait of longing.
ideas: Tennov coined limerence to describe the involuntary state of being in love with another person, marked by constant thoughts of them and a strong wish that they return the feeling.
The central feature is intrusive thinking. The limerent person keeps returning to the other, and the thoughts feel hard to stop.
The state depends on uncertainty. A little hope keeps it going, and Tennov says that a love that is certain tends to feel different.
Limerence mixes joy with fear. The person can swing between elation at a sign of interest and misery at a sign of rejection.
Tennov describes a process of crystallisation, borrowed from Stendhal, in which the limerent person comes to see the other as nearly flawless and reads small gestures as meaningful.
She separates limerence from sexual desire and from affection. A person can feel one without the others, and the three can pull in different directions.
Tennov found that some people say they have never experienced limerence. She treats this as a real difference and not as a failure to love.
Tennov uses the term limerent object for the person who is the target of limerence. The limerent person reads every sign from the object closely, and treats small gestures as significant.
She gives limerence a typical duration of about eighteen months to three years. It can end through reciprocation turning into another kind of bond, or through fading, or through lasting loss.
Limerence has bodily signs, including trembling, weakness, an aching in the chest and shyness in the other's presence. Tennov takes these as part of the state itself and not as side effects.

books.thesis: Love is a skill and an activity. You don't simply fall into it.
books.summary:
Erich Fromm, a psychoanalyst and social thinker, argues that most people treat love as a matter of being lovable and finding the right object. His question is why we do so little to learn the skill of loving. He says love is an activity that takes discipline, concentration, patience and practice, much like any art.

He begins with the human need to overcome the anxiety of separateness and then describes different kinds of love, including the love of parent for child, brotherly love, erotic love, self-love and the love of God. He also criticises modern capitalist society for turning people into things to be exchanged. Some readers find his picture of mature love idealistic, and some find it dated in places. The book is short and still widely read.
ideas: Fromm says that love is an art and demands knowledge and effort. Most people treat it as a matter of luck, of finding the right person.
He roots love in the human need to overcome separateness. Being cut off from others is the deepest anxiety, and love is the mature answer.
Mature love has four elements: care, responsibility, respect and knowledge. Without all four, he argues, what we feel is something less.
Fromm distinguishes mature love from symbiotic union, in which two people merge and lose their independence. In mature love, each stays whole while being close.
Self-love is not selfishness. Fromm argues that we cannot love others if we are unable to love ourselves, because respect for a person includes oneself.
He criticises a market-oriented society in which people see themselves and each other as goods to be exchanged. In that setting, love is hard to practise.
Fromm describes several forms of love, including brotherly love, motherly love and erotic love, and says they share the same basic elements.

Fromm says love is an orientation of character and not a relation to a single object. A person who loves only one other and is indifferent to the rest of the world has, in his view, a symbiotic attachment and not love.
He says that practising any art needs discipline, concentration and patience, and that love is no different. He thinks these qualities are rare in a culture that prizes speed and comfort.
Fromm treats the love of God as a form of love that parallels the person's development. He sees religion moving from a mother-centred to a father-centred picture and then to a more mature one.

books.thesis: Intimacy and desire need different conditions, and a long relationship has to hold both.
books.summary:
Esther Perel is a Belgian-born couples therapist, and this book asks why desire so often fades in long relationships even when love is strong. Her observation is that the qualities that make a home safe, such as closeness, predictability and care, can work against erotic excitement, which seems to need distance and mystery.

She draws on her practice and on conversations with couples. Rather than offering a technique, she argues that security and adventure are both human needs and that a couple has to hold both. Desire, she says, often needs a space of one's own, a touch of the unknown and a willingness to take part in imagination. Critics find some of her points hard to generalise, and her examples come from a limited range of clients. The book is thoughtful and widely read.
ideas: Perel argues that intimacy and desire work on different principles. Love seeks closeness and certainty, while desire thrives on distance, novelty and the sense of something not yet possessed.
Human beings need both security and adventure. A relationship that offers only one will feel either stifling or unstable, and the couple has to live with the tension.
Too much care can dampen desire. When one partner becomes a caretaker, the erotic charge can slip, because it is hard to want someone you are responsible for.
Separateness matters. Perel says that desire often needs a gap between two people, and that seeing your partner as an independent person can bring it back.
Fantasy and imagination are central to erotic life. Perel argues that couples need permission to have an inner erotic life, even if it is not shared.
She describes how couples sometimes treat sex as a measure of the relationship's health, and argues that this pressure can make desire harder.
Eroticism, for Perel, is a way of playing with risk and uncertainty. Committed couples may have to deliberately create room for these.
Perel uses the term erotic intelligence for the ability to bring imagination, play and attention to desire. She treats it as a skill that couples can develop, and not as a gift that some people lack.
She questions the idea that total transparency is always good for a couple. Mystery and privacy keep some distance between partners, and Perel says that distance can feed desire.
Egalitarian marriage, with its stress on fairness and negotiation, can flatten erotic tension. Perel argues that power, difference and play have a role in desire that equality alone does not provide.

books.thesis: Infidelity is often less about the partner than about a longing for another version of yourself.
books.summary:
Esther Perel follows her earlier book with an examination of infidelity. She asks why people stray, even when they are not unhappy at home, and what the betrayal does to those involved. Her observation from years of practice is that an affair is often less about the partner than about a part of the self the person feels they have lost.

The book draws on case stories and interviews, with details changed. She defines an affair by three elements, which are secrecy, an emotional connection and a sexual element. She also considers how today's expectation that one person will be everything has raised the stakes. Perel is interested in what couples can build afterward, which sometimes means ending and sometimes a stronger partnership. Some readers think she is too forgiving, and others find her account balanced.
ideas: Perel defines an affair through three elements: secrecy, emotional connection and sexual alchemy. She says all three have to be present for it to feel like an affair.
Many people who cheat say they are not leaving a partner. They are looking for a version of themselves that they miss, and the other person is its mirror.
Modern couples expect one partner to provide security, passion and friendship. Perel argues that this expectation is historically new and sets up intimate relationships to fail.
For the betrayed partner, the injury is often the discovery that their picture of the relationship was false. The lies hurt as much as the sex.
Perel notes that affairs can be a response to deadness as well as unhappiness. People sometimes look outside to feel alive, even when the marriage is stable.
She describes how couples can recover, and she says some use the crisis to rebuild. It does not always work, and she argues that either choice can be reasonable.
The book notes that infidelity is viewed differently across cultures and eras, and that today's focus on honesty and romantic fulfilment shapes how we judge it.
Perel discusses the growing number of affairs among women and links it to changes in women's independence and expectations. She does not treat these affairs as a reversal of the male pattern.

She considers the effect of technology, including messaging and dating sites, on how affairs begin and are discovered. Possibilities for secrecy and contact have expanded, and so have the means of exposure.
In recovery, she asks the partner who strayed to answer questions and to acknowledge the hurt. The couple may in time build a shared account of what happened, which she treats as a step toward trust.

books.thesis: Couples fight in predictable attachment patterns. They repair by reaching for each other.
books.summary:
Sue Johnson, a clinical psychologist, developed Emotionally Focused Therapy for couples, and this book presents it to a general audience. She asks why couples get stuck in the same fights and how they can get out. Her answer is that adult partners are attachment figures to one another, so a conflict is often a protest about whether the other person is there when needed.

The book describes patterns of conflict that she calls demon dialogues, then guides readers through seven conversations meant to move a couple from distance to connection. The underlying idea is that vulnerable reaching, as opposed to blame, is what renews a bond. Critics note that the approach does not fit every couple and that the research backing is stronger for some groups than others. The book is clear and practical in tone.
ideas: Johnson says that adult romantic partners serve as each other's attachment figures. Arguments often come from fear that the other person is not reliably available.
She describes three demon dialogues. In Find the Bad Guy, both blame, in the Protest Polka one pursues and the other withdraws, and in Freeze and Flee both shut down.
The pursue and withdraw pattern is one of the most common. One partner protests to get a response, and the other retreats to avoid conflict, and each makes the other worse.
Johnson uses the shorthand A.R.E., meaning accessibility, responsiveness and engagement, for the questions partners are really asking: are you there, will you respond, do I matter to you.
Under anger and criticism sit softer feelings such as fear and hurt. The therapy aims to help people say those feelings directly.
Past injuries, such as a betrayal or a moment of abandonment, can leave a lasting wound. The book describes a conversation for forgiving injuries that helps partners repair it.
The seven conversations in the book are designed to be done together, with the aim of moving from distance toward emotional closeness.
Johnson speaks of effective dependency, the ability to turn to a partner and to be turned to in return. She argues that this kind of dependence supports independence and does not weaken it.

The approach is Emotionally Focused Therapy, which Johnson developed. She cites research reporting that most couples who complete it improve, and she presents it as built on evidence and not only on clinical impression.
Touch and sex are treated as expressions of the attachment bond. Johnson describes how sex can serve a search for closeness or an escape from it, and says that emotional safety shapes lovemaking.

books.thesis: A popular guide to adult attachment styles and the ways they collide.
books.summary:
Amir Levine, a psychiatrist, and Rachel Heller, a psychologist, wrote this popular book to apply attachment research to adult dating and partnership. They ask why some people feel at ease in close relationships while others feel anxious or crowded, and why certain pairs repeatedly cause each other pain. The answer is that people differ in attachment style, a pattern in how they handle closeness.

The authors describe three styles, anxious, avoidant and secure, and give signs to help readers identify theirs and their partner's. They argue that anxious and avoidant partners often fall into a painful cycle. Their advice is to understand your own style, and to seek a secure partner or become more secure. Critics point out that the styles are simplified into categories and that people are more flexible than the book may suggest. It is easy to read.
ideas: The book sorts adults into three attachment styles: anxious, avoidant and secure. Each describes how a person responds to closeness and to the risk of losing someone.
Anxious people crave closeness and worry about rejection. They tend to read small signals as signs that the partner is pulling away.
Avoidant people value independence and feel uneasy when a partner gets close. They often keep some distance, and they may pull back when intimacy grows.
Secure people are comfortable with closeness and also with independence. The authors say they tend to communicate directly and respond well to a partner's needs.
The anxious-avoidant trap describes a pairing in which the anxious partner's need for reassurance triggers the avoidant partner's withdrawal, which in turn heightens the anxiety.
Protest behaviours are the actions an anxious person uses to get a partner's attention. Deactivating strategies are the habits an avoidant person uses to keep feelings at bay.
The authors suggest that people can shift their attachment style. A relationship with a secure partner may help, and so can learning to communicate needs clearly.
The authors estimate that around half of adults are secure, with the rest divided mainly between anxious and avoidant. A small group is both anxious and avoidant, and shows features of each.
The fourth pattern, anxious-avoidant, combines a wish for closeness with a fear of it. People with this style may swing between pursuing and pulling away.
The authors recommend effective communication, meaning saying what you need plainly, without blame and without games. They say this is the quickest way to find out whether a partner can respond.

books.thesis: A love affair taken apart with philosophy, from idealization through to disillusion.
books.summary:
Alain de Botton's first book is a novel built as an essay. A narrator meets a woman named Chloe on a flight from Paris to London, and the story follows the relationship from first attraction to its end. At each turn he stops to think about what is happening with the help of philosophers. The question underneath is why a love that feels so special can also seem so ordinary once examined.

The book works by pairing small scenes with short bursts of reflection. It looks at idealisation, at the fear of seeming needy, at what we want from being known by someone, and at how love can shift into doubt. Critics have found its tone arch and its characters thin, while others enjoy the wit. The book does not offer advice, but it does treat ordinary courtship as worth close attention.
ideas: The narrator meets Chloe on a flight, and the early days are told with close attention to small details. Ordinary events become charged when we are falling for someone.
Falling in love involves idealising the other. We attach hopes to a person who we hardly know, and the book treats this as both pleasing and risky.
The narrator wonders how it can be possible to love someone he has just met. The book asks whether we love the person or a picture we have made.
De Botton explores the strain of wanting to be loved. Any sign of interest or coolness is read at length, and the narrator is aware of how silly this seems.
Early on, love feels like fate, as if the two people were made for each other. The book looks at how this belief is both thrilling and a poor guide.
The book takes real philosophers and uses their ideas to light up ordinary romantic moments, so abstract thought is tested against a small private event.
As the relationship matures, disillusion sets in. The book treats it as an expected result of seeing the other person more clearly, and not simply a failure.
De Botton calls the belief that beauty means goodness the romantic fallacy. The narrator assumes that because Chloe is lovely she must also be wise and kind, and finds this hard to hold.
The book is a novel with a philosophical commentary running through it, divided into short chapters. De Botton uses the story to illustrate ideas and not merely to tell it.
After the relationship ends, the narrator tries to explain why. De Botton shows that the explanation is built after the event, and that the real causes were small and mixed.

books.thesis: What comes after falling in love? The long, unromantic work of staying.
books.summary:
Alain de Botton's later novel picks up where love stories usually stop. It follows a couple, Rabih and Kirsten, from their first meeting through marriage, children and the strains of ordinary life. The question is what really happens after the romance, and what it takes to stay with someone. His answer is that love, in the long run, is a skill and a series of small acts.

The narrative is interrupted by short essays that comment on the couple's troubles, and these set out de Botton's view that Romanticism has given people unrealistic ideas about love. He argues that frustration and disappointment are normal, and that compatibility is something couples build over time. The tone is wry and gentle. Critics say the characters are used mainly to illustrate his ideas, but many readers find the situations familiar.
ideas: The book follows Rabih and Kirsten through marriage, children and the dull routines of ordinary life. It treats the long middle of a relationship as the real subject of love.
De Botton argues that Romanticism taught us to expect effortless love. When difficulty appears, we assume something is wrong, when it is a normal part of any partnership.
Compatibility is presented as something that emerges from working through differences, and not as a quality that two people have at the start.
The couple's quarrels often start from small matters. De Botton shows how a trivial complaint can stand in for a larger sense of being unappreciated.
Each partner has a damaged side that grows from childhood, and the book suggests that these damaged sides collide in a marriage.
The book considers the pull of an affair or of another person, and treats it as a response to ordinary frustration. It also stresses the cost of acting on it.
De Botton suggests that love is learned, and that the willingness to understand and forgive a partner is a skill that has to be practised.
The book treats sulking as a recurring problem. One partner expects the other to guess what is wrong, and the failure to say so openly leaves both feeling misunderstood.
De Botton says the Romantic view assumes a true partner will understand us without explanation. He traces this wish to the way a parent first met a baby's needs without being told.
The text alternates between narrative and essay-like passages that comment on the couple. This lets De Botton step back and name the pattern while Rabih and Kirsten are still living it.

books.thesis: Love is a practice of care, respect and responsibility. It isn't a feeling we passively receive.
books.summary:
bell hooks wrote this book to ask what love really means, in a culture that talks about it constantly and practises it badly. She argues that we often use the word to cover neglect, control or abuse, and that confusion about the definition keeps people from loving well. She proposes that love is better understood as an action.

She borrows a definition from the psychiatrist M. Scott Peck, who described love as the will to nurture one's own or another's growth. From there, she looks at honesty, commitment, community, spirituality and the ways in which male-dominated society distorts love for both men and women. The tone is personal and direct, and she draws on her own experience. Some readers want more evidence, but many value the plain moral clarity of her argument.
ideas: hooks argues that love is a verb. It is something we do through care, commitment, respect, trust and honesty, and not a feeling that arrives on its own.
She takes up the definition of love as the will to nurture growth, which she draws from M. Scott Peck, and she says that this makes love a matter of choice.
Love and abuse cannot exist together. If a person is harming or controlling us, hooks says, it is not love, however much feeling is involved.
Honesty is the base of love. hooks argues that lying and secrecy, even in the name of kindness, wear away trust.
She says our culture is confused about love, as it often treats it as a commodity or a source of excitement, and so people lack a clear model.
Patriarchy harms love by teaching boys to suppress feeling and girls to give care without receiving it. hooks says change is needed from both sexes.
Love is also a public matter. hooks links love to community and justice, and she argues that a society built on domination cannot teach people to love.
hooks speaks of a love ethic, where love guides how we live with others and not only in private. She draws on Martin Luther King Jr and his idea of the beloved community.
She argues that many people learn to confuse love with control or punishment in childhood. A parent who hurts a child in the name of love teaches that care and harm can go together.
hooks writes that love has a spiritual side and that seeking it can be a way to approach the divine. She sees a spiritual practice as helping a person stay with love when it is hard.

books.a: Thomas Lewis, Fari Amini and Richard Lannon
books.thesis: Our nervous systems regulate each other, which makes love partly a physiological bond.
books.summary:
Three psychiatrists, Thomas Lewis, Fari Amini and Richard Lannon, ask why relationships shape us so deeply and why therapy works. Their proposal is that human beings regulate each other physiologically. A nervous system is not self-contained, and close relationships help set the rhythm of the body and the mind. Love, in this view, is partly a biological bond.

They combine accounts of brain structure with clinical stories. Drawing on the idea of a three-part brain, they describe how the emotional centres respond to others and how early experience leaves lasting patterns. They also criticise Western culture for treating emotion as secondary to reason. Their brain model is now regarded by many neuroscientists as too simple, and some claims run ahead of the evidence. The writing is lively, and the central point about connection remains persuasive.
ideas: The authors argue that the human nervous system is open, meaning that relationships help regulate heart rate, mood and stress. A person alone is a different thing from a person with others.
Limbic resonance is their term for the way two mammals can attune to each other's emotional states. They suggest this is the basis of empathy and closeness.
Limbic regulation describes how a close relationship steadies the body. A calm companion can help calm us, and an upset one can unsettle us.
Limbic revision is the idea that relationships can change the emotional patterns laid down early in life, which is how they explain what happens in psychotherapy.
The book uses the triune brain model, which describes reptilian, limbic and cortical layers. Many neuroscientists now think this model is too crude.
Early care leaves a lasting pattern in the infant's brain. The authors cite studies of infants deprived of contact to show how much love affects development.
They argue that Western culture overvalues reason and neglects emotional life, and that our habit of treating the self as independent hides how much we rely on others.
The authors stress implicit memory, the emotional learning laid down early that works without words. This is why old patterns of feeling can persist even when a person knows better.
They argue that the main work of psychotherapy is the relationship itself and not the insights offered. A therapist who can attune to the patient helps change the patient's emotional patterns.
The ideal of self-sufficiency, they say, runs against our biology. People are built to be regulated by others, and a culture that prizes the lone individual works against this.

books.t: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
books.thesis: Decades of couple research found that contempt, criticism, defensiveness and stonewalling predict breakup.
books.summary:
Some marriages last and some quietly fall apart, and from the outside the difference is hard to see. John Gottman spent decades watching couples talk in a research lab, then followed them for years to see who stayed together. This book, written with Nan Silver, asks what the stable couples actually do differently, and whether those habits can be taught.

The answer is less dramatic than most advice. Gottman reports that happy couples are not the ones who avoid conflict. They are the ones who keep a friendship underneath it, who notice small bids for attention, and who repair a fight before it hardens. The book sets out seven principles, each with exercises, and warns about four patterns he found predicted divorce. Critics note that the research samples were limited and that prediction is not the same as cure. Still, the book's core claim is that how a couple handles ordinary moments matters more than any single big disagreement.
ideas: Gottman found that couples who split tended to show four habits in arguments: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. He called them the Four Horsemen, and contempt was the most damaging.
A love map is detailed knowledge of your partner's inner world, including worries, hopes and daily details. Couples who keep updating it cope better with stress and change.
Fondness and admiration work as an antidote to contempt. Couples who still hold a respectful story about each other tend to weather conflict better than those who have rewritten the past.
Turning toward means answering the small bids a partner makes, like a remark about the news or a sigh. Gottman says these ordinary exchanges build trust.
Gottman says husbands who resist their wives' input are at more risk of splitting. Willingness to share power is treated as a sign of a stable marriage.
A harsh startup predicts a bad ending. Gottman advises raising a complaint gently, describing the issue without blame, because conversations usually end the way their first minutes begin.
Many conflicts never get solved because they come from lasting differences in personality. Gottman suggests discussing them with humor and curiosity, and looking for the dream beneath each position.
Repair attempts are efforts to calm an argument as it unfolds, such as a joke, an apology or a touch. Gottman finds that stable couples make these and that their partners accept them.

Flooding is the state of being overwhelmed by physiological arousal in a fight, with a racing heart and a loss of clear thought. Gottman advises taking a break of at least twenty minutes to calm down before continuing.

The last principle is creating shared meaning, through rituals, roles, goals and symbols that the couple holds in common. Gottman says that couples who share such a sense of purpose are better able to withstand conflict.

books.thesis: We meet others in one of two ways, as objects to use or as presences to encounter.
books.summary:
Martin Buber's short, strange book begins with an observation about how we stand toward the world. Sometimes we treat a person or a tree as a thing with features, something to use, measure or understand. Other times we meet it whole, and something happens between us that cannot be reduced to either party. Buber asks which of these relations makes a human life, and what is lost when the first crowds out the second.

He argues in a compressed, almost scriptural style, with numbered fragments instead of a step-by-step case. He names the two stances I-It and I-Thou, and says the second cannot be produced on demand, only entered when one gives oneself fully. It also cannot last, and every Thou eventually settles back into an It. Buber finds the source of all such meeting in an eternal Thou, which he calls God. Readers disagree on how literally to take this, and whether the book is philosophy, theology or poetry.
ideas: Buber says a person speaks two basic words. I-It describes experience and use, and I-Thou describes meeting. The I is different in each, so the self is not fixed.
In I-It, the other is a bundle of qualities placed in space and time. Buber says this mode is necessary for ordinary life and is not itself a fault.
I-Thou happens with the whole being and cannot be done halfway. Buber describes it as relation that is mutual and immediate, with no goal or technique standing between the two.
A Thou cannot be held onto. Every I-Thou meeting fades and the other becomes an It again, which Buber treats as the sad but ordinary rhythm of life.
Buber describes relation as open to three spheres: nature, other people and spiritual beings. A tree can be met as a Thou in a moment of real attention.
Grace and will both play a part. Buber says we cannot seek a Thou directly, yet we must be ready, so the right posture is openness, with no scheme to get anything.
Every particular Thou points to the eternal Thou. Buber links this to God as the one who is never an It, and he suggests prayer is a kind of address.
Buber speaks of the between as the place where meeting happens. The relation belongs to neither person alone, but to the space that opens when both are present.
Love, for Buber, is not a feeling that one has but something that happens between I and Thou. Feelings are possessed, while love is a responsibility of one person for another.
The book is written in a poetic, aphoristic style in three parts. Its form makes it read more like an address than an argument, and Buber meant it to be experienced and not only studied.

books.thesis: Romantic love runs on the brain's reward systems, which is why it can feel like addiction.
books.summary:
Why do people fall in love with one person and not another, and why does it feel like something that happens to us? Helen Fisher, an anthropologist, takes the question to the brain. She asks whether romantic love is an emotion, a drive or something closer to a craving, and what that would mean for how we treat heartbreak and long relationships.

Her case rests on brain scans she and colleagues ran on people who were newly in love, plus cross-cultural surveys and animal work. She proposes three linked systems, lust, attraction and attachment, which can run partly apart. She argues that romantic attraction is a drive like hunger, tied to dopamine and reward circuits, and that rejection can intensify it. The book is lively and sometimes speculative, and critics say that brain activity maps onto love less cleanly than the title promises. What Fisher offers is a naturalist's view of passion as old, widespread and hard to argue with.
ideas: Fisher scanned the brains of people who said they were intensely in love, and she reports activity in dopamine-heavy reward areas, including one near the brainstem.
She proposes three brain systems for mating, lust, romantic attraction and attachment. They can run apart, which might explain deep attachment to one person alongside lust for another.
Romantic love, she argues, is a drive and is not simply an emotion. It has a goal, it can be focused on one person and it can last, like hunger or thirst.
Lovers show intrusive thinking, craving, mood swings and focus on one person. Fisher notes these resemble features of addiction, and links them to reward chemistry.
Romantic love appears in nearly every culture she surveyed, in songs, poems and stories. She treats that spread as evidence that it is a human universal and not a Western invention.
Rejection can make attraction stronger. Fisher says that obstacles and being abandoned can push the reward system harder, which she offers as one reason people keep chasing someone who has left.
Fisher suggests that the attraction phase is built to last for a limited time, while attachment can carry a couple through child rearing and beyond.

Fisher's scans showed activity in the ventral tegmental area and the caudate nucleus, parts of the brain tied to reward and motivation. She uses this to say that romantic love works like a drive and not only an emotion.
She points to lowered serotonin as a likely basis for the obsessive thinking of new love. She also raises concern that antidepressants that raise serotonin may dull romantic feelings.

Fisher discusses what shapes who we fall for, including timing, familiarity, mystery and early experience. She suggests that we carry an unconscious pattern of what we find attractive, formed long before we meet anyone.

books.thesis: Growth requires accepting that life is difficult. Love is the will to extend yourself for another.
books.summary:
M. Scott Peck was a psychiatrist who noticed that his patients often wanted relief without change. His book opens with a plain sentence, life is difficult, and asks what follows if we accept that instead of resenting it. It mixes case stories, moral argument and some religion, written for ordinary readers.

Peck argues that growth depends on discipline, which he breaks into delaying gratification, accepting responsibility, dedication to truth and balance. He then offers a definition of love as the will to extend oneself for another person's spiritual growth, and separates it from the feeling of falling in love. Late in the book he turns to grace and to religion, which many readers find the weakest part. Critics say the tone can be moralizing and that the case material is thin as evidence. The book still sells because its central request, to stop expecting an easy life, is hard to dismiss.
ideas: Peck says life is difficult, and that the pain starts to ease once we stop expecting it to be otherwise. Complaining about the difficulty makes it heavier.
Delaying gratification, he says, means facing the painful part of a task first so the rest can be enjoyed. He treats this as the base of every other discipline.
Accepting responsibility means admitting a problem is yours to solve. Peck contrasts neurotics, who take too much blame, with character disorders, who take too little.
Dedication to truth requires constant testing of your own map of reality. Peck argues that we avoid this because revising the map hurts, and that avoidance is a root of mental illness.
Peck defines love as the will to extend oneself to nurture another person's growth. He says it is an act of will and not a feeling.
Falling in love is, in his view, a temporary collapse of ego boundaries driven by instinct. It can start a relationship but it is not love in the sense he means.
Laziness is named as a form of original sin, the pull toward ease that fights growth. Peck also writes about grace, a force he says helps us grow without being earned.

Balancing is Peck's fourth tool of discipline. It includes the flexibility to give up one thing for another and the practice of bracketing, which means holding back a strong feeling long enough to act well.
Peck separates love from dependency. A dependent person wants to be taken care of and calls it love, while real love looks to the growth of the other.
Some readers object that Peck mixes psychiatry with religious belief in a way that is not scientific. His claims about grace and evil in particular go beyond what clinical evidence can support.

books.thesis: The great novelists (Cervantes, Stendhal, Flaubert, Proust, Dostoevsky) saw that desire is borrowed from a mediator, and their heroes' "romantic lie" is believing it's spontaneous.
ideas: Girard's central claim is that desire is triangular. We want an object because a model wants it, so the model stays in the picture and the thing wanted is secondary.
Don Quixote chooses knight-errantry by imitating the legendary Amadis. Girard uses him as the clearest early case of a hero whose wishes are borrowed from a mediator.
External mediation means the model is far away and cannot be a rival. A fictional hero or a distant king can be imitated with little conflict and little shame.
Internal mediation means the model is close enough to compete. As models and imitators grow closer, desire turns into rivalry, obsession and resentment.
The romantic lie is the belief that our wants are our own. Girard says modern heroes cling to it, and the novelistic truth is its exposure.
Snobbery, vanity and jealousy are treated as forms of imitation rivalry. Girard reads Proust's social climbers and Stendhal's proud men as people who want what others seem to want.
Girard sees many great novels ending with the hero's recognition of the lie, a sort of conversion that comes late. In Dostoevsky, this sometimes costs the hero everything.
Girard calls the later stage of triangular desire metaphysical desire. The object matters less and less, while the mediator becomes the real aim, and the desiring person wishes to be like the model.
Stendhal's vain characters and Flaubert's Emma Bovary show imitation in different settings. Emma takes her wants from romances she has read, while Stendhal's vain men act for the eyes of a rival.
Dostoevsky's Underground Man is Girard's extreme case of internal mediation. He is drawn to the very people who humiliate him, and his hatred and admiration are mixed together.
books.surprise: Girard argues the novels themselves record their authors' conversion: they only see mimetic desire after renouncing their own.
books.crit: The theory explains everything it touches, which makes it hard to falsify.
books.summary:
We usually think our wants come from inside us. René Girard noticed that the heroes of great novels do not want things freely. They want what some admired other seems to want, and they hide this from themselves. His first book asks what Cervantes, Stendhal, Flaubert, Proust and Dostoevsky understood about desire that readers and the characters themselves tend to miss.

Girard reads these novelists side by side and finds a shared structure he calls triangular desire. There is a subject, an object and a mediator whose wanting makes the object attractive. The hero's romantic lie is the belief that the desire is spontaneous, and the novelist's truth is the exposure of it. The closer the mediator stands, the more rivalry and misery follow. Girard sees many of the novels ending in a kind of conversion, where the hero finally sees the lie. Later readers debate how far this theory of imitation explains real behavior.

books.thesis: Take away emotion and reasoning breaks down, because feelings guide decisions through bodily signals.
books.summary:
Philosophers have long pictured reason as clean thinking that works best when emotion is kept out. Antonio Damasio, a neurologist, saw patients who seemed to prove the opposite. After brain damage to certain frontal regions, they kept their intelligence yet made terrible choices in daily life. His book asks what role feeling plays in good decisions, and why the old split between mind and body keeps misleading us.

He builds the argument from clinical cases, including the famous railway worker Phineas Gage and a patient he calls Elliot. He proposes the somatic marker hypothesis, in which bodily states tied to past outcomes quietly steer us toward or away from options before we deliberate. The title refers to Descartes' separation of mind from body. Damasio does not claim emotion replaces reason. He says that reason without it falters. Scientists still dispute the details of the hypothesis, though the broad point has been influential in psychology and economics.
ideas: Phineas Gage survived an iron rod through his frontal lobe, yet his social behavior changed. Damasio uses the case, and modern brain studies of it, to link specific brain regions to judgment.
Elliot, a patient whose frontal damage came from a tumor, scored well on intelligence tests but could not decide simply or manage his life. Damasio notes he felt little about his misfortunes.
The somatic marker hypothesis says bodily feelings attached to past outcomes mark options as good or bad. They narrow the choices so that reasoning has less to sort through.
Damasio proposes that the body sends signals to the brain that shape thought. He describes a body loop, and a shortcut he calls the as-if loop where the brain simulates those signals.
Descartes' error, as Damasio puts it, was to separate the thinking mind from the body. He says the mind is embodied and depends on the whole organism.
The book separates emotion from feeling. An emotion is a bodily and brain response, and a feeling is the perception of that state, which comes after.
Damasio argues that the ventromedial prefrontal cortex links situations to emotional memories. Damage there leaves reasoning intact on paper while real-life decisions fall apart.

Damasio distinguishes primary emotions, which are inborn responses such as fear to certain stimuli, from secondary emotions, which arise as we link situations to experience. The ventromedial frontal region is needed for the second kind.
His team reconstructed the probable path of the iron rod through Gage's skull from the remains. This gave a firmer anatomical basis to what had been a famous but vague case.

Critics say the evidence for the somatic marker hypothesis is less clear than the book suggests, and that other accounts can explain the patients' deficits. The idea remains influential, but it is still debated.

books.thesis: Consciousness grows out of the brain's map of the body's state.
books.summary:
What is consciousness made of, and where does it come from in a brain that is mostly handling the body? Antonio Damasio starts with a simple observation. When we are awake, there is a sense that these events are happening to me. The book asks how a brain produces that sense, and why it seems so close to feeling.
