Reciprocity means we feel obliged to return a favor, even a small, uninvited one. Cialdini describes charities giving small gifts first, which raised donations.
Commitment and consistency describe our wish to act in line with what we have already said or done. A small initial commitment can lead to larger ones.
Social proof says we look to what others are doing to decide what is correct, especially when we are uncertain. Laugh tracks and the bystander effect are examples.
Liking is the tendency to say yes to people we like. Similarity, compliments and cooperation raise liking, and persuaders use all of them.
Authority works because people defer to apparent experts and symbols of rank. Cialdini discusses obedience research, including Milgram's, to show how strong the pull can be.
Scarcity makes things more desirable when they are limited or about to be lost. Cialdini ties this to a wish not to lose freedom of choice.

Cialdini describes the contrast principle, where a thing seems more different when presented right after something else, as in a seller who shows an expensive item first so that a later one seems cheap.
He gives the rejection-then-retreat technique, also called door-in-the-face, in which a large request is refused and then a smaller one is more likely to be accepted because of reciprocity.
Cialdini offers advice on defense, such as treating the feeling of being rushed into compliance as a warning sign and asking whether the trigger is being used to deceive, to resist these tactics.

books.thesis: We're poor at predicting what will make us happy.
books.summary:
We are constantly deciding things on the basis of how we think we will feel later, and Daniel Gilbert says we are not very good at that. His book asks why the future we imagine, a raise, a move, a breakup, so often fails to match the future we live through, and what that means for how we pursue happiness.

Gilbert, a psychologist, argues that imagination works by filling in gaps without telling us, and that it leans on the present. We overestimate how long and how intensely events will affect us, a pattern called impact bias. He also describes a psychological immune system, a set of unconscious ways of making sense of bad events that we forget to count when we predict our feelings. Some of the specific studies have been questioned in later work. The advice is gentle, to ask people who have been through a situation instead of trusting our own simulation.
ideas: Gilbert says imagination fills in missing details automatically and without telling us. We fail to notice what our mental pictures leave out, so they feel more complete than they are.
Presentism describes how our current state colors our predictions. When we are hungry or happy now, we imagine the future feeling the same way.
Impact bias is the tendency to overestimate how strongly and for how long future events, good or bad, will affect our mood.
The psychological immune system helps us come to terms with misfortune. Gilbert says we forget it exists when we predict how bad things will feel.
Synthetic happiness is what we make when we do not get what we wanted. Gilbert argues it is as real as natural happiness and that people do not expect it.
Because other people's experience is a better guide than our simulation, Gilbert suggests asking people who have been in a situation, called surrogates, how it felt.
We see our own choices as clearly better than alternatives once they are made, and rationalize more when the decision is irreversible. This helps explain why we adapt to our circumstances.
Gilbert describes the way we are poor at predicting how we will feel, partly because we imagine the future by filling in details from the present and leaving out features that will matter.

He reports studies, including one with photography students, in which people grew happier with a choice they could not reverse than with one they could, because the psychological immune system works harder when there is no way out.
Gilbert argues that the human brain is the only one that can plan far ahead, and that the frontal lobe's capacity for simulation is both what makes us unique and what leads us astray.

books.thesis: We mistake luck for skill and noise for meaning.
books.summary:
Some traders look brilliant, and some of them are simply the survivors of a very large number of coin flips. Nassim Nicholas Taleb, a former trader, asks how often we mistake luck for skill, and why it is so hard for us to see randomness in a record that looks like a story.

Taleb argues through anecdote, mathematics and polemic. He introduces survivorship bias through the idea of the cemetery of failed traders we never hear from, and he asks us to judge a decision by the alternative histories that could have happened. He distinguishes frequency from magnitude, noting that someone can be right nearly always and still be ruined by a rare event. He draws on Hume's problem of induction and Popper on falsification. The style is combative, and critics find some of the jabs unfair. Its central point, that outcomes are a poor guide to the quality of decisions, remains widely cited.
ideas: Taleb says we mistake luck for skill because we see winners and not the many losers. A successful record can be what is expected from a large pool of random players.
Survivorship bias is illustrated by the cemetery of silent failures. Taleb says we study the visible winners and draw conclusions that the hidden losers would contradict.
He proposes judging a decision by thinking about alternative histories. A good outcome may come from a bad decision that happened to get lucky.
A strategy that wins small and often can hide a rare large loss. Taleb argues that the size of an outcome matters as much as how often it happens.
Taleb draws on the problem of induction to show that no number of observations proves a general rule, and one counterexample can overturn it.
We see patterns in noise and build stories around them. Taleb argues that the media and many professionals encourage this by explaining random movements.
Taleb urges accepting randomness in ordinary life and remaining modest about prediction. He advises building a life that can survive being wrong.
Taleb presents the problem of skewness and asymmetry, saying that how often one is right matters less than how much one gains when right and loses when wrong.
He discusses the idea of the rare event and the peso problem, where a trader's record looks good until a rare crash that wipes out the gains.
Taleb describes the concept of noise versus signal in the media, arguing that more frequent observation of data leads to more attention to noise, which harms judgment.

books.thesis: Rare, extreme events shape history, and we only explain them afterwards.
books.summary:
Before Europeans reached Australia, they took it for granted that all swans were white, and one black swan overturned the rule. Nassim Nicholas Taleb uses that image for events that are rare, have huge impact and, once they have happened, seem to have been foreseeable. His book asks why we keep being surprised by them and why our models and experts keep ignoring them.

He argues that history is driven more by such rare events than by the gradual changes we like to study. He contrasts Mediocristan, where the average describes things well, with Extremistan, where single cases dominate. He criticizes the narrative fallacy, our habit of telling tidy stories after the fact, and the misuse of the bell curve. His advice is to accept that some things cannot be predicted and to limit exposure to bad surprises while staying open to good ones. Critics find his tone abrasive and some claims loosely argued.
ideas: A black swan has three features, as Taleb describes it. It surprises the observer, it has large impact, and afterwards people explain it as if it had been predictable.
Mediocristan covers domains such as height, where no single case moves the average much. Extremistan covers things like wealth or book sales, where one case can dominate the total.
The narrative fallacy is our urge to create tidy causal stories, which makes history look more understandable and predictable than it was.
In the turkey problem, a turkey fed daily concludes that the farmer is friendly until the day before Thanksgiving. Past safety gives no information about a sudden change.
The ludic fallacy is the habit of treating real-world uncertainty like the controlled odds of a game. Taleb says this misleads those who rely on neat probability models.
Taleb criticizes the use of the bell curve in finance and social science, arguing it underestimates extreme events and leads to false confidence in forecasts.
Expert prediction is poor in fields with a lot of uncertainty, Taleb argues, and the experts are rarely held to account. His advice is to guard against ruin.
Taleb distinguishes Extremistan from Mediocristan, and sets out the scalable and non-scalable distinction, in which one observation can dominate the total in the former, as with wealth or book sales.
He describes the idea of the silent evidence and the Casanova or Diagoras example of the drowned worshippers, to explain how the dead and failed are missing from our view.
Taleb advises a barbell approach for the unpredictable, advising that one be hyperconservative in some areas and take a small amount of risk with high upside in others, rather than the middle road.

books.thesis: Some things gain from shocks and disorder, and shielding them from all stress weakens them.
books.summary:
Some things break under stress, some resist it, and some get better from it. Nassim Nicholas Taleb says our language has no word for the third kind, so he made one, antifragile. His book asks how to build lives, businesses and institutions that gain from shocks and disorder, and why so much modern effort goes into removing the very stressors that would strengthen them.

He lays out the triad of the fragile, the robust and the antifragile, and links it to the shape of payoffs, where limited downside and open-ended upside favor volatility. He draws on biology, finance and ordinary habits such as exercise. He recommends a barbell strategy, extreme caution in one area and bold risk in another, and the removal of harmful things before adding helpful ones. He also criticizes interventionists who cause harm while trying to help, and insists that decision makers carry their own risk. Critics find some claims stretched.
ideas: Taleb divides things into three types. The fragile is harmed by volatility, the robust is unaffected and the antifragile improves with it, gaining from shocks, error and time.
Antifragility depends on the shape of payoffs. When losses are limited and gains are open-ended, random variation helps, which he links to option-like structures.
Hormesis in biology, where a small dose of a stressor strengthens an organism, is used as a model. Taleb applies the idea more widely to muscles, bones and other systems.
The barbell strategy combines extreme safety in one part of a portfolio or life with a small share of high-risk bets, and avoids the middle.
Via negativa suggests that subtracting harmful elements often works better than adding new ones. Taleb applies it to health, decisions and advice.
Iatrogenics is harm caused by the healer. Taleb warns against naive intervention, especially in intricate systems where side effects exceed benefits.
He argues for skin in the game, meaning decision makers should bear the consequences of their choices. Without it, risk is passed onto others who cannot respond.
Taleb introduces the Procrustean bed and the idea of the lecturing-birds-how-to-fly effect, in which academic theory is credited with achievements that came from practice and tinkering.
He discusses the Lindy effect, which suggests that for non-perishable things such as books or ideas, each additional year of survival adds to the expected remaining life.
Taleb describes the neomania of modern life and the fragilista, a person who naively imposes planned solutions and underrates the hidden costs of removing small stressors.

books.thesis: Moral intuitions come first and reasoning follows, which is why politics divides good people.
books.summary:
Haidt asks why decent people split so bitterly over politics and religion, and why each side finds the other baffling. He starts from moral psychology and argues that we behave less like judges weighing evidence and more like lawyers, building a case for a verdict that a quick gut reaction has already delivered.

To get there he combines experiments, cross-cultural research and evolutionary thinking. He proposes that human morality rests on several foundations, including care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity and liberty, and that liberals and conservatives weight them differently. He also argues that people are partly groupish, able to lose themselves in a team or a congregation, and that this helps explain religion and tribal politics. His practical conclusion is modest: understanding the other side's moral outlook is a better route to civility than out-arguing them. Critics dispute the list of foundations and the group selection argument, and both remain debated.
ideas: Moral judgments usually arrive as fast intuitions, and conscious reasoning mostly turns up afterward to defend them, the way a lawyer serves a client rather than a judge seeking truth.
Haidt pictures the mind as a small rider, our reasoning, sitting on a large elephant of automatic feeling. The rider can advise and steer a little but rarely commands.
Stories of harmless taboo violations, such as consensual sex between adult siblings, make many people condemn first and then struggle to find reasons, a state Haidt calls moral dumbfounding.
Haidt argues that morality has several foundations, among them care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity and liberty, and that political camps lean on different subsets of them.
Many people in Western, educated, industrialized, wealthy, democratic societies build their morality mostly on care and fairness, while much of the rest of the world uses a wider range.
People are about ninety percent chimp and ten percent bee: mostly self-interested, yet able to flip a hive switch and feel joy in merging with a group.
Haidt treats religion as something that binds groups and builds trust, a view tied to group selection, which many evolutionary biologists still reject.
Haidt tells the story of the moral dumbfounding studies, in which people hold on to a judgment even when they cannot give a reason, and says that this shows reasoning comes after intuition.
He describes the claim that liberals draw mainly on the care and fairness foundations while conservatives use all of them more evenly, and offers this as a way to understand political disagreement.
Haidt proposes the hive switch, the capacity to lose oneself in a group through rituals and shared experience, and ties it to group selection as a part of human evolution.

books.thesis: Ancient wisdom, tested against modern psychology.
books.summary:
Haidt takes big ideas about the good life from ancient traditions, including Buddhist, Greek, Hebrew, Christian and Stoic teachings, and asks which of them survive contact with modern psychology. The question underneath is where happiness actually comes from and whether old wisdom can be trusted on the subject.

Each chapter sets one old idea beside the research and keeps what holds up. Some claims fare well, such as the value of loving relationships and the way people adapt to good fortune. Others are qualified or overturned. Haidt does not argue that happiness lives entirely inside us or entirely in our circumstances. He suggests it arises from getting the relationships right between oneself and other people, between oneself and work, and between oneself and something larger. He is open that some of the science he cites is young and may change, and several findings from this period have since been questioned.
ideas: The mind is divided, and Haidt introduces his image of a rider on an elephant here: reason is the small rider, automatic emotion and habit are the far stronger animal.
People spot faults in others far more easily than in themselves, so hypocrisy comes naturally. Haidt links this to the old teaching about the speck and the plank.
Adaptation: people get used to most changes, good or bad, so new possessions and raises give short boosts. Noise and commuting are among the things people do not fully adapt to.
Haidt offers a rough formula in which happiness equals a biological set point, plus life conditions, plus voluntary activities, and argues that conditions and activities are where change is possible.
Passionate love tends to fade within a couple of years, and lasting relationships rely on a quieter companionate love grounded in attachment and trust.
Engagement and absorption in work matter for wellbeing, and Haidt draws on research on flow and on strengths and virtues to argue that a sense of purpose supports it.
Happiness comes from between: from fitting yourself well to other people, to your work and to something beyond yourself, so that neither inner effort nor outside luck alone settles it.
Haidt discusses the idea that the pursuit of virtue and meaning is a path to a good life, drawing on ancient thinkers such as Buddha, Plato and the Stoics to test their ideas against modern research.
He reports the progress principle, that people are happier from making progress toward goals than from reaching them, along with the finding that vigorous pursuit can matter more than success.
Haidt describes the vital engagement and the need for a sense of purpose, and writes of the human need for a moral life with relationships, work and beliefs that connect to something larger.

books.t: Mistakes Were Made (but Not by Me)
books.thesis: Why do people justify bad decisions and hurtful acts? The answer is cognitive dissonance.
books.summary:
Tavris and Aronson ask why people who do wrong, whether a spouse in a quarrel, a police officer, a doctor or a politician, so seldom say sorry and often seem to believe their own defence. Their answer is cognitive dissonance, the discomfort of holding two clashing ideas, such as "I am a good person" and "I did something harmful."

The book follows self-justification through memory, marriage, medicine, law and politics. The authors argue that people usually reduce dissonance by bending the story rather than admitting the error, and that the effect grows when the person is committed, skilled or proud. Wrongful convictions are a central case, since prosecutors and police who have staked their reputations on a suspect often discount later evidence. The authors end on a hopeful but limited note. Awareness helps, and so do outside checks, but nobody escapes the pull.
ideas: Cognitive dissonance is the tension felt when beliefs, or a belief and an action, clash. People ease it by changing whichever side is easiest, often protecting their self-image.
The pyramid of choice: two almost identical people stand at the top and make a small decision, each justifies it, and the justifications carry them to opposite ends at the base.
Memory is shaped by self-justification. People reshape the past so their choices look sensible, and the authors liken memory to a historian working for the defence.
Most people see themselves as more objective than others. We spot bias easily in rivals and rarely in ourselves, which keeps the blind spot intact.
In wrongful convictions, police and prosecutors who have committed to a suspect tend to explain away contrary evidence, even DNA results, because admitting error threatens their sense of competence.
In marriage, each partner's self-justification can harden small grievances into a standoff in which both feel wronged and each defends their own account.
Change is possible when people can separate the self from the act, saying "I did a bad thing" instead of "I am bad," and when institutions build in outside review.
The authors discuss naive realism, the belief that we see things as they are and that reasonable people will agree with us, which leads to the view that those who differ must be biased.
They look at the way memory errors, such as false memories in therapy and recovered memory cases, can come from the wish to make sense of one's life and can cause real harm.
The book describes how ambitious people in organizations, including doctors and scientists, resist admitting error and how institutions can build checks, such as outside review, to counteract this.

books.thesis: The original theory: inconsistency is uncomfortable, so we change our beliefs to reduce it.
books.summary:
Festinger proposes that people carry many pieces of knowledge, opinion and belief about the world and about their own behaviour. When two of them do not fit, the person feels a tension he calls dissonance. The book asks what that tension does to us and how it can be measured and predicted.

It is a short, technical book. Festinger defines terms, states hypotheses, and then applies them to decisions, forced compliance, exposure to information and the role of social support, citing experiments and observations. His central claim is that dissonance acts like a drive. Just as hunger pushes us toward food, dissonance pushes us to reduce it by changing a belief, changing behaviour, or adding new justifications. He also says people will avoid information likely to increase it. Later researchers debated whether inconsistency itself is the trigger or whether threat to self-image does the work, and the theory has been revised accordingly.
ideas: Two cognitions are dissonant when one follows from the opposite of the other. The resulting discomfort is a motivating state that pushes the person toward reducing the clash.
The strength of dissonance depends on how important the beliefs are and on the proportion of dissonant to consonant cognitions that bear on the same matter.
Dissonance can be reduced in three broad ways: change a behaviour, change a belief, or add new beliefs that make the conflict seem smaller.
After a hard decision, people tend to rate the chosen option as more attractive and the rejected one as less so, easing the doubt that comes with having given something up.
Forced compliance: when someone is induced to say or do something against their belief, a small reward leaves more dissonance than a large one, and so predicts more private change.
Selective exposure: people look for information likely to support what they have chosen and avoid information that might add dissonance, especially right after committing.
Social support can reduce dissonance, because finding others who agree makes a belief easier to hold. Disagreement from others, in turn, creates pressure to resolve the clash.
Festinger states that dissonance is a motivating state, like hunger, which pushes a person to reduce it, and the greater the dissonance, the greater the pressure to do so.

He describes the famous experiment of one dollar versus twenty dollars, in which those paid less to lie about a boring task came to believe it was more enjoyable, with insufficient justification as the explanation.
Festinger discusses the effects of unfavorable information on a person who has made a decision, such as the way that smokers react to evidence of harm, and the strategies of minimizing it.

books.a: Leon Festinger, Henry Riecken and Stanley Schachter
books.thesis: A study of a doomsday group, and how its members grew more committed after the world failed to end.
books.summary:
Social psychologists infiltrated a small group in the 1950s whose members believed a great flood would destroy the world and that they would be rescued by visitors from another planet. The book asks a simple question: what happens to believers when the prophecy fails.

The authors joined the group as apparent converts and kept notes on meetings, messages and preparations. When the appointed night passed with no flood and no rescue, they expected disappointment. Instead the members who were most committed, and who were together at the time, became more convinced and began seeking publicity. Those who faced the moment alone were more likely to abandon the belief. The authors use Festinger's dissonance theory and state conditions under which conviction can deepen after disproof, including commitment and social support. Critics have questioned whether the observers shaped events and whether the group was as eager to convert others afterward as the book claims.
ideas: The book opens with older cases of failed predictions, such as nineteenth-century movements expecting the end of the world, to ask whether disproof usually weakens belief.
The group was led by a woman who received messages through automatic writing from beings who warned of a coming flood, and the authors used pseudonyms for her and others.
Followers had made costly commitments before the date. Some left jobs, gave away possessions or cut ties, which made abandoning the belief expensive.
The authors list conditions for conviction to grow after disproof: a firmly held belief, hard-to-reverse commitment, a clear refutation that is acknowledged, and social support from fellow believers.
The researchers joined as believers to see the group from inside. This gave unusual access but raises the worry that their presence influenced what happened.
Before the failed date the group avoided publicity and turned away would-be followers. Afterward members sought out journalists and tried to convert others.
Members who spent the critical hours alone tended to lose faith, while those gathered with fellow believers held on, which the authors read as evidence for the role of social support.
The group in the study centered on Mrs. Keech, who predicted a great flood, and the authors gave the people pseudonyms, as their study was of a group they called the Seekers.
The authors show that after the prophecy failed, the group received a new message saying that their faith had saved the world, and then began to seek publicity and recruit people.

They conclude that social support is necessary and that the belief in a group is kept alive when members can reinforce each other, which is a central lesson for the study of how such groups handle disconfirmation.

books.thesis: More options can leave people less satisfied, not more.
books.summary:
Schwartz points out that a modern shopper can face dozens of kinds of jam, jeans or retirement plans, and asks whether all that freedom leaves people better off. His argument is that up to a point choice helps, and beyond it choice can bring paralysis, regret and a lingering sense that we could have done better.

He separates maximizers, who search for the very best, from satisficers, who accept what is good enough, and reports research suggesting maximizers often feel worse even when they end up with better results. He adds opportunity costs, rising expectations, social comparison and self-blame, since with so many options a bad outcome seems to be our own fault. His advice is to choose when to choose, to satisfice more often, to lower expectations and to accept some constraints as a relief. Later research on choice overload has been mixed, and critics note that effects depend on context and on how people feel about the decision.
ideas: Having more options has real costs. Time, attention and worry rise with each added choice, and Schwartz argues the rise can outweigh the benefit of getting a slightly better fit.
Maximizers try to find the best option, while satisficers settle on one that meets their standards. Maximizers in Schwartz's research tended to report more regret and less happiness.
Opportunity costs: choosing one option brings to mind the attractive features of everything given up, which makes the chosen thing feel less satisfying.
Anticipated regret can make people delay a decision or avoid it, because the fear of choosing wrongly looms larger when there are many ways to be wrong.
Expectations rise with the number of options. A result that might delight someone with few choices can disappoint someone who believes a perfect one must exist.
With many options, failure feels personal. Schwartz suggests this self-blame may contribute to rising unhappiness and even depression, though he treats the link as tentative.
In a well-known jam study, a display with many flavours drew more shoppers but fewer purchases than one with a few. Later replications have given mixed results.
Schwartz describes the idea of choice overload and the tyranny of freedom, arguing that a culture that values choice can leave people feeling paralyzed or unhappy with the result.

He discusses the effect of adaptation and the hedonic treadmill on consumer decisions, noting that people adjust quickly to what they buy and that this makes the effort to find the best option less rewarding.
Schwartz suggests that people can benefit from choosing when to choose, using self-imposed constraints and rules, and from practicing gratitude to reduce the pull of comparing with other options.

books.thesis: Optimal experience comes from absorption in a challenge matched to your skill.
books.summary:
Csikszentmihalyi asks when people feel most alive. After studying thousands of people, he found that rock climbers, chess players, surgeons and factory workers described a strikingly similar state: absorbed, clear about what to do, and unaware of the time. He calls it flow, and the book asks what produces it and what it implies for how to live.

His answer is that flow tends to arise when a task has clear goals, quick feedback and a level of challenge that stretches but does not overwhelm a person's skill. Too hard brings anxiety, too easy brings boredom. Because flow depends on how attention is used, he argues that people can reshape work, relationships and spare time to produce more of it, and that control over consciousness shapes the quality of life. The evidence rests heavily on self-report, which critics find hard to measure. He also admits that flow can be found in harmful activities, so it is not a guide to goodness by itself.
ideas: People report their best moments during effortful, voluntary pursuits that stretch them, and rarely during passive relaxation, which Csikszentmihalyi calls optimal experience.
Flow tends to need clear goals, immediate feedback on progress and a challenge matched to the person's skill, so that attention can settle fully on the task.
If a challenge exceeds skill, people feel anxiety, and if skill exceeds challenge they feel boredom. Flow sits in the channel between, and it shifts as skill grows.
In flow, self-consciousness drops away and the sense of time bends. Hours can feel like minutes, and the person acts without hearing an inner critic.
The Experience Sampling Method signalled people at random moments, by pager, to note what they were doing and how they felt. It gave data on everyday states.
Some people have an autotelic personality: they do things for their own sake, and find flow in many settings, including routine ones, because they set goals and attend closely.
People often reported more flow at work than in leisure, yet said they wished to be elsewhere, a puzzle that suggests we misjudge where satisfaction lies.

Csikszentmihalyi describes the structure of the self and the idea of psychic entropy, the disorder in consciousness when information conflicts with our goals, and contrasts it with the order that flow brings.
He discusses the way people can shape the quality of experience through control of attention, and that the activity of daily life, such as work and relationships, can be reshaped to be more engaging.
The book gives examples from rock climbers, chess players, surgeons and dancers, and argues that the elements of flow are the same in different activities, from play to ritual.

books.thesis: Some ordinary people predict events far better than experts do. Humility and updating make the difference.
books.summary:
Tetlock and Gardner ask whether anyone can predict political and economic events with real accuracy and, if so, what sets those people apart. Tetlock's earlier research had found that well-known experts forecast only a little better than chance. This book looks at the exceptions: ordinary volunteers who repeatedly beat the crowd.

The evidence comes from the Good Judgment Project, a forecasting tournament in which thousands of volunteers estimated probabilities on questions about world events. The best, called superforecasters, tended to break problems into parts, start from base rates, think in finely graded probabilities, update often in small steps and keep score of their own accuracy. They were more foxlike than hedgehog-like, willing to hold several ideas. The authors say the skill has limits, since forecasts far into the future remain unreliable, and some critics argue that rare, large shocks escape any such method. The book makes a case for humility, but not for helplessness.
ideas: Earlier work by Tetlock found that famous experts often did little better than chance. He contrasted hedgehogs, who rely on one big idea, with foxes, who draw on many.
The Good Judgment Project ran a multi-year tournament in which volunteers gave probability estimates on real questions. Top performers beat the average and, reportedly, some trained analysts.
Superforecasters break big questions into smaller parts, in the spirit of Fermi estimates, so that they can reason about pieces rather than guess at the whole.
They start from the outside view, asking how often similar events happen, and then adjust with case-specific detail instead of anchoring on a gripping story.
They revise forecasts often and in small increments as news arrives, avoiding both stubbornness and overreaction.
Forecasts are scored with the Brier score, which punishes confident mistakes. The method also exposes vague wording such as "likely," which can hide a wide range of probabilities.
Tetlock accepts that long-range prediction is mostly beyond reach, and that forecasting works best on questions with a horizon of months or a few years.
Tetlock describes the difference between foxes and hedgehogs, with foxes drawing on many ideas and hedgehogs using one big idea, and finds that foxes forecast better.
He discusses the importance of a growth mindset and grit among forecasters, as well as active open-mindedness, and notes that forecasters improve through practice with feedback.
The book describes the benefit of teams and of extremizing aggregated forecasts, as well as the commandments for forecasters, including balancing under- and over-reaction to new evidence.

books.thesis: Seeing things as they are is a skill, and motivated reasoning is its opposite.
books.summary:
Galef contrasts two ways of treating what we believe. The soldier defends a position against threats. The scout tries to draw an accurate map, even when the terrain is unwelcome. The book asks why we so often think like soldiers and what changes if we treat seeing clearly as the goal.

She argues that motivated reasoning pays real emotional dividends, such as comfort, self-esteem, motivation, persuasiveness and belonging, but that most of them can be had without distorting reality. The book offers practical checks, including a double standard test, an outsider test and a conformity test, along with advice on calibration, betting on beliefs and holding identity lightly. Galef treats the scout mindset as a habit to be practised, not a native talent. She concedes that self-deception can sometimes help in the short term, while arguing that its benefits are usually overstated. The book is plainly written and light on theory.
ideas: Soldier mindset defends what you already believe. Scout mindset wants to know what is true, and Galef says most people mix the two without noticing.
Motivated reasoning offers comfort, self-esteem, morale, persuasion and social belonging. Galef argues you can get most of these without bending your view of the facts.
The double standard test asks whether you would judge the same behaviour or evidence the same way if it came from the other side.
The outsider test imagines a newcomer taking over your situation with no history, and asks what they would do, to loosen the pull of sunk costs and past choices.
Calibration means matching your confidence to how often you are right. Galef suggests putting numbers on beliefs and checking your track record over time.
Beliefs tied to identity are harder to revise. Galef recommends holding identity lightly, so that changing your mind feels less like losing yourself.
Seeking out thoughtful critics, and treating a changed mind as something to reward, builds scout habits that make being wrong less costly.
Galef describes the bet test, in which you ask whether you would put money on a belief, as a way to discover how confident you really are and where the self-deception lies.
She discusses the way that people can feel good without lying to themselves, by using self-compassion and by accepting that a decision can be sound even if the outcome is bad.
Galef gives the Dreyfus affair as a historical example, showing how motivated reasoning can lead intelligent people to maintain a false belief even in the face of strong evidence.

books.thesis: How we explain bad events shapes whether we give up.
books.summary:
Seligman begins with a laboratory finding. Dogs given shocks they could not escape later failed to escape even when escape became possible. He calls this learned helplessness, extends it to people, and asks why some who face setbacks recover while others give up.

His answer is explanatory style, the habit of explaining bad events to ourselves. Pessimists tend to see causes as permanent, pervasive and personal, and optimists see them as temporary, specific and external. He links the pessimistic style to depression, weaker school and sports results, and poorer sales. The book then teaches a cognitive method for disputing gloomy interpretations and treating them as claims to be tested. Seligman cautions that optimism is a tool and not a creed, and that realism matters when risks are real. Critics point out that the correlations do not prove cause, and Seligman himself later revised the animal findings, suggesting passivity is the default and control is what is learned.
ideas: In the helplessness experiments, animals exposed to uncontrollable shocks stopped trying to escape later, and Seligman argued that humans can also learn that their actions do not matter.
Explanatory style has three dimensions: permanence, pervasiveness and personalization. Pessimists say "it will last, it ruins everything, it is my fault" about setbacks.
A pessimistic explanatory style predicts a higher risk of depression, and Seligman argues it works as a habit that can be changed rather than a fixed trait.
Life insurance agents who scored as optimists sold more and quit less than pessimists in a study Seligman describes, and he uses it to argue that style predicts performance.
The ABCDE method: note the adversity, your beliefs about it, the consequences, then dispute the belief with evidence and notice the energy that follows.
Seligman says optimism is not always the right stance. It suits situations where the cost of failure is small, and pessimism may serve when risk is real.
Children pick up explanatory style partly from how adults, such as parents and teachers, explain failure to them, which Seligman says can shape how they respond to setbacks.
Seligman describes learned helplessness in humans as well as animals, and notes that about a third of the animals and people did not become helpless, which led him to the study of resilience.
He discusses the idea of disputing pessimistic thoughts by using evidence, alternatives, implications and usefulness, as a way to challenge one's own explanations.
Seligman reports that optimistic candidates did better in elections and that pessimistic explanatory style in athletes and students predicted worse performance than ability alone would suggest.

books.thesis: Belief in your own capability shapes what you try and how long you persist.
books.summary:
Bandura asks why people with similar skills perform differently. His answer is belief: whether a person feels able to carry out the actions needed to reach a goal. The book gathers decades of research into social cognitive theory and argues that these beliefs shape what we try, how hard we try and how long we persist.

Bandura identifies four sources of efficacy: mastery experiences, watching similar others succeed, social persuasion, and the way we read our own bodily and emotional states. He applies the idea to health, education, athletics, work and groups. He says efficacy is tied to particular domains and is not a general trait, and that it differs from simply expecting good outcomes. Strong efficacy goes with higher goals, persistence and less stress under pressure. He allows that slightly optimistic self-beliefs can be useful. Critics note that it is hard to separate efficacy from earlier performance, and the book is dense, closer to a research handbook than to a popular read.
ideas: Self-efficacy is the belief that you can organize and carry out the actions a task needs. It differs from expecting a good outcome, since you can expect rewards and doubt your ability.
Mastery experiences, actually succeeding at something hard, are the strongest source of efficacy, while easy wins build only a fragile belief.
Vicarious experience matters: seeing people similar to you succeed raises your belief that you can too, and seeing them fail lowers it.
Social persuasion helps when it is realistic and comes from a credible person. Empty encouragement is quickly undone by failure.
People read arousal, such as a racing heart, as a sign of threat or readiness, and these readings change how capable they feel.
Efficacy is domain specific. A person can feel highly capable at public speaking and not at maths, so Bandura treats it as a belief about tasks, not a personality trait.
Groups also hold collective efficacy, a shared belief about what they can achieve together, which Bandura links to how teams and communities act under strain.

Bandura distinguishes efficacy expectations, the belief that one can carry out a behavior, from outcome expectations, the belief that the behavior will lead to a given result, and says that both affect action.

He describes the way that efficacy beliefs influence the choices people make, the effort they spend and how long they persist in the face of obstacles, as well as their thought patterns and emotional reactions.

Bandura discusses triadic reciprocal determinism, in which personal factors, behavior and environment influence each other, and uses it to explain why people are both products and producers of their circumstances.

books.thesis: Reason evolved to argue and persuade. It didn't evolve to find the truth alone.
books.summary:
Mercier and Sperber ask why humans, called the rational animal, reason so badly. We favour our own side, rationalize our choices and are easily swayed. The usual story says reason is a tool for sharper individual thinking that often fails. They propose that reason evolved for a social purpose, to justify ourselves to others and to evaluate what others tell us.

They call this the interactionist view. On it, the oddities of reasoning look like features. People are quick to produce one-sided arguments and tougher at judging other people's, and groups that disagree and share a goal often reason better than individuals. The authors set this within an account of the mind as many intuitive inference systems, with reason one of them. They draw on psychology, evolution and anthropology. Critics say the view overstates the case, and it remains debated whether reasoning ever helps a lone thinker find truth. The book does not claim that it never does.
ideas: The intellectualist view holds that reason exists to improve individual thinking. The authors argue that its many familiar failures are hard to square with that idea.
Much of our thinking comes from unconscious intuitions. Reason, in this account, is a mechanism that supplies reasons for conclusions we have already reached.
Confirmation bias may be a feature of producing arguments. Searching for support for your own view is an efficient way to build a case to put to others.
People are far better at judging other people's arguments than at generating their own, which suggests that reason does its best work in exchange.
Groups that share a goal but disagree often perform better than their individual members, for example on reasoning puzzles that most people fail when working alone.
Reason helps us justify our actions and keep our standing among others, which matters for a species that relies heavily on cooperation and reputation.
When people reason alone or only with like-minded companions, the lopsidedness is unchecked and can drive them to more extreme positions.

Mercier and Sperber propose the interactionist or argumentative theory, which says that reason evolved to justify ourselves to others and to evaluate their arguments, instead of for solitary reasoning.

They discuss epistemic vigilance, the set of mechanisms by which people judge whom to trust and which messages to accept, and they argue that it is needed because communication can be used to deceive.

The authors suggest that the reasons people give are often rationalizations that come after the fact, as shown by studies where people explain choices they did not actually make, and that reasons are meant for social use.

books.thesis: What is rationality, why does it seem so scarce, and why does it matter?
books.summary:
Pinker asks how a species that built vaccines and spacecraft can also believe in conspiracies, astrology and fake cures. His book explores what rationality is, why it seems so scarce, and why it matters. He defines rationality as using knowledge to reach goals, which makes it a matter of means and not a rejection of feeling.

The bulk of the book is a tour of tools: logic, probability, Bayesian updating, expected utility, signal detection, game theory, and the difference between correlation and causation. Pinker argues that people make mistakes because their intuitions developed for small groups and concrete problems, and because beliefs about politics and identity often serve as badges rather than as maps. He rejects the idea that people are hopelessly irrational, noting that they reason well in everyday settings where they face consequences. His answer is to teach the tools and build institutions that reward accuracy. Critics say he gives too little weight to why people want to believe.
ideas: Rationality means using knowledge to achieve goals. It does not require being unemotional, and Pinker says a person can pursue emotional goals rationally.
Bayesian reasoning updates a prior belief with new evidence. Pinker uses medical tests to show how ignoring base rates leads people to overrate what a positive result means.
People often fail abstract logic puzzles but do much better when the same structure is dressed in a familiar social rule, such as checking who is old enough to drink.
Signal detection explains why every decision trades misses against false alarms, and how the right threshold depends on the cost of each error.
Expected utility and rational choice give a way to weigh outcomes by probability and value, and Pinker explains why some apparent paradoxes arise from framing.
Correlation is not causation. Confounds, selection effects and the logic of randomized trials are central tools for telling what causes what.
People reason soundly about the everyday world, the reality mindset, yet hold other beliefs in a mythology mindset where they work as badges of belonging.

The availability heuristic leads people to judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind, which is why vivid risks like plane crashes or terrorism loom larger than car accidents or heart disease.

Game theory shows how choices that are rational for each person can leave everyone worse off, as in the prisoner's dilemma and the tragedy of the commons, and Pinker uses it to explain why cooperation needs rules or shared expectations.

Pinker stresses myside bias, the tendency to reason in defence of one's own camp, and argues that rationality is a social achievement that depends on institutions such as peer review, open debate and fact checking.

books.thesis: Milgram's full account of his experiments, and of the agentic state.
books.summary:
Milgram asks how ordinary people come to carry out orders that harm others. In his experiments at Yale in the early 1960s, volunteers acted as teachers and were told to give increasing electric shocks to a learner for wrong answers. The shocks were not real. The book gives his full account of the studies and his theory of why the results came out as they did.

In the baseline version about two thirds of participants went to the top of the shock scale. Milgram ran many variations, changing how close the victim was, who gave the order and whether others refused, and the results shifted sharply. To explain them he proposed the agentic state, in which a person sees themselves as an instrument of authority and hands over responsibility. Many participants showed obvious distress while obeying. The studies remain controversial. Critics raise ethical objections and doubts about how many participants believed the shocks were real.
ideas: The setup: a volunteer plays teacher, a confederate plays learner, and a shock generator labelled up to 450 volts is used for wrong answers, with an experimenter urging the teacher on.
In the baseline condition, roughly two thirds of participants continued all the way to the highest shock, a result far above what Milgram's psychiatrist colleagues had predicted.
Agentic state: when people see themselves as carrying out another's wishes, they feel less responsible for the consequences, shifting from autonomous to agent.
Variations mattered. Obedience fell when the victim was physically close and rose when the authority was present and had institutional standing.
When peers who appeared to be other participants refused to continue, most real participants also defied the experimenter, showing that obedience is shaped by other people.
Many obedient participants showed visible strain, sweating, trembling or nervous laughter, so Milgram argued that obedience does not require cruelty and may feel unpleasant.
Critics raise ethical concerns about the deception and distress and dispute how closely the experimenter followed the script and how many participants believed the shocks were real.
Milgram repeated the study in a run-down office building under the name Research Associates of Bridgeport, without Yale's prestige, and obedience was lower but still substantial.

He lists binding factors that keep a person in the situation, including the shocks rising in small 15 volt steps, so that each new step differs little from the last, and the awkwardness of breaking off a task already begun.
Milgram says conscience does not vanish under authority but is redirected, so that moral concern shifts from the victim to how well one performs as a good subject carrying out the job.

books.thesis: Situations can make good people do evil. Its key experiment is now heavily disputed.
books.summary:
Zimbardo asks how good people turn cruel, and where the line between good and evil really falls. The book centres on the 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment, in which students were assigned to play guards and prisoners in a mock jail, then extends the argument to real cases such as the abuse at Abu Ghraib, where he served as an expert witness for one of the accused.

His case is that situations and systems have more power over conduct than most people believe, and that blaming a few bad apples ignores the barrel. He lists mechanisms such as deindividuation, dehumanization and diffusion of responsibility, and ends with a hopeful chapter on ordinary heroism. The key experiment is now heavily disputed. Later critics, using archive recordings and interviews, argue that the guards were coached to be tough and that participants were partly acting to meet expectations. Zimbardo has rejected that reading. Other research supports the broader claim that context shapes behaviour.
ideas: Zimbardo opens with the image of Lucifer as an angel who fell, to ask whether the line between good and evil is a thin boundary people can cross.
In the Stanford Prison Experiment, students were randomly assigned as guards or prisoners in a mock prison. The planned two-week study was stopped after about six days.
Zimbardo contrasts bad apples, bad barrels and bad barrel makers, arguing that the system that creates a situation often matters most when people behave badly.
He interprets the abuse at Abu Ghraib as a failure of the system, with poor oversight, pressure and boredom, rather than only the failings of a few soldiers.
He describes mechanisms that ease harmful acts, including deindividuation, dehumanizing others, diffusion of responsibility and step-by-step escalation from small acts to larger ones.
Critics who studied archive tapes and interviewed participants claim the guards were encouraged to be harsh and that some prisoners acted distress for effect, which damages the study's value.
The book closes on the heroic imagination, the idea that ordinary people can resist pressure and that heroism, like cruelty, is influenced by situation.

Zimbardo ties the guards' behaviour to anonymity: they wore uniforms and mirrored sunglasses, while prisoners wore smocks, numbers and stocking caps, and he argues these cues encouraged deindividuation.

He gives weight to the evil of inaction, the good people who watch and do nothing, and notes that it was a visiting colleague, Christina Maslach, who objected to the conditions and pushed him to end the study.
Zimbardo served as an expert witness for one of the Abu Ghraib guards, Ivan Frederick, and argued that the situation and the system should be weighed alongside individual blame.

books.thesis: Modern power watches, measures and normalizes us, until we learn to discipline ourselves.
books.summary:
Foucault opens with a gruesome public execution in 1757 and, a few decades later, a prison timetable. He asks what changed in how societies punish, and why punishment moved from the body to the soul and behind walls. It is a history of the prison that doubles as a history of power.

His argument is that reform was not only humane. New techniques of power developed in armies, schools, workshops, hospitals and prisons, built on hierarchical observation, normalizing judgment and the examination. Bentham's Panopticon, a prison design in which inmates can be watched but never know when, serves as his model of how visibility makes people police themselves. Foucault adds that the prison's failure to reduce crime may be part of its use, since it produces a class of delinquents who can be managed and watched. He concludes that discipline spreads through society as a way of producing orderly, useful, docile people. Critics find the sweep too broad and the picture of resistance thin.
ideas: The book opens with the execution of Damiens in 1757 and a prison timetable from decades later, a contrast that frames the shift in how power treats the body.
Public torture displayed the sovereign's power. The crowd watched the law reassert itself on the criminal's body in a ritual of spectacle.
Later punishment aims at the soul, at habits and character as well as acts, so that reform, assessment and treatment become part of what a sentence means.
Discipline works on bodies through control of time, space and movement, producing what Foucault calls docile bodies that are useful and easy to direct.
Foucault names three instruments of discipline: hierarchical observation, normalizing judgment that measures people against a norm, and the examination that combines both.
The Panopticon makes inmates visible without showing when they are watched, so they internalize the gaze and become their own guards. Foucault treats it as a diagram of modern power.
Foucault argues that the prison's failure to cut crime may be useful, since it creates delinquents who can be policed, and links this to wider control.

Foucault describes a carceral archipelago, in which the methods of the prison spread into schools, factories, barracks and hospitals until disciplinary power forms a continuous network across society.

Power and knowledge imply each other in his account. The human sciences, such as criminology and psychology, grew out of disciplinary practices of observing and examining people, and in turn gave those practices authority.
Foucault notes that public executions carried a risk, since crowds could sympathize with the condemned or turn on the authorities, which helped push punishment out of sight and behind walls.

books.thesis: How reason defined itself by confining and excluding the mad.
books.summary:
Foucault asks how Western societies came to treat madness as mental illness, and how the border between reason and unreason was drawn. The book begins with leprosy houses, which emptied as the disease declined and left structures of exclusion that, he suggests, were later filled by other outcasts, among them the mad.

He argues that in the seventeenth century madness was confined alongside the poor and idle, notably after the founding of the Hôpital Général in Paris in 1656, in what he calls the great confinement. Later reformers such as Pinel and Tuke removed chains but, Foucault says, substituted moral treatment that instilled guilt and obedience. Psychiatry's authority rests on a monologue of reason about madness, since earlier dialogue had been silenced. Historians have disputed the scale and timing of the confinement and his handling of sources. The book leaves open what it would mean to listen to madness on its own terms, and it still divides readers.
ideas: Leprosy houses emptied after the Middle Ages, but the habits of exclusion remained. Foucault suggests madness later took leprosy's place as the thing a society must set apart.
In Renaissance images and literature, the ship of fools carries the mad from town to town. Foucault argues that madness then still spoke, with a kind of strange truth.
The great confinement: in 1656 the Hôpital Général in Paris began locking up beggars, the idle and the mad together, treating unreason as a moral and social problem.
Because the mad were confined with the poor and idle, madness came to be judged as a failure of work and morals, not as a disease with its own medicine.
Reason defined itself by excluding unreason, and a dialogue between the two ended. Psychiatry later spoke about the mad without letting madness answer back.
Pinel and Tuke are remembered for freeing patients from chains, but Foucault argues that moral treatment replaced physical restraint with internalized guilt, surveillance and authority.
Historians have challenged the scale, timing and sources of the great confinement, and the book's sweeping claims are still debated among specialists.
Foucault reads Descartes' Meditations as ruling madness out of the grounds for doubt, a sign that reason had come to exclude madness, and Derrida later disputed this reading.
In the classical age, he says, the confined mad were often treated as animals, kept in cells and sometimes shown to visitors, on the belief that animality made them insensible to cold or hardship.
The full 1961 book was long known in English only through a heavily abridged translation titled Madness and Civilization, and a complete English translation did not appear until 2006.

books.thesis: Sexuality wasn't simply repressed. Power produced endless talk about it.
books.summary:
Foucault challenges the familiar story that sexuality was silenced from the seventeenth century on, and that speaking freely about it is liberation. He calls this the repressive hypothesis and asks a different question: why are we so eager to say we are repressed, and why do we keep talking about sex?

His answer is that modern power did not mainly forbid talk of sex but encouraged it. Confession, medicine, psychiatry, education and population science all produced a stream of discourse that sorted people into types, such as the homosexual, and made sex a route to truth about the self. Power here is productive and works through relations, and he introduces biopower, the management of bodies and populations. This is the first volume of a planned series, and he later shifted his focus to antiquity. Critics, including many feminist scholars, say it neglects gender and rests on thin evidence. Readers still disagree over how much of his picture holds up.
ideas: The repressive hypothesis says sex was silenced by modern society and that speech frees us. Foucault doubts it and notes that talk about sex multiplied.
Confession began as a religious practice and later spread into medicine, schooling and psychiatry, making sex something a person was expected to speak about in order to know themselves.
Foucault contrasts ars erotica, in which pleasure is passed on as a craft, with scientia sexualis, which treats sex as a field of truth to be studied and classified.
Earlier law punished sodomy as an act, but the nineteenth century made the homosexual a type of person with a case history. Categories made identities.
Four figures became targets of study and control: the hysterical woman, the masturbating child, the couple regulated for the sake of population, and the perverse adult.
Power is not just a ban from above. It works through relationships everywhere, produces knowledge and desire, and Foucault says resistance arises inside it.
Biopower refers to power over life, working through discipline of individual bodies and regulation of populations, such as birth rates and public health.
Foucault contrasts the older deployment of alliance, built on kinship and marriage rules, with the newer deployment of sexuality, which works through bodies, sensations and pleasures.
He describes a shift in power from the sovereign's right to take life or let live toward a power to foster life or disallow it to the point of death.
This first volume was meant as an introduction to a longer project, and Foucault later changed course, turning to ancient Greek and early Christian ideas of the self in the later volumes.

books.thesis: Totalitarianism grows out of loneliness, rootlessness and mass movements.
books.summary:
Arendt wrote this after the Second World War to ask how Nazi Germany and Stalin's Soviet Union became possible, and why they were unlike older tyrannies. The book has three parts, on antisemitism, imperialism and totalitarianism, and it treats the regimes as something new, not as old despotism in modern dress.

She argues that no single cause explains them. Elements crystallized together, including imperialist racism and bureaucracy, the decline of the nation-state, the statelessness of refugees, and a mass society of lonely, atomized people drawn toward movements and ideology. In power, such movements rely on terror and an ideology followed to its logical end, and the camps serve as a laboratory for total domination. Arendt concludes that the aim is to make human beings superfluous. Critics dispute whether Nazism and Stalinism belong in one category, and many historians challenge parts of the antisemitism section. The book is more a work of political theory than a narrative.
ideas: The book is organized around antisemitism, imperialism and totalitarianism. Arendt argues that earlier hatreds and colonial practice supplied elements, not a direct line to the regimes that followed.
After the First World War, stateless people lost the protection of any government, which led Arendt to describe the loss of a right to have rights.
The boomerang effect: methods of racial rule and bureaucratic administration developed overseas in imperial settings came back to shape politics in Europe.
Totalitarian movements drew on masses of atomized individuals lacking class ties. Arendt separates isolation from loneliness, the feeling of being abandoned by all other people.
Ideological thinking follows a single premise to its logical end and ignores experience. Arendt argues that this sealed logic made believers resistant to facts.
Terror is the essence of totalitarian rule, not merely a tool. It replaces the stability of law with constant movement toward a predetermined end.
The camps worked as laboratories for total domination, and Arendt argues the project aimed to make human beings superfluous, stripping spontaneity and individuality.
Arendt examines the pan-movements, Pan-Slavism and Pan-Germanism, as forms of tribal nationalism that claimed a people's destiny beyond the borders of any state.
She discusses the Dreyfus affair as a preview of modern antisemitism, in which a mob and parts of the elite joined in a hostility that the institutions of the state failed to contain.
Arendt argues that totalitarianism is a new form of government, distinct from tyranny and dictatorship, because it rests on ideology and terror and aims to remake human beings.

books.thesis: Labour, work and action. What do we lose when life is reduced to producing and consuming?
books.summary:
Arendt asks a plain question: what are we doing when we are active? She separates the activities of life into labour, work and action. The book was written in the age of Sputnik and growing automation, and its worry is what we lose when life is reduced to producing and consuming.

Labour answers biological needs and its products are quickly consumed. Work makes lasting objects and builds a shared world. Action, speaking and acting among equals, reveals who a person is and begins something new, a capacity she ties to natality, the fact that each birth is a fresh beginning. Arendt argues that the modern age exalted labour and shrank the public realm, as the household and the economy took over what had been political. Forgiving and promising are her remedies for the unpredictability and irreversibility of action. Critics find her categories too tidy and her picture of the Greek polis idealized. The book offers no programme.
ideas: Labour belongs to the cycle of biological need. It must be repeated endlessly, and its products are consumed, leaving nothing lasting behind.
Work is making. It produces durable objects, from tools to buildings, and with them the human world that outlasts any one life.
Action is speaking and acting together in public. Arendt says it depends on plurality, since it needs others to see, answer and remember.
Natality: every birth brings a new beginning into the world, and Arendt sees this as the root of our capacity to act in unexpected ways.
Arendt draws a line between the private realm of necessity and the public realm of freedom, a division based on the Greek polis that critics see as idealized.
The rise of the social blurs the line, as household concerns and the economy become public matters, and society treats people as behaving, not acting.
Forgiving and promising answer the irreversibility and unpredictability of action: forgiving releases us from past deeds, and promising gives some stability to the future.
The book opens with the launch of Sputnik, which Arendt reads as a sign of a wish to escape the earth, and she calls the resulting distance from our home planet world and earth alienation.
Action and speech, she says, disclose who a person is rather than what a person is, and this revelation is only possible among others and cannot be controlled by the speaker.

Arendt distinguishes the vita activa from the vita contemplativa and argues that the tradition placed contemplation above all action, while the modern age has inverted that order in favour of making and labouring.

books.thesis: Great evil can be done by people who are neither monstrous nor fanatical. They're just thoughtless.
ideas: The banality of evil: Arendt found a man who was neither sadist nor monster but frighteningly ordinary, so that great harm could flow from shallow, unremarkable motives.
Thoughtlessness was the key. Arendt saw in Eichmann an inability to think from another's standpoint, not a lack of intelligence.
Officialese and clichés served as tools that blocked thinking. Eichmann's stock phrases shielded him from reality and from the people his work destroyed.
Eichmann claimed to have lived by Kant's moral law, which Arendt noted he twisted into a duty to act as if the Führer would approve.
Arendt criticised the staging of the trial as a lesson in Jewish history and a showpiece, while accepting that he had to be tried and held responsible for his acts.
Her account of the Jewish councils was the book's most controversial part. She argued that some leaders' cooperation worsened the toll, and critics called it unfair.
Later historians say Eichmann was more ideologically committed than Arendt allowed, and the phrase she coined is still contested and often misunderstood.
Arendt reports that Eichmann felt a kind of Pontius Pilate relief at the Wannsee conference, since leading officials approved the plan and he no longer had to decide anything himself.

She argues the crime had no precedent and called for it to be understood as a crime against humanity, not only a crime against the Jewish people, and she discusses the legal problems of the abduction and the court's jurisdiction.
She points to Denmark, Bulgaria and Italy as places where officials or populations refused to cooperate, and says this shows that resistance was possible and that moral choices were open.
books.surprise: Arendt thought the trial's prosecution was right about the crime and wrong about the man.
books.crit: Stangneth's research shows Eichmann was a committed ideologue. Arendt's tone toward victims was criticised as cold.
books.summary:
Arendt covered the 1961 trial of Adolf Eichmann in Jerusalem for The New Yorker, and this book grew from that reporting. She asks what kind of man Eichmann was, what he could be held responsible for, and what a courtroom can say about crimes on this scale. Its subtitle is A Report on the Banality of Evil.

She portrays Eichmann as a diligent careerist who spoke in stock phrases and seemed unable to see anything from another person's point of view. In her reading, he was neither a demon nor a fanatic but thoughtless, and that was the disturbing part. She also criticised how the trial was staged, and she wrote about the cooperation of some Jewish leaders, which brought fierce condemnation. Later historians, drawing on interviews Eichmann gave in Argentina, argue that he was a committed antisemite, and the phrase banality of evil is often misread as saying evil is ordinary. That remains debated.

books.thesis: Modern freedom isolates. When people can't bear that isolation, they give their freedom up to authority, destruction or conformity.
ideas: Freedom from versus freedom to. Medieval people were secure but bound, modern people free but alone, and only spontaneous love and work give freedom a positive content.
Individuation: as a child grows apart from its mother, it gains independence and loses security. Fromm sees the same arc in the history of the West.
Fromm argues that Luther and Calvin, in stressing the individual's solitary relation to God, deepened anxiety and powerlessness, which later fed the drive for work and success.
The authoritarian character is masochistic toward those above, craving submission, and sadistic toward those below, craving control, and both come from the fear of standing alone.
Destructiveness is an escape in which a person tries to eliminate the world outside, relieving the feeling of powerlessness by removing what threatens to dwarf them.
Automaton conformity is the most common escape in democracies. People adopt the expected opinions and tastes and lose the sense of a self of their own.
Fromm reads Nazism's appeal through the lower middle class, whose economic insecurity and sense of lost status made submission to a strong leader attractive.
Fromm uses the idea of social character, the shared core of personality in a group, which makes people want to act as the society needs them to act.
He analyses Hitler's writing and speeches, arguing that they show an authoritarian character that combines worship of power with contempt for the weak.

Fromm closes by saying that real freedom needs a democratic economy in which people have actual control over the forces that shape their lives, since formal political freedom alone leaves them isolated.
books.surprise: Fromm argues that the Reformation, not just the 20th century, began the psychological crisis behind fascism.
books.crit: The historical argument is broad-brush; the solution ("spontaneity") is vague.
books.summary:
Fromm, a German psychoanalyst writing in exile in 1941, asks why so many people welcomed fascism and gave up freedom they had only recently won. His answer starts from a paradox. Modern life freed people from the fixed ties of the medieval world, but this freedom from brought isolation and anxiety along with independence.

Some people find freedom to, a spontaneous way of living through love and work. Others flee, and Fromm describes three escapes: submitting to authority, destroying what makes them feel small, and conforming like an automaton. He traces the roots of this anxiety to the Reformation and the rise of capitalism, then reads the appeal of Nazism for the lower middle class through it. He mixes Freud with Marx, drawing on a theory of social character. Critics say his claims about historical psychology are broad and thinly supported, though the book remains influential in discussions of authoritarianism and conformity.

books.thesis: A whole society can be sick, and adjusting to it isn't the same as being healthy.
books.summary:
Fromm asks whether an entire society can be unhealthy, and what a healthy one would look like. He challenges the assumption that being well adjusted to society means being sane. If the society itself is sick, then a person who fits in perfectly may be suffering from what he calls the pathology of normalcy.

He starts from basic human needs, among them relatedness, transcendence, rootedness, identity and a frame of orientation, and judges societies by how well they meet them. Modern capitalism, he argues, produces alienation, since people come to see themselves as things and as commodities with a market value. He criticizes Soviet communism on similar grounds. His own proposal is a humanistic communitarian socialism with smaller groups and worker participation, which many readers find vague and utopian. Fromm points to alcoholism, suicide and violence in wealthy countries as signs that prosperity is no proof of health. The book is a work of social criticism rather than strict empirical research.
ideas: The pathology of normalcy: a defect shared by the majority is not felt as a defect, so a whole society can be ill without anyone noticing.
Fromm names basic human needs: relatedness, transcendence, rootedness, a sense of identity and a frame of orientation, and judges societies by how well they meet them.
Alienation means experiencing oneself as a thing, cut off from one's own powers and from others, and Fromm sees it as the typical condition of modern industrial life.
The marketing orientation: people treat their own personalities as goods to be sold, and their worth seems to depend on success in the market.
Fromm criticizes both Western capitalism and Soviet communism as bureaucratic, alienated systems that treat people as means to economic ends.
He cites rates of suicide, alcoholism and violence in prosperous countries as evidence that material comfort does not guarantee mental health.
His remedy is a humanistic communitarian socialism, with decentralized, face-to-face groups and workplace participation, a proposal critics find sketchy.
Fromm warns of robotism, the danger that people will become automatons who are well fed and adjusted but no longer experience themselves as active agents.
He defends normative humanism, the claim that mental health can be judged by universal human needs, and rejects the view that sanity is simply whatever a culture treats as normal.
Fromm describes regressive attempts to meet the need for rootedness, such as fixation on blood, soil, nation or idols, and calls them false solutions compared with brotherly love and reason.

books.thesis: Two modes of existence: having things, or being engaged with life.
books.summary:
Fromm describes two ways of living. In the having mode, we relate to the world as property, and that includes our knowledge, our love, our beliefs and our own selves. In the being mode, we are alive and active, engaged with people and things for their own sake. The book asks which mode shapes us and our society.

He illustrates the contrast with everyday examples, such as students taking notes, the difference between owning a memory and remembering, and the way love can turn into possession. He draws on Meister Eckhart, the Buddha and Marx as models of being. Fromm argues that industrial society cultivates having, at a psychological cost and an ecological one, and he calls for a new kind of person and a new society. Critics find the opposition too tidy, and his practical proposals are brief. The book is more a moral appeal than an argument built from data, which is both its strength and its limit.
ideas: In the having mode, a person's sense of worth rests on what they own, and this extends to knowledge, status and even relationships treated as things to hold.
In the being mode, a person is alive, active and responsive, giving up the ego's grip, and Fromm separates this from mere busyness.
Students in the having mode listen to a lecture to copy it down and keep it. Students in the being mode listen, question and let it change how they think.
Fromm points to language: saying "I have a problem" turns an experience into a possession, while "I am troubled" keeps it a state of being.
Love in the having mode tries to possess and control the other person. In the being mode, loving is an activity that gives without demanding.
Fromm draws on Meister Eckhart, the Buddha and Marx as thinkers of being, and reads them as sharing a call to detach from possessions.
He warns that an economy built on endless having and consumption endangers the planet, and he calls for a new kind of society and a new person.
Fromm separates existential having, the possessions needed to survive, from characterological having, a passion to hold and keep that shapes how a person relates to everything.
Faith in the having mode is the ownership of a creed or an authority to lean on, while in the being mode it is an inner orientation of confidence and openness.
He says that knowing in the having mode means gathering information and certainties, whereas in the being mode it means penetrating a subject to understand it and be changed by it.

books.thesis: Consumer society manufactures needs and absorbs all opposition.
books.summary:
Marcuse argues that advanced industrial society, whether capitalist or Soviet, flattens thought and politics into a single dimension that affirms what exists. He asks why a society so wealthy and apparently free produces so little real opposition, and why people feel content with arrangements that limit them.

His answer is that technology, affluence and mass media create needs that feel like our own but are shaped from outside, which he calls false needs.
