The working class is integrated into the system, protest is absorbed, and even sexual freedom serves it through what he calls repressive desublimation. Language and thought are narrowed to what is useful and measurable, and critical negation fades. The book is pessimistic. Marcuse places what hope there is in outsiders, such as the unemployed, minorities and the marginal, and in a Great Refusal. Critics say he is elitist in judging which needs are true, and that he underrates how real the gains of affluence were.
ideas: One-dimensional thought has lost the negative, critical edge that compares reality with what could be. The existing order seems the only rational option.
False needs are those imposed by advertising and industry in the name of the individual's wants. Marcuse says people identify with them and so cannot see what they lack.
Affluence and organized labour integrate the working class into the system, which Marcuse sees as draining its revolutionary potential.
Repressive desublimation: relaxing sexual restraint within consumer society integrates people into it rather than freeing them, because the new freedom is easy to sell.
Technological rationality presents efficiency as neutral, but Marcuse says it hides a form of domination in how society is organized.
Language narrows into functional, operational terms that close the universe of discourse. Words that point beyond the existing order lose their meaning.
The Great Refusal is a rejection of the system. Marcuse says hope lies with outsiders such as the unemployed, minorities and the marginalized, and he is not optimistic.
Marcuse describes the result as a comfortable, smooth, reasonable, democratic unfreedom, in which domination is accepted because it delivers goods.
The happy consciousness is the belief that the real is rational and the system delivers the goods, which makes people content and dulls their urge to protest.
He criticizes positivism and ordinary language philosophy as one-dimensional philosophy that accepts the given and treats questions about what could be as meaningless.

books.thesis: Reason turned into domination, and mass culture became a factory of conformity.
books.summary:
Horkheimer and Adorno wrote this in exile during the Second World War and ask why the Enlightenment, which set out to free people from fear and myth, ended in a new kind of barbarism. Their question is about reason itself, and why progress in knowledge and technology seemed to bring domination rather than freedom.

They argue that enlightenment turned into mastery of nature and then of people, so that myth is already a kind of enlightenment and enlightenment reverts to myth. They read Odysseus as an early model of the calculating self, and they criticize the culture industry, where film, radio and magazines supply standardized amusement that trains people to conform. The book is written as essays and fragments and avoids system on purpose. Habermas later charged it with a total critique that leaves no exit, and others find the attack on mass culture elitist. It leaves its central question largely open, and readers disagree on whether it offers any way out.
ideas: The central claim is that enlightenment aims to dispel myth but becomes a new myth of domination, as the effort to control nature slides into control of people.
Instrumental reason treats thought as the calculation of means, and the world, including other people, becomes material to be measured and used.
Odysseus bound to the mast and his rowers with wax in their ears show an early form of the self: it survives by self-control and cunning, at the price of renunciation.
The culture industry delivers film, radio and magazines in standardized form. Amusement becomes an extension of work, preparing people for more of the same.
Mass culture offers pseudo-individuality, small variations on a pattern that feel like choice and keep the pattern in place.
They treat antisemitism as a product of mass society, an outlet for frustration and rage at difference, rather than only an inherited prejudice.
Written in fragments, the book offers no clear route of escape, and critics such as Habermas say its critique of reason is too total to allow any.
In an excursus on Sade and Kant, the authors argue that formal reason, cut off from substantive ends, can be put to the service of any purpose, including cruelty.

They distinguish false projection, where the persecutor places inner hostility onto a victim, from reflective thought that returns the world to the self, and treat antisemitism as an example of the first.
The book was written during the Second World War by German Jewish exiles living in California, was first circulated in 1944 as Philosophical Fragments, and was published in 1947.

books.t: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
books.thesis: Social life as theatre, where we perform roles and manage impressions.
books.summary:
Goffman asks how everyday encounters work, using the language of theatre. People present a version of themselves, and others read it and respond. The question is what keeps interaction running smoothly, and how we manage the impressions we give off, whether we mean to or not.

The book draws on observation, including fieldwork in a hotel on a Shetland island, and introduces terms such as front, front stage, backstage, team and the definition of the situation. Goffman argues that interaction depends on shared agreement about what is going on, that slips cause embarrassment, and that audiences often cooperate to save the performer's face. He does not say that everything is fake. By the end he suggests the self is partly an effect of performance and not something hidden behind it. Critics find the picture cynical, and Goffman himself treats the theatre comparison as a scaffold to be dropped once it has done its work.
ideas: Impression management: people shape how they appear to others, using words, clothes, manner and setting, and they also give off impressions they do not intend.
The front is the set of expressive equipment, including setting, appearance and manner, that a person uses to define the situation for the audience.
Front stage is where a performance is given to an audience. Backstage is where performers relax and drop the act, such as a restaurant kitchen out of customers' sight.
Performances are often team efforts, and members cover for one another, share secrets and protect the impression the team is trying to give.
Performers tend to present idealized versions of themselves that fit the values of their society, and they hide behaviour that does not fit.
Audiences help sustain a performance through tact. They ignore slips and play along, because exposing the performer would embarrass everyone.
Goffman ends by suggesting that the self is an effect of a successful performance, not a hidden thing beneath it.
Goffman lists discrepant roles, such as the informer who pretends to be a team member, the shill, the spotter and the go-between, who hold secrets that threaten the team's performance.
Performers can be sincere, believing in their own act, or cynical, using it to manage the audience, and Goffman notes people can move between the two.
His examples draw on fieldwork in a Shetland Isle community, including a hotel, along with writing on service workers and other settings.

books.thesis: How do people manage a "spoiled identity" in the eyes of others?
books.summary:
Goffman looks at people who carry a trait that leads others to disqualify them from full acceptance, producing what he calls a spoiled identity. The book asks how people with visible or hidden marks manage ordinary encounters, and how those without such marks respond.

He draws on memoirs, case histories and published accounts of people with disabilities, disfigurement, mental illness, criminal records and minority status. He separates the discredited, whose difference is visible, from the discreditable, whose difference can be hidden, and he describes covering, passing and the careful control of information. He also writes of the wise, who are sympathetic outsiders, and the own, who share the stigma. His central point is that stigma lives in a relationship of expectations, not in the trait itself, and that everyone can be on either side at some time. The book is short and observational, and it describes more than it prescribes.
ideas: Stigma is a trait that is very discrediting in a particular social setting. Goffman insists that it is a language of relationships rather than of attributes.
He names three kinds of stigma: abominations of the body, blemishes of individual character, and tribal stigma of race, nation or religion.
The discredited person's difference is known or visible. The discreditable person's difference is hidden, so they must decide whether and when to reveal it.
Passing means hiding a stigma to be taken as normal, and covering means playing it down so that it intrudes less in interaction.
Information control is a constant task for the discreditable, who manage who knows what, and weigh the costs of disclosure against concealment.
The wise are people who are not stigmatized but understand the situation and are accepted by those who are. The own are others who share the stigma.
Normal and stigmatized are roles within interactions, not kinds of people, and Goffman notes that everyone has some trait that could be judged this way.
Goffman distinguishes virtual social identity, the character we assume of a person, from actual social identity, the attributes they really have, and stigma opens when the two do not match.
Courtesy stigma is the discredit that spreads to people close to the stigmatized, such as family members, who share some of the difficulty.
Stigma symbols draw attention to a flaw, while disidentifiers, such as a style of dress, are used to suggest a person is something other than what the stigma implies.

books.thesis: Total institutions strip people of their identities and then remake them.
books.summary:
In the mid-1950s Goffman spent about a year at a large public mental hospital in Washington, observing patients as an assistant to the recreation staff. He asks what life inside a total institution does to a person. He defines such a place as a setting where many people, cut off from wider society, live an enclosed and formally administered life.

His examples include prisons, barracks, monasteries and asylums. He describes the mortification of the self at admission, when personal belongings, names and routines are taken away, and the privilege system of small rewards. He also describes the underlife, the secondary adjustments through which inmates keep some selfhood. Goffman argues that much of what looks like symptom is a response to institutional treatment. The book fed into debates about deinstitutionalization. Critics note that it rests on one hospital and one observer, and say it may underrate the reality of illness.
ideas: A total institution is a place of residence and work where many people, cut off from the wider society, lead an enclosed, formally administered round of life. Prisons, barracks and asylums fit.
Mortification of the self happens at admission. Possessions and clothes are taken, the person is given a number, and old roles are stripped away.
A wide gap separates staff and inmates. Each side holds stereotypes of the other, and information and decisions flow one way.
A privilege system of small rewards and punishments, such as access to a ward or a yard, shapes behaviour and makes obedience pay.
Underlife and secondary adjustments are the unofficial ways inmates get around rules and keep a sense of self, such as hidden items and private rituals.
The moral career of the mental patient describes the stages from becoming a patient to life inside, with each stage reshaping how the person sees themselves.
Goffman suggests that a lot of what is read as symptom is shaped by the institution and by the patient's reaction to confinement.
Goffman did the fieldwork for the book over a year in the mid 1950s at St Elizabeths Hospital in Washington, working as an assistant to the athletic director.

He sorts total institutions into five kinds, including those for people thought incapable and harmless, incapable and a threat, dangerous to the community, work based, and retreats such as monasteries.
Inmates adapt in several ways he names, including situational withdrawal, the intransigent line, colonization, conversion, and playing it cool.

books.thesis: Taste in food, art and music marks social class and helps reproduce it.
books.summary:
Bourdieu asks whether taste is a private, natural gift or something tied to social position. Using surveys carried out in France in the 1960s, he maps preferences in music, art, food, clothing, sport and furnishing across occupation and education, and asks what they reveal about class.

He introduces concepts such as cultural capital, habitus and field. His argument is that the upper classes hold an advantage in what counts as legitimate taste, learned early at home and in school and then experienced as natural. He contrasts a working-class taste of necessity, which favours the practical and filling, with a bourgeois taste that values form, restraint and distance from need. Taste therefore classifies the person who displays it, and helps pass advantage across generations. Critics say the data are tied to one country and period and that the theory is too deterministic, and later studies of cultural omnivores complicate the picture. The book is long and dense.
ideas: Taste classifies the classifier. Choices of music, food or decor mark where a person stands and reveal social position to others who read the signs.
Habitus is the set of durable dispositions people absorb from family and class, which guide perception and choice without conscious thought.
Cultural capital is knowledge, ease and credentials in legitimate culture. Families pass it on, and schools tend to reward it as if it were natural talent.
Social space has two main axes, the amount of economic capital and cultural capital a person has, and the balance between them shapes lifestyle.
The taste of necessity favours the practical and filling. The taste of luxury favours form over function, because those freed from need can put style first.
Bourdieu argues that Kant's pure aesthetic, a disinterested contemplation of art, is itself a product of privilege and distance from necessity.
Critics note that the data come from France in the 1960s and that later work on cultural omnivores finds people of high status enjoying a wider mix.
Bourdieu says taste is first of all distaste, the disgust provoked by other people's tastes, so that class boundaries are drawn partly by what each group rejects.
The petite bourgeoisie shows cultural goodwill, a striving and anxious effort to acquire legitimate culture, while the dominant class displays ease, as if its taste came naturally.
Symbolic violence is the way dominated groups accept the legitimacy of the dominant taste and judge themselves by it, so inequality works through misrecognition rather than open force.

books.t: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
books.thesis: Religious anxiety over salvation helped build the modern compulsion to work.
books.summary:
Weber asks why modern capitalism, with its discipline, its devotion to steady work and its habit of earning money as an end in itself, first took hold in parts of northern Europe with a strong Protestant presence. Greed and trade existed everywhere. What seemed unusual to him was the sense of duty attached to earning.

His argument is that Calvinist ideas, especially predestination, produced anxiety about whether one was saved. Success in a worldly calling became a sign of grace, and an ascetic ethic of hard work and restrained spending led to saving and reinvestment. With time, he says, religion faded and left an economic order that people must serve, the iron cage. Weber presents religion as one factor in a larger picture and does not claim to replace economic explanations with spiritual ones. Historians have disputed his evidence and the link between Protestantism and capitalist growth, and the debate has not settled.
ideas: The spirit of capitalism treats earning more as a duty and a goal in itself. Weber uses Benjamin Franklin's maxims on thrift and industry as an example.
The idea of a calling comes from Luther's view that worldly work is a task assigned by God, giving ordinary labour moral weight.
Calvinist predestination held that God had already decided who is saved. Believers could not know their fate, and that produced intense anxiety.
Worldly asceticism combined hard, methodical work with restrained spending, so that profit was reinvested and not enjoyed, and Weber saw this as a driver of capitalism.
Weber also looks at Pietism, Methodism and the Baptist sects, arguing that several Protestant movements shared an ascetic outlook in daily life.
The iron cage describes a rationalized economic order that outlives the religious motives that built it, so people keep working because the system requires it.
Weber insists that he is not replacing a materialist account with a spiritual one. Historians continue to dispute the evidence and the strength of the link.
Weber stresses the disenchantment of the world, in which Protestantism stripped away magic and sacraments as means of salvation and left the believer to prove himself through conduct.

He describes traditionalism, with the example of workers who earned less when piece rates went up because they only wanted to earn what they were used to, as what the capitalist spirit had to overcome.
Weber ends with the remark that the modern order produces specialists without spirit and sensualists without heart, a warning about where rationalization leads.

books.thesis: Suicide rates follow social bonds. Too little integration or too little regulation kills.
books.summary:
Durkheim asks whether suicide, which seems the most private of acts, has social causes. He compares rates across countries, religions, marital statuses and periods, and finds that they are stable within a society and vary in regular ways. The question is what social facts could explain such patterns.

He proposes four types: egoistic suicide, from too little integration into groups, altruistic suicide, from too much, anomic suicide, from too little regulation of desires, and fatalistic suicide, from oppressive regulation, which he treats briefly. He finds higher rates among Protestants than Catholics, and relates anomic suicide to sudden economic change. The book also served to establish sociology as a discipline with its own subject matter. Critics point to unreliable official statistics, the risk of reading individual causes from group data, and his treatment of religion. Even so, it remains a founding work, and the link between social bonds and wellbeing still shapes research.
ideas: Suicide rates are steady within a society and differ between groups, which Durkheim takes as a sign of social forces that psychology alone cannot explain.
Egoistic suicide comes from weak integration. People without strong ties to family, religion or community lack something to anchor them.
Altruistic suicide comes from excessive integration, where individuals are so bound to a group that they give up their lives for it, as in some military settings.
Anomic suicide arises when the regulation of desires breaks down. Durkheim links it to sudden economic booms and crashes that unsettle people's expectations.
Fatalistic suicide, which Durkheim treats only in a footnote, comes from excessive regulation, as with people whose future is blocked and whose lives are tightly controlled.
Protestants showed higher suicide rates than Catholics in the data Durkheim used, and he attributed this to Protestantism's weaker communal integration.
Critics note that official statistics were unreliable and that group-level patterns do not prove individual causes, though the book established sociological method.

Durkheim treats suicide as a social fact, something to be explained by other social facts, and he rules out individual explanations such as mental illness, race, climate and imitation as accounting for the rates.
He finds that marriage and family life protect against suicide, and that married men and parents have lower rates, while divorce is linked with higher rates, especially among men.
Rates of suicide fall during wars and national crises, which Durkheim explains by the way shared events strengthen social integration.

books.thesis: Even among the comfortable, social rank predicts health and lifespan.
books.summary:
Marmot, an epidemiologist, asks why people lower down the social ladder get sicker and die sooner, even in wealthy countries with health care and stable jobs. His starting point is the Whitehall studies of British civil servants, which found that death rates rose steadily as one moved down the grades of employment.

The pattern is a gradient, not a divide between poor and prosperous: each step down is associated with worse health. Marmot argues that standard risk factors such as smoking and diet explain only part of it. A key idea is control. Low autonomy at work and in life, and limited social participation, seem to matter and probably act through chronic stress. He then argues for policy that reduces inequality and invests in early childhood and working conditions. Critics raise questions about the direction of causation and about confounding, and the translation into policy is debated. The book remains a major argument that health is a social matter.
ideas: In the Whitehall studies, civil servants in lower employment grades had higher mortality than those in higher grades, though all had steady jobs and access to health care.
The pattern is a gradient. Health worsens at each step down the ladder, even among people who are far from poverty, so it is not only about material deprivation.
Smoking, blood pressure, diet and other standard risk factors explain only part of the gradient, which pushed Marmot to look at social and psychological causes.
Low control at work, meaning high demands with little say, was linked to higher risk of heart disease in the Whitehall research.
Marmot stresses autonomy and social participation, having a say in one's life and being involved with others, as central to health.
Early childhood matters. Conditions in the first years of life shape health and opportunities later on, and Marmot says early investment matters.
He argues that reducing inequality is a health policy, while critics ask how far the findings show cause and how well they translate into policy.
Marmot considers whether illness lowers status instead of the other way round and argues that the evidence points mainly to social position affecting health.
He proposes chronic stress as a pathway, with stress hormones and effects on the heart and immune system linking a low sense of control to disease.
Marmot discusses the sharp rise in mortality among men in Russia and Eastern Europe in the 1990s as an example of how social upheaval and loss of control can affect health.

books.thesis: Human life is organized around games of status, and we rarely admit we're playing.
books.summary:
Storr argues that human life is organized around games of status, in families, workplaces, online communities and ideologies, and that we rarely admit we are playing. The book asks why status matters so much to us and how the drive to gain it shapes our sense of who we are, what we believe and how we judge others.

He separates dominance games, won by force or fear, virtue games, won by showing moral worth, and success games, won by skill and achievement. He draws on psychology, evolutionary thinking and studies of cults, extremists and social media. He suggests we each tell ourselves a story in which we are the hero, and that the beliefs of a group often work as badges of belonging as much as claims about the world. Playing is unavoidable. His advice is to notice which game you are in and to prefer ones that are good for others too. Critics say that explaining so much through status risks being unfalsifiable.
ideas: Status is a basic human need. We are sensitive to how others rank us, and loss of standing hurts, which is why people go to great lengths to avoid it.
Storr names three kinds of game: dominance games won by force or intimidation, virtue games won by displaying moral worth, and success games won by skill and achievement.
Each game has its own rules, players and prizes, and people move between them without noticing. Knowing which game is on explains behaviour that otherwise looks irrational.
The brain is a storyteller that edits our life into a narrative with ourselves as hero, which helps us hold a stable self and defend our status.
Group beliefs often work as badges of belonging, so that holding the right view signals loyalty and earns standing, a pattern he sees in cults and in political movements.
Social media turns status into a visible scoreboard of likes and followers, which intensifies the games and rewards displays of virtue and outrage.
Storr advises noticing which game you are playing and choosing games that benefit others as well, since opting out entirely is not possible.
Storr separates status from wealth. It is the respect and influence that others grant, and it is felt as a matter of how one is seen, which is why the loss of it can hurt more than the loss of money.
In virtue games, rank is lifted by condemning those who break the group's moral code, so public displays of outrage and shaming bring rewards.
He argues that the hunger for status is an old social adaptation shared with other primates, and that it shapes both our worst behaviour and many of our most admired achievements.

books.thesis: Why does worry about our standing hurt so much, and how do philosophy and art respond?
books.summary:
de Botton asks why worry about our standing hurts so much, even when we are comfortable. He defines status anxiety as the fear that we are failing to meet society's ideals of success and that we may be stripped of dignity and respect. The book asks where it comes from and what philosophy and art can offer in response.

The first part looks at causes, including lovelessness, the demand for esteem, rising expectations, snobbery and the idea that success is earned by merit. The second part looks at remedies, drawn from philosophy, art, politics, Christianity and bohemia. Throughout he writes as an essayist, with humour and examples from painters and philosophers. He does not promise a cure. The response is closer to consolation, offering ways of seeing that loosen the grip of other people's opinions. Critics say the remedies are gentle and personal and say little about structural inequality.
ideas: Status anxiety is the fear that we are failing to meet society's ideals of success and may lose the respect of others, and it persists even in comfortable lives.
Lovelessness: de Botton argues that we seek status partly to win the attention and affection that we feel we lack, because respect brings a kind of love.
Envy is strongest toward people near us. We compare ourselves with those we see as similar, so a neighbour's success stings more than a king's.
Meritocracy sharpens the pain. If rank is believed to reflect worth, low position feels like a verdict on the person and not a stroke of bad luck.
Philosophy offers a remedy by questioning whose opinions deserve our concern. Socrates and the Stoics suggest we should weigh the judgment of others against truth.
Art can widen our sense of what is worthy, and tragedy and realist painting treat ordinary or suffering people with dignity.
Bohemia rejects the dominant measures of success and builds alternative communities with their own values, a remedy that comes with its own risks.
Snobbery, in de Botton's account, is the habit of judging a person's worth by their rank or occupation, and it makes people feel their value depends on a job title.
Expectation raises anxiety in modern societies. As people are told they are equal and can rise, they set their hopes higher and feel greater disappointment when they do not.
De Botton also discusses Christianity as a remedy, since it taught the vanity of worldly rank and the humility of every person before God.

books.thesis: You gain power through empathy and lose it when power erodes it.
books.summary:
Keltner asks how people gain power and why they lose it. His answer, drawn from his research and others' on groups, is that power usually comes from enhancing the lives of others, through empathy, generosity and cooperation. Once people hold power, those same qualities tend to fade, and people with power become impulsive, self-focused and less able to read others.

He argues that the Machiavellian picture of power as force and manipulation does not match how influence works in ordinary groups. Power is a relationship, granted by others, and it can be kept by continuing to serve them. The abuse of power is often a result of the experience of power itself, which lowers empathy. The book draws on studies of teasing, touch, laughter and status in groups. It ends with practices such as gratitude and generosity. Some social priming studies in the wider field have struggled to replicate, so some experimental claims deserve care.
ideas: Power is the capacity to make a difference in other people's lives, and Keltner stresses that it can be gained and kept through giving as well as force.
In many groups, those who rise are the ones who show enthusiasm, kindness and attention to others, not the most dominant or aggressive.
The power paradox is that the qualities that win power, such as empathy and generosity, tend to decline once a person holds it.
People with power tend to become more impulsive and self-focused, and less accurate at reading other people's emotions or taking their perspective.
Keltner draws on studies of playful teasing, laughter and touch to show how small gestures build trust, and how people with power sometimes lose these habits.
The Machiavellian view that power comes from force and manipulation is, in Keltner's account, a poor fit for everyday influence, which depends on the consent of others.
He suggests that practising gratitude, generosity and humility helps hold onto empathy, though some priming studies behind similar claims have been hard to replicate.

In the cookie experiment, three students worked together with one assigned to lead, and the leaders were more likely to take the extra cookie and eat messily, a small sign of how power loosens manners.
Keltner points to primate research suggesting that high rank often depends on building coalitions, sharing and making peace, not on bullying alone.
He argues that the effects of power on behaviour are strongest when people feel unchecked, and that accountability and reminders of one's own vulnerability help keep empathy alive.

books.thesis: Many people think their own jobs are pointless, and that belief does real harm.
books.summary:
Graeber began with a short essay in 2013 and received a flood of letters from people saying their own jobs were pointless. The book asks why, in a society that praises work, so many workers feel their jobs accomplish nothing, and why such jobs persist. He defines a bullshit job as paid work so pointless that even the person doing it cannot justify it.

He gathers testimonies and sorts them into five types: flunkies, goons, duct tapers, box tickers and taskmasters. He argues that the damage is real, since people feel ashamed, depressed or cut off from any sense of making a difference. He explains the persistence of these jobs through managerial hierarchy and politics instead of market efficiency, and through a moral belief that paid work is a virtue. Graeber floats universal basic income as a way out. Critics note that the argument leans on self-reports and that a worker's sense of pointlessness is subjective, and some economists dispute the scale he proposes.
ideas: A bullshit job, in Graeber's definition, is paid work so pointless that even the worker feels they must pretend it has a purpose.
He sorts these jobs into five types: flunkies who make others look important, goons, duct tapers who patch problems, box tickers and taskmasters.
The idea started with a 2013 essay in an online magazine, which drew so many replies from people describing their own pointless work that Graeber expanded it into a book.
The harm is psychological. People paid to do nothing useful often feel ashamed, depressed or trapped, and Graeber calls this a kind of spiritual violence.
Bullshit jobs are often well paid, while much essential work, such as care and teaching, is low paid, and Graeber sees an inverse link between social value and pay.
Graeber explains such jobs by managerial feudalism, in which firms hire retainers to display rank, and he doubts that market efficiency can account for them.
A moral belief that paid work makes people good sustains these jobs, and Graeber proposes universal basic income as one way to loosen that belief.
Graeber starts from Keynes's prediction that technology would let people work fifteen hours a week by the end of the twentieth century, and asks why it did not happen.
He separates bullshit jobs from shit jobs. The latter are useful but poorly paid and often degrading, while bullshit jobs are pointless but may be comfortable.
A YouGov poll he cites found that about 37 percent of British workers thought their job made no meaningful contribution to the world.

books.thesis: Debt is older than money, and it has always been moral as well as economic.
books.summary:
Graeber challenges the textbook story in which barter came first, then money, and only later credit. He says anthropologists have not found societies that ran on barter, and that credit and debt came before coins. The book asks what debt is, and how an economic relation became a moral idea.

He surveys five thousand years, from Mesopotamia through the Axial Age, medieval religion and the modern empires, tracing alternating eras of credit money and metal coin. He proposes three moral foundations of social life, everyday communism, exchange and hierarchy, and argues that debt turns human relationships into impersonal exchange. The idea that debts must always be paid, he says, is moral and often tied to violence. Historians and economists dispute many of his claims, and some chapters are speculative. The book's lasting provocation is the suggestion that the moral language of debt hides its political uses, a point that readers continue to argue over.
ideas: The myth of barter: economics textbooks say money grew out of barter, but Graeber argues that anthropology finds no society that ran mainly on direct swaps.
Debt is older than coin. Temples in ancient Mesopotamia ran credit accounts that were kept on tablets long before coined money appeared.
Graeber describes three moral principles of social life: everyday communism, exchange and hierarchy, and says each shapes how people understand obligation.
The idea that you must always pay your debts is a moral claim that has often been used to justify violence and servitude.
Rulers in the ancient Near East periodically cancelled debts, jubilees that kept indebtedness from tearing societies apart.
Coinage spread alongside armies and slavery, and Graeber ties precious metal to the paying of soldiers and the trade in captives.
Debt can slide into servitude when people pledge themselves or family members against a loan, and Graeber argues the pattern recurs across history.
Graeber describes human economies, as found among groups such as the Tiv, where money is used to create and rearrange relations between people, such as marriages, and not to buy and sell goods.
He proposes that history alternates between ages of virtual credit money and ages of bullion, with coin and metal dominating in periods of war and plunder.
He relates the Axial Age, roughly 800 BCE to 600 CE, to coinage, war and the rise of the major world religions, and he calls debt a promise corrupted by math and violence.

books.thesis: Early humans experimented with many social forms, and inequality wasn't inevitable.
books.summary:
Graeber and Wengrow challenge the standard story in which humans moved from small egalitarian bands to farming, cities and states, with inequality as the price of progress. They ask how we came to accept that story, and why we assume that large societies must have rulers and hierarchy.

They draw on archaeology and anthropology to argue that early societies experimented with many forms of life. Some groups changed their political arrangements with the seasons, some built large settlements without evident kings, and farming spread slowly and unevenly. They also argue that Indigenous critiques of European society influenced Enlightenment thought. They propose that people have lost three basic freedoms, to move away, to disobey and to reshape social relations. Specialists dispute parts of the evidence, and critics say the authors choose examples that suit them. The book is best read as a challenge to a settled story and not as a final account, and the debate over its claims is lively.
ideas: The standard story of human history, with Rousseau's lost innocence and Hobbes's brutal origins, presents a one-way ladder, and the authors argue the evidence does not fit it.
Some societies changed their social structure by season. Groups such as certain Indigenous peoples shifted between looser and more hierarchical arrangements through the year.
Large early settlements, such as sites in Ukraine and the city of Teotihuacan, show no clear signs of kings, which the authors use to question the link between scale and hierarchy.
Farming did not arrive as a single revolution. It spread slowly and unevenly, and some groups tried it, left it, or mixed it with other ways of living.
The authors argue that Indigenous thinkers such as Kandiaronk criticised European society, and that these critiques helped shape Enlightenment ideas about freedom and equality.
They propose three basic freedoms that societies have allowed or taken away: to move away, to disobey orders, and to reshape social relations.
Specialists dispute parts of the evidence and the authors' selection of cases, so the book is better read as a provocation than as a settled account.

Schismogenesis is the process by which neighbouring societies define themselves in opposition to each other, and the authors use it to explain why groups might deliberately choose different ways of life.
The authors name three sources of domination, control of violence, control of information and personal charisma, and argue that societies can have one without the others.
They describe early cities such as those in Mesopotamia and the Mesoamerican polity of Tlaxcala as governed by councils or assemblies, which they use to challenge the idea that cities require rulers.

books.thesis: Humans conquered the world by cooperating around shared fictions.
books.summary:
Sapiens tells the story of our species from the cognitive revolution tens of thousands of years ago to the present day. Harari asks why one ape among several human species ended up running the planet. His answer begins with something odd about us. We can believe in things nobody has ever touched, such as nations, gods, corporations and money, and enough people believing the same story lets strangers work together at huge scale.

The argument moves through three revolutions, the cognitive, the agricultural and the scientific, with empire and money tying them together. Harari keeps asking whether each step made individuals happier, and he often suggests it did not, describing farming as a trap. The final chapters turn to biotechnology and the chance that sapiens will redesign itself. Specialists dispute some of his claims, and critics say the sweep forces simplification. The book leaves open what we should want to become, now that we can choose.
ideas: Harari proposes that flexible language let sapiens gossip about each other and also describe things that do not exist, which made cooperation in large groups possible.
Gods, nations, corporations and money exist because enough people believe in them. Harari calls these shared fictions, and they allow millions of strangers to act together.
He calls the agricultural revolution history's biggest fraud. Wheat tamed people as much as the reverse, and most farmers worked harder and ate worse than foragers.
Hierarchies such as caste and race are presented as natural. Harari argues they are imagined orders, kept going by shared belief, habit and force.
Money is described as the most universal system of mutual trust, letting people who share no gods or customs still trade with each other.
The scientific revolution starts with admitting ignorance. Harari ties it closely to European empires and capital, which paid for exploration and research.
Harari questions whether history made people happier, noting that material gains do not clearly bring contentment, and ends on bioengineering that might replace sapiens itself.

The Cognitive Revolution, around 70,000 years ago, is when Harari says sapiens began to use language in new ways, and he links their spread to the extinction of large animals in Australia and the Americas.
The luxury trap is his term for how comforts, such as the ones farming brought, become necessities that people then work harder to keep.
Harari names money, empires and universal religions as the three great unifiers that brought the world's peoples into larger shared systems.

books.thesis: What happens to humanism when algorithms know us better than we know ourselves?
books.summary:
Homo Deus begins from a claim that famine, plague and war, once treated as fate, have mostly become problems of management. Harari asks what humanity will want next. His guess is immortality, lasting happiness and upgraded abilities, which amounts to a bid for godlike powers. The deeper question is about authority. Modern humanism trusts human feelings as the final guide, and the book asks what happens to that trust once algorithms can read us better than we read ourselves.

Harari argues by sketching scenarios and says he offers possibilities, not prophecies. He draws on biology and neuroscience to doubt that free will works the way liberal thought assumes. He describes an emerging faith in data flow, which he calls Dataism, and worries about people who lose economic value to machines. The book does not tell us what to do. It ends on questions about whether intelligence can separate from consciousness, and what we would still value if it did.
ideas: Harari says famine, plague and war have become problems of management rather than fate, so the human agenda shifts toward immortality, happiness and enhanced abilities.
Humanism replaced God as the source of authority. The voter, customer and viewer are supposed to know best, and personal feeling becomes the final guide.
He argues the liberal idea of free will does not survive biology and neuroscience, which describe us as complex biochemical algorithms rather than free agents.
Drawing on research like Kahneman's, Harari separates the experiencing self from the narrating self, and notes that the storyteller often makes our decisions.
Dataism is his name for an emerging creed that treats the universe as data flows and judges anything by its contribution to processing information.
Advances in artificial intelligence could create a useless class of people who lack economic or military value, a prospect Harari treats as a political danger.
If algorithms come to know us better than we know ourselves, we may hand over choices about careers, partners and votes. Harari frames this as a scenario, not a forecast.
Harari describes three forms of humanism, liberal, socialist and evolutionary, which differ on whether the individual, the collective or the species is the source of meaning.
He calls the modern bargain a covenant in which humans give up meaning in exchange for power, trusting science and growth to make up for the loss of a cosmic plan.
He devotes space to the industrial treatment of animals, using it as a warning of how a more capable intelligence might treat humans who lose their economic value.

books.thesis: In a crowd, individuals lose responsibility and become suggestible. Influential, and dated.
books.summary:
The Crowd was published in 1895 and tries to explain what happens to people when they gather in large numbers. Le Bon watched strikes, revolutions and mass politics in France and asked why ordinary individuals act so differently together than alone. His answer is that a crowd forms a kind of collective mind. Inside it, people lose a sense of personal responsibility and become suggestible, emotional and quick to follow.

Le Bon argues through assertion and examples more than evidence. He describes anonymity, contagion and suggestion as the mechanisms, and says crowds think in images and respond to leaders who repeat bold claims with confidence. He saw his own era as the age of crowds and feared for the future of civilization. The book was widely read and influenced later writers on propaganda and mass psychology. Critics say it is dated, snobbish about the lower classes and short on proof, and later research has found crowds far more varied than he allowed.
ideas: Le Bon claims a crowd forms a collective mind, so people together think and feel differently from how any one of them would alone.
Numbers and anonymity give the individual a feeling of invincible power, and the restraint that comes from being identifiable and accountable drops away.
Feelings and acts spread through a crowd by contagion, to the point where a person will give up personal interest for the collective one.
He compares the crowd member to a hypnotised subject, who acts on impulse and suggestion while the conscious personality fades.
Crowds, he says, think in images rather than arguments. Vivid, exaggerated and simple statements move them far better than reasoning does.
Leaders sway crowds through affirmation, repetition and contagion, helped by what Le Bon calls prestige, a kind of authority that is felt and rarely examined.
Le Bon saw his age as the era of crowds and feared for civilization. Critics call this alarmist and class-biased, and note that later studies found crowds less uniform.
Le Bon sorts crowds into heterogeneous kinds, such as street crowds and juries, and homogeneous kinds, such as sects, castes and classes, and describes the sorts of leaders and moods that suit each.
He says crowds hold convictions in an absolute and religious way, so they are intolerant, authoritarian and impatient of doubt.
The book influenced later thinkers, and Freud engaged with it in Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego, while Le Bon's ideas on race are now widely rejected.

books.thesis: Mass movements attract people who are fleeing a spoiled self.
books.summary:
Eric Hoffer was a self-taught longshoreman, and The True Believer is his attempt to explain what draws people into mass movements. He asks why such different causes, religious, nationalist or revolutionary, seem to gather the same sort of follower. His answer is that movements attract people who are frustrated with their own lives and want to escape a self they find spoiled or unbearable.

Hoffer argues in short, aphoristic chapters and relies on observation and history, not on formal study. He says joiners trade individual identity for the group, find pride in a holy cause, and are held together by hatred of a common enemy. Doctrine matters less than the intensity of faith, so a fanatic can move from one movement to its opposite. He also sketches how movements pass from thinkers to fanatics to administrators. Critics say he generalizes too boldly, and some of his claims rest on thin evidence. Many readers still find the portrait of the fanatic hard to forget.
ideas: Hoffer holds that mass movements draw the frustrated, people whose lives feel spoiled and who want to be rid of a self they cannot bear.
Movements with opposite creeds attract similar temperaments, which explains why a convert can switch from one fanatical cause to another with little change in manner.
Self-renunciation is the main offer. Joiners give up individual identity for the group and gain pride and purpose they could not find through their own efforts.
Hatred acts as glue. Hoffer says movements can do without a god but not without a devil, and a common enemy keeps followers united.
Doctrine works best when it cannot be tested. Hoffer says faith needs to be shielded from facts, so obscure and unprovable teaching serves a movement well.
He describes a sequence in which men of words prepare the ground, fanatics carry the movement forward, and practical administrators eventually take over and consolidate it.
Movements keep followers busy with marches, causes and campaigns. Hoffer suggests action holds a movement together, while critics say his sweeping claims outrun his evidence.
Hoffer was a self-taught San Francisco longshoreman, and he wrote the book from observation and reading rather than from an academic post.

He lists the kinds of people prone to join movements, including the poor, misfits, the bored, the ambitious, minorities and sinners, and says what they share is a sense of frustration with themselves.
Hoffer names several unifying agents of movements, including hatred, imitation, persuasion, coercion, leadership and action, and says that the strongest movements use many of them together.

books.thesis: Civic and social bonds in America have frayed, and it has had real costs.
books.summary:
Bowling Alone starts with a small observation. More Americans bowl than before, but fewer bowl in leagues. Putnam uses this to ask whether Americans have been drifting away from the clubs, congregations, unions and neighbourhood ties that once held communities together. He gathers survey data across decades and finds a decline in many forms of civic and social participation from the 1960s onward.

Putnam builds his case around social capital, the networks and norms of trust that help people cooperate. He weighs possible causes, giving a large share to generational change and television, with time pressure and suburban sprawl as further factors. He then argues the decline has costs for schools, safety, health and the working of democracy. The book ends with a call for renewal, drawing on an earlier period of American civic invention. Critics ask whether he undercounts new kinds of association, including online ones, and how firmly the costs can be tied to the decline.
ideas: Social capital is the book's central term. It means the networks and norms of trust that make groups work and let people cooperate for shared goals.
The title image is the rise of solo bowling alongside the fall of league bowling, which Putnam uses as a small symbol of fading group life.
Putnam documents declines over late decades in membership of civic groups, PTAs, unions and congregations, and in informal habits such as hosting dinners or visiting friends.
He separates bonding social capital, within similar groups, from bridging social capital, across differences, and says healthy communities need both.
He weighs several causes, giving much of the weight to generational replacement and television, and smaller shares to busy schedules, commuting and suburban sprawl.
Putnam links higher social capital to better schools, safer neighbourhoods, better health and more responsive government, though critics say causation is hard to show.
The closing chapters call for civic renewal and look to the early twentieth century as a precedent. Critics ask whether the internet changes the picture.

Putnam names a long civic generation, born roughly between 1910 and 1940, as unusually active in community life, and says its gradual replacement by less engaged cohorts is a main cause of the decline.
His earlier study of Italian regions, Making Democracy Work, found that regions with stronger civic traditions had better governments and economies, and this shaped the book's argument.
He distinguishes generalized reciprocity, helping now without expecting an immediate return because you trust that others will help you in time, as the core of a trusting community.

books.thesis: Life has become a spectacle, with social relations mediated by images.
books.summary:
The Society of the Spectacle is a short book of 221 numbered theses written by Guy Debord, a leader of the Situationist movement. He asks what happens to social life when images and commodities stand between people. The spectacle, in his usage, is more than television or advertising. It names a social relation among people that is mediated by images, in which living is replaced by watching.

Debord writes in dense aphorisms, borrowing from Hegel and Marx and extending Marx's idea of commodity fetishism to the whole of modern life. He argues that consumers become passive spectators who are separated from each other even as they seem to be united by the same images. The book offers no program in the usual sense. It points toward Situationist tactics such as turning existing images against themselves. Readers disagree on whether it is a precise theory or a mood, and its density is part of the reputation.
ideas: Debord says the spectacle is not a pile of images. It is a social relation between people, mediated by images.
What was once directly lived has turned into representation. Life gives way to watching, and watching comes to stand in for acting.
He extends Marx's commodity fetishism, arguing that the commodity has taken over social life so fully that people mainly contemplate it.
The spectacle separates people while appearing to unite them. The more we contemplate the images offered to us, the less we live our own lives.
The spectacle speaks in a one-way monologue. What appears is declared good, and the only demanded response is passive acceptance.
Debord describes the time of consumer society as a repeating, pseudo-cyclical time of work, weekends and holidays, which hides the sense of history.
The Situationists proposed detournement, which means taking existing images and texts and turning them against their original message. The book itself reuses lines from earlier writers.
The book is made up of 221 numbered theses in nine chapters, written in aphorisms in the style of Hegel and Marx, and it does not argue in a step by step way.
Debord separates the concentrated spectacle, found under totalitarian regimes with a single leader, from the diffuse spectacle of abundant commodities in Western societies.
In his chapter on the proletariat, he favours workers' councils as an alternative, in which people control their own conditions of life instead of watching them.

books.thesis: Signs no longer point to reality. They replace it.
books.summary:
Simulacra and Simulation is a set of essays in which Baudrillard argues that signs and images no longer point to reality, they replace it. He asks what remains of the real when copies multiply and models come first. His claim is that modern life is increasingly lived in the hyperreal, a space made of representations with no original behind them.

Baudrillard works by provocation and example more than by sustained proof. He lays out stages in the life of an image, from reflecting reality to masking its absence to bearing no relation to it at all. He uses Disneyland, Watergate and Borges's fable of the map to illustrate. The tone is gnomic, and the book is often quoted for its title idea and rarely read through. Critics say it offers a mood more than an argument and gives readers little way to test its claims. Supporters say it names a real feature of media saturated life.
ideas: Baudrillard sketches four phases of the image. It first reflects reality, then distorts it, then hides that reality is absent, and finally becomes a pure simulacrum.
He retells the fable of the map that covers the territory, then says today the map comes first and models generate the real.
The hyperreal is his term for copies without originals. Such things can seem more real than reality because they are cleaner and more coherent.
Disneyland, he says, is presented as imaginary so that the rest of America can look real, when in fact it is just as simulated.
He reads Watergate as a scandal whose exposure helped persuade people that moral order otherwise exists, hiding the fact that political life is already staged.
Simulating differs from pretending. Someone who feigns an illness can be found out, but one who produces its symptoms blurs the line between real and false.
Critics say the book is more provocation than argument and hard to test. Admirers say it names a genuine feature of media saturated life.
Baudrillard discusses the Tasaday, a group said to have been found untouched in the Philippines, as an example of how anthropology needs a preserved primitive to prove its own reality.
He reads the American television series about the Loud family as a case where real life and its televised version merge, and the family becomes a model of itself.
The Beaubourg effect, named for the Pompidou Centre in Paris, is his image for an institution of culture that absorbs and neutralizes the masses it claims to serve.

books.thesis: Nobody else disciplines us anymore. We exploit ourselves and call it freedom.
books.summary:
The Burnout Society is a short essay by Byung-Chul Han about the sickness of an age that no longer needs to be told what to do. He asks why depression, attention disorders and burnout have become typical complaints, in place of the infections and repression of earlier eras. His answer is that we have moved from a society of commands and prohibitions to a society of achievement, where the slogan is that we can do anything.

Han argues that in such a world the person becomes both exploiter and exploited. There is no master to blame, so failure turns inward as exhaustion and self reproach. He sets this against an older order described by Foucault and uses ideas from Heidegger, Benjamin and others. He proposes that deep boredom and contemplation have been lost to constant stimulation and multitasking, and that some kinds of tiredness might be worth recovering. The essay is compressed and assertive rather than empirical, and some readers find it persuasive and others find it too sweeping.
ideas: Han says the twentieth century disciplinary society of prohibitions and commands has been replaced by an achievement society driven by the belief that we can do anything.
The achievement subject is both exploiter and exploited. With no outside master to resist, failure is felt as personal fault, and exhaustion follows.
He argues the typical illnesses of our time are neural, such as depression, attention deficit and burnout, rather than infections, and he calls the cause a violence of positivity.
Too much openness to stimuli, options and information leaves little to push back against. Han says the immune model of defence against an outside enemy no longer fits.
Multitasking is described as a regression toward the divided attention of an animal watching for threats, while deep attention is a cultural achievement we are losing.
Han defends deep boredom and idleness as conditions for contemplation and creativity, and says a culture that never pauses loses the ability to see.
He contrasts an isolating, exhausting tiredness with a shared, inspiring one, an idea he borrows from Peter Handke. Whether this is a real remedy is left open.
Han draws on Alain Ehrenberg's idea of the weariness of the self, and links depression to a self that must keep producing and optimizing itself without end.
He engages Arendt's contrast between the vita activa and the vita contemplativa and argues that modern life has made activity absolute, losing the contemplative side.
Han says the disappearance of otherness, the negativity of what is foreign and resists us, leaves a society of sameness, where more of the same is the only thing that can happen.

books.thesis: Societies keep mimetic violence in check by uniting against a scapegoat.
books.summary:
Violence and the Sacred asks why religion everywhere seems tied to sacrifice and ritual killing. Girard starts from an observation about human desire. We learn what to want by copying others, so rivals end up wanting the same things and becoming alike. He asks how communities survive when that copying produces escalating conflict and endless vengeance.

His proposal is that societies resolve such crises by turning against a single victim. The group's tension is discharged on this scapegoat, and peace returns. The victim is then honoured as sacred, since the killing seemed to save everyone. Ritual sacrifice repeats the event in controlled form, and myths hide the original violence. Girard reads Greek tragedy, myth and anthropology to support this. Many anthropologists reject his evidence, and critics say the theory explains everything and so cannot be checked. Others find it unusually good at describing how groups pick targets.
ideas: Girard says we want what others want. Imitation, more than the worth of an object, drives desire, and it pushes people into rivalry.
As rivals copy each other they become doubles, and differences between them blur. Girard says this sameness escalates conflict instead of calming it.
Violence is contagious and vengeance has no natural stopping point, so left alone it can destroy a community in a spiral of retaliation.
The scapegoat mechanism has a group turn unanimously on one victim. Tension drains away, and the victim is blamed first and then treated as sacred.
Ritual sacrifice repeats the founding act in controlled form, using a surrogate victim who cannot be avenged, so that violence is spent and order renewed.
The sacred, Girard says, is violence in disguise. The gods who terrify also protect, because the same mechanism produces both the threat and the peace.
Judicial systems replace sacrifice by giving vengeance to an institution. Girard's readings of tragedy and myth are contested, and critics call the theory hard to falsify.
Girard reads Oedipus the King as a story of a plague and a crisis in which differences collapse, and Oedipus is cast out as the community's scapegoat.
The sacrificial crisis is his term for the breakdown of ritual order, when differences are lost and sacrifice no longer works to contain violence.
Girard faults Freud's Totem and Taboo and the Oedipus complex, and the structuralism of Levi-Strauss, for missing the role of violence and mimetic rivalry.

books.thesis: How persecution texts hide their victims' innocence.
books.summary:
The Scapegoat follows Girard's earlier work by looking closely at texts written by persecutors. He asks how such accounts of crimes, plagues and monstrous outsiders can be read so that the victim's innocence shows through. The book starts from a medieval account of the Black Death in which Jews were blamed, and treats it as a model case of a story told by the crowd.

Girard argues that persecution texts share recurring features, and that the persecutors usually believe what they write. He contrasts myths, which tell the story from the crowd's side, with the Gospels, which tell it from the victim's side and so expose the mechanism. He claims this exposure weakens the scapegoat effect in modern societies. That Christian reading is the most contested part of the book. Many scholars doubt that the Gospels are unique in this way, and critics say he flattens differences between texts. Even so, his method of reading accusations with suspicion has been widely borrowed.
ideas: Girard reads a medieval account of the Black Death in which Jews are blamed, to show how a persecutor's text can hide the innocence of its victims.
He lists four recurring features of persecution stories: a social crisis, accusations of crimes that dissolve distinctions, signs that mark the victim, and collective violence.
Persecutors usually sincerely believe the victim is guilty. Girard treats that conviction as part of the mechanism and not a lie told afterward.
Myths, in his reading, tell the story from the crowd's side and keep the victim guilty, while the Gospels tell it from the victim's side and reveal innocence.
He reads the account of Peter's denial in the Passion story as an example of how the pull of a crowd can make a person join in against a victim.
Girard holds that once victims' innocence is widely recognised, scapegoating works less well, which he thinks leaves modern societies with fewer ways to contain violence.
His claim that the Gospels are unique in siding with victims is contested, and critics note that other traditions also show sympathy for the persecuted.
Girard argues that the crowd's unanimity is what makes the accusation look self-evident, since if everyone agrees the victim must be guilty.
He reads the saying about Satan casting out Satan as a description of the mechanism by which disorder is driven out by turning on a single victim.
The persecutors' difficulty, he says, is that they do not see themselves as persecutors, which he links to the Gospel line that they know not what they do.

books.thesis: Alienated labour and human nature, as the young Marx saw them.
books.summary:
These notebooks were written by the young Marx in Paris and were not published until the 1930s. He asks what happens to a person whose work belongs to someone else. His answer is alienation. Under capitalism, the worker is cut off from what he makes, from the activity of making it, from other people, and from what Marx calls species-being, the human capacity for free, conscious production.

Marx argues by criticizing the political economists, who treat private property as a given, and by borrowing and reworking Hegel. He claims private property is the result of alienated labour, and he treats money as a force that inverts human qualities. The text is unfinished and often fragmentary, with passages on communism that remain sketchy. Scholars still argue about whether the humanist themes here continue in his later work or were left behind. For many readers the manuscripts are the most personal and philosophical Marx, interested in what work does to a life.
ideas: The worker's product confronts him as an alien power. Marx says the more the worker produces, the poorer he becomes in the world of things he has made.
Work under capitalism is external to the worker and forced. People feel at home only outside work, and so work becomes a loss of self rather than an expression of it.
Marx describes species-being as the human capacity to produce freely and consciously and to shape nature. Alienated labour reduces it to a means of survival.
If the product and the activity belong to another person, then that person controls the worker's life. Alienation from others follows from alienation in work.
Marx reverses the political economists. He argues private property is the result of alienated labour, and treats it as something to be explained instead of assumed.
Citing Shakespeare's Timon and Goethe's Faust, he argues money inverts human qualities, since it can buy what one is not and so turns ugliness or cowardice into their opposites.
The manuscripts stayed unpublished until the 1930s, and scholars still debate whether this humanist young Marx stands apart from the later economist.
In the final manuscript Marx criticizes Hegel's Phenomenology, saying Hegel understood labour as the self creating itself but only as abstract mental labour.
He criticizes crude communism, which wants to level everyone by turning private property into common property, as universalized envy that has not yet understood what property means.
Marx says that under the wage system the worker is reduced to a commodity whose fate depends on demand, and who sinks to the level of a thing that must be kept alive to work.

books.thesis: More unequal societies do worse on almost every social measure, though the statistics are debated.
books.summary:
The Spirit Level begins from a puzzle. Among rich countries, average income tells us little about how well a society does on health and social problems. Wilkinson and Pickett ask what does. Their answer is the size of the gap between rich and poor. They gather data on life expectancy, violence, imprisonment, mental illness, teenage births and trust, and compare countries and American states.

They argue that more unequal societies do worse on nearly all of these measures, and that the effect reaches beyond the poor to most of the population. Their proposed mechanism is status anxiety, the stress of being judged and ranked, and they argue for reducing inequality as a shared benefit. The book was influential in policy debates and also attacked. Critics say the countries were picked selectively, that correlation is not cause, and that results weaken with other data. The authors have answered these points, and the dispute continues.
ideas: Among rich countries, average income matters little to social outcomes, while the gap between top and bottom tracks them closely.
The authors combine measures such as life expectancy, obesity, mental illness, violence and imprisonment into an index, and compare it with inequality across countries.
The same pattern is reported among US states, offered as a check that the result is not an accident of which countries were chosen.
Their proposed mechanism is status anxiety. Where differences are larger, people feel judged more, and chronic social stress harms health and behaviour.
The effects are said to reach beyond the poor. Even well-off people in unequal societies are reported to do worse on several measures than counterparts in equal ones.
Trust and community life are weaker in unequal societies, which the authors link to the social strain that wider gaps create.
Critics say the countries were selected and that correlation is not cause, and that results weaken with other data. The authors dispute these objections.
The book notes that equality can be reached by different routes, with Japan having small pre-tax income gaps and Sweden relying more on taxes and benefits, and both doing well on the index.
The authors report that countries with more inequality have lower social mobility, so that where you start matters more, which they link to the idea of the American Dream.
They draw on research on social evaluative threat, which shows stress hormones rise when people feel judged or looked down on, to support the claim that inequality works through social stress.

books.thesis: How does prejudice form, and how can contact reduce it? This is the classic analysis.
books.summary:
The Nature of Prejudice is Allport's classic attempt to understand how people come to dislike others for belonging to a group. He asks how prejudice forms in the individual, how it is kept alive in society, and what can be done about it. He defines it as antipathy based on a faulty and inflexible generalization, one that holds even when the facts say otherwise.

Allport argues that sorting people into categories is a normal habit of thought, and prejudice is an exaggerated and rigid form of it. He reviews historical, economic, psychological and cultural causes and warns against any single explanation. He describes a ladder of rejection from careless talk to violence. His most cited idea is that contact between groups can reduce prejudice when certain conditions hold. Later research has largely supported a version of this, though critics note it is hard to meet the conditions in real life, and that attitudes can change more easily than institutions.
ideas: Allport defines prejudice as antipathy resting on a faulty and inflexible generalization, felt or expressed, and directed at a group or at an individual because of membership in it.
The mind works with categories, and Allport treats prejudice as a rigid, exaggerated version of an ordinary habit that helps us cope with a complicated world.
Preferring the in-group does not require hating the out-group. Allport suggests loyalty to what we know usually comes first, and hostility is a further step.
He describes degrees of rejection, from antilocution, which is hostile talk, through avoidance and discrimination to physical attack and extermination.
Contact between groups can lessen prejudice when the groups have equal status, share goals, cooperate, and have the support of authorities or custom.
Allport discusses personality, noting that some people need rigid certainties and clear categories, and these are more likely to hold strong prejudices.
He reviews many causes, historical, economic, social and psychological, and warns against explaining prejudice by any single one.
Allport discusses scapegoating, linking it to frustration and displaced aggression, in which hostility that cannot reach its true source is turned on a weaker group.

A chapter on traits due to victimization covers how persecuted groups react, including withdrawal, obsessive concern, in-group solidarity and clowning, and Allport warns that these reactions can be mistaken for the group's nature.
Prejudgment turns into prejudice only when it is not reversible on exposure to new knowledge, so for Allport the test is whether a person can change their mind.

books.thesis: Our moral instincts serve the tribe, so cooperating across tribes takes slower thinking.
books.summary:
Moral Tribes asks why people who each think they are decent can still fail to agree, and sometimes fight. Greene argues that our moral instincts evolved to help us cooperate within groups, which solves the problem of Me versus Us. They do much less well on the problem of Us versus Them, where each tribe's intuitions feel obviously right to its own members.

Greene draws on psychology and brain imaging, including studies of trolley problems, and describes two modes of thought. One is fast and automatic and the other is slower and deliberate. For disputes between tribes, he proposes using the manual mode to find a common currency, and he argues that utilitarian reasoning, which he calls deep pragmatism, can serve. Many philosophers object. They say he treats intuitions too lightly and that utilitarianism yields results most people will not accept. The book is a clear statement of a contested position.
ideas: Greene says morality evolved to solve Me versus Us, the tension between selfish and group interests, by making people cooperative inside their own groups.
The tragedy of commonsense morality is that the same instincts that make us cooperate within a tribe leave us unable to settle disputes between tribes.
He compares the mind to a camera with automatic settings for speed and a manual mode for flexibility. Moral thinking has both, and they can disagree.
In trolley cases, people accept switching a track but resist pushing a man off a footbridge. Greene links the difference to emotional responses seen in brain imaging.
Appeals to rights and moral intuition are often used as weapons, he says, letting each side feel righteous while rationalizing its own tribe's position.
Between tribes we need a common currency, and Greene proposes happiness, weighed impartially, as the shared standard. He calls this approach deep pragmatism.
Critics reply that he dismisses intuitions too quickly and that utilitarian reasoning can lead to conclusions most people reject.
Greene frames Me versus Us with the tragedy of the commons, the parable of herders sharing a pasture, and calls Us versus Them the problem that morality does not solve by itself.
He uses Peter Singer's drowning child and related cases to ask why we feel strongly about a child in front of us but weakly about children far away.

Greene argues that our automatic settings are reliable for familiar problems, such as dealing with kin and neighbours, but unreliable for unfamiliar ones such as distant strangers or new technologies.

books.thesis: Human beings are animals who know they'll die, and character, culture and heroism are largely defences against that knowledge.
ideas: Becker describes a dual nature. We have a symbolic self that can imagine forever and a body that decays, and living with that gap is the human predicament.
Character armour is personality seen as a structure built early to avoid terror, narrowing a person so that life feels manageable.
Following Freud's idea of repression, Becker puts the fear of death at its root, which makes ordinary normal life look like a kind of managed denial.
Heroism is an immortality project. We want to matter on a cosmic scale and to be more than an animal that will be forgotten.
Culture supplies the hero system, the scripts and rewards through which people can feel that their lives count beyond death.
Transference and love hand the burden of meaning to another person, who is asked to be the answer to everything. Becker says no one can bear that.
He leaves the problem open. Because illusions seem unavoidable, he points toward faith in something larger than the self, and admits that is not a proof.

Becker draws on Otto Rank, who held that the neurotic refuses the loan of life to avoid the debt of death, and he treats the creative person as someone who tries to fashion a lasting work from limits.
Creatureliness is the horror of being an animal with a body that decays, and Becker, following Kierkegaard, sees human beings as gods who excrete and die.
The book won a Pulitzer Prize shortly after Becker's death in 1974, and it later became the basis for terror management theory in experimental social psychology.
books.surprise: Becker reads Freud through Kierkegaard. Neurosis isn't just repression; it's a refusal of the full truth of the human condition, and so is "normal" adjustment.
books.crit: Totalizing: almost everything becomes death denial. The experimental programme it inspired (TMT) has struggled with replication.
books.summary:
The Denial of Death argues that human beings are unusual animals. We are creatures who know we will die and also have a self that imagines living forever. Becker asks how a mind can carry that gap and still get through a day. His answer is that much of what we call character, culture and ambition is built to keep the terror of death out of view.

Becker draws on Freud, Otto Rank and Kierkegaard, and revises Freud by putting the fear of death at the root of repression rather than sex. He argues that we protect ourselves through personality, heroic projects and love, and that none of these fully works. The book won wide readership and shaped later research in terror management. Critics find the sweep too large and the evidence mostly interpretive. It ends without a cure, only a hope that a person might live with fewer illusions, perhaps through faith in something larger.

books.thesis: Human evil grows out of the attempt to deny death and win immortality.
books.summary:
Escape from Evil is Becker's follow-up to The Denial of Death, and it asks where human evil comes from. His thesis is that much of it grows out of ordinary people trying to deny death and win some kind of immortality. He takes up the question across history and culture, asking why humans have been so willing to hurt and kill each other for causes that feel holy.

Becker argues that every culture is a hero system offering ways to feel that one's life counts. Rival systems threaten each other, because another culture's existence suggests that ours may not be the real route to permanence. He suggests we then project our fear and guilt onto victims and try to destroy them. He draws on Otto Rank and Norman O. Brown.
