He gives little program for change and only hopes that seeing the motive might loosen its hold. Critics find the claims broad and speculative, and some doubt a single motive can explain so much.
ideas: Becker argues that much human evil comes from ordinary people seeking to secure immortality, and he disputes that it mainly flows from a simple instinct to aggress.
Each culture works as an immortality system, giving its members heroic roles and a sense that their lives will count beyond death.
Rival hero systems feel threatened by each other, so war can be a contest over whose version of heroism is real and whose is false.
Scapegoating lets people unload their guilt and mortality onto others. Destroying the victim feels like cleansing, so evil can be done in the name of good.
Following Norman O. Brown, Becker treats money as a symbol of immortality, so that accumulation becomes a way of denying that one will die.
He follows others in saying that unease about our animal bodies gets projected onto groups seen as dirty or lowly, so contempt helps keep the creaturely at a distance.
Becker closes without a program. He suggests only that seeing the motive may loosen its hold, and he is unsure we can live without victims.
Becker finished the book as he was dying of cancer, and it appeared posthumously in 1975 as a kind of sequel to The Denial of Death.
Following Rank, he argues that people feel guilt for being alive and try to pay for it with a sacrifice, so that other people become the price of their own immortality.
He holds that modern ideologies, such as nationalism and revolutionary politics, take over the religious job of offering immortality, and so can become holy wars.

books.thesis: Meaning is the primary human motive, and it can be found even in suffering nobody can change.
ideas: Frankl describes how prisoners reacted in stages, from shock on arrival to apathy to a bitter disillusion after liberation, and treats the stages as psychological patterns.
The last human freedom is choosing your attitude. Circumstances can be taken from a person, and Frankl says the choice of one's response remains.
He sets the will to meaning against Freud's will to pleasure and Adler's will to power, claiming meaning is the more basic motive.
Meaning can be found through work or deeds, through love, and through the stance taken toward unavoidable suffering. Frankl says avoidable suffering should be avoided.
Happiness ensues. It cannot be pursued directly, and it appears as a side effect of living for something beyond oneself.
The existential vacuum is his name for the sense of emptiness that shows up as boredom, and he calls it a mark of modern life.
Prisoners with a task or a person to live for seemed to endure better, a point Frankl ties to Nietzsche's remark about having a why to live.
The second part of the book sets out logotherapy and two techniques, paradoxical intention and dereflection, which help people stop fixing on a symptom or on themselves.
Frankl closes with tragic optimism, the capacity to say yes to life despite pain, guilt and death, by turning suffering into achievement, guilt into change and transience into responsible action.
He argues that freedom must be balanced by responsibility, and suggests that the Statue of Liberty on the East Coast be supplemented by a Statue of Responsibility on the West Coast.
books.surprise: Frankl is unsentimental about fellow prisoners. He writes that the best did not return, and that survival often depended on luck and ruthlessness.
books.crit: It can be read as implying that meaning helped people survive, when survival was overwhelmingly a matter of chance.
books.summary:
Man's Search for Meaning has two parts. The first is Frankl's account of surviving Nazi camps, and the second sets out logotherapy, the approach to psychology he developed. He asks what keeps people going when almost everything has been taken. His answer is that the drive to find meaning is primary in human life, and that a person can find it even in suffering that cannot be changed.

Frankl writes in a plain, observational voice and offers his own experience and that of fellow prisoners as evidence. He set the will to meaning against Freud's pleasure and Adler's power. He says meaning can come through work, love, or the stance we take toward unavoidable suffering. The book is short and has sold in huge numbers. Critics point out that it rests on one man's observations and is not a systematic study, and some worry that it can be read as making suffering sound useful. Frankl is careful to say suffering is only meaningful when it cannot be avoided.

books.thesis: The absurd is the clash between human longing for meaning and a silent world. The right response is revolt, neither suicide nor hope.
ideas: Camus opens by saying the question of whether life is worth living is the one truly serious philosophical problem, and everything else comes after it.
The absurd is not located in the world or in the person. It arises from the confrontation between human longing for meaning and a silent universe.
Philosophical suicide is leaping to a meaning that is not there. Camus accuses thinkers such as Kierkegaard, Jaspers and Husserl of making this leap.
He draws three consequences of the absurd, which are revolt, freedom and passion, and means by them living without appeal to anything beyond this life.
Absurd heroes include the seducer, the actor, the conqueror and the artist, each of whom lives fully inside limits without hoping for something beyond them.
Camus favours the quantity of experience over its quality, because without a higher measure the aim is to live as much as possible.
The book ends with Sisyphus and the line that one must imagine him happy, since the struggle itself is enough to fill a heart.
An appendix on Kafka argues that his work holds both the absurd and a hope that Camus treats as a leap, and Camus reads the novels as a play between the two.
Camus uses Kirilov in Dostoevsky's The Possessed as a case of logical suicide, someone who kills himself to prove his freedom, and he disagrees with the conclusion.
Suicide would end the absurd by removing one of its two sides, so Camus argues the absurd person rejects it and keeps the confrontation alive.
books.surprise: Camus's main targets aren't nihilists. They're the existentialists, whom he accuses of escaping into hope.
books.crit: Some philosophers find the argument more lyrical than rigorous; Sartre thought Camus avoided politics.
books.summary:
The Myth of Sisyphus opens with a blunt claim. Whether life is worth living is, Camus says, the one truly serious philosophical question. He asks what to do when human longing for meaning meets a world that gives no answer. That collision is the absurd, and it lives in the meeting of the two, not in either alone.

Camus argues that there are two cheap exits. One is suicide, and the other is what he calls philosophical suicide, a leap into faith or a system that promises meaning the world does not supply. He rejects both and proposes revolt, which means living with the absurd and refusing to look away. He sketches absurd figures such as the seducer, the actor, the conqueror and the artist. The essay closes on Sisyphus pushing his rock, whom we are told to imagine happy. Critics ask whether revolt is a real answer or only a mood, and some say Camus misreads the thinkers he criticizes.

books.thesis: Revolt affirms a shared human value, and it loses itself when it justifies murder.
books.summary:
The Rebel takes up where The Myth of Sisyphus left off. If life is absurd, does anything permit murder? Camus asks what revolt means, and whether it can be kept from sliding into the killing done in the name of revolution. He starts from the figure of the rebel who says no, and he argues that the no also carries a yes to some value that the rebel believes belongs to everyone.

Camus traces the history of revolt through metaphysical rebellion, against creation itself, and historical rebellion, against rulers. He discusses Sade, the Romantics, Ivan Karamazov, Nietzsche, Hegel and Marx, and the terror of the French and Russian revolutions. His claim is that revolt loses itself when it justifies murder for a future end. He argues for limits and a Mediterranean sense of measure. The book led to a public break with Sartre and the Left, and critics still disagree on whether his alternative is practical or only a moral stance.
ideas: The rebel says no, but in saying it also affirms a value he takes to be shared by everyone, which is why revolt is more than refusal.
Camus turns Descartes into a formula of solidarity. I rebel, therefore we exist, because revolt takes for granted a common human dignity.
Metaphysical rebellion is revolt against the human condition and creation itself, and Camus follows it through Sade, the Romantics, Ivan Karamazov and Nietzsche.
Historical revolutions, he argues, betray the revolt that began them when they justify killing for a future end. He points to the French Terror and Soviet Russia.
Revolt implies a limit. Because it starts from an affirmation of human worth, it cannot consistently justify unlimited murder.
Camus appeals to a Mediterranean idea of measure, setting it against ideologies that treat history as an absolute to which people can be sacrificed.
The book's publication led to a public break with Sartre and his circle, and the dispute over whether Camus weakened the left continues.
Camus separates revolt from ressentiment. Revolt gives and affirms a value, while ressentiment is the bitter product of long powerlessness and only poisons.

He praises the Russian terrorists of 1905, such as Kaliayev, who accepted that killing is a crime and paid for it with their own lives. He sets them against later revolutionaries who treated murder as routine.
A chapter on rebellion and art argues that the artist also says no to the world as given and then rebuilds it with a unity and style that reality lacks.

books.thesis: Consciousness is freedom, and bad faith is how we run from it.
books.summary:
Being and Nothingness is Sartre's large attempt to describe what it is to be conscious. He asks how a being that can question, imagine and deny relates to the solid world of things. His answer is that consciousness is a kind of nothingness, always lacking and never fixed, and that this makes it free. There is no human nature that settles in advance what a person must do.

Sartre argues through detailed descriptions of everyday scenes, such as a waiter acting out his role and the shame of being watched through a keyhole. He treats freedom as a source of anguish, and bad faith as the many ways we deny it by pretending to be things or by pretending to have no choice. Other people appear as a threat to our freedom, and love turns out to be a doomed attempt to possess another consciousness. The book is long and difficult, and critics question whether his picture of relations is too bleak.
ideas: Sartre separates being-in-itself, solid and complete like a stone, from being-for-itself, which is consciousness and is defined by what it lacks.
Consciousness brings nothingness into the world. We can see an absence, such as a friend who is not in the cafe where we expected to find him.
Anguish is the awareness of our own freedom with nothing to lean on. Sartre compares it to vertigo on a narrow path, where the fear is of our own possible act.
Bad faith is lying to oneself about one's freedom. His example is a waiter who plays at being a waiter as if it were his fixed nature.
We are always both facticity, the given facts of our situation, and transcendence, our projection beyond them. Bad faith tries to live as only one.
The Look of another person turns me into an object. Sartre uses the shame of being caught peeping through a keyhole to show it.
Relations with others tend toward conflict, and Sartre treats love as a project to possess another's freedom, which cannot succeed. Critics find this account too bleak.

Sartre says human beings are driven by a desire to be both in-itself and for-itself, solid like a thing yet conscious, which is the project of being God. He concludes that this is impossible and calls man a useless passion.
His example of bad faith in a woman on a first date shows it at work. She leaves her hand in her companion's hand and does not decide what it means, treating it as neither giving nor withdrawing it.
Sartre proposes existential psychoanalysis, which looks for a person's fundamental project, the original choice of self behind particular desires, in place of Freud's unconscious drives.

books.thesis: A short lecture. Existence precedes essence, so we are responsible for what we become.
books.summary:
Existentialism Is a Humanism began as a public lecture in Paris in 1945 and was published the next year. Sartre was answering critics, Catholics who saw despair in his work and Communists who saw self-absorbed idleness. He lays out in plain terms the idea that existence comes before essence. A human being has no fixed nature, and we become what we do and choose.

Sartre argues by example and by contrast. A paper knife is made for a purpose, and people have no maker whose purpose defines them. From this he draws abandonment, anguish and despair as the mood of a world without ready made values. In choosing for ourselves we also say how people ought to be, so we are answerable to everyone. He illustrates with a student torn between his mother and the Resistance, and says no rule can decide for him. Sartre later expressed regret about the lecture's simplifications, but it remains the most readable door into his thought.
ideas: With a paper knife, the maker's idea comes before the object. People have no maker, so existence comes first and we define ourselves through what we do.
In choosing for myself I also choose an image of what a person ought to be, so Sartre says each choice carries responsibility for all humanity.
Anguish is the awareness of that responsibility. Sartre likens it to a military leader who knows his decisions will cost others their lives.
Abandonment means there is no God to supply values and nothing written in the sky. We are left with our choices and their consequences.
Despair, for Sartre, means acting without counting on hopes beyond our control, relying only on what lies within our power to do.
A student must choose between caring for his mother and joining the Free French. Sartre says no moral theory settles it, so he must choose and invent his own answer.
Sartre calls existentialism a humanism because humans are always still in the making, not because humanity is to be worshipped. He later expressed regret about the lecture.
The lecture answers two kinds of critic. Communists said existentialism was quietist and gloomy, and Christians said it was subjective and left no firm ground for morals.
Sartre denies there is a fixed human nature, since there is no God to have conceived one. He still allows a universal human condition, the limits of being in the world, that every person must face.

A person is nothing other than the sum of his actions, he says. The coward makes himself a coward by what he does, and could have chosen otherwise, so there is no excuse from temperament or circumstance.

books.thesis: Freedom is real but situated, and my freedom requires the freedom of others.
books.summary:
The Ethics of Ambiguity was Beauvoir's first book on moral philosophy, written in the years just after the war. She asks how to act when human life is irreducibly ambiguous. We are free subjects who make meaning, and also objects in the world with bodies, limits and a death. She argues that ethics should begin there, instead of trying to escape one side of ourselves.

Beauvoir builds on Sartre but disagrees with him in places. Her central claim is that freedom wills itself and, in doing so, must also will the freedom of others. She describes failed ways of facing freedom through character types such as the serious man, the sub-man, the nihilist and the adventurer. She takes oppression seriously as a limit on what some people can choose. The book is clear and compact, and critics debate whether her answer on violence against oppressors is settled or left uneasy. She seems content to leave it uneasy.
ideas: Ambiguity is the human condition. We are both free subjects and objects in the world, and Beauvoir says ethics must start from that tension.
Freedom must will itself, and to will oneself free is also to will others free. My freedom needs other people's to have any meaning.
The serious man takes values to be given from outside and absolute. He gives up his freedom by treating them as things to obey.
Beauvoir sketches the sub-man, the nihilist, the adventurer and the passionate man as failed ways of facing freedom, each avoiding part of the human situation.
Children live in a world of ready made values and are not asked to justify them. Some adults, she suggests, retreat into that world to avoid choice.
Freedom is real but situated. People kept in conditions where choosing is hard cannot simply be told that they are free anyway.
She grants that violence against oppressors may sometimes be unavoidable, but treats it as a tragic cost and not as a clean solution.
Beauvoir holds that freedom is the source from which all values spring, so it cannot be sacrificed for any value that depends on it. This is her ground for refusing to let ends justify any means.
She argues against systems that dissolve the individual into History or the universal. Each person's separate existence and death is a fact that cannot be argued away.

The book opens by noting that philosophers have tended to deny ambiguity, and she says the attempt to escape it, by calling man pure spirit or pure thing, is what produces much of the evil in the world.

books.thesis: Woman has been defined as man's Other, and womanhood is something one becomes.
books.summary:
The Second Sex is Beauvoir's long study of what it has meant to be a woman. She asks why women have been treated as secondary, and how a person comes to live as one. Her starting point is that man is taken as the human norm and woman as his Other, defined in relation to him. The famous line says that one is not born a woman but becomes one.

The book has two parts. The first examines biology, psychoanalysis and historical materialism, and finds that none of them fully explains women's position. It then reads the myths of the Eternal Feminine in literature. The second follows women's lived experience through childhood, puberty, marriage, motherhood and old age. Beauvoir argues that economic independence is needed for liberation, though not enough alone. Some of her claims have been criticized as dated or as drawing too much from a narrow class of women. It nonetheless set the terms for much later feminist thought.
ideas: Beauvoir's best known line says a woman is made by upbringing and social pressure, and is not simply born. Gender is learned over a lifetime.
Man is treated as the subject and the norm, while woman is the Other, described in relation to him and rarely allowed to define herself.
She tests biology, psychoanalysis and historical materialism in turn, and finds that each helps but none explains women's subordination on its own.
Beauvoir reads myths of the Eternal Feminine in male writers, who cast woman as mystery, nature or muse and so fix her in an image.
Girls are taught to see themselves as objects for others to look at, and Beauvoir traces how puberty and menstruation can sharpen this self-consciousness.
She criticizes marriage and domestic life as an institution that ties women to repetitive work, trapping them in immanence while men pursue projects.
Economic independence is needed for liberation, she argues, though it is not enough alone. The hope is relations between people who see each other as equals.

Women, Beauvoir says, are dispersed among men, living with them in homes and classes, and lack a shared history or solidarity of their own. That is why their case differs from that of other oppressed groups.

The chapter on the woman in love describes love as self-abandonment, in which she makes herself an object for a man's sake. Beauvoir hopes for a love of two free people who recognise each other as equals.

Her literary examples include Montherlant, D. H. Lawrence and Breton, whom she criticises for casting woman as a mirror for the male hero. The first English translation by Parshley was abridged, which long limited how the book was read in English.

books.thesis: What does it mean to exist? Thrown into the world, lost in the They, facing death.
books.summary:
Being and Time asks a question Heidegger thinks philosophy has forgotten. What does it mean to be? He starts with the one being who can ask it, which he calls Dasein, roughly the human way of existing. Rather than treating us as minds looking at objects, he describes us as always already in a world, involved with tools and other people, and living in time.

Heidegger works by close description of ordinary life. We are thrown into circumstances we did not choose, and we mostly live as the They do, following what one does. Anxiety and the awareness of our own death can pull us out of that and open the chance of authenticity. The book is famously hard, its vocabulary is new, and it was never finished, since the planned second half did not appear. Heidegger's later involvement with the Nazi party has also complicated how readers receive it. Its influence on existentialism and psychotherapy is large.
ideas: Heidegger says the question of the meaning of Being has been forgotten, and he starts by asking about the kind of being that asks it. He calls this Dasein.
We are always already in the world, involved with things. A hammer is ready to hand in use, and only shows up as an object when it breaks.
Thrownness is finding ourselves in a time, place, family and language we did not choose, and having to live from there.
The They is the anonymous everyone whose habits, opinions and tastes we follow in daily life. Doing what one does spares us the burden of deciding.
Anxiety is unlike fear. It has no object and reveals the world as without support, pulling us out of the comfort of the They.
Death is always one's own and cannot be handed to anyone else. Facing it, Heidegger says, can make a person's life authentic.
He names the structure of Dasein as care and argues its meaning is time. The announced second half never appeared, and the book remains unfinished.

Everyday life, Heidegger says, falls into idle talk, curiosity and ambiguity. We repeat what is said, chase novelty and cannot tell real understanding from its show, and he calls this tendency fallenness.
Mood, which he calls attunement, is how the world matters to us before we think about it. Moods are not private colourings of inner states but a way the situation is disclosed.
The call of conscience summons Dasein out of the They toward its own potential, and resoluteness is the answer. Heidegger insists the call carries no content and no moral instruction.

books.thesis: Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac, and the leap of faith that goes beyond ethics.
books.summary:
Fear and Trembling is written under the pseudonym Johannes de Silentio and takes up the story of Abraham and Isaac. Kierkegaard asks what it would mean to obey a command to sacrifice your own son, and why we praise Abraham instead of treating him as a murderer. The narrator admits he cannot understand Abraham, and he approaches him with awe, from the outside.

The book works by retelling the story in several ways, then setting Abraham beside tragic heroes such as Agamemnon, who sacrifice a child but stay within what a community can understand. Abraham cannot explain himself, so he is silent. Kierkegaard calls what he does a teleological suspension of the ethical and describes faith as believing by virtue of the absurd. Readers dispute what this means. Critics ask whether the argument could excuse any killing done on a claimed divine order, and the book does not settle that worry. It leaves faith both admirable and disturbing.
ideas: The pseudonymous narrator, Johannes de Silentio, says he cannot understand Abraham. He writes as an admirer who stands in awe from outside faith.
The book retells the Genesis story several times in different versions, partly to show how easily familiar tellings smooth away the horror.
The knight of infinite resignation gives up what he loves. The knight of faith does the same and then believes he will get it back, and looks like an ordinary citizen.
Faith by virtue of the absurd means Abraham believed he would receive Isaac back in this life, even though everything made that impossible.
The tragic hero, such as Agamemnon, sacrifices his child for a cause the community can understand, so he stays within ethics. Abraham has no such public reason.
Kierkegaard calls Abraham's case a teleological suspension of the ethical, meaning the individual stands in relation to God in a way that outranks the universal.
Abraham is silent because he cannot make himself understood. Critics ask if this defence could excuse any murder, and the book does not settle it.

The book is organised around three Problemata: whether there is a teleological suspension of the ethical, whether there is an absolute duty to God, and whether Abraham's silence toward Sarah, Eliezer and Isaac can be defended ethically.

Kierkegaard targets the Hegelian view that the ethical is the universal and that the individual is justified only by fitting into it. Abraham, he says, stands as the single individual in an absolute relation to the absolute.
He complains that his age wants to go beyond faith, treating it as a first step to leave behind. For him faith is the hardest task and no one finishes with it.

books.thesis: Two ways to live, the aesthetic and the ethical, each written from the inside.
books.summary:
Either/Or is Kierkegaard's first major book, published under a pseudonymous editor who claims to have found two sets of papers in a secondhand desk. One set is by a young man called A, who lives for aesthetic interest and pleasure. The other is by Judge William, an older married man who defends the ethical life of commitment and duty. The title poses the question of which way a person should live.

Kierkegaard does not argue the case in his own voice. Instead each life is written from the inside, so the reader meets A's wit and melancholy and the Judge's warmth and moral earnestness. A's pages include the Diary of the Seducer and an essay on rotating the crops against boredom. The Judge replies in long letters on marriage and on choosing oneself. The book gives no clear verdict, and the final sermon points beyond both. Many readers see it as setting up Kierkegaard's later religious stage, though that reading is debated.
ideas: A pseudonymous editor, Victor Eremita, says he found the papers of two men, A and Judge William, in a desk, which lets Kierkegaard avoid speaking in his own voice.
A's aesthetic life aims at interest and pleasure, and his essay on rotating the crops suggests beating boredom by varying how one approaches things rather than where.
The Diary of the Seducer shows pursuit turned into a cold art. Johannes the seducer manipulates a young woman, and the story exposes the cruelty of the aesthetic life.
A's opening aphorisms show a bored and melancholy writer, so the aesthetic life seems to carry its own despair along with its wit.
Judge William argues that marriage keeps romantic love alive by giving it duration and commitment, instead of letting it fade as a fleeting mood.
For the Judge, ethical choice is the choice of oneself, to become a self with a history and responsibilities, and not only to pick among options.
The book gives no clear winner, and a closing sermon points past both lives. Many readers take it as pointing toward a religious stage.

The essay on Mozart's Don Giovanni, in the section on the immediate erotic stages, argues that the figure is best expressed in music because he is sensuous desire in general, not an individual character.
In the speech of the unhappiest man, A describes a person who is always absent from himself, living in hope or memory and never in the present. He suggests this is a mark of the aesthetic life.
The closing sermon, the Ultimatum, holds that in relation to God we are always in the wrong. It points past Judge William's ethics toward a different kind of seriousness.

books.thesis: Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom.
books.summary:
The Concept of Anxiety is a short, dense book published under the name Vigilius Haufniensis. Kierkegaard asks what anxiety is and how it connects to freedom and sin. He starts from the story of Adam and the idea of inherited sin, but his real subject is the moment before a choice. Anxiety, he says, differs from fear because it has no object. It is anxiety about possibility itself.

He argues through an image of vertigo. A person looking into an abyss feels dizzy not only because of the drop but because of their own freedom to jump, and he calls anxiety the dizziness of freedom. He treats sin as entering through a leap that psychology cannot fully explain. The book is written in a technical style and is often read alongside his other pseudonymous works. Readers disagree about how much is theology and how much psychology. It is influential partly because it treats anxiety as a sign of human possibility.
ideas: Fear has an object, while anxiety is about nothing in particular. Kierkegaard says it is the anxiety of possibility, the sense that anything could happen.
Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom. Looking into an abyss makes us dizzy because of our own freedom to jump, as well as the drop.
In the story of Adam, the prohibition awakens the possibility of freedom, so anxiety is present in innocence before any sin has taken place.
Sin enters through a qualitative leap that psychology cannot fully explain. Kierkegaard says explaining it away or denying it are both mistakes.
Anxiety is ambiguous. It is a sympathetic antipathy and an antipathetic sympathy, something that both attracts and repels us.
Anxiety educates. Whoever has learned to be anxious in the right way, Kierkegaard says, has learned the ultimate, because it teaches us about our freedom.
The demonic is shut-upness, the condition of a person who closes himself off from the good and refuses to be opened out, from fear.
The book appeared under the pseudonym Vigilius Haufniensis, the watchman of Copenhagen. Its subtitle calls it a simple psychological deliberation on the dogmatic issue of hereditary sin.
Kierkegaard describes the human being as a synthesis of soul and body held together by spirit. Anxiety arises when spirit tries to posit that synthesis and meets its own freedom.
On hereditary sin, he says Adam is both himself and the race. Each individual repeats the beginning of sin for himself, and so no one is merely a product of Adam's fall.

books.thesis: Despair is the failure to be a self, and most people are in it without knowing.
books.summary:
The Sickness unto Death is written under the pseudonym Anti-Climacus. It asks what a self is and why so many people are in despair without realizing it. Kierkegaard defines the self as a relation that relates itself to itself, grounded in something beyond it. Despair is a failure of that relation. It is called a sickness unto death because it cannot be cured by dying, and one cannot die of it.

Kierkegaard describes despair through pairs such as the finite and infinite, possibility and necessity, and the many ways a person can go wrong. He says despair can be unconscious, as in the person who is cheerful and busy, or defiant, as in the person who wants to be a self on his own terms. The cure is faith, in which the self rests transparently in the power that established it. Readers disagree over how much the book depends on Christian belief. For those who do not share it, the diagnosis still reads as an unusually exact portrait of self-evasion.
ideas: Kierkegaard defines the self as a relation that relates itself to itself, and says it is grounded in another power. Despair is a misrelation within it.
Despair is called a sickness unto death because one cannot die of it. The torment is that the self cannot be used up and ended.
The misrelation can show up in pairs such as the finite and the infinite, or possibility and necessity, each ending in a different despair.
Unconscious despair is the most common. A cheerful, busy person who thinks he is fine may be in the deepest despair, simply because he has no idea.
In defiant despair a person wants to be a self entirely on his own terms. In weak despair he wants to be rid of the self altogether.
Kierkegaard distinguishes despair over the earthly, despair of the eternal and despair about one's own sin, a sequence that intensifies as the person becomes more aware.
The cure is a formula. The self, by relating to itself and willing to be itself, rests transparently in the power that established it. Kierkegaard calls this faith.

The book is written by the pseudonym Anti-Climacus, whom Kierkegaard presents as a higher Christian standard than his earlier Johannes Climacus. The subtitle calls it a Christian psychological exposition for upbuilding and awakening.
In the second part, despair is shown to be sin, and Kierkegaard says the opposite of sin is not virtue but faith. Despair means living before God while refusing to rest in him.
The degree of despair rises with the degree of consciousness of self. The more a person knows of what a self is, the more intense the despair, and the farther he is from the unconscious kind.

books.thesis: After the death of God come the overman, eternal recurrence and saying yes to life.
books.summary:
Thus Spoke Zarathustra is Nietzsche's most poetic book, written as a kind of mock scripture. A prophet descends from ten years in the mountains to teach people that God is dead and that they should live toward something beyond themselves. The question under it all is what to do with life once the old sources of meaning lose their authority.

Nietzsche answers through speeches, parables and songs and not through argument. Zarathustra offers the overman as a goal, warns against the last man who wants only comfort, and tells of the camel, the lion and the child as stages of the spirit. The most testing idea is eternal recurrence, the thought of living this life again without end. Readers still argue about what the overman means, and the book has been misused by political movements that Nietzsche would have despised. Many find its style exhilarating, while others find it overheated and hard to pin down.
ideas: Zarathustra comes down from ten years alone and tells a town that God is dead. The crowd, waiting for a tightrope walker, is not much interested.
The overman is offered as a goal. Humanity is something to be overcome, as the ape is to the human, and Zarathustra asks his hearers to remain faithful to the earth.
The last man is the comfortable, small, blinking figure who says he has found happiness. Nietzsche presents him as a warning about contentment without aspiration.
The three metamorphoses describe the spirit as a camel that bears burdens, a lion that says no, and a child that begins again and creates new values.
Zarathustra urges loyalty to the earth and warns against otherworldly hopes that teach people to despise the body and this life.
Eternal recurrence asks whether you could will to live this life again, endlessly. It works as a test of whether you can say yes to your existence.
The book is parable and poem, so readers still disagree about what the overman is supposed to be, and what exactly Nietzsche meant.

In the speech on the despisers of the body, Zarathustra says that body I am entirely, and nothing more, and that soul is only a word for something about the body. The body is a great reason, wiser than the thinker.
In the vision and the riddle, he shows a dwarf the gateway called Moment, from which two paths run endlessly back and forward. This is where eternal recurrence is first put to the reader as an image.
Nietzsche writes in a style that parodies the Bible, with parables, sermons and a prophet and disciples. The form lets him mock the voice of religion while teaching something opposed to it.

books.thesis: Philosophers' moral systems turn out to be confessions of their drives.
books.summary:
Beyond Good and Evil is a collection of aphorisms and short essays in which Nietzsche turns his suspicion on philosophers. They claim to pursue cold, impartial truth, yet their systems tend to defend moral prejudices they inherited. He asks why we want truth at all, and what drives lie behind the arguments of thinkers who say they have none.

His method is to read a philosophy as a symptom of the person who wrote it. He questions Descartes's confidence in an I that thinks, treats knowledge as seeing from many perspectives, and proposes the will to power as a hypothesis for psychology and life. He contrasts a noble morality and a slave morality and calls for free spirits who will test their own convictions. The book is playful and uneven, with some passages that readers find offensive. It does not build a system, and Nietzsche seems to prefer leaving the reader unsettled.
ideas: Philosophers claim to pursue cold truth while defending inherited prejudices. Nietzsche asks the odd question of why we want truth in the first place.
Every great philosophy, he says, is the personal confession of its author and a kind of involuntary memoir, with moral intentions hidden inside it.
He challenges the Cartesian I think, saying a thought comes when it wants and not when I want, so Descartes assumes more than he has shown.
Truth is perspectival. Knowing means looking from many angles, and a false judgment is not an objection to it if it helps preserve and promote life.
The will to power is offered as an experimental hypothesis, which Nietzsche tests as an account of psychology and of life, not as settled doctrine.
He distinguishes master morality, which starts from self-affirmation, from slave morality, which starts from the reaction of the weak and values humility and pity.
He calls for free spirits and philosophers of the future who treat their own convictions with suspicion and are willing to experiment.
He mocks the Stoic ideal of living according to nature. Nature is indifferent and wasteful, he says, and the Stoics read their own values into it and then claim to have found them there.
The aphorism on the abyss warns that whoever fights monsters should take care not to become a monster, and that when you gaze long into an abyss the abyss gazes into you.
In Peoples and Fatherlands he ridicules the nationalism of his day and hopes for good Europeans. He thinks the future lies in a mixing of peoples and not in a stiffening of national pride.

books.thesis: Morality has a history, and much of it is ressentiment.
books.summary:
On the Genealogy of Morality is made of three essays that ask where our moral ideas came from. Nietzsche's wager is that morality has a history, and that tracing it may reveal origins we would not call noble. He asks what good and evil, guilt and conscience, and the ideals of self-denial actually did for the people who invented them.

In the first essay he contrasts the noble good and bad with the later good and evil, and links the latter to the ressentiment of the powerless. The second derives guilt from the idea of debt and bad conscience from instincts turned inward. The third asks what ascetic ideals mean, and suggests that priests gave suffering a purpose, so that people would rather will nothing than not will at all. Scholars debate whether this is history or polemic. Nietzsche himself says we need a critique of moral values, which still seems unfinished.
ideas: Moral values have a history, Nietzsche says, and tracing it may show origins that we find unflattering instead of the pure ones we assume.
He contrasts a noble good and bad, which begins from the self-affirmation of the strong, with a later good and evil, which begins from reaction.
The slave revolt in morality comes from ressentiment. Those who cannot act turn their imagination to revenge, and call their powerlessness a virtue.
Guilt, Nietzsche suggests, grows out of debt. The German word for guilt is close to the word for debts, and punishment began as repayment.
Bad conscience comes from instincts turned inward when society closes in, so humans learn to suffer from themselves and from their own cruelty.
Ascetic ideals give suffering a meaning. Nietzsche says humans would rather will nothingness than not will at all, and priests exploit this need.
He asks for a critique of moral values and wants to know their worth. Scholars debate whether the genealogy is real history or a pointed polemic.

The second essay describes breeding an animal with the right to make promises. This needs active forgetting, a power that keeps the mind clear, and ends in the sovereign individual who answers for himself.
In the third essay, Nietzsche argues that science is not the opposite of the ascetic ideal but its latest form, since it still believes in truth as unconditionally valuable.
He calls for perspectival seeing and knowing. The more eyes we can use for one matter, the more complete our idea of it will be, and there is no view from nowhere.

books.thesis: The book where Nietzsche announces the death of God and first poses eternal recurrence.
books.summary:
The Gay Science is a book of aphorisms, poems and short essays by Nietzsche, first published in 1882 and expanded in 1887. The title refers to a knowledge that is light, joyful and close to poetry. It is the book where he first announces that God is dead and first poses eternal recurrence, and both ideas arrive in short passages that are easy to read past.

In the well known scene of the madman, a man runs into a marketplace with a lantern and tells people they have killed God. His listeners, who do not believe, only laugh, and he says he has come too early. The consequences, Nietzsche suggests, have not yet been felt. Elsewhere he asks us to love fate, to give style to our character, and to question the importance given to consciousness. The book is more varied than systematic. It is often called his warmest, and some readers take that lightness as a serious philosophical position.
ideas: A madman with a lantern in the morning tells a marketplace that we have killed God. The crowd laughs, and he says he has come too early.
The death of God is presented as a cultural event. The beliefs that held up morality are losing their footing, and the consequences have not yet been felt.
In the demon passage, a demon asks whether you would welcome living your life again, exactly as it was, for ever. It is the first appearance of eternal recurrence.
Amor fati is the love of fate. Nietzsche wants to see what is necessary in things as beautiful, and to say yes even to what he cannot change.
The gay science is knowledge held with lightness and joy. The book mixes aphorisms, verse and songs, and treats thinking as an art as well as a task.
He argues consciousness is overrated. It developed for the sake of communication, he says, and so tends to flatten experience into what can be shared.
One should give style to one's character, Nietzsche says, shaping strengths and weaknesses into a unified plan, so that even faults become part of a pleasing whole.

The second edition of 1887 added a new preface, a fifth book, and an appendix of songs. Book Five, We Fearless Ones, says that with the death of God the horizon seems open again, and the sea lies open.

In the section on polytheism, Nietzsche says its great advantage is that it lets an individual create his own ideal and give himself his own laws. Monotheism he calls the rigid rule of a single normal human type.

The title echoes the Provencal gai saber of the troubadours, and the book carries verses and a closing set of songs. Nietzsche presents his cheerfulness as something won after illness, not as a simple temperament.

books.t: The World as Will and Representation
books.thesis: Reality is blind striving, so life swings between pain and boredom.
books.summary:
The World as Will and Representation opens with the claim that the world is my representation, which means we know only how things appear to a subject. Schopenhauer builds on Kant and then asks what lies behind appearances. His answer is that we can know it from within, through our own body and its urges. Underneath everything is will, a blind striving without purpose or end.

From this he draws a bleak picture. Because will never rests, wanting is endless, satisfaction is brief, and life swings between pain and boredom. Relief comes only in moments, mainly through art, with music given a special place, and through compassion, which recognizes the same will in others. The deepest relief is the denial of the will, as practised by saints and ascetics. Critics point to a tension between his pessimism and the comfortable life he led, and many doubt that the will explains as much as he thought. His influence on Nietzsche, Wagner and Freud is clear.
ideas: The book opens with the claim that the world is my representation. We know things only as they appear to a subject, and Schopenhauer extends Kant on this point.
The will is the thing in itself. We know it from inside through our bodily urges, and the same blind force runs through all of nature.
Because will has no final aim, wanting never ends. Satisfaction is brief and lack is lasting, so life swings between pain and boredom.
Aesthetic contemplation briefly lets us forget the will, since we lose ourselves in disinterested attention. The relief is real but it does not last.
Music has a special place. Schopenhauer treats it as a direct expression of the will itself, which he says explains its power over us.
Compassion is the basis of ethics. Seeing another's suffering is recognising that the same will is at work in them as in me.
The denial of the will, practised by saints and ascetics, offers the deepest relief. Critics note the tension with his own comfortable life.

Schopenhauer rests the book on the principle of sufficient reason, which he had set out in an earlier work. Our representations are tied together by causes, reasons and motives, but the will itself lies outside that principle.
He denies free will in the usual sense. Our acts follow necessarily from our character and motives, though he allows that we are free in the sense that the will itself is not subject to causes.

Taking the veil of Maya from Indian thought, he says that individuation is an appearance, and that seeing past it makes one feel for others as for oneself. He argues suicide is no denial of the will, since it destroys only the body.

books.thesis: Essays by Schopenhauer on suffering, love, death and the wisdom of life.
books.summary:
Parerga and Paralipomena is a two volume collection of essays and fragments that Schopenhauer published late in life. The title means something like appendices and omissions, and the pieces extend or supplement his main philosophy. The question running through them is practical. Given what he takes to be the character of life, how can a person live reasonably well? The book, rather than his major work, finally made him famous.

The essays range widely, from the famous Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life to pieces on suffering, solitude, religion, reading and writing. Schopenhauer argues that happiness depends more on what a person is than on what one has or how one is seen, and he tells the parable of porcupines who cannot stand to be too close or too far apart. His tone is sharp and often witty. Some pieces, notably his essay on women, are widely seen as prejudice and not argument. Readers tend to take what they like and leave the rest.
ideas: The title means appendices and omissions. The essays supplement his major work, and this book, published in 1851, finally brought him the fame he had waited for.
In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he argues that happiness depends more on what one is than on what one has or how one appears to others.
He argues pain is the positive reality and pleasure only its absence, so a good life is mostly one in which suffering is kept small.
The porcupines huddle for warmth and prick one another with their quills, and learn a moderate distance. Schopenhauer says that is how people should treat each other.
Solitude suits those with much within themselves. He argues that the more a person has inside, the less he needs others, and the less others can touch him.
His pieces on reading and writing urge people to think for themselves, read less, and be wary of the pull of whatever is newest.
His essay on women is widely criticized as prejudice dressed as argument, a reminder that wisdom literature carries its author's blind spots.
The essay on university philosophy attacks professors who bend thought to their jobs and the state. He aims much of the scorn at Hegel, whose prose he calls nonsense used to impress.
In a speculation on the apparent intention in the fate of the individual, he suggests that a life may be arranged like a novel by a hidden hand. He offers this as a conjecture, not as proof.

Against Leibniz, Schopenhauer says this is the worst of all possible worlds, meaning that a slightly worse one could not continue to exist. Optimism, he thinks, is a bitter mockery of human suffering.

books.thesis: Courage is affirming yourself in spite of anxiety about death, meaninglessness and guilt.
books.summary:
The Courage to Be is Tillich's study of what it takes to affirm oneself in the face of what threatens our existence. He asks what courage is and what it requires. His definition is that courage is self-affirmation in spite of non-being, the possibility of ending, emptiness or condemnation. Anxiety, as he uses the word, is the awareness of that threat, and unlike fear it has no particular object.

Tillich names three forms of anxiety. They are anxiety of fate and death, of emptiness and meaninglessness, and of guilt and condemnation. He suggests that each dominated a different age. He describes the courage to be as a part, finding oneself in a group, and the courage to be as oneself, standing alone, and says both risk loss. His answer draws on theology, in a God above the God of ordinary belief that survives doubt. Critics find this vague, and some secular readers set the theology aside and keep the analysis of courage and anxiety.
ideas: Tillich defines courage as self-affirmation in spite of what threatens being. Everything in the definition turns on the phrase in spite of.
Anxiety is the awareness of non-being. Unlike fear, it has no definite object, and that is what makes it so hard to meet directly.
He names three forms of anxiety, of fate and death, of emptiness and meaninglessness, and of guilt and condemnation, and suggests each marked a different age.
Neurotic anxiety is an attempt to avoid non-being by avoiding being, shrinking the self into a small area where it feels safe.
There is a courage to be a part, finding oneself within a group, and a courage to be oneself. Tillich says each carries its own risk of losing the self.
He treats certain existentialist writers as showing the courage to face meaninglessness, taking despair seriously instead of covering it.
Tillich points to a God above the God of theism, the ground of being, that survives doubt. Critics find this vague, and secular readers often leave it aside.
Tillich treats courage as a response to the polarity of individualization and participation. The self must be itself while belonging to a world, and courage can fail by losing either side.

He reads Stoicism as the ancient courage to be oneself in the face of death and fate. He sees medieval Christianity as answering anxiety of guilt, and the modern age as answering anxiety of meaninglessness.
Religiously, he translates justification by faith as accepting acceptance. One has courage to be when one accepts being accepted in spite of being unacceptable.

books.thesis: Anxiety is more than a symptom. It's a condition of being free.
books.summary:
The Meaning of Anxiety grew out of Rollo May's doctoral work and treats anxiety as more than a symptom to be removed. He asks what anxiety actually is, and why it seemed to be spreading in his time. His answer is that anxiety is the response to a threat to values that a person holds essential to their existence as a self. This is why it feels different from fear of a specific harm.

May surveys earlier thinkers, including Kierkegaard, Freud, Kurt Goldstein and Harry Stack Sullivan, and finds each partial. He leans most on Kierkegaard's link between anxiety and freedom. He separates normal anxiety, which is proportionate and can be faced, from neurotic anxiety, which is out of proportion and involves repression. He ties anxiety to its time, pointing to competition and weakened shared values. Therapy, in his view, cannot promise an end to anxiety. It can help a person bear it and use it. The book is an early statement of American existential psychology.
ideas: Anxiety is a response to a threat to values the person holds essential to their existence as a self, which is why it differs from fear of a specific harm.
May surveys Kierkegaard, Freud, Goldstein and Sullivan, among others, and finds each partial. He leans most heavily on Kierkegaard.
He takes from Kierkegaard the link between anxiety and freedom. Anxiety goes with possibility, and a person who grows must move through it.
Normal anxiety is proportionate to the threat and can be faced constructively. Neurotic anxiety is out of proportion, involves repression, and blocks growth.
May ties anxiety to its time. He cites competitiveness and the loosening of shared values in modern Western society as reasons it was spreading.
Facing anxiety allows a person to grow, while avoiding it narrows life. New freedom tends to arrive with some measure of anxiety.
Therapy cannot promise to end anxiety. May says its job is to help a person bear it and make use of it.
May wrote the book while recovering from tuberculosis in a sanatorium, where he read Kierkegaard. It became his doctoral dissertation at Columbia, and Paul Tillich was his advisor.

Goldstein's work with brain-injured patients is used to show a catastrophic reaction, in which a person overwhelmed by a task falls into a disordered state. May treats it as anxiety when a person's world is shaken.

May traces Freud's shift in theory, from anxiety as transformed libido to anxiety as a signal of danger to the ego. He thinks the later version is closer to the truth but still lacks a view of the self.

books.thesis: Modern people have more freedom than ever, and less will to use it.
books.summary:
Love and Will looks at a modern puzzle. People have more freedom than before, and especially more sexual freedom, yet many report feeling numb, empty and unable to commit. Rollo May asks what has gone wrong with love and will, and suggests the answer lies in apathy, a defence against feeling too much. He draws on his work as a therapist as well as on literature and philosophy.

May separates sex from eros, the drive toward union and creation, and says our culture has reduced eros to technique. He describes the daimonic, a natural power that can take over a whole person and is destructive when denied but creative when integrated. He also separates wish from will and argues that each fails without the other. Throughout, care is the root. Critics call the book wide-ranging and loose, and some of its claims are better as observations than as proof. It remains a lively account of how feeling and choice depend on each other.
ideas: May starts from apathy. In an age of sexual openness many people feel numb, and he reads that numbness as a defence against feeling too much.
Eros is the drive toward union and creation, while sex is a physiological need. May says the culture reduced eros to technique and so lost its force.
The daimonic is any natural power, such as sex, anger or eros, that can take over the whole person. Denied, it erupts, and integrated, it can become creative.
A wish is imagining a possible act, while will is organising oneself toward it. May argues each is empty without the other.
Intentionality is the structure that gives experience its meaning, and May treats it as the bridge between wish and will.
Care is the root of both love and will. Without it, people become either detached from what happens or unable to act on their wishes.
May discusses pseudo-innocence, the claim to be harmless that is used to avoid owning one's power and its effects on others.
May distinguishes four kinds of love from the Greek, which are sex, eros, philia and agape. He holds that a mature love contains all four and that modern culture has flattened them into sex.

He criticises the new puritanism of technique, where sex becomes performance and measurement, as seen in the work of Kinsey and of Masters and Johnson. He says feeling is lost when function is the only goal.
May argues that violence grows from impotence and from the need to feel significant. When a person cannot affect the world, the daimonic can take over in destructive form.

books.thesis: Therapy built around four facts: death, freedom, isolation, meaninglessness.
books.summary:
Existential Psychotherapy is Yalom's textbook on a way of doing therapy that begins from the givens of human life. He asks whether psychological conflict comes only from repressed drives or also from our confrontation with certain facts of existence. He names four ultimate concerns, death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness, and organizes the book around them.

Yalom argues that each concern sets up a conflict between the awareness of a given and our wish to avoid it, and that many symptoms are ways of managing that conflict. He draws on philosophers such as Kierkegaard, Sartre and Frankl, and mixes in clinical examples from his own practice. He describes therapy as a real encounter between two mortal people, more than a technique. Critics ask how well the framework can be tested, and some find it long and uneven. It has been widely used in training, and it brought existential ideas into mainstream therapy.
ideas: Yalom proposes that psychological conflict comes from confronting the givens of existence, and not only from repressed drives. The four he names are death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness.
Death anxiety often shows up in disguise. Yalom describes two main defences, a belief in one's personal specialness and a belief in an ultimate rescuer.
Confronting mortality can also awaken a person. Yalom reports that those who face death sometimes shift their priorities and live more fully.
Freedom means we are responsible for our own lives, and that nothing outside us gives them structure. Yalom draws on Sartre and May here.
He distinguishes interpersonal isolation, isolation within oneself, and existential isolation. Relationships can ease the last but cannot remove it.
We seem to need meaning in a universe that supplies none. Yalom suggests that meaning tends to follow engagement with life more than direct pursuit.
The therapist is a fellow mortal and not a detached expert, so the relationship itself is central to the work. Critics ask how testable the framework is.
Yalom separates cosmic meaning, a scheme laid on the universe, from terrestrial meaning, found in purposes inside a life. He thinks people can live well with the second even without the first.
He describes how patients dodge responsibility, for instance by seeing themselves as victims of forces they did not choose. Therapy aims to show them their own part in creating their situation.
Following Jaspers, he points to boundary situations such as a death or a diagnosis, which can break through everyday routine and push a person to reconsider how to live.

books.thesis: Face death head on and life gets richer.
books.summary:
Staring at the Sun is Yalom's late, personal book about death anxiety. After decades as a therapist, he believes the fear of death often lies behind other complaints, and that most of us spend our lives trying not to look at it. The title borrows from La Rochefoucauld's remark that neither the sun nor death can be looked at steadily, and the book is an attempt to look anyway.

Yalom mixes stories from his practice with candid notes on his own aging and fears. He describes awakening experiences, in which a brush with mortality changes how a person lives, and the idea of rippling, in which our influence continues through others. He discusses Epicurus and the thought experiment of eternal recurrence as aids. The advice is modest and offered as experience, and critics find it uneven or too reassuring. Readers who want a treatise will not find one. What the book offers is a sober, humane account of how facing death might loosen its grip.
ideas: Yalom believes death anxiety often hides beneath other complaints, and after decades of practice he sees it as common and usually unspoken.
Awakening experiences are moments, often after loss or illness, when awareness of mortality changes a person's priorities and sometimes permanently shifts how they live.
Rippling is the idea that our influence passes outward through other people. It is a kind of survival that does not depend on personal immortality.
He discusses Epicurus, who held that nonexistence after death is like nonexistence before birth. Yalom admits the argument comforts some people far more than others.
Yalom suggests that the more unlived life a person carries, the greater the fear of death, so living more fully may lessen it.
He uses the thought experiment of eternal recurrence as a test. Imagine living your life again exactly as it was, and notice the regrets that appear.
The title borrows La Rochefoucauld's remark that neither sun nor death can be looked at steadily. The book mixes case stories with Yalom's own fears.
Yalom revisits two defences against death anxiety, the belief in personal specialness and the belief in an ultimate rescuer. He shows how each can fail when a person meets real loss.
He credits Ernest Becker's The Denial of Death as a major influence. Yalom takes Becker's claim that fear of death shapes our lives and applies it in the consulting room.
He suggests that talking openly about death, in therapy or in groups, makes it less frightening. Isolation with the fear, he thinks, makes it worse.

books.thesis: Medicine is good at fixing bodies and struggles with what matters at the end of life.
books.summary:
Atul Gawande is a surgeon who realised that his training had taught him to fix bodies and had said almost nothing about how people age and die. The book asks what a good end of life looks like once medicine can no longer cure, and what doctors, families and institutions get wrong when they treat old age as a problem to be solved.

Gawande moves through nursing homes, assisted living, hospice and his own father's illness. He argues that safety and survival have been allowed to crowd out autonomy, meaning the chance to keep living by one's own priorities. He suggests clinicians should ask patients what they fear, what they hope for and what trade-offs they would accept, and then help them act on the answers. The book offers no formula. It leaves open how to weigh a longer life against a better one when patients, families and doctors disagree, .
ideas: Gawande's medical training prepared him to rescue patients and left him unready to talk with people who could not be rescued, a gap he came to see as built into the profession.
Nursing homes often put safety and routine ahead of what residents want, so a long life can end up with little say over meals, schedules or possessions.
Physician Bill Thomas brought plants, dogs, cats and birds into a nursing home where he worked, and the book reports that residents became livelier and needed fewer drugs.
Keren Brown Wilson's assisted living idea started from giving frail people their own rooms with doors that lock and keys of their own, so privacy and choice survive dependence.
He describes doctors who decide for patients, doctors who only hand over information, and doctors who help patients work out what they want, and he favours the last kind.
The book reports that seriously ill patients who accepted hospice or palliative care sometimes lived as long as, or longer than, those who kept pursuing aggressive treatment.
A useful end-of-life conversation asks what the patient understands, what they fear and hope for, what they would give up, and what outcome they could not accept.
Gawande contrasts the modern institutional treatment of old age with his grandfather in rural India, who was cared for at home by his family and held status for his age.
He writes about his own father, a surgeon with a spinal tumour. The family had to work out what he valued before deciding which risks were worth taking.
A young pregnant woman with terminal lung cancer keeps hoping for more treatment, which shows how hard it is for patients and doctors to move from fighting disease to caring for comfort.

books.thesis: Interviews with dying patients, and the source of her famous five stages. Research doesn't support them as a sequence.
books.summary:
In the 1960s Elisabeth Kübler-Ross, a Swiss-born psychiatrist working in Chicago, began sitting with terminally ill patients and asking them what dying was like. Hospitals at the time mostly avoided the subject, and patients were often not told how ill they were. The book asks what dying people actually experience and what the living, especially medical staff, can do for them.

She builds the book from interviews and seminars and from the patients' own words. Out of these she describes denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance as reactions she kept seeing, with hope running through them. She urged doctors and nurses to listen rather than deflect. Later research has not found that people move through these reactions in order, and she herself said they were not meant as rigid steps. Many readers now value the book most for the permission it gave to talk with the dying, while the five stages remain the contested part.
ideas: Dying patients in hospitals were often avoided or kept in the dark, and she argued that this protected the staff from their own discomfort with death more than it protected the patient.
Her method was simple. She invited terminally ill patients to talk about their situation, often in front of students, and she treated their accounts as the main source of knowledge.
Denial comes first for many patients. Shock and disbelief at a terminal diagnosis act as a temporary buffer, and she saw it as a defence to respect rather than to break.
Anger shows up as the question of why this is happening to me. It often lands on nurses and relatives, who she said should try to understand it.
Bargaining is the attempt to postpone the end in exchange for good behaviour or promises. Depression follows as grief for what has already been lost and what is still to be lost.
Acceptance, in her account, is not happiness. It is a quiet, nearly feelingless stage in which patients are tired, want fewer visitors, and have made some peace with what is coming.
The stages were observations, not a schedule. Later studies have not found that people pass through them in order, and Kübler-Ross warned against treating them as fixed steps.
Hope persists through all the stages, she writes, even in patients who accept death. She advises staff not to take hope away, since it gives meaning to suffering.
The families of dying patients go through similar reactions and need support of their own. She asks staff to include relatives in conversations and not treat them as bystanders.
The work began with a seminar at the Chicago hospital where she taught, after theology students asked for help understanding crisis in human life. Her interviews with the dying became its material.

books.a: Sheldon Solomon, Jeff Greenberg and Tom Pyszczynski
books.thesis: Terror Management Theory argues for itself here: death anxiety drives culture.
books.summary:
The title borrows from William James, and the book follows Ernest Becker in asking why humans do so many things that look unrelated to survival, such as building monuments, fighting over beliefs and chasing status. Its answer is Terror Management Theory. We are animals who know we will die, and the authors say the resulting dread shapes much of culture.

Solomon, Greenberg and Pyszczynski lay out Becker's argument and then bring in experiments from their own labs and others. In a typical study, people reminded of their own death grow more attached to their worldview and harder on those who reject it. The authors connect this to religion, self-esteem, prejudice, politics and consumption. The book is written by the theory's founders, so it reads as a case for the theory rather than a neutral survey. Critics ask whether death is special or whether any threat to meaning would produce the same reactions.
ideas: Following Becker, they say humans combine animal bodies with minds that can picture their own death, and that this pairing produces a terror which must be managed somehow.
Cultures supply protection by offering a worldview that gives life meaning and a way to count as lasting, either through literal afterlives or symbolic ones such as legacy, nation or family.
Self-esteem works as a buffer. Feeling that one is a valuable person within a worldview that gives life sense is presented as the main way individuals calm their death anxiety.
They argue people distance themselves from their animal nature, which helps explain disgust at bodily functions and unease about the physical side of sex, since bodies remind us we will decay.

In mortality salience experiments, participants asked to think about their own death often judged people who share their beliefs more kindly and critics of their group more harshly than control participants did.
Because a rival worldview threatens the one that shields us, the authors tie death anxiety to prejudice, conflict and war, suggesting groups can treat different beliefs as a danger to life.
Some researchers question whether death is special or whether any threat to meaning produces similar reactions, and some mortality salience results have struggled in replication attempts.
The title comes from William James, who spoke of the worm at the core of our usual happiness. The authors take it to mean that awareness of death underlies ordinary life.
In one study, municipal judges who were reminded of death set a much higher bond for an alleged prostitute than judges who were not. The authors read it as defence of cultural values.
They argue that after the September 11 attacks, reminders of death helped raise support for George W. Bush. They cite experiments in which such reminders increased preference for a strong leader.

books.thesis: The existentialists as people: their lives, arguments and breakups.
books.summary:
Sarah Bakewell tells the story of existentialism through the people who made it, including Sartre, Beauvoir, Heidegger, Husserl, Camus and Merleau-Ponty. The book asks what a philosophy of freedom, authenticity and responsibility looks like when it is lived by real people with jealousies, politics, lovers and bad decisions.

She weaves biography together with plain explanation of the ideas. The story starts with an apricot cocktail in a Paris bar, moves through Husserl's call to return to the things themselves and Heidegger's account of being in the world, and follows Sartre and Beauvoir's partnership, the war years and the quarrels that broke up friendships. She does not hide Heidegger's embrace of the Nazis, and she leaves open how far a philosophy can be separated from the person who wrote it. The book closes by suggesting that questions about freedom and choosing a life keep returning, whatever happens to the label.
ideas: The story opens with an apricot cocktail, over which Raymond Aron told Sartre that phenomenology could make philosophy out of an ordinary drink, and Sartre reportedly reacted with excitement.
Husserl's phenomenology asked philosophers to go back to the things themselves, describing experience as it appears before explaining it, and this method shaped nearly everyone in the book.
Heidegger argued that we meet the world first as a place of tools and tasks we are involved in, not as detached observers looking at objects.
Heidegger joined the Nazi party in 1933. Bakewell shows how that sits uneasily with his thought and leaves readers to decide how to read him.
Sartre claimed that existence comes before essence, that people are condemned to be free, and that pretending we have no choice is bad faith, a form of self-deception.
In The Second Sex, Beauvoir applied existentialist ideas to women's situation, arguing that womanhood is shaped by society and history instead of being fixed by nature.
Camus broke with Sartre in the early 1950s over politics and the Soviet Union, and he also rejected the label existentialist for himself.
Merleau-Ponty appears as the thinker of the body. In his account, perception is not a mental act but something we do as embodied beings immersed in the world.
In 1935 Sartre took mescaline, and for some time afterward he felt followed by lobsters and other creatures. Bakewell says the episode shaped his sense of the dark side of consciousness.
After the war existentialism became a fashion in Saint-Germain, with cellar clubs, jazz, Juliette Greco, and Boris Vian's parodies. Sartre and Beauvoir found themselves cast as celebrities.

books.thesis: Life is short. Productivity can't change that, and accepting it helps.
books.summary:
An average human life lasts around four thousand weeks. Oliver Burkeman starts from that number and asks why so many people feel overwhelmed despite owning more time-saving tools than any earlier generation. His question is what we should do with a life that is short and in which we cannot do everything.

He argues that productivity advice treats time as a resource to be mastered, which quietly assumes that with enough efficiency we could fit it all in. We can't, so every yes closes off other possibilities. Drawing on Stoics, Buddhist teachers, Heidegger and modern psychology, he suggests accepting limits, choosing what to neglect, and finding some relief in how little any one life matters on a cosmic scale. Critics point out that the advice suits people who already have some control over their hours. The book leaves open how to live with the constant sense of missing out.
ideas: Four thousand weeks is roughly an eighty-year life, a number Burkeman uses to make finitude concrete and to remove the fantasy that there is plenty of time later.
The efficiency trap says that clearing tasks faster tends to bring more of them, so reaching the bottom of the inbox simply makes you the person who gets more work.
Staying busy has become a badge of importance, and Burkeman argues that the to-do list will never end, so peace has to come from accepting that rather than from finishing.
Every choice costs other choices. He recommends the joy of missing out in place of the fear of missing out, since a full life requires giving things up on purpose.
Treating time as a tool to be used leads people to treat the present as a means to some future that never quite arrives, which empties out the time they actually have.
Because neglect is unavoidable, he suggests deciding in advance which important things to do badly or skip, and keeping fewer projects open at once.
Cosmic insignificance therapy is his name for the relief of seeing that one's life matters little in the grand scheme, which can lower the pressure to make every week count.
Burkeman suggests paying yourself first with time. Put the most important work first in the day or week, and accept that other things will be done less well or not at all.
He argues that rest should be valued for itself and not used to recharge for more work. Treating leisure as a means to productivity, he says, keeps us in the same frame of mind.
He recommends limiting work in progress to a few projects and finishing before starting new ones. A small number of open tasks keeps the sense of a finite life from being buried.

books.thesis: Chasing security makes us anxious. Meaning lives in the present.
books.summary:
Alan Watts wrote this short book in 1951 and gave it the subtitle A Message for an Age of Anxiety. It asks why people who are safer and more comfortable than their ancestors still feel anxious, and why the more we try to secure ourselves, the less secure we feel.

The book is a set of essays rather than a tight argument. Watts draws on Buddhism, Taoism and Christian mysticism and returns to one point from several angles. The mind grabs at the future and the past, which exist only as thought, and so overlooks the one place where experience actually happens. Pleasure and pain, life and death come bundled together, and trying to keep only half of each produces tension. His remedy is to stop resisting impermanence and to pay attention to what is here now. Critics find him loose and more persuasive than rigorous, and the book leaves open what such acceptance looks like in practical choices.
ideas: Watts says the desire for security and the feeling of insecurity are the same thing, so the anxious grasping for safety is what produces the sense of being unsafe.
He separates faith from belief. Faith is an open mind willing to meet whatever turns out to be true, while belief is clinging to a fixed idea for comfort.
Pleasure and pain are bound together, so efforts to keep one and banish the other tend to create more tension than they remove.
Memory and anticipation take place in the present as thoughts, and people often live in these mental pictures of past and future instead of in the experience in front of them.
We confuse symbols with the things they stand for, and Watts's example is money mistaken for wealth, or reading the menu and calling it dinner.
The present moment is the only point at which anything is actually experienced, and he treats attention to it as the practical answer to worry about what comes next.
The sense of a separate self standing apart from experience is an illusion for Watts, since the thinker and the thought, the feeler and the feeling, are one process.
Watts describes his time as an age of anxiety. He says medicine and religion are tried as ways to buy security, and that the more they promise it, the more people worry.
He uses music as an analogy. We play a piece for the playing and do not hurry to the last note, and he says life should be treated the same way, without reducing it to a goal.
To try to hold on to life, he says, is like trying to grasp water, which runs away the tighter the fist closes. Living well means moving with the flow and not fixing it.

books.thesis: Private notes from a Roman emperor on controlling what you can and accepting what you can't.
books.summary:
Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180, and the notes later called Meditations were written in Greek for his own use, often while on military campaign. He never meant them for readers. They ask how a person with great duties can act well, stay steady and treat others fairly while facing loss, annoyance and death.

The book is a series of reminders, not a treatise, and the same points come back in different forms.
