He follows Stoic ideas: our judgments and actions are up to us, while other people's behaviour, our bodies, reputations and the events around us are not. The universe is orderly, everything passes, and humans belong to one community. Scholars still debate how systematic the notes are and how much is private venting. Some readers worry that the advice tips into resignation. Others read it as a training manual, written by someone who knew he often failed to follow it.
ideas: The notes were written to himself, in twelve books, with no known audience, and they read like exercises meant to correct his own tendencies and moods.
Each morning he reminds himself that he will meet meddling, ungrateful and arrogant people, and he says they act out of ignorance of what is good and bad.
Distress comes from how we judge events, and judgment is something he can change, so his task is to separate what is up to him from what is not.
He recommends the view from above, picturing the Earth and its crowds from a great height so that ambition, quarrels and worries shrink to proper size.
Fame does not last. Those who praise you will die and so will those who remember them, which he offers as a reason to stop craving reputation.
An obstacle to action becomes material for action, and what stands in the way can be turned into the way, which is his advice for setbacks.
Humans are made to cooperate, like hands or feet, so acting against other people goes against our own nature and treats a shared community as if it were not there.
Book One lists debts to those who shaped him, from his grandfather and mother to teachers and the emperor Antoninus. It reads as a record of gratitude and of the habits he learned from each.
He often says the universe is either providence or atoms, and that the right response is much the same either way. Either we belong to a rational whole, or there is nothing to fear in dissolution.
The past and future are not ours to lose, and only the present can be taken from us. He tells himself to retreat into his own mind, the inner citadel, where nothing external can reach.

books.thesis: Letters on time, death and friendship, and on living according to reason.
books.summary:
Seneca was a Roman statesman and, for a time, tutor and adviser to Nero. In his last years he wrote 124 letters to his friend Lucilius, a provincial official in Sicily, and they are usually read in selection. The letters ask how to live by reason when time is short, fortune is unreliable and a ruler can order your death.

Each letter is brief and practical, built around one theme, such as using time, choosing friends, facing poverty, fearing death or reading wisely. Seneca borrows freely from Epicurus and presents himself as a learner who has not reached the Stoic ideal of the wise person. Critics have long pointed out the gap between his praise of simple living and his great wealth. Nero eventually ordered him to kill himself, in 65, which gives the letters on death a grim backdrop.
ideas: The first letter urges Lucilius to claim his time for himself, since people guard money carefully and waste hours as if they cost nothing.
Seneca recommends reading a few authors thoroughly rather than many authors lightly, because a mind that wanders through many books settles into none of them.
On friendship, he advises thinking carefully before choosing a friend and then trusting completely, and he treats shared life with a friend as one of the great goods.
He suggests practising hardship, living for a few days on poor food and rough clothes, so that the fear of losing wealth loses some of its hold.
Death is not a single event ahead of us. Each day uses up part of life, so we are dying all along and have no reason to dread only the last step.
Travelling will not cure restlessness. A person who is unhappy at home carries the same mind abroad, and the work has to be done on oneself.
He argues that enslaved people are human beings and should be treated with decency, though critics note that he lived in wealth supported by that system.

In the letter on crowds, Seneca warns that mixing with them leaves one more greedy, cruel and inhuman. He describes the games where gladiators were killed and says he came home worse for having watched.
He quotes Cleanthes, that fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling. The Stoic path is to want what happens, so that necessity feels like choice.
In the letter on suicide, he holds that a person may leave life when it can no longer be lived well. He treats the freedom to die as a final guard against being forced to live in disgrace.

books.thesis: Personal identity isn't what matters. Once you see that, ethics looks different.
books.summary:
Derek Parfit's book asks what a person is and whether the answer matters for how we should live. It starts from the fact that our everyday views about self-interest, identity and morality seem to assume something we may not be able to find on inspection.

It has four parts, on self-defeating theories, rationality and time, personal identity and future generations. Parfit argues for reductionism, the view that a person's existence just consists in physical and psychological facts, with no further deep fact such as a soul. He uses thought experiments, including teletransportation and split brains, to show that what matters is continuity of memory and character rather than strict identity. He says this made death seem less bad and his own life less enclosed. The last part turns to population ethics and a conclusion he disliked and could not escape. Critics resist his reductionism, and he treated the book as unfinished work.
ideas: Parfit argues that some theories of self-interest and morality can be self-defeating, since everyone following them can leave everyone worse off, as in prisoner's dilemma cases.
Being nearer in time is no rational ground for caring more about an experience, he says, and he questions the common bias toward whatever is coming over what has passed.
In the teletransporter case you are scanned, destroyed on Earth and rebuilt on Mars from the scan, and Parfit asks whether the person who wakes up is you.
Reductionism holds that persons exist through bodily and psychological continuity, with no extra fact such as a soul or Cartesian ego that makes identity deeper than those links.
In the fission case each half of your brain is placed in a different body and both people continue your life, so identity cannot be what matters.
Parfit says that accepting this view felt like leaving a glass tunnel, because his own life seemed less separate from others and death felt less bad.

On the Repugnant Conclusion, certain reasonable-looking assumptions imply a vast population with lives barely worth living could be better than a smaller happy one, and Parfit never found a satisfying way out.
Parfit proposes that what matters in survival is Relation R, psychological connectedness and continuity with the right kind of cause. Identity is not what matters, and this relation comes in degrees.

The non-identity problem notes that a policy can change which people come to exist. If a depletion policy gives rise to different people than conservation would, it is hard to say anyone has been harmed.

In the section on mistakes in moral mathematics, he argues that acts can do harm together without harming anyone alone. In the case of the harmless torturers, each small shock is unnoticeable but the sum is agony.

books.thesis: An Epicurean poem: the world is atoms and void, and death is nothing to fear.
books.summary:
Lucretius wrote this Latin poem in six books to explain the philosophy of Epicurus to a Roman audience. It asks what the world is made of and what follows for how people should feel about gods and death. The poem's stated aim is to free readers from fears he thought were based on ignorance.

The argument begins with atoms and empty space. Everything is atoms and void, nothing comes from nothing, and nothing returns to nothing. The soul is material and disperses at death, so there is no afterlife to dread. The gods exist but take no interest in us, and thunder, disease and the rest have natural causes. Lucretius compares his verse to honey on the rim of a cup of bitter medicine. The poem seems unfinished and ends with a plague. Modern readers disagree about whether his arguments against fearing death succeed, since some say that death can still deprive us of good things.
ideas: Lucretius says he is putting hard doctrine into sweet verse, like honey on the rim of a cup of bitter medicine, so that readers will take it in.
Nothing comes from nothing and nothing is destroyed into nothing. Things are made and unmade by matter rearranging, which is why the world renews itself without a creator.
Everything is made of invisible atoms moving in empty space, and differences in shape and arrangement explain the many properties of the things we see.
Atoms sometimes swerve unpredictably, a idea Lucretius uses to break strict necessity and leave room for free will.
The mind and soul are material and made of fine atoms that spread out when the body dies, so nothing remains to suffer after death.
We feel no distress about the endless time before we were born, and Lucretius says the same calm should apply to the time after we are gone.
The poem opens with Agamemnon sacrificing his daughter Iphigenia, offered as an example of the evil that religion can inspire, while he insists the gods live untroubled and do not meddle.

Book Two opens with the line that it is sweet to watch from shore the struggle of a ship in a storm. Lucretius says it is sweet to see from what troubles you are free, and he uses it to praise philosophic calm.
Book Four takes love apart. He argues that passion for a single person is a kind of illusion and an affliction, and advises taking the physical side lightly instead of becoming bound to one lover.
The poem ends with the plague of Athens, described in grim detail. Many readers have found it an odd ending, and have debated whether it was meant to be finished.

books.thesis: Our moral language is a heap of fragments. Virtue, the book says, needs community and tradition.
books.summary:
Alasdair MacIntyre opens with a thought experiment. After a catastrophe, science is wiped out, and later generations keep only scraps of its vocabulary and rules without the understanding that gave them sense. He says modern morality is in that condition. The book asks why moral arguments today seem endless and why we lack any shared standard to settle them.

He traces the story from Aristotle's ethics of virtue through the Enlightenment attempts to ground morality in reason alone. He argues those attempts failed, leaving a culture in which moral claims often work as expressions of preference. His proposal is to recover virtue by understanding it through practices, through the shape of a whole life as a story, and through the traditions that carry such stories. Critics call this nostalgic and worry it leads to relativism or to ethics tied to small communities. The book leaves open whether tradition-based ethics can work in a pluralist society.
ideas: MacIntyre imagines a world where science is destroyed and only fragments of its language survive, and he claims our moral vocabulary has lost its original context in just that way.
Emotivism is the view that moral judgments only express feelings or preferences, and MacIntyre says people use moral language that way while pretending to appeal to impersonal standards.
The Enlightenment project of justifying morality by reason alone, in Kant, Hume and others, failed in his view because it discarded the idea of a human purpose that gave moral rules point.
He puts the choice as Nietzsche or Aristotle. Either morality is a mask for the will to power, or we should return to a purpose-based ethics of the virtues.
A practice is a cooperative human activity with its own standards of excellence, such as chess or farming, and the virtues are the qualities needed to achieve the goods internal to it.
A human life has a narrative unity, a story in which we are characters with a quest, and we make sense of actions by seeing where they fit in that story.
Moral reasoning happens inside traditions carried by communities, and the book ends by hoping for another, very different, St Benedict to help local communities sustain civility.

A practice has internal goods, which can only be had by taking part, and external goods such as money or fame. MacIntyre's example is teaching a child chess by offering sweets, so the child must come to value excellence itself.
He describes three social characters who embody emotivism, the Aesthete, the Manager and the Therapist. Each treats ends as given and asks only how to get what one wants.

He holds that rival moral arguments in modern debates, on justice, war and abortion, are interminable because they use premises that cannot be weighed against each other. The disagreement is deep, not merely about facts.

books.thesis: How do people change morally? Through attention, by learning to see others without the ego.
books.summary:
This short book collects three essays by Iris Murdoch, written when moral philosophy was dominated by pictures of the self as a will making clear choices. She asks how people actually change morally, and she suspects the answer lies in what happens before any choice is made.

Her answer is attention. Moral work is the slow, continuous effort to see other people and the world justly, against the pull of an ego that spins comforting stories. She gives the example of a mother-in-law who revises her opinion of her daughter-in-law without doing or saying anything, and a hovering kestrel that pulls her out of her own worries. Goodness for her is real and draws us, and cannot be reduced to our wishes or decisions. She criticises both existentialist and behaviourist pictures of the person. The essays give no method for becoming good and leave open how far the Good can be defended without religion.
ideas: Murdoch criticises the picture of a lonely will choosing between options, saying it overrates the moment of decision and neglects the vision that shapes what choices look possible.
The moral life is continuous, because what matters happens in how we look at people and situations over time, long before we face a decision.
In her example, a mother-in-law sees her son's wife as vulgar and then looks again and sees her as fresh and spontaneous, and all the change takes place inside her.
Attention, a term she borrows from Simone Weil, is a just and loving gaze directed at an individual reality, and she treats it as the main moral skill.
The selfish ego is a fantasy machine that builds flattering stories and distorts what we see, so that clear sight of others takes constant effort.
A hovering kestrel makes her forget her own anxious preoccupations, and she uses the moment to show how nature and art can draw us out of the self.
The Good is real, attracts us like a centre of gravity, and cannot be defined away as a human invention, even though we lack a clear picture of it.
Murdoch uses unselfing for what happens when great art or nature pulls us out of our small concerns. She sees this as training in moral perception, not mere pleasure.

Love, she says, is the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real. It is the main discipline of moral attention, and it is opposed to the ego's urge to turn others into figures in its own story.
She takes up Plato's image of the sun as the Good. She argues that moral progress is a movement toward perfection, which is known only dimly and still guides us as a standard.

books.thesis: Some of what we get blamed for comes down to luck. Moral theory struggles to admit it.
books.summary:
Bernard Williams published these essays between 1973 and 1981, and they share a worry about ethical theory that aims at purity. The title essay asks how much of what we are praised or blamed for depends on matters outside our control, and why moral philosophy has tended to pretend it does not.

Williams works through examples rather than a single argument. The painter Gauguin leaves his family to work in Tahiti, and whether he was justified depends on whether the painting succeeds, which he could not know beforehand. A lorry driver who is not at fault runs over a child and feels a regret that no bystander shares. Williams uses such cases to attack the Kantian hope that morality is shielded from luck, and to argue that utilitarian and Kantian demands can alienate people from the projects that give life a point. He offers no neat replacement and leaves open how to hold people responsible once luck is admitted.
ideas: The book is a collection of essays from 1973 to 1981, held together by Williams's suspicion that ethical theory tries to make morality neat and shielded from the accidents of life.
The Kantian picture says moral worth depends only on the will, and Williams argues that this hope of immunity from luck is a comforting fantasy.
Gauguin leaves his family for Tahiti to paint. Williams says whether the choice is justified depends partly on his turning out a great painter, which no one could know beforehand.
A lorry driver is blameless but runs over a child. Williams says he will feel agent-regret, a special regret for what he did, which a mere onlooker does not feel.
A man who can save only one of two people, one of them his wife, and stops to check whether it is permissible has, Williams says, had one thought too many.

Moral theories that demand impartial sacrifice can alienate people from their own commitments, so that integrity, the loyalty to projects that make life worth living, gets treated as mere self-indulgence.
In the essay on internal and external reasons, he argues that a person has a reason to act only if it connects with something already in their motivations.

Thomas Nagel wrote a reply to Williams's essay, and the two together are the usual starting point for the debate. Nagel adds a taxonomy that includes luck in results, circumstance, constitution and cause.
In the essay on practical necessity, Williams uses Luther's I can do no other to show a necessity found in deliberation. A person can feel that some options are not open to them without being forced.

In the essay on ethical consistency, he argues that when moral claims conflict, the one that loses leaves a remainder. Regret and a sense of what was owed are not mistakes, so ethics is not a tidy system.

books.t: Ethics and the Limits of Philosophy
books.thesis: Moral theories can't deliver what they promise. That is no reason to stop thinking.
books.summary:
Bernard Williams starts from the Socratic question of how one should live and asks whether moral philosophy can answer it by theory. He doubts the main contenders, utilitarianism and Kantianism, can deliver what they promise, which is a reasoned foundation that any rational person must accept.

He distinguishes ethics from what he calls the morality system, a narrow scheme built around obligation, blame and voluntariness. Real ethical life, he says, is broader, and uses thick concepts such as cruelty, courage and gratitude that mix description with evaluation. He worries that theory can wreck the ethical confidence it hopes to justify. On relativism he allows that we may not judge distant societies, while insisting that nearer ones can challenge us. The book is no argument for giving up reflection. It presents philosophy as a way to understand and criticise our ethical lives, and leaves open how to reason without a neutral standpoint outside them.
ideas: Williams begins with Socrates asking how one should live, a question wider and messier than what a person's duty is in some narrow case.
The morality system, which he calls a peculiar institution, centres on obligation, blame and guilt, and he thinks it misrepresents much of what matters in ethical life.
Thick ethical concepts like coward, brutal or grateful describe and evaluate at once, belong to particular communities, and can still carry real knowledge.
Reflection can destroy ethical knowledge, because theory can undermine confident habits and give nothing equally dependable in their place.
What he calls relativism of distance says it makes little sense to praise or condemn societies that are too remote to be real options for us.
There is no Archimedean point, no neutral place outside our ethical life from which theory could prove its foundations, and he doubts utilitarianism or Kantianism can supply one.
The Greeks, especially Aristotle and the tragedians, receive credit for treating character, luck and shame more honestly than modern morality does.
Williams contrasts science with ethics. Science might converge on an absolute conception of the world, but he thinks ethical thought has no such convergence to hope for.
He doubts Aristotle's hope of deriving an ethics from a theory of human nature. Even if we knew our nature, he says, it would not settle how to live among competing ways of life.
He assigns philosophy a more modest role. It should help us understand and criticise our ethical life from within and not lay a foundation for it from outside.

books.thesis: Fair principles are the ones you'd pick without knowing your place in society.
books.summary:
John Rawls asks what principles should govern the basic institutions of a society of free and equal people. He wants an alternative to utilitarianism, which he thinks allows some people's basic claims to be traded away for a larger total of happiness. His answer is called justice as fairness.

The method is the original position. Imagine representatives choosing principles for society behind a veil of ignorance, without knowing their class, talents, race or even their view of the good life. Rawls argues they would pick two principles: equal basic liberties for everyone, and inequalities allowed only if there is fair equality of opportunity and they benefit the least well off. Critics came from several directions. Nozick defended strong property rights, communitarians questioned the picture of the self, and feminists asked about the family. Rawls revised his view later. The book leaves unsettled how its principles apply to global justice.
ideas: Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought, so a law or arrangement has to be reformed if it is unjust, however efficient.
Utilitarianism fails to take seriously the separateness of persons, since it can justify sacrificing some people's basic interests for a greater sum of advantage to others.
The original position is a hypothetical situation in which people choose principles of justice together, set up so that the choice reflects fairness and not bargaining power.
Behind the veil of ignorance, nobody knows their class, talents, social position or conception of the good, which is meant to prevent self-serving principles.
The first principle gives everyone an equal set of basic liberties and takes priority over the second, so liberty cannot be traded for economic gain.
The difference principle allows social and economic inequalities only when they work to the benefit of the least advantaged, and when offices are open under fair equality of opportunity.
Rawls says people behind the veil would protect themselves against the worst position, and critics like Harsanyi reply that this reasoning is too cautious and expected utility is a better guide.

The subject of justice is the basic structure of society, meaning how major institutions assign rights, duties and shares of social benefits. Rawls leaves individual conduct and the private associations within it to other principles.

He uses reflective equilibrium, a method of adjusting principles and considered judgments against each other until they fit. The original position is justified by how well it matches our firm convictions.

Principles are judged by an index of primary goods, such as rights, liberties, opportunities, income and the social bases of self-respect. These are things any rational person is assumed to want whatever else they want.

books.thesis: Where did the modern self come from, and what moral sources does it still draw on?
books.summary:
Charles Taylor traces how people in the modern West came to understand themselves as having inner depths, as owing respect to all humans, and as entitled to affirm ordinary life. The book asks where this modern identity came from and what moral sources it still draws on, whether or not we admit it.

He proceeds historically, through Plato, Augustine's turn inward, Descartes's disengaged reason, Locke, Montaigne, the Romantics and modern writers. His central claim is that having an identity means having an orientation in moral space, a sense of what is worth doing and being, which a purely naturalistic picture of the person cannot capture. Some readers find the story too confident and too shaped by Taylor's Catholic sympathies. He admits that the moral sources behind modern ideals are contested, and the book ends without deciding whether they can sustain themselves without the religious background that first fed them.
ideas: Knowing who I am means knowing where I stand on questions of what is good and worth doing, so identity depends on an orientation in moral space.
Strong evaluation is the capacity to rank desires as higher or lower, and to judge them worthy or base, and not just to feel which is stronger.
Some goods, which Taylor calls hypergoods, rank above others and give a framework for judging the rest, and people usually hold such frameworks without stating them.
Augustine shifted attention inward, locating the path to God inside the self, and Taylor treats this as an early step in the modern sense of inner depth.
Descartes and Locke brought a disengaged, objectifying stance toward the self, in which we stand back and remake ourselves by control and method.
The Reformation and later movements affirmed ordinary life, work and family as places of real value, which overturned older ideas that the highest life lay in contemplation or war.
Romantic expressivism treated inner nature as a source of moral direction and said each person has an original way of being human, which prepared the modern ideal of authenticity.
Taylor argues that frameworks are inescapable. A person with no orientation toward the good would not be free but in an identity crisis, unable to tell what matters or who they are.

He distinguishes life goods, the things we value, from constitutive goods, the sources that make them worth valuing. These moral sources can empower us, and a loss of faith in them leaves ideals hard to sustain.

In the modern period, writers such as Joyce, Eliot and Pound use epiphanies, moments in which a deeper meaning shows itself. Taylor reads these as a late form of the Romantic search for sources inside the self.

books.thesis: Authenticity is a real ideal. Without something beyond the self to answer to, it collapses into narcissism.
books.summary:
Charles Taylor wrote this short book from lectures given in Canada, and he asks a question about ordinary culture. Is the modern emphasis on self-fulfilment a sign of decline, or does it hold an ideal worth saving? He wants to stand between those who mock it as narcissism and those who simply celebrate it.

He names three malaises of modernity: a narrowing individualism, the dominance of instrumental reason, and a drift toward soft despotism in politics. Against the critics, he argues that authenticity is a real moral ideal that grew out of thinkers like Rousseau and Herder, the idea that each person has their own way of being human to live out. But this ideal needs something beyond the self. Choices matter only against horizons of significance, and identity is shaped in dialogue with others. Without that background it shrinks into self-absorption. Taylor does not claim the culture can easily be repaired.
ideas: Individualism brings real gains in freedom to choose one's own life, but Taylor says it can also narrow people's concern, leaving them less interested in others and in larger purposes.
Critics of modern culture see narcissism and defenders see liberation. Taylor says both miss that authenticity is a moral ideal with its own demands.
Herder's idea that each person has an original way of being human, a measure of their own to live up to, is a source of the modern ideal of authenticity.
The dialogical self takes shape in conversation with significant others, so recognition matters, and no one can work out an identity entirely alone.
Choices only count against horizons of significance, a background of things that matter independently of my choosing them, such as history, nature, community and the demands of others.
Soft relativism, the idea that everyone has a right to their own values, undermines itself because it rests on the value of self-choice, which is itself a value beyond what anyone chooses.
Following Tocqueville, he warns of soft despotism, where people absorbed in private lives leave decisions to a distant administrative power that treats them gently and gives them little say.

Taylor names three malaises of modernity: individualism, the primacy of instrumental reason, and the loss of freedom through soft despotism. The book is an attempt to take them seriously without wishing for the past.

Instrumental reason is the kind of rationality that seeks the best means to a given end. Taylor warns that when it dominates, technology and cost-benefit thinking crowd out other ways of valuing things.

The book began as the 1991 Massey Lectures, published in Canada as The Malaise of Modernity. Taylor's strategy is retrieval, which means finding the moral ideal behind a degraded practice and not simply praising or condemning it.

books.thesis: How did belief become one option among many, and what does that do to meaning?
books.summary:
Charles Taylor's long book starts from a contrast. Around 1500 in Latin Christendom it was almost impossible not to believe in God, and today belief is one option among many and often a contested one. The question is how that change came about and what it has done to the way people find meaning.

He rejects what he calls subtraction stories, in which science removes religion and leaves humanism as what remains. Humanism was itself an invention. His account follows the shift from the porous self, open to spirits and powers, to the buffered self, and the rise of disciplined reform from the Reformation onward. The result is the immanent frame, a way of understanding the world that can be read as open or closed to the transcendent. People live under cross-pressures between belief and unbelief. Critics say his story centres on Latin Christianity. The book leaves open how a sense of fullness can be sustained.
ideas: Taylor separates three senses of secular: public spaces emptied of God, declining belief and practice, and a condition where belief is contestable, and the third is his main concern.
Subtraction stories say that when science and religion part, humanism is what remains. Taylor says humanism had to be invented and was a real new option.
The premodern self was porous, open to spirits, demons and forces outside the mind. The modern self is buffered, protected from them, and that change alters what experiences feel like.
Reform movements starting before and during the Reformation pushed people to remake themselves and society by discipline, a push he treats as one driver of disenchantment.
The immanent frame is the natural and social order as understood without reference to anything transcendent, and it can be lived either as closed or as open to something beyond.
People feel cross-pressures, tugged between belief and unbelief, and the number of positions available grows in what Taylor calls the nova effect.
People sense that life has a place of fullness, where things come together, and modern disenchantment brings a feeling of flatness that they respond to in many different ways.

Taylor describes three stages of the link between religion and society: paleo-Durkheimian, where church and state are bound together, neo-Durkheimian, where belonging is through a denomination, and post-Durkheimian, where spirituality is individual.

He tells of a Great Disembedding in which people came to be seen as individuals with rights and not as members of fixed orders. This change in the social imaginary made a moral order of mutual benefit seem natural.
He thinks the 1960s began an age of authenticity, where each person is encouraged to find their own way. Religion survives, but as one option among many and often on the terms of the self.

books.thesis: How much of a good life is at the mercy of luck? Greek tragedy and philosophy take it up.
books.summary:
Martha Nussbaum asks how much of a good human life is at the mercy of luck. Can a person be good and flourish whatever happens, or does flourishing depend on friends, health, politics and chance? She takes up the question through Greek tragedy and Greek philosophy side by side.

She reads Plato as trying to make goodness secure against fortune by setting reason above love and need. Aristotle, she argues, allows for a more exposed kind of good life, in which friendship, political activity and responsiveness to particular situations matter and can be damaged. The tragedians, especially in Agamemnon and Hecuba, show conflicts between real values and characters broken by events. She suggests that these vulnerable goods are valuable partly because they can be lost. Scholars dispute her readings of Plato in particular, and the book does not settle whether a life open to loss is worth its price.
ideas: The central question is how far a good life depends on things outside our control, such as friends, health, political circumstances and sheer chance.
In Agamemnon, the king must choose between sacrificing his daughter and abandoning the fleet, and Nussbaum says his anguish shows that even a right choice can leave real moral remainder.
Hecuba shows a person of good character broken by catastrophe, which Nussbaum uses to suggest that virtue can be damaged by what happens to us.
Plato's early dialogues hope that a science of measurement could remove luck from ethics, and Nussbaum presents this as an attempt to make goodness invulnerable.
She reads the Symposium as urging us to leave behind love of particular persons, and the speech of Alcibiades as a reminder of what that ascent would cost.
For Aristotle a good life needs friends, resources and a trained perception of particular cases, so practical wisdom responds to the situation instead of applying fixed rules.
She argues that vulnerability is part of the value of friendship, love and civic life, and that the fragile goods of a human life are like a plant, unlike a jewel.

In Antigone, Nussbaum sees a conflict between two real claims, family piety and civic duty. She says Creon fails by seeing only one, and she thinks the play shows that a good person can be forced into wrongdoing.

She reads the Phaedrus as a change of view by Plato, who now allows that madness and passion can be sources of the greatest goods. The self-sufficient reason of the middle dialogues is partly given up.
Aristotle, she notes, says Priam's disasters can damage his happiness. A good life can be undone by bad luck, though a good person will bear it nobly and not become wretched.

books.thesis: Emotions think. They are intelligent judgments about what we value.
books.summary:
Martha Nussbaum asks what emotions are and what part they should play in ethical and political life. Her answer in the subtitle, The Intelligence of Emotions, is that they are judgments about things that matter to our flourishing, not blind surges that reason must hold in check.

The book begins with her grief at her mother's death, which she uses to show that emotion recognises the importance of another person. Building on the Stoics but rejecting their wish to stamp emotions out, she says they reveal how needy and vulnerable we are. She draws on developmental psychology and on literature and music, including Proust, Augustine, Dante and Mahler, to explore love, disgust, shame and compassion. She argues that just societies need cultivated public emotions. Critics ask whether she makes emotions too cognitive, and whether compassion can sit comfortably with impartial justice. The book leaves that tension partly open.
ideas: Nussbaum opens with grief after her mother's death, using it to argue that an emotion can be a way of seeing someone's value, not an irrational upset.
Emotions are evaluative judgments about things outside our control that matter to our flourishing, which makes them closer to thoughts than to mere feelings.
Emotions expose our neediness. We grieve, fear and hope because we depend on people and things we cannot command, which she thinks a mature view should accept.
Drawing on psychology, she shows that adult emotions carry the history of infancy, including helplessness, dependence and early experiences of shame and disgust.
The ascent of love, a Platonic and Christian ladder from particular persons toward something higher, is examined through Plato, Augustine and Dante, and she is wary of leaving individuals behind.
Compassion needs three judgments: that the suffering is serious, that it was not deserved, and that I could meet something similar, so I count the other as part of my world.
She argues that societies need public emotions such as compassion cultivated through art, education and law, since just institutions depend on citizens who feel for others.

Her starting point is the Stoic view that emotions are judgments of value. She accepts this cognitive account but rejects the Stoic aim of removing emotions, since they track what we truly care about.

She writes about music and emotion, with Mahler's Third Symphony as a case, and argues that music can express emotional patterns without words. She uses this to widen her account beyond what can be stated in propositions.
Novels like Proust's In Search of Lost Time are read as studies of love, jealousy and memory. Nussbaum holds that narrative is a good way to learn how emotions work, since it shows their history.

books.thesis: Before any theory, the face of the other calls me to responsibility.
books.summary:
Emmanuel Levinas asks what comes before knowing, before theory and before any system of thought. His answer is the encounter with another person. He argues that Western philosophy has tended to reduce everything, other people included, to something the thinker can grasp and absorb, which he calls totality.

Against that, he describes the face of the other as something that exceeds every concept I form, and he calls this infinity. The face is an expression that addresses me and makes a demand, and the first thing it says is that I may not kill. My responsibility for the other person is asymmetrical, since I owe it without expecting anything back. Ethics therefore comes before ontology, the study of being. The book is dense and moves between phenomenology and Jewish thought, and many readers find it hard going. It leaves open how a face-to-face relation becomes justice among many people.
ideas: Totality is Levinas's name for the habit in Western philosophy of reducing everything to a single system of the Same, including other people, who become objects of knowledge or use.
Before the other person appears, the self lives in enjoyment and dwelling, at home in the world, and the encounter interrupts that self-contentment.
The other person exceeds any idea I form of them. Levinas calls this infinity, since the other can never be contained in a concept.
The face is not an object I look at. It is an expression that addresses me, calls for a response and cannot be mastered.
The first word of the face is that I may not kill, which Levinas treats as the origin of ethical obligation, whether or not it is heard.
My responsibility for the other is asymmetrical. I am responsible for them without waiting for them to be responsible for me, and it is not a contract.
Ethics is first philosophy, because the relation to the other comes before knowledge and before being, and the rest of philosophy depends on it.

The opening section says that Western philosophy has often taken ontology as first philosophy, a philosophy of power. Levinas ties this to war, which he says is the state in which beings are reduced to roles in a whole.
He sets Ulysses against Abraham as two figures. Ulysses returns home and keeps to the Same, while Abraham leaves his country for an unknown land and answers a call.
Fecundity, the relation to a child, is a way of being beyond oneself. Levinas says it opens a time that continues after one's own death, without making the child a mere extension of the parent.

books.thesis: Fragments on attention and affliction, and on detaching from the ego.
books.summary:
This book is a selection from the notebooks of Simone Weil, arranged by her friend Gustave Thibon and published in 1947, four years after her death. It is made of fragments rather than chapters. Its question is how a person can turn toward the good when the ego and the pull of nature keep dragging the soul down, as gravity drags a stone.

Weil's answers come in short entries on attention, affliction, the void and what she calls decreation. Grace is what comes from outside and lifts us, and we cannot produce it by effort, only make room for it. She mixes Christian mysticism with Plato, Greek tragedy and Indian texts. Because the entries were selected and ordered by Thibon, who shaped the result to his own religious view, scholars treat the arrangement with caution. The book cannot be read as a system, and it leaves open how a reader without her faith might use it.
ideas: Gravity is her image for the natural forces, including self-interest and the ego, that pull the soul downward as reliably as physical laws, while grace comes from beyond.
Attention is the practice of turning toward what is real without forcing it. Weil saw it as the substance of prayer and as the rarest kind of generosity.
Affliction differs from suffering. It joins physical pain, social humiliation and a sense of being crushed, and it can destroy a person's feeling of being someone.
She says we should accept the void and not fill it with imaginary consolations, since false comfort blocks the openness that grace needs.
Decreation means undoing the self's claim to be the centre of things, giving up the ego so that something real can take its place.
Beauty is for Weil a trace of the good in the material world, something that holds our attention without any wish to possess it.
Imaginary evil is varied and exciting while real evil is monotonous and dull, and imaginary good is boring while real good is always new and surprising.
The book was assembled by Gustave Thibon from notebooks Weil left with him in 1942, and published after her death. It is a sequence of aphorisms and not a systematic treatise.
Creation, for Weil, is an act of withdrawal. God lets the world exist by retreating, which means the absence of God from the world is a sign of love and not of neglect.

She uses Plato's Great Beast for the social, the collective force that gives out opinion and approval. Real goodness, she argues, must resist its pull, and false good often comes dressed as the social.

books.thesis: Includes "Two Concepts of Liberty", on negative and positive freedom.
books.summary:
Isaiah Berlin's 1969 collection has four essays: one on political ideas in the twentieth century, one on historical inevitability, the famous Two Concepts of Liberty, and one on John Stuart Mill. The question running through them is what freedom means, and why people have done terrible things in its name.

Berlin separates negative liberty, being left alone by others, from positive liberty, being one's own master. He treats both as legitimate but warns that positive liberty can be bent into a doctrine that some rational elite knows people's true selves and may force them to be free. Behind this lies value pluralism, his belief that human goods are many and can conflict without a hidden harmony. Critics, including MacCallum, argue the distinction is too sharp because freedom always involves an agent, an obstacle and a goal. The essays leave open how to balance liberty against other values.
ideas: In Historical Inevitability, Berlin attacks the idea that history follows laws that excuse individuals, arguing that it would dissolve praise, blame and moral responsibility.
Negative liberty is the area in which a person can act without being obstructed by others, and Berlin treats it as the core of what most liberals value.
Positive liberty is the wish to be one's own master, a subject rather than an object, steering one's life by one's own purposes.
Positive liberty becomes dangerous when it splits the self into a real, rational self and an ordinary one, since that split can justify coercing people for their own good.
Value pluralism says that human goods such as liberty, equality and justice are many and sometimes conflict, so some loss is unavoidable and harmony is a dangerous fantasy.
Berlin reads Mill as defending liberty because people are fallible and differ in the ends they pursue, so a society needs room for experiments in living.
Critics like MacCallum say there is really one concept of freedom, since it always involves an agent, an obstacle and a goal, and Berlin's two categories blur.

Two Concepts of Liberty was his inaugural lecture at Oxford in 1958, and the 1969 volume added a long introduction answering critics. There Berlin clarifies that his two concepts are historical strands and not a strict logical split.

Berlin insists that liberty is liberty and not equality, justice or culture. Poverty may make freedom worthless to a person, but he says it does not make it absent, and the two should not be confused.

He describes the retreat to the inner citadel, where a person escapes coercion by shrinking what he wants. This is a form of positive liberty that gains freedom by changing the self, and Berlin thinks it can be a way of giving up.

books.thesis: The bullshitter doesn't care if what he says is true. That makes him worse than a liar.
books.summary:
Harry Frankfurt wrote this essay in the 1980s and published it as a small book in 2005. He begins with the observation that there is a great deal of bullshit around and very little theory about what it is. The book asks what bullshit is, why it is so common and how it differs from lying.

His central claim is that the liar and the bullshitter stand in different relations to truth. The liar knows the truth and works to hide it, so he is still tied to it. The bullshitter does not care whether what he says is true, only what impression it makes. For this reason Frankfurt says bullshit is a worse enemy of truth than lying. He suggests it flourishes when people feel obliged to speak on matters they know little about, and when scepticism about objectivity leads people to prize sincerity instead. Critics say his line between liar and bullshitter is too tidy.
ideas: Frankfurt notes that bullshit is everywhere yet we lack a clear account of it, and he sets out to say what it is.
Drawing on the idea of humbug, he describes bullshit as a kind of pretence short of lying, especially about one's own thoughts, feelings and attitudes.
A liar needs to care about the truth in order to avoid it, whereas the bullshitter has no concern with it either way.
Bullshit arises when circumstances demand speech beyond one's knowledge, as when people feel obliged to give opinions on every subject.
He recounts Fania Pascal telling Wittgenstein she felt like a dog that had been run over, and Wittgenstein replying that she did not know what that felt like.
People who doubt that any account of reality can be correct often fall back on sincerity, being true to oneself, and Frankfurt calls that stance bullshit as well.
A bullshitter's statements may even be true by accident. What matters is that they were picked for their effect, not for their accuracy, which is why they erode the habit of caring.
Frankfurt's essay first appeared in 1986 in the journal Raritan, and was published as a small book in 2005. Its sales surprised many people, who found the topic timely.
He argues that bullshit is a greater enemy of truth than lies, because the liar still respects the truth enough to hide it. The bullshitter loosens the hold of any distinction between true and false.
He contrasts bullshit with the bull session, where people speak freely, trying out ideas without committing to them. Everyone understands that the talk is not meant as a serious statement of belief.

books.thesis: Our final reasons come from what we love.
books.summary:
Harry Frankfurt asks where our reasons for acting finally come from. Moral rules, self-interest and reason itself all seem to run out at some point, and he suggests that what we care about and love provides the last ground. The book is a short set of essays on caring, love, necessity and the meaning of a life.

He defines love as a disinterested concern for the existence and good of the beloved. He reverses the usual order of explanation, saying that love does not respond to the value of what we love but creates it. Parents love their children without having chosen to, and that is his model case. He also writes of volitional necessity, the fact that some things we simply cannot bring ourselves to do, and he ties identity and meaning to what we cannot help caring about. Critics ask whether this leaves love's authority arbitrary, and whether it can account for love of unworthy objects.
ideas: Practical reason cannot be the final foundation of action, since reasons come to an end somewhere, and Frankfurt places the end in what we care about.
Love is a disinterested concern for the existence of the beloved and for what is good for them, rather than a means to some benefit for ourselves.
Frankfurt reverses the common picture and says that love creates the value of the beloved, instead of responding to value that was already there.
A parent's love for a child is the main example, since it is neither earned by the child's merits nor chosen after weighing reasons.
Volitional necessity describes limits of the will. There are things we cannot bring ourselves to do, and these limits show what we love and who we are.
What a person cares about determines the shape of their life, so meaning comes from wholehearted care for something and not from an external standard.
Critics ask whether love can ground reasons if it can attach to unworthy objects, and the book gives only a partial answer.
Love is always of a particular person and not of a list of qualities, so the beloved cannot be swapped for someone who has the same traits, and this particularity is part of why love gives reasons.
Frankfurt contrasts volitional necessity with the rational necessity of Kant, saying that what binds us most deeply is what we cannot bring ourselves to will against, not what reason alone commands.
He treats wholeheartedness, being free of inner conflict about what one cares about, as a mark of a good life, and ties it to a kind of self-love that means caring about one's own ends.

books.t: The Open Society and Its Enemies
books.thesis: Certainty about utopia ends in tyranny. Open societies can correct their mistakes.
books.summary:
Karl Popper wrote this book in New Zealand during the Second World War and later called it his contribution to the war effort. It asks what ideas helped make totalitarianism possible and what kind of society can resist it. Its two volumes treat Plato first, then Hegel and Marx.

Popper argues that these thinkers share historicism, the belief that history follows laws that let us predict where it must go, and that this belief licenses leaders to override individuals for the sake of a promised future. He opposes utopian social engineering with piecemeal reform that can be tested and reversed. The open society, as he describes it, is one where citizens can criticise policy and replace rulers without bloodshed. Many classicists and Hegel scholars say he caricatures his targets. Popper also raises the paradox of tolerance and leaves open how an open society can defend itself without losing what it defends.
ideas: Popper described the book as his war effort, written in New Zealand during the Second World War as a response to the rise of fascism and communism.
In a closed society, customs are treated as fixed and sacred, and in an open one individuals face personal decisions and can criticise their institutions.
He reads Plato's Republic as a blueprint for a closed society, with rule by philosopher-kings, censorship and fixed classes, though many classicists say this is unfair.
Historicism is the belief that history follows laws we can discover and use to predict the future, and Popper argues it is mistaken and dangerous.
Utopian engineering aims to rebuild society according to a blueprint and tends to require authority and silencing of dissent, while piecemeal reform fixes specific problems and can be reversed.
Democracy for Popper is defined less by who rules and more by whether a people can remove a government without violence.
The paradox of tolerance says that unlimited tolerance can destroy itself, so a society may have to defend itself against the intolerant.
Popper treats Hegel as a defender of the authoritarian state and Marx as a historicist whose prophecies could not be tested, while crediting Marx with a sincere humanitarian motive.
He argues that political action should aim to reduce avoidable suffering and not to maximise happiness, since the first goal is clearer, less open to abuse and easier to agree on.
Popper speaks of the strain of civilization, the unease people feel when they leave the sheltered life of the tribe and must take responsibility for their own choices.

books.thesis: Meaning is use. Private experience can't be what language rests on.
books.summary:
Wittgenstein's late book, published after his death in 1953, asks how words come to mean anything, what it is to follow a rule, and why philosophical problems seem so hard to leave alone. It begins by quoting Augustine's account of how a child learns language, as if every word were a name for an object.

Rather than offer a theory, Wittgenstein gives numbered remarks, examples and imagined scenes. He introduces language-games, family resemblance, the argument about rule-following and the argument against a private language. His view of philosophy is therapeutic: confusion arises when language is taken out of the contexts where it does its work, and the aim is to show where the confusion started. Interpreters disagree sharply about what he concludes, especially on rules, where Kripke's reading is both influential and disputed. The book has no single doctrine and leaves open what philosophy should be once its old questions are dissolved.
ideas: Augustine's picture says words name objects and sentences combine names. Wittgenstein argues this describes only a small part of what we do with language.
Language-games, such as builders calling for slabs and blocks, show that words acquire meaning from the activities in which they are used.
For a large class of cases, the meaning of a word is its use in the language, so to understand a word is to know how it is used.
Games share no single feature that all of them have, only overlapping similarities like members of a family, and many everyday concepts work the same way.
A rule cannot interpret itself, so following one depends on shared practice and agreement in how people go on, not on an inner act of grasping.
The beetle in the box suggests that if each person had a private thing they called a beetle, it could play no role in the meaning of the word.
Philosophy aims to show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle. Problems arise when language goes on holiday, and the remedy is to see how words are used.

The private language argument says that a word for a purely private sensation would have no check on correct use, since whatever seems right to the speaker would be right, and that removes any sense of being right or wrong.

Pointing at something to define a word does not settle its meaning by itself, because the same gesture can be taken in many ways, so ostensive definition already assumes a background of shared training.
In the later part he discusses seeing-as, using the duck-rabbit figure to show that noticing an aspect is neither plain seeing nor plain interpretation.

books.thesis: What can be said can be said clearly. Of what we can't speak, we must stay silent.
books.summary:
Wittgenstein's first book was published in 1921 and written partly while he served in the First World War. It asks how language can represent the world and what limits that places on what can be said. It begins with the sentence that the world is all that is the case.

The core idea is the picture theory. A proposition pictures a possible state of affairs by sharing its logical form. Compound propositions are built from simple ones by logical operations. What cannot be said, such as logical form itself, ethics, aesthetics and the mystical, can only be shown. Near the end, Wittgenstein says that anyone who understands him will see his own propositions as nonsense and will throw away the ladder after climbing it. Interpreters disagree sharply over whether this means there are unsayable truths or whether the book aims to show that supposed truths are plain nonsense. Wittgenstein later rejected much of it.
ideas: The book opens by saying the world is all that is the case, meaning the world is the totality of facts, not of things.
In the picture theory, a proposition represents by sharing logical form with the situation it describes, as a map or model does.
Compound propositions are truth-functions of elementary ones, so all sayable language can be broken down into simple propositions about how things stand.
Some things can be shown but not said. Logical form is visible in the way language works, yet any attempt to state it produces nonsense.
The limits of my language mean the limits of my world, a line that has been read as pointing toward a kind of solipsism.
Ethics, value and the mystical lie outside what can be said, and he describes the feeling of the world as a limited whole as something that cannot be put into propositions.
The closing pages call the book's own propositions nonsensical, a ladder to be thrown away, and end by saying that whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.
The book is numbered in a decimal system, with seven main propositions and sub-propositions that mark how much logical weight each carries, so the form of the text mirrors its structure.
Tautologies and contradictions say nothing about the world, and Wittgenstein holds that the propositions of logic are tautologies, so logic has no subject matter of its own.
Names in elementary propositions refer to simple objects, which form the unchanging substance of the world, though he never gives an example of one.

books.thesis: We perceive with a lived body. No detached mind involved.
books.summary:
Merleau-Ponty asks how perception works and what kind of being does the perceiving. He rejects two dominant pictures. One, empiricism, builds perception from bits of sensation. The other, intellectualism, says the mind constructs it through judgment. Instead he starts from the experience of a body living in a world.

His central claim is that the body is the subject of perception. We do not have a body the way we have a coat. We are our bodies, and they give us a practical grip on the world before any reflection. He supports the point with cases from psychology and neurology, such as phantom limbs and the patient Schneider, whose injury shows a gap between concrete and abstract movement. Perception is always from a viewpoint, so things show only some sides. The book is dense and demanding, and readers disagree over how fully it escapes the mind and body split. He also writes about other people and freedom.
ideas: Perception is where knowledge starts. Science builds on the world as we live it, and Merleau-Ponty asks us to return to that lived experience.
Empiricism assembles perception from separate sensations and intellectualism says judgment constructs it, and he argues both misdescribe the experience of seeing something as a whole object.
The lived body is the subject of perception. I am my body, and it gives me a way of having a world, in contrast to a thing I own.
The body schema is a practical, pre-reflective sense of where my body is and what it can do, which lets me reach for a cup without measuring.
The patient Schneider could perform concrete movements such as scratching a mosquito bite, but not abstract ones like pointing on command, which shows that action has its own kind of understanding.
In a phantom limb, a person keeps feeling a missing limb as part of their habitual world, and Merleau-Ponty says neither a purely bodily nor a purely mental account explains this.
Perception always has a point of view, so objects show only some sides and carry a horizon of more to see, and that incompleteness belongs to how real things appear.
Motor intentionality is the idea that consciousness is first of all not an I think but an I can, so the body is directed toward the world in action before any thought about it.
Drawing on Gestalt psychology, he argues that we perceive structured wholes, a figure against a ground, and not collections of atomic sensations.
Speech is described as a kind of gesture, and thought completes itself in being expressed, so meaning is not a private idea that language merely labels.

books.thesis: How phenomenology works: bracket your assumptions, then describe experience itself.
books.summary:
Husserl's 1913 book sets out how phenomenology is supposed to work. It asks how knowledge can be grounded in consciousness and how philosophy might become a rigorous science of experience, starting from what is given rather than from theories about the world.

The method begins with the natural attitude, in which we take the world to be simply there. Husserl proposes the epoché, a suspension of the belief that the world exists, so that we can study experience itself. Consciousness is always consciousness of something, which he calls intentionality, and he separates the act of experiencing from the object as experienced. By varying examples in imagination, he says we can grasp essences. The book moves toward transcendental idealism, where the world depends on consciousness for its sense. Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty took the method in other directions and rejected that turn, and it remains debated whether the bracketing Husserl asks for can be carried out.
ideas: The natural attitude is our ordinary stance, in which we treat the world as simply there and take its existence for granted, and Husserl starts by describing it.
The principle of all principles says that whatever presents itself in intuition, as it is given, is a legitimate source of knowledge within the limits in which it is given.
Eidetic reduction means varying an example in imagination to see what cannot change, and this is how Husserl thinks we reach the essence of a kind of thing.
The epoché brackets our belief that the world exists, without denying it, so that experience can be examined on its own terms.
Intentionality is the claim that consciousness is always consciousness of something, directed toward an object, whether that object is real, remembered or imagined.
Husserl separates noesis, the act of perceiving or judging, from noema, the object as it is experienced, so he can describe experience without settling what exists outside it.
The reduction leads to pure consciousness, and Husserl argues that the world's sense depends on it, a transcendental idealism that Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty rejected.
Husserl wants philosophy to become a rigorous science without presuppositions, and he opposes psychologism, the view that the laws of logic are just facts about how minds happen to work.
He separates sciences of fact from eidetic sciences of essence, such as geometry, and presents phenomenology as an eidetic science of consciousness and not an empirical one.

Physical things are given only through changing perspectival profiles, which he calls adumbrations, while consciousness is given directly, so he treats consciousness as absolute and the world as relative to it.

books.thesis: Desire produces things. Capitalism and psychoanalysis both try to capture it.
books.summary:
Deleuze, a philosopher, and Guattari, a psychoanalyst, wrote this book in the aftermath of 1968 as the first volume of Capitalism and Schizophrenia. It asks what desire is and why people so often come to want their own repression. It is aimed at Freudian psychoanalysis and at the forms of power that capitalism supports.

Their central move is to treat desire as productive. They say it does not come from lack. It makes connections, flows and things, and they describe desiring-machines to capture this. Psychoanalysis, in their account, shuts the unconscious inside the family triangle of mother, father and child. Capitalism frees flows of money and labour, then re-captures them. They praise the schizophrenic process as a way of breaking through, while distinguishing it from the suffering of patients in hospitals. The style is dense and playful, and critics call it obscure and romantic about madness. The authors offer schizoanalysis as an alternative and leave its politics open.
ideas: Desire is productive. It makes connections, flows and new things, and treating it as a lack to be filled is, they say, a mistake that suits those in power.
Desiring-machines are their image for desire at work, always connecting to something else, as a mouth connects to a breast or a hand to a tool.
They accuse psychoanalysis of reducing the unconscious to the family triangle of mother, father and child, which they say domesticates desire into a private drama.
Following Spinoza and Reich, they ask why people fight for their servitude as if it were their salvation, a question they apply to fascism.
The body without organs, a phrase taken from Artaud, is a surface on which desire is recorded and which resists being organised into a fixed hierarchy of functions.
Capitalism decodes older social codes and frees flows of money and labour, then re-captures them, and in their view it works only by constantly approaching its own limits.
Schizoanalysis is their alternative to psychoanalysis, and they praise the schizophrenic process as a breakthrough while separating it from the clinical patient, a distinction critics find romantic.
They describe three syntheses of the unconscious, connective, disjunctive and conjunctive, as the ways desire joins, divides and distributes its elements.
History is sorted into three social machines, the primitive territorial one, the despotic one and the capitalist one, each with its own way of coding and managing flows of desire.
Foucault's preface calls the book an introduction to the non-fascist life, and the authors set a paranoid, fascist pole of investment against a schizophrenic, revolutionary one.

books.thesis: Speech does not outrank writing. Meaning is always deferred.
books.summary:
Jacques Derrida asks why Western thought has ranked speech above writing, treating the spoken word as close to thought and writing as a pale copy. He calls this tendency phonocentrism, part of a wider logocentrism that looks for a source of meaning that is fully present.

He reads Saussure, Lévi-Strauss and Rousseau to show how each says writing is secondary while relying on features that belong to writing. He introduces différance, the idea that meaning comes from differences between signs and from endless deferral, and the trace, the mark of what a sign differs from. He also describes the supplement, something that both adds to a thing and replaces it. The famous line that there is nothing outside the text is often read as claiming only words exist. Defenders say it means no reading can step outside context. Critics such as Searle called the argument obscure and exaggerated, and the debate has not closed.
ideas: Logocentrism is Derrida's name for the long habit of treating spoken presence as the source of meaning and writing as a secondary copy of speech.
Saussure treats writing as external to language, yet Derrida argues his account of language relies on differences between signs, a feature he says belongs to writing.
Rousseau treats writing as a dangerous supplement to speech, and Derrida says a supplement both adds to something and substitutes for it, so the original was never complete.
Lévi-Strauss describes writing among the Nambikwara as a violence brought by outsiders, and Derrida replies that this view idealises speech and overlooks forms of violence that predate writing.
Différance names both difference and deferral. A sign gets its meaning from how it differs from other signs, and that meaning is never fully settled.
Every sign carries a trace of the others it differs from, so no meaning is purely present, and there is no unmarked origin to find.
The line that there is nothing outside the text is often read as saying only books exist. Defenders say it means no reading can step outside context.
Archi-writing is Derrida's name for a general structure of marks and traces that makes both speech and ordinary writing possible, so writing in the narrow sense is not a late addition to speech.
He argues that the privilege given to phonetic writing is ethnocentric, and that Western thinkers have misread non-phonetic scripts such as Chinese as less developed.
The first half surveys the logocentric tradition, and the second half is a close reading of Rousseau's Essay on the Origin of Languages, where the theory of the supplement is worked out.

books.thesis: Take one consistent principle, equal consideration of interests, and apply it to hard cases.
books.summary:
Peter Singer takes a single principle, equal consideration of interests, and applies it to hard practical questions. The book asks how we should act on matters such as animals, abortion, euthanasia, poverty and the environment if we try to be consistent and follow the argument without relying on tradition.

The principle says that like interests should count equally, whoever has them. Singer argues that this puts animal suffering on the moral map and that preferring human interests simply because they are human is speciesism, comparable to racism. He holds that what makes killing wrong depends on features such as self-awareness and having plans for the future, and he draws controversial conclusions about disabled newborns. He argues that people in wealthy countries are obliged to give much more to the poor. Disability activists protested strongly, and other philosophers dispute his utilitarian reasoning. The book leaves open how far consistency should override moral intuitions.
ideas: Equal consideration of interests does not mean equal treatment. It means similar interests count the same whoever has them, whatever their race, sex or species.
Speciesism is giving less weight to an animal's interests purely because of its species, and Singer compares this to racism and sexism as an unjustified prejudice.
Persons, in his sense, are self-aware beings who see themselves as existing over time, and killing them wrongs them in ways that killing beings without such awareness may not.
Singer rejects the sanctity of human life as a basis for ethics and argues that a newborn's severe disability can be morally relevant to decisions, a claim that remains highly controversial.
Voluntary euthanasia should be permitted in some circumstances, he argues, because people have a right to make decisions about their own death, with safeguards against abuse.
The drowning child analogy says that if we would ruin our shoes to save a child, we should also give to relieve distant suffering, which makes ordinary affluence morally demanding.
Disability activists protested his views and some philosophers say his consistency comes at the price of discarding strong moral intuitions that should count as evidence.
Singer defends preference utilitarianism, which weighs the satisfaction of interests and preferences of all affected beings and not only their pleasure and pain.

He applies the principle of equal consideration to food, arguing that the suffering caused by factory farming outweighs the minor benefit of human taste, and that this makes eating animals hard to defend.
On abortion he argues that moral weight depends on capacities such as sentience and self-awareness, and that birth is not a morally decisive line, a position that many readers reject.

books.thesis: Six philosophers take on unpopularity, money, love, inadequacy, a broken heart and difficulty.
books.summary:
Alain de Botton asks whether philosophy can console us for everyday troubles. The book takes six philosophers, Socrates, Epicurus, Seneca, Montaigne, Schopenhauer and Nietzsche, and sets each against a problem, in order: unpopularity, not having enough money, frustration, inadequacy, a broken heart and difficulty.

His premise is that philosophy began as a guide to living well, and that academic philosophy has often drifted from that purpose. The chapters mix short biography, plain explanation and everyday scenes, and each philosopher is read as an adviser rather than a system builder. Socrates says to follow reason over the crowd, Epicurus says friends and freedom matter more than luxury, and Seneca tells us to adjust our expectations. Professional philosophers have often dismissed the book as popular and tidy. It makes no claim to settle disputes between the thinkers, and it leaves open whether consolation is the same as being right.
ideas: De Botton argues that philosophy began as a practical guide to living well, and that much academic philosophy has moved away from helping people with their troubles.
Socrates is the guide for unpopularity. He accepted a death sentence rather than abandon his reasoning, and the lesson is that logic should decide a matter, not majority opinion.
Epicurus is cited on money. He held that happiness needs friends, freedom and time for thought, none of which depend on luxury.
Seneca is matched with frustration. Anger and disappointment grow from false expectations, so we should remember how much of life is outside our control.
Montaigne is the guide for inadequacy, easing shame about the body and the mind by pointing out that even the great sit on their own behinds.
Schopenhauer is offered for a broken heart. His pessimism consoles by reminding us that suffering is common and part of life, which helps us feel less singled out.
Nietzsche is the voice for difficulty. He suggests that hardship is a condition of growth and that what looks like an obstacle may be necessary to achievement.
The book is aimed at general readers and builds each chapter around a vivid scene or image from a philosopher's life, which makes it easy to read but light on argument.
Epicurus separates natural and necessary desires from vain ones, and De Botton uses this to question advertising that presents luxury as the route to happiness.
Critics note that offering quotations from six thinkers as remedies turns philosophy into self-help and passes over the disagreements between them.

books.thesis: One question, twenty answers, all drawn from Montaigne's life and essays.
books.summary:
Sarah Bakewell uses the life of Michel de Montaigne to pursue one question, how to live, and gives it twenty different answers. Each chapter takes up a way of living that Montaigne tried or described, so the book works as a biography and as a reflection on what a life might be.

The structure follows the man. Montaigne withdrew to his tower library around the age of thirty-eight and began writing essays about himself and everything else. He mourned his friend La Boétie, nearly died after a riding accident, served as mayor of Bordeaux in a time of plague and religious war, and kept asking what he really knew. Bakewell draws out answers such as paying attention, questioning everything and guarding a private space within public life. She also traces how readers over centuries found themselves in his essays. None of the answers is final, and the book does not claim that Montaigne had the last word on living.
ideas: The book takes the form of one question, how to live, followed by twenty attempts at an answer, and none of the answers is meant to be final.
Montaigne retired to his tower library at about thirty-eight, after his father's death, and began writing the essays that made him famous.
His friendship with La Boétie ended with La Boétie's death, and Bakewell shows how that loss shaped Montaigne's thinking about friendship and grief.
After being thrown from his horse and nearly killed, Montaigne found the experience peaceful, which fed into his view that we should not worry about death.
One answer is to read a lot and forget most of what you read. Montaigne said he had a poor memory, and he treated it as a lesson in thinking for oneself.
His motto, usually given as What do I know, expressed a habit of doubt, and Bakewell presents scepticism as part of his curiosity instead of a pose.
Montaigne recommends keeping a back shop, a private inner room, while serving in public life as mayor of Bordeaux during plague and war.
In the essay on cannibals, Montaigne suggests that people call barbarous whatever is not their own custom, and Bakewell uses it to show his early taste for comparing cultures with an open mind.
Montaigne said that he was himself the matter of his book, and Bakewell shows how his essays became a self-portrait that wanders from topic to topic without a plan.
His travels through Italy and Germany to take spa waters for kidney stones show his curiosity about other customs and about the body, and Bakewell treats his illness as one of his teachers.

books.thesis: Feel accepted with no conditions attached, and people grow toward health.
books.summary:
Carl Rogers collected these papers under the subtitle A Therapist's View of Psychotherapy. They ask what helps people change in therapy and what kind of person emerges when someone is freed to grow. He writes from experience as a psychologist who began to trust his clients more than his theories.

His argument is that therapy works when the therapist offers certain conditions: genuineness, unconditional positive regard and empathic understanding. Given these, he says clients move away from facades and from what they feel they should be, toward trusting their own experience and living more fully, a direction he described as becoming a fully functioning person. Rogers was one of the first to record sessions so they could be studied. Critics say the picture of human nature is too optimistic and the claims hard to test, and later work has debated whether these conditions are enough. The book leaves open how far growth is a natural tendency.
ideas: Client-centred therapy trusts the client's own capacity to find direction, so the therapist follows instead of interpreting from above.
Congruence, or genuineness, means the therapist is real in the relationship rather than hiding behind a professional front.
Unconditional positive regard means accepting the client as they are, without judging or requiring them to earn approval.
Empathic understanding means sensing the client's inner world as if it were one's own, without losing the as-if quality.
