Rogers describes therapy as a process in which people move from fixed, distant relations to their feelings toward flowing and owning them.
Many clients begin by hiding behind facades and asking who they really are, and Rogers describes them gradually dropping masks that they felt they had to wear.
The fully functioning person is open to experience and trusts their own organism, and critics say this view is too optimistic about human nature.
Rogers speaks of the locus of evaluation, and says healthy change moves it from outside the person, in the approval of others, to inside, in the person's own sense of what is right.
He was among the first to record therapy sessions and to study outcomes empirically, which brought psychotherapy into the research laboratory.
In his essay on communication he says the main barrier is the tendency to evaluate, and he proposes that each side restate the other's view to the other's satisfaction before replying.

books.thesis: Why study only illness? Psychology should study growth and self-actualization too.
books.summary:
Abraham Maslow asks why psychology spends so much of its effort on illness and so little on health. He argues that a field studying only damaged people gives a distorted picture of human nature, and he wants a psychology that also studies growth, creativity and the best that people can be. The book is a landmark of what he called the third force.

He distinguishes deficiency motivation, driven by needs we must fill, from growth motivation, which seeks fulfilment. He describes self-actualization, peak experiences of wonder and unity, and what he called Being-values such as truth, beauty and goodness. His evidence came from case studies of people he judged to be unusually healthy. Critics point out that those people were chosen by his own standards, the sample was small, and the framework reflects a particular culture. He insists that science should include values. The book leaves open whether these ideas can be tested.
ideas: Maslow argued that psychology had been built on the study of the sick and that a fuller account needs to study healthy, creative and fulfilled people as well.
Deficiency motivation arises from needs that must be filled, such as safety, while growth motivation is the drive toward fulfilment and does not stop when a need is met.
Self-actualization is the tendency to become what one is capable of becoming, which he saw as the mark of psychological health.
Peak experiences are brief moments of intense joy, wonder or unity that he found many people report, and he treated them as glimpses of healthy functioning.
Being-values such as truth, beauty, goodness and wholeness are what self-actualizing people tend to care about, and Maslow treats them as real motives, not just preferences.
His healthy subjects were people he chose by his own judgment, which critics say makes the evidence thin and the conclusions subjective.
Every child faces a choice between safety and growth, and healthy development depends on safety needs being met enough that growth becomes attractive.
Maslow contrasts B-cognition, seeing something for its own sake and as a whole, with D-cognition, seeing it in terms of what it can do for our needs.
He distinguishes B-love, which accepts the other person as they are and does not try to use them, from D-love, which arises from need.
He presents humanistic psychology as a third force beside behaviourism and Freudian psychoanalysis, one that studies the whole person and human potential.

books.thesis: The book the hierarchy of needs came from.
books.summary:
This is the book in which Maslow set out his hierarchy of needs, first sketched in a 1943 paper. It asks what moves people and proposes that human needs are organised by priority. He wanted a theory of motivation that treated the person as a whole and was neither reduced to drives nor to responses to stimuli.

He describes physiological needs, safety, love and belonging, esteem and self-actualization. The lower needs tend to dominate until they are reasonably met, after which higher ones come forward, and a need that is satisfied stops motivating. He studied people he considered self-actualizing, including historical figures such as Lincoln. Maslow says the order is flexible and has exceptions. The familiar pyramid does not appear in the book and was drawn later by others. Research has not strongly backed a strict order, and cultural studies suggest priorities vary. The book leaves unresolved how to test growth and fulfilment scientifically.
ideas: Physiological needs such as hunger, thirst and sleep come first, and a person who is truly starving finds that most other concerns shrink or disappear.
Safety needs cover order, predictability and protection from threat, and they show most clearly in children and in times of disaster or insecurity.
Belonging and love form the next level, the need for affection, friends and a place among others, and Maslow says that frustration of it is a major cause of poor adjustment.
Esteem has two forms, self-respect and the respect of others, and Maslow connects it with confidence, achievement and a sense of being useful.
Self-actualization is the need to become what one is capable of being, and Maslow studied people he judged to be examples, including Lincoln.
Lower needs tend to dominate until they are reasonably satisfied, after which higher needs emerge, and a satisfied need stops acting as a motivator.
Maslow said the order is flexible with many exceptions, the pyramid is not in the book, and later research has not strongly confirmed a strict sequence.
Beside the five levels, Maslow describes cognitive needs, the desire to know and understand, and says that curiosity is a basic human drive and not only a tool for survival.
His portrait of self-actualizing people lists traits such as spontaneity, a focus on problems outside themselves, a need for privacy, autonomy, a democratic outlook and frequent peak experiences.

He gives rough percentages, suggesting that an average person is satisfied perhaps 85 percent in physiological needs but only about 10 percent in self-actualization, and presents them as illustration and not as data.

books.t: Cognitive Therapy and the Emotional Disorders
books.thesis: Distorted thoughts keep depression and anxiety going. They can be examined and changed.
books.summary:
Aaron Beck was trained as a psychoanalyst and noticed that his patients had streams of automatic thoughts running alongside what they said. This 1976 book asks what keeps depression, anxiety and related problems going, and argues that the way people interpret events is central to how they feel and act.

Beck proposes that emotions follow from interpretations, and that people with emotional disorders show systematic distortions such as arbitrary inference, selective abstraction, overgeneralization, magnification and minimization. In depression he describes a negative view of the self, the world and the future. Therapy is a collaboration in which patient and therapist treat beliefs as hypotheses and test them against evidence and behavioural experiments. Later research gave this approach a large evidence base. Critics have said that it may overstate the causal role of thinking compared with biology and circumstances. The book leaves open how much cognitive change is a cause of recovery and how much a result.
ideas: Beck began as a psychoanalyst and noticed that patients reported streams of rapid, automatic thoughts, which led him to treat thinking as the place to intervene.
The cognitive model says that emotions follow from how a situation is interpreted, so two people can react very differently to the same event.
In depression Beck describes a cognitive triad, a negative view of oneself, one's experiences and the future, which feeds on itself.

He lists thinking errors such as arbitrary inference, selective abstraction, overgeneralization, and magnifying or minimizing events, which are ways of reading facts that bias them toward threat or loss.
In anxiety, people overestimate danger and underestimate their ability to cope, so a harmless situation can feel overwhelming.
Collaborative empiricism treats beliefs as hypotheses that patient and therapist test against evidence, with behavioural experiments, instead of arguing the patient out of them.
Underlying schemas, stable beliefs formed early, bias interpretation, and critics say the approach may overstate thinking's causal role compared with biology and circumstances.
Beck argues for content specificity, meaning that depression centres on themes of loss and defeat while anxiety centres on danger and threat.
For depressed patients he describes behavioural methods such as activity scheduling and graded task assignment, which counter inertia and give evidence against the belief that nothing can be done.
He acknowledges earlier influences such as Albert Ellis, George Kelly and the Stoic idea that people are disturbed by their view of events and not by the events themselves.

books.thesis: Trauma, from war to abuse, follows common patterns. Recovery happens in stages.
books.summary:
Judith Herman asks what links the damage done by combat, rape, domestic violence and political terror, and why knowledge about that damage keeps being lost. Her starting observation is that psychiatry has studied trauma in bursts and then forgotten it, and that each revival followed a political movement, first around hysteria, then shell shock, then the Vietnam veterans and the women's movement.

The book argues that the aftermath looks similar whatever the cause. She describes the core symptoms, then makes the case that long captivity, as in abusive homes or camps, produces a wider pattern than the standard diagnosis covers. Recovery, she says, runs through three stages: safety, remembrance and mourning, and reconnection with ordinary life. She stresses that the stages overlap and that no one does them alone. Whether this wider pattern deserves its own diagnosis is still debated, but her staging remains a common reference for clinicians.
ideas: Herman traces a repeating cycle in the history of psychiatry: trauma is studied, denied and forgotten again, and it returns only when a social movement forces the subject open.
Trauma symptoms fall into three groups: hyperarousal, in which the body stays on alert, intrusion, in which the event returns uninvited, and constriction, in which feeling and action shut down.
Prolonged abuse in a situation of control, such as a violent home or a prison camp, changes a person more broadly than a single frightening event does.
Herman compares domestic abuse with political captivity and argues that coercive control works the same way in both, through fear, isolation and the loss of any sense of choice.
Recovery begins with safety, in the body and in the person's surroundings. She argues that uncovering the past before safety exists tends to do harm.
The second stage is remembrance and mourning, where the survivor tells the story in full and grieves what was lost, with a witness who can bear to hear it.
The last stage is reconnection. Survivors rebuild trust and a place among others, and Herman says healing happens in relationships, with group settings often useful because they end isolation.
Herman proposes complex post-traumatic stress disorder as a diagnosis for survivors of prolonged abuse, since the standard picture of PTSD does not capture the damage to identity and relationships.
She calls the central conflict the dialectic of trauma, the pull between the wish to deny horrible events and the wish to proclaim them aloud.
Bystanders are pushed to take a side, and she notes that it is tempting to side with the perpetrator, who asks only that people do nothing, while the victim asks them to share the burden.

books.thesis: Trauma lives in the body, the book argues. Hugely influential, and criticized for overstating the neuroscience.
books.summary:
Bessel van der Kolk, a psychiatrist who worked with Vietnam veterans and with abused children, asks why trauma so often outlasts the event and why talking alone sometimes fails. His answer is in the title: the body holds what the mind cannot put into words, and survivors are stuck reacting to a past that feels present.

The book mixes patient stories, brain imaging findings and his own clinical history. He argues that trauma disturbs the systems that sense danger and regulate the body, and he backs treatments that work through the body as well as speech, such as EMDR, yoga and neurofeedback. He also pushes for a wider diagnosis for traumatised children. Critics say he overstates what brain scans show and leans on small studies, and some of his preferred therapies have thinner evidence than the book suggests. Even so, it changed how many general readers talk about trauma.
ideas: Traumatised people often react to a harmless moment as if it were the original danger, because the brain's alarm system keeps treating the past as the present.
Van der Kolk describes the thinking brain going quiet during a flashback, which he links to imaging studies, and says this is why survivors struggle to put what happened into words.
Many survivors lose the ability to sense their own bodies, so they cannot tell what they feel. He treats rebuilding that awareness as a first task of therapy.
The book discusses the large study of adverse childhood experiences to show that early neglect and abuse are common and tied to later illness and troubled lives.
He argues that children raised amid abuse show a pattern the standard adult diagnosis misses, and he campaigned for a separate diagnosis, which the diagnostic manual declined to adopt.
Treatments he describes include EMDR, yoga, neurofeedback and theatre work, on the view that the body needs a way to feel safe that talk cannot supply.
Critics argue the book claims more certainty about brain mechanisms than the research supports, and that its picture of trauma stored in the body is more metaphor than finding.
Van der Kolk draws on Stephen Porges's polyvagal ideas to explain how social safety calms the stress response, a theory that some researchers question.
He uses the triune brain model, with reptilian, mammalian and thinking layers, to explain why reason fails when the alarm system takes over, though the model is widely seen as outdated.
He cites animal studies of inescapable shock to explain why traumatised people may freeze or stay passive when they could act to protect themselves.

books.thesis: Ten therapy stories about people up against death, freedom and isolation.
books.summary:
Irvin Yalom is an existential psychiatrist, and this book asks what happens in the consulting room when people run into the facts they most want to avoid: that they will die, that they are responsible for their own lives, and that each of us is finally alone. Ten stories, each built around one patient, show those facts coming up through symptoms like obsession, grief, weight and loneliness.

The book works by telling, not by arguing a system. Yalom writes as a fallible participant, admitting irritation, doubt and mistakes, and he disguises his patients. His claim is that therapy is mostly an honest meeting between two people, and that real change often comes when someone stops fighting these givens and starts looking at them. Readers who want evidence will not find it here. What they get is a vivid, sometimes self-critical account of one therapist's method, which helped make the case for therapy as storytelling.
ideas: Yalom organises his therapy around three givens: death, freedom and isolation. His claim is that many everyday symptoms are an attempt to dodge one of them.
Death anxiety often shows up disguised. Patients complain of other troubles while their fear of ending sits underneath and shapes what they do.
Freedom means that each person has to author a life with no ready design. Yalom presents responsibility as frightening, and sees much passivity as a way to avoid it.
The title story concerns a woman consumed by obsessive love for a former lover. Yalom treats the obsession as something to be worked through, even to be killed off, and not indulged.
He is open about his own reactions to patients, including dislike and aversion, and he argues that a therapist's honest feelings are useful clinical information.
The therapeutic relationship itself is the main tool. What happens between the two people in the room is treated as a live sample of how the patient lives.
Because he tells these cases as stories, Yalom shows therapy as a human encounter with uncertainty. Patients are changed names and details, so the book offers narrative, not data.
Yalom adds meaninglessness to death, freedom and isolation as a fourth ultimate concern, and says that people who lack a sense of purpose often show it as boredom or restlessness.
In the story of the woman he calls Fat Lady, he describes his first revulsion toward an obese patient and shows how admitting that feeling to himself opened the work.
His existential approach draws on Nietzsche, Kierkegaard and Sartre and not on Freud's drive theory, treating anxiety as a response to the human situation and not a sign of buried urges.

books.thesis: Decades of practice in short lessons.
books.summary:
The Gift of Therapy is Irvin Yalom's attempt to hand on what he learned over decades of practice, addressed to younger therapists and, he says, to their patients as well. It asks a plain question: what actually helps in the room? The answer is spread across dozens of short chapters, each a single piece of advice.

There is no single argument. Yalom offers rules of thumb and the reasoning behind them, drawn from his own sessions, and he is frank about where he thinks the field has gone wrong, including its drift toward manuals and quick fixes. The recurring view is that the relationship between therapist and patient does most of the healing and that techniques matter less. He leaves open how much of his advice would suit a therapist with a different temperament, and he says as much. The short format makes it easy to read in pieces, and the lessons reflect his existential outlook throughout.
ideas: The relationship between therapist and patient is the agent of change. Technique matters, but Yalom says it works mainly through the bond it supports.
He urges therapists to attend to the here and now, to what is happening between the two people in the session, since it shows how the patient treats others.
Yalom advises building a new therapy for each patient and warns against forcing everyone into one model or a manual.
He argues for careful, honest self-disclosure. A therapist who shares real feelings, in moderation, gives the patient permission to be honest too.
He treats dreams as useful material in therapy, a way to reach what the patient has not yet said, and he recommends asking about them directly.
Yalom is wary of leaning on diagnostic labels, and says they can narrow the therapist's view of the person sitting in the room.
He thinks therapists should have therapy themselves, and should look at their own fear of death, because unexamined anxieties leak into their work.
The book is made of 85 short chapters, each a piece of advice for younger therapists, so it reads like a notebook of working habits and not a theory.
Yalom urges therapists to look out of the patient's window, trying to see the world as the patient sees it, and to remember that therapist and patient are fellow travellers.
He draws on his group therapy research to stress the instillation of hope, saying that a patient's belief that therapy can help is itself part of the cure.

books.thesis: A psychiatrist writes about living with her own bipolar disorder.
books.summary:
Kay Redfield Jamison is a psychiatrist who studies mood disorders, and in this memoir she tells how she has lived with manic-depressive illness since adolescence. The book asks what the illness is like from inside, and what it costs and gives a person who also treats it for a living.

She does not argue so much as report. Jamison describes the early highs, the crashes that followed, a suicide attempt, and the years she kept the diagnosis private for fear of her career. She writes about the lure of mania as well as its wreckage, and about how hard it is to keep taking medication when part of you misses the illness. Her conclusion is that lithium and psychotherapy together kept her alive and functioning, and that the love of others mattered as much. She leaves open whether she would give the illness back, and she is honest that the answer is not simple.
ideas: Jamison describes her first manic episode as a teenager as intoxicating, with racing thoughts, boundless energy and confidence, before the crash that followed it.
Mania is not only wreckage. She admits that it felt wonderful and that missing those highs makes it harder to stay on medication.
She attempted suicide in her twenties, and writes about it plainly, using it to show how deeply depression can distort judgment.
For years she hid her illness from colleagues and kept her treatment quiet, fearing that disclosure would cost her licence and standing in psychiatry.
Lithium is central to her account. It brought stability but came with side effects, and she resisted taking it, as many patients do.
She argues that medication alone was not enough, and that psychotherapy gave her a place to make sense of the moods.
Jamison writes of the support of family, friends and her husband, and presents steady relationships as part of treatment, not an extra.
Jamison was a professor of psychiatry who studied mood disorders while living with one, so her account carries both clinical knowledge and personal experience.
She describes how untreated mania led to reckless spending, damaged relationships and risky behaviour, and how the wreckage left behind added shame to the illness.
Her long relationship with her own psychiatrist is shown as steady and humane, and she credits that care with keeping her alive.

books.thesis: An atlas of depression: personal, clinical and cultural.
books.summary:
Andrew Solomon asks what depression is, where it comes from and why it has been so hard to understand and treat. He writes as a sufferer, drawing on his own breakdowns, and as a reporter who spent years interviewing patients, doctors and researchers. The book won the National Book Award for nonfiction.

It is built as an atlas. Chapters cover the experience itself, causes, treatments, suicide, addiction, poverty, history and politics. Solomon argues that depression is partly biology, partly circumstance and partly the stories a society tells, and that no single framework explains it. He is open about his own use of medication and therapy, and he weighs other treatments with a mix of curiosity and doubt. His conclusion is cautious. Depression is a common human condition and not a failure of will, and finding a way to live with it often needs several kinds of help. He leaves the deeper causes unresolved.
ideas: Solomon describes depression as the opposite of vitality more than of happiness. A person can lose the capacity to feel anything at all.
He draws on his own breakdowns and shows how the illness arrived gradually, with ordinary tasks turning into things he could not do.
The book argues against one cause. Genes, brain chemistry, loss, stress and social conditions all feed in, and different people reach depression by different routes.
Treatment is covered at length, from medication and talking therapy to electroconvulsive therapy and alternatives, and he gives each a hearing without pretending any one works for everybody.
He gives a chapter to suicide and treats it as a real outcome of depression, not only a moral failing or an act of choice.
Solomon looks at poverty and social hardship and notes that depression is shaped by circumstance as well as biology, and that people in poor places seldom get care.
He reads depression across history and cultures and shows that the way it is named and judged changes with the age, though the suffering recurs.
The title comes from the medieval idea of acedia, the noonday torpor that monks feared, and Solomon uses it to link old accounts of despair with modern depression.
He calls depression the flaw in love, the pain of being unable to care or connect, and says it is love's absence turned into a condition.
The book rests on many interviews with other sufferers, which he uses to show how varied the illness is and to keep his own story from standing for everyone's.

books.thesis: Severe depression described from inside, briefly and exactly.
books.summary:
William Styron, the novelist, wrote this short book after his own severe depression in 1985 and an essay he had already published about it. It asks a narrow question and answers it with care: what does the illness actually feel like, and why does ordinary language fail to describe it?

Styron argues that the word depression is too weak for what he went through, since it sounds like a low mood and not a storm in the mind. He describes the dread, the loss of the ability to read or write, the sense of being watched by his own despair, and the way suicide began to seem reasonable. He points to a possible trigger in giving up alcohol, and to the suicides of other writers. He admits he does not know why he recovered, and says rest and the hospital helped. The book is brief, plain in manner, and humble about what anyone can explain.
ideas: Styron objects to the word depression. He thinks it sounds like a dip in mood and has no weight for the agony he went through.
He describes a pain that is hard to compare with anything physical, a drowning feeling, and says that people who have not had it cannot easily imagine it.
He reports losing the ability to concentrate, and he describes his writing and reading falling away, which shows how the illness invades the work a person lives by.
The onset followed his sudden decision to stop drinking, and he suggests, with caution, that giving up alcohol may have helped open the way for the collapse.
He writes about thoughts of suicide as a growing, calm kind of logic and not a moment of rage, and he places his own near-miss alongside writers who died that way.
Hospitalisation, rest and removal from his usual pressures were part of how he recovered, and he gives no tidy medical account of why it lifted.
He argues that those who have not been through it should be slow to judge, and that sufferers need patience, not advice to pull themselves together.
The book grew from an essay, and it opens with a 1985 trip to Paris to receive a literary prize, where Styron's dread and disorientation first became clear.
He suspects that a sedative he was taking, Halcyon, worsened his condition, and uses this to warn that medications can interact with the illness in unpredictable ways.
The night he nearly killed himself, he heard a passage of Brahms from a film, thought of his family and the life he would destroy, and checked himself into hospital.

books.t: Maybe You Should Talk to Someone
books.thesis: A therapist in therapy, and how people hide from what hurts.
books.summary:
Lori Gottlieb is a therapist who, after a sudden breakup, finds herself sitting in a therapist's office as a patient. The book asks why people avoid the thing that hurts, and what changes when they stop. It follows her own sessions with a therapist she calls Wendell, alongside several of her patients, whose details she has altered.

Her argument is shown in the cases. People arrive complaining about one thing, a partner or a boss, and the real trouble turns out to be underneath. She finds she does the same, and that her own therapy shows her what she tells patients. A newly married young woman facing terminal illness, an older woman threatening to end her life, and a difficult television writer are among those she describes. The book concludes that change needs honest looking and often a witness, and that therapists are as stuck as anyone. It is a memoir, not a study, so it offers observation, not evidence.
ideas: Gottlieb's own breakup brings her to therapy, and she finds that the crisis she names is not the thing she is really stuck on.
Patients often come asking for someone else to change, a partner or a parent, and therapy turns slowly toward what they themselves can do.
Therapists are people with their own blind spots, and the book shows one in the patient's chair learning how it feels to be seen.
She describes a young newlywed with terminal cancer to show how people face the end, and how presence can matter more than advice.
One patient, an older woman, says she will end her life on a coming birthday unless things improve, and the book uses her to show how despair gets stated as an ultimatum.
People often hide behind a story about their lives, and Gottlieb argues that the story protects them from grief or fear they have not allowed themselves to feel.
She presents good therapy as steady, honest company over time, and she resists the idea of a quick technique that fixes a life.
Gottlieb's own therapist appears under the name Wendell, and the book shows how he answers her questions and holds back advice, as the therapist she has been to others.
She follows four patients across a year while describing her own therapy, so the reader sees both sides of the room.
Change, she suggests, involves loss, since giving up an old way of coping means grieving what it once protected.

books.thesis: The Grant Study asks how men's defences matured, and what that predicted.
books.summary:
George Vaillant followed a group of Harvard men chosen as college students in the late 1930s and early 1940s, in what became known as the Grant Study. Adaptation to Life asks how these men coped with the strains of adult life, and whether the way they handled inner conflict predicted how their lives went.

The book reports on their careers, marriages, health and psychological troubles into middle age, and ranks their unconscious defences from immature, like projection, to mature, like humour, altruism and anticipation. Vaillant argues that defences change over adulthood and that the more mature ones tend to go with better outcomes. He leans on interviews and his own clinical judgement, which makes some of the ratings subjective. The sample was narrow, and critics doubt the findings carry over to other groups. The book's main point is that adults keep developing and that how someone copes matters more than what happened to them.
ideas: The study followed Harvard students chosen in their college years, tracking jobs, marriages, health and mental state to see what lives actually looked like decades later.
Vaillant treats defence mechanisms as unconscious ways of managing anxiety and conflict, and he argues that they can be observed and rated from interviews.
He ranks defences from immature, such as projection, through neurotic ones, to mature ones such as humour, altruism, suppression and anticipation.
Men who used more mature defences tended to do better at work, in love and in health, while heavy use of immature ones went with trouble.
Defences are not fixed. Vaillant reports that many men moved toward more mature ones over the years, so character keeps changing in adulthood.
Some men who looked well adjusted early on later struggled, and some who started poorly improved, so early promise predicted less than expected.
The group was male, white and from an elite college, so critics doubt the findings apply broadly, and the ratings relied on the judgement of the interviewers.
Vaillant groups defences into four levels, psychotic ones such as delusional projection, immature ones, neurotic ones such as intellectualisation and repression, and mature ones.
He links the men's lives to Erikson's stages, such as intimacy, career consolidation and generativity, and uses them to show how adult development unfolds.
He treats defences as ways of coping and not as pathology, since even immature ones protect a person from pain that would otherwise be unbearable.

books.thesis: Seventy-plus years of the Grant Study, and one finding: warm relationships predicted flourishing.
books.summary:
Triumphs of Experience reports on the Harvard Grant Study after more than seventy years, with the men now old. George Vaillant, who directed the study for decades, asks what actually predicted a good life and a good old age, and he tries to sort the strong findings from the weak ones.

His answer is plain. Warm relationships, in childhood and across adult life, predicted more than most other things, including wealth and early career success. He reports that heavy drinking did serious damage, to marriages and to health, and that mature defences and a capacity to learn from experience helped men recover from hard starts. He compares the Harvard men with two other groups in the wider research on adult development, a group of working-class Boston men and a group of gifted women. The sample remains narrow, and measuring something like flourishing is debatable, but the pattern about close relationships has been widely repeated.
ideas: The central finding is that warm relationships predicted flourishing in later life more reliably than income, status or early intelligence did.
A loving childhood, especially a warm bond with a parent, was linked with better health, work and mood well into old age.
Alcohol abuse emerges as a major wrecker, tied to divorce, depression and early death, and Vaillant treats it as a leading cause of ruined lives.
Men with hard childhoods could still do well later, and Vaillant credits mature defences and the ability to take in warmth from others.
He places the Harvard men beside other groups in the long research on adult development, including working-class men from Boston and women of high ability, to test whether patterns held.
Retirement, ageing and the later stages of life are covered, and many men found new meaning in generativity, in caring for those who come after them.
The sample was narrow, mostly white men from Harvard, and critics note that the study cannot say what caused good outcomes, only what went with them.
Vaillant sums up the study by saying that what matters in life is love, and he reads the whole record of the men as support for that claim.
He reports that a man's satisfaction with his relationships at midlife predicted health at eighty better than physical risk markers such as cholesterol.
Some men with troubled midlives became warm and engaged in old age, which he offers as evidence that development continues late in life.

books.thesis: The research showing shame and guilt push behaviour in opposite directions.
books.summary:
June Tangney and Ronda Dearing, psychologists, ask a question that sounds like a quibble: are shame and guilt the same feeling, or do they lead people in different directions? Their book collects years of research to answer it, using questionnaires that ask people how they would feel in everyday situations.

The distinction is that guilt is about something you did, and shame is about what you are. They report that guilt-proneness goes with empathy, apology and repair, while shame-proneness goes with anger, blaming others, withdrawal and a range of psychological troubles including depression. They argue that shame is not the moral motivator it is often thought to be, and that guilt works better. The findings come mostly from self-reports, and some critics think the two feelings overlap more in real life than the research allows. Still, the book moved the field toward separating them.
ideas: Guilt focuses on a behaviour, as in I did something bad. Shame focuses on the whole self, as in I am bad, and that difference shapes what people do next.
Guilt-prone people tend to feel empathy for those they have hurt, and are more likely to apologise, make amends and try to put things right.
Shame-prone people are more likely to respond with anger, to blame others and to see the fault as outside themselves.
Shame-proneness is linked with depression, anxiety and other psychological symptoms, while guilt-proneness, once shame is accounted for, shows far less of such a link.
The researchers measured these tendencies with scenario questionnaires that ask how a person would react to a described situation, and this method is also the main target of criticism.
They examine links with risky behaviours and addiction, and find shame-prone people at greater risk, though the evidence is correlation and not proof of cause.
The authors argue that shaming people, in schools, prisons and families, tends to make matters worse, and that helping people feel guilt about acts may work better.
Shame and guilt are presented as self-conscious emotions, which arise when we evaluate ourselves, and the authors distinguish them from simple emotions such as fear or anger.
They discuss how parenting shapes the two tendencies, with explaining the consequences of harm tending to build guilt and humiliating discipline tending to build shame.
Shame-prone people tend toward personal distress, a self-focused reaction to another's pain, and are less able to feel empathy directed at the other person.

books.thesis: Shame is a central emotion in human life, and it often stays hidden.
books.summary:
Gershen Kaufman, a psychologist, argues that shame is among the most important and least discussed emotions in human life. His book asks why shame stays hidden, how it forms, and what it does to a person who carries a lot of it. He builds on the affect theory of Silvan Tomkins, where shame is an inborn emotion.

Kaufman says shame arises when the bond between a person and someone they depend on is broken, and that repeated experiences of this kind can become internalised, so shame turns into part of identity. People then defend against it with rage, contempt, perfectionism or by withdrawing, and those defences hide the original feeling, often even from the person. He suggests that healing means repairing the bridge between people, through care and acceptance. The book is clinical and theoretical more than experimental, so its claims rest on case experience, and later researchers have tested parts of them.
ideas: Shame is an inborn emotion, in the line of Silvan Tomkins, and not a learned moral idea, which makes it central to everyday life.
Kaufman says shame is triggered when the connection with another person, a parent or a friend, is suddenly broken.
Repeated shaming can be internalised, so the person starts to feel shame without anyone present, and it becomes part of who they think they are.
Shame tends to hide itself, and people often feel it as something else, which is why it is easy to overlook in daily life and in therapy.
People defend against shame with rage, contempt, perfectionism and the urge to be in control of others, and these defences often cause more harm than the shame.
A person bound by shame can feel ashamed of the shame itself, which makes a loop that is hard to break from the inside.
Healing, he argues, comes from restoring the interpersonal bridge, so that the person feels accepted and connected again, and the book leans on clinical experience for this.
Kaufman describes the shame-bound person, in whom other feelings such as anger, fear and excitement have become tied to shame, so the person feels ashamed of having them.
Following Tomkins, shame acts as a brake on interest or enjoyment, appearing when something wanted is blocked, which is why it shows in a lowered head and averted eyes.
Shame passes down in families, since parents who carry shame tend to shame their children, so patterns repeat across generations.

books.thesis: The first account of depression as learned helplessness, later revised.
books.summary:
Martin Seligman's Helplessness set out the idea of learned helplessness and proposed it as a model of depression. The book asks why some people and animals stop trying even when escape is possible, and whether that passivity can explain a human illness.

It starts from laboratory work in which dogs given shocks they could not control later failed to escape shocks they could have avoided. Seligman argues that what matters is experiencing events as uncontrollable, and that this learning carries over to new situations. He then compares the resulting passivity with features of depression and discusses development and death. The theory was soon revised. Researchers argued that how people explain bad events matters, which led to the attributional version, and in later work Seligman and Maier reversed the story, saying passivity is the default and control is what gets learned. The 1975 book is best read as a first account that opened a long line of research.
ideas: The core experiments gave dogs shocks they could not stop. Many of them later failed to escape shocks that were easy to avoid.
Seligman argues that the key factor is uncontrollability. What the animal learns is that its actions and outcomes are unrelated.
Helplessness spreads. After learning that nothing works in one setting, animals and people become slower to try in a different one.
He sets out parallels with depression, including passivity, reluctance to start tasks and trouble believing that effort will pay off.
The book also treats how early experience of control or its absence may shape children, and how helplessness might bear on health and death.
Seligman's own theory was later revised. Researchers argued that the way people explain bad events, as lasting and personal, decides who becomes helpless.
Decades later, Seligman and Maier proposed that passivity is the default response, and that the brain has to learn that control is possible.
The key experiments used a triadic design, in which one group could stop the shock, a yoked group got the same shocks with no control, and a third got none, which isolated the effect of control.
Seligman describes helplessness as three deficits, a motivational one in which the animal stops trying, a cognitive one in which it fails to learn that responding works, and an emotional one.
Prior experience of control can act as an immunisation, and animals that first learned to escape were less likely to become helpless later.

books.thesis: Human nature is real, and denying it has cost us.
books.summary:
Steven Pinker asks why so many thinkers have resisted the idea that people come with a built-in nature, and what that resistance has cost. The Blank Slate argues that human nature is real, shaped by evolution and visible in the brain, and that denying it has distorted science, art and politics.

Pinker names three dogmas he wants to retire: the blank slate itself, the noble savage and the ghost in the machine. He reviews work from genetics, twin studies, neuroscience and cognitive science to argue that minds have structure from the start,. Critics say he attacks a straw opponent, since few serious scholars ever held that the mind is entirely blank, and that he overreads some of the evidence on sex and genes. His conclusion is that knowing our nature helps us to work with it.
ideas: Pinker takes aim at three ideas: the blank slate, the noble savage and the ghost in the machine, each of which he says rests on faulty assumptions.
Twin and adoption studies show that personality and ability are partly heritable, and he argues that families and culture are not the only forces shaping children.
Human universals, features found in every known culture, are his evidence that a shared nature underlies the surface variety of customs.
He argues that people fear human nature because they link it with inequality, with unchangeability, with determinism and with nihilism, and he says these fears rest on mistakes.
The mind is described as a set of evolved faculties, so learning depends on built-in structures and is not poured into an empty container.
He discusses differences between the sexes and argues that average differences may have biological roots, a claim that critics dispute and that he presents with qualifications.
Critics say Pinker overstates his opponents, as few scholars have held that the mind is wholly blank, and that his case for innateness sometimes goes beyond the data.

Pinker uses Thomas Sowell's idea of two visions of human nature, a constrained one and an unconstrained one, to argue that political positions often rest on hidden assumptions about what people are like.
He takes Margaret Mead's work on Samoa as a case of anthropology that was too eager to find cultures without human nature, and cites Derek Freeman's criticisms of it.
He argues that modernist and postmodern art lost its audience by rejecting the human taste for beauty, which he sees as part of the same denial of nature.

books.t: The Better Angels of Our Nature
books.thesis: Violence has declined over history, though some historians contest the claim.
books.summary:
Steven Pinker's book asks whether violence has declined over the long run of history and, if so, why. His answer is that it has, and that most of us live in what may be the most peaceful era of our species, though it rarely feels that way because we notice what makes the news.

The argument is organised around six trends, five inner demons and four better angels. Pinker draws on archaeology, homicide records and war statistics to claim that deaths from violence fell with the rise of states, commerce, literacy and the spread of rights. He credits empathy, self-control, moral norms and reason for the change. The book has drawn heavy criticism. Statisticians say rare catastrophes make trends hard to read, and historians question his data on early societies and his treatment of recent wars. He accepts that the decline could reverse, and that the causes are not settled.
ideas: Pinker uses archaeological and historical evidence to argue that violent deaths were a much larger share of deaths in early societies than in modern ones.
The Pacification Process describes how settled states, by monopolising force, cut down the feuding and raiding of earlier life.
The Civilising Process, a term from Norbert Elias, describes how manners and self-restraint spread across Europe and made everyday violence less acceptable.
The Humanitarian Revolution covers the end of practices such as judicial torture and public execution, as new ideas about the worth of individuals took hold.
He lists five inner demons, among them predation, dominance, revenge and sadism, set against four better angels: empathy, self-control, a moral sense and reason.
The long peace after 1945 and the fall in wars between states are central to his case that great powers have grown less willing to fight.
Critics dispute his statistics, arguing that rare very large wars make trends hard to read, and Pinker himself concedes that the decline is not guaranteed to continue.
Pinker draws on Hobbes's three causes of quarrel, gain, safety and glory, and describes the Hobbesian trap in which fear of a first strike leads each side to attack.
He names five historical forces behind the decline, the Leviathan, gentle commerce, feminization, cosmopolitanism and the escalator of reason.
Through the escalator of reason, he links the rise of measured intelligence, the Flynn effect, to more abstract thinking that makes it easier to see violence from another's point of view.

books.thesis: Evolution works on genes, and that explains selfishness and some altruism too.
books.summary:
Richard Dawkins asks what natural selection is really acting on, and why animals so often behave as if they were out for themselves or, sometimes, for others. His answer is the gene's eye view: genes are the units that get copied, and bodies are machines that genes build to carry them on.

The book argues that selfish is a figure of speech and not a claim about motives. Genes that make copies of themselves become common, and that can explain aggression, parental care, cooperation among relatives and even some apparent altruism. It uses kin selection and game theory to show how helping behaviour can spread, and in its final chapter it introduces the meme as a cultural replicator. Critics argue that selection also acts on individuals and groups, and that the gene's eye view is a way of seeing and not a separate theory. Dawkins closes by saying humans can, uniquely, rebel against their genes.
ideas: Dawkins puts the gene, not the organism or the species, at the centre. Genes are replicators, and bodies are survival machines that carry them.
The word selfish describes what the genes do, not what animals feel. Most of the animals he writes about have no intentions at all.
Kin selection explains why animals may help relatives. A gene that makes an animal help a sibling can spread because the sibling shares copies of it.
Using game theory, he shows how stable strategies such as cooperating only when others do can persist in a population, and how mixed behaviour can be an equilibrium.
Reciprocal altruism describes how unrelated individuals can benefit from trading favours, so long as cheaters can be recognised and not helped again.
The meme is introduced as a unit of cultural copying, such as a tune or an idea, that spreads from mind to mind much as genes spread through bodies.
Dawkins ends by saying that humans, alone among animals, can understand the selfish replicators and choose to go against them, a view critics find hard to square with his own picture.
Dawkins imagines a primeval soup in which the first replicators arose, and argues that good replicators are marked by longevity, fecundity and copying fidelity.
He treats parent-offspring conflict as a result of genes, since each child is more related to itself than to its siblings, so a child and parent can disagree about how much care should be given.
The hawk and dove example, with retaliator strategies added, shows how an evolutionarily stable strategy can arise without any group planning.

books.thesis: Evolutionary psychology turned on love, status, morality and Darwin's own life.
books.summary:
Robert Wright asks what evolution can tell us about the way people love, climb in status, deceive themselves and decide what is right. The Moral Animal is a popular account of evolutionary psychology, and Charles Darwin's own life runs through it as a case study.

Wright reasons that the mind was built by natural selection to serve the survival and spread of genes, so our feelings about sex, family, friendship and conscience have reasons we do not see. He uses Darwin's marriage, ambitions and worries to show the theory at work in one real life. He argues that the moral sentiments evolved partly to manage cooperation and reputation, and that self-deception is part of the design. Critics call some of the explanations just-so stories that are hard to test, and some feel the book reads too neatly. Wright says that understanding these pressures may help us resist them, and that the theory does not excuse anyone.
ideas: Wright says the mind is the product of natural selection, so our feelings, including love and guilt, have evolutionary reasons even when we sense nothing of the kind.
Darwin's own life, his cautious courtship, his marriage and his anxiety about status, serves as a running example of how these pressures play out in a person.
Differences in what men and women seek in partners are explained through the cost of parental investment, an argument many critics find too tidy.
Reciprocal altruism, helping others who will help you back, is used to explain friendship, gratitude, anger at cheaters and why reputation matters so much to us.
Conscience and moral feeling are described as tools shaped by selection to regulate cooperation, not as a window onto absolute right and wrong.
Self-deception is treated as a design feature. We tend to see ourselves as better than we are because that makes it easier to convince others.
Critics say many of the explanations are just-so stories, but Wright holds that understanding these urges gives us room to resist them.
Wright builds on the work of George Williams, William Hamilton and Robert Trivers, and presents them as the founders of the modern view of social behaviour.
He argues that human mating is mildly polygynous, which means men vary more than women in reproductive success and compete harder for mates and status.
Wright addresses the is-ought gap, saying that knowing where a moral feeling comes from does not tell us whether it is right, and he cites studies of stepparent abuse by Daly and Wilson as a case.

books.thesis: Evolutionary psychology, the book says, backs the Buddhist claim that the mind deludes us.
books.summary:
Robert Wright asks whether the Buddhist claim that ordinary experience misleads us has support from modern science. He argues that it does. Evolution, he says, shaped minds to chase pleasure and avoid threat, not to see clearly or to be happy, and that is why craving and anxiety keep pulling us around.

The book blends evolutionary psychology with accounts of meditation, including Wright's own retreat experience. He claims that the mind is a set of semi-independent modules and that there is no single self in charge, in line with the Buddhist teaching of not-self. Mindfulness, he says, lets us notice feelings as passing events and weaken their hold. He focuses on a modern, secular strand of Buddhism and sets aside the rebirth and ritual. Critics say the book leans on selective science and that it reads Buddhism through an evolutionary lens it never had. Wright admits he picks and chooses, and that the claim is not a proof.
ideas: Wright says natural selection built minds for gene survival, not for truth or contentment, so feelings about what matters are often unreliable guides.
The Buddhist diagnosis is that suffering comes from craving and clinging, and Wright links this to the way evolution keeps us wanting more.
Pleasure fades quickly by design, since lasting satisfaction would stop us seeking, and this explains why getting what we want rarely makes us happy for long.
The mind is described as a set of modules that compete for control. No single inner boss exists, which fits the Buddhist teaching of not-self.
Mindfulness meditation lets people watch feelings arise and pass without being swept along, and Wright reports brain studies on this, with caution about how strong they are.
He describes his own experience on a silent retreat and says some of its effects supported the book's central claims.
Wright favours a secular, modern Buddhism and leaves out rebirth, and critics say this selection bends the tradition toward his argument.
Taking the red pill, the image from The Matrix, is Wright's picture of seeing through the illusions that evolution built into the mind.
He explains emptiness as the way we project essences and value onto things, so a thing seems to carry its goodness or badness within itself when the feeling comes from the mind.
He cites Michael Gazzaniga's split-brain work and the interpreter idea, a module that narrates our actions after the fact, to support the claim that there is no unified self in charge.

books.thesis: People are more decent than cynical theories assume, and some famous studies show less than they claimed.
books.summary:
Rutger Bregman asks whether people are, underneath, selfish and dangerous, as many theories of civilisation assume. Humankind argues that most people are more decent than that, and that the opposite belief, which he calls veneer theory, has shaped institutions in ways that do harm.

He goes back to famous studies and stories and retells them. He claims that the Stanford prison experiment was staged more than it was discovered, that the tale of boys stranded on a Pacific island ended very differently from Lord of the Flies, and that stories of bystanders ignoring crime were exaggerated. He then describes cases of cooperation, from soldiers in the First World War to schools and prisons run on trust. Critics say Bregman picks evidence to suit his case and treats his own sources less sceptically than his targets. Even so, several of the studies he challenges have been seriously questioned by others.
ideas: Bregman calls the belief that goodness is a thin coat over human selfishness veneer theory, and says it is old, popular and mostly unsupported.
He retells the story of six boys stranded on a Pacific island and says they looked after one another, the reverse of Lord of the Flies.
The Stanford prison experiment, he argues, was shaped by its organisers, so it does not show that ordinary people turn cruel when given power.
The famous story that many neighbours watched a woman's murder and did nothing is shown, in his account, to have been inflated by the press.
He argues that humans evolved to cooperate, and that the same traits that make us friendly also make us easy to teach and to trust.
He describes soldiers in the First World War who held fire or shared the lines at Christmas, as signs that people resist killing.
Critics say Bregman is selective and applies less scrutiny to evidence that fits his view, and he admits that people can also be cruel.
Bregman describes the Homo puppy hypothesis, that humans selected for friendliness and in effect domesticated themselves, and he cites the Russian fox experiment as a parallel.
He revisits Milgram's obedience studies and argues that many people went on not from blind obedience but because they were persuaded they were doing something worthwhile.
He rejects the story that Easter Island was ruined by its own people, and says disease and slavery brought by outsiders did most of the damage.

books.thesis: Culture made humans successful. Raw intelligence didn't.
books.summary:
Joseph Henrich asks why humans, who are not especially strong or fast, ended up dominating the planet. He argues that raw intelligence is not the answer. Instead, our success comes from culture, from the way groups accumulate and pass on knowledge across generations, much of which no individual could work out alone.

The book argues that humans are cultural learners who copy what works, especially from people who seem successful or prestigious, and that this has shaped our bodies and brains through gene and culture evolving together. He gives examples of cultural know-how that works without anyone understanding why, such as food processing that removes toxins, and of European explorers who died in places where locals had long thrived. Critics say he gives too little weight to individual reasoning and that cultural evolution is hard to test. His broad conclusion is that we are smart because of the collective brain, not that our brains alone make us so.
ideas: Humans owe their success to cumulative culture, the slow build-up of skills and knowledge over generations, more than to any one person's cleverness.
Henrich tells of European explorers who starved in places where local people lived well, because they lacked the locals' inherited knowledge.
Methods for preparing certain foods, such as detoxifying cassava, protect people from poison even though those following them may not know why they work.
People learn by copying, and they copy most from those who seem successful or prestigious, which lets useful practices spread without anyone checking them.
Experiments comparing young children with other apes suggest that children are not better at physical puzzles but far better at learning from other people.
Culture and genes shape each other. Cooking and group living changed our bodies and brains, which in turn made us better able to learn from others.
Critics say Henrich undervalues individual reasoning, and that cultural evolution is hard to test, but the book makes a case that is hard to ignore.
Henrich describes conformist transmission, the human tendency to copy the majority, and says it lets useful practices spread and stabilise in a group.
The collective brain idea says that larger and better connected populations sustain more complex technology, and Henrich points to Tasmania, which lost tools after it was cut off from the mainland.
He argues for cultural group selection, in which groups with better norms and institutions outcompeted others, shaping human cooperation.

books.t: The WEIRDest People in the World
books.thesis: Western psychology is the odd one out, shaped by its cultural history.
books.summary:
Joseph Henrich asks why people in Western societies think and act so differently from most people in history and across the world. The term WEIRD, standing for Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic, comes from earlier work he did with colleagues, who pointed out that psychology had mostly studied people from these societies.

His argument is that WEIRD psychology, individualistic, analytic, trusting of strangers and prone to guilt over shame, is the product of a particular cultural history. He claims that medieval Church rules about marriage and family broke up the tight kin groups that had organised most societies, and that this opened the way for new institutions, new habits of trust and, later, widespread reading. The thesis is bold and critics say it rests on a single cause and sometimes confuses correlation with explanation. Henrich holds that psychology cannot understand people while it treats one odd population as typical, and that point is widely accepted.
ideas: The acronym WEIRD stands for Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic, and Henrich notes that most psychology studies draw their participants from just such societies.
WEIRD people tend to be more individualistic and analytic, to value personal choice, and to put the self ahead of group ties.
They also show more trust in strangers and impersonal institutions, which Henrich links to the rise of markets and law.
He argues that Church policies on marriage, such as bans on marrying relatives, weakened the extended clans that had once organised life in most societies.
Learning to read changes how the brain works, and Henrich links the spread of literacy, helped by the Protestant stress on reading scripture, to later psychological differences.
Guilt-based moral thinking, which concerns private conscience, is stronger in WEIRD societies, while shame, which concerns reputation, is stronger in many others.
Critics say the thesis leans on one cause for a huge historical change, and that correlations across regions do not prove his explanation.
He uses illusion experiments such as the Muller-Lyer figure to show that even basic perception differs across populations, so WEIRD samples cannot stand for all people.
Economic games such as the ultimatum game show that people in market-integrated societies offer fairer splits to strangers than people in small-scale societies.
He credits voluntary associations such as guilds, monasteries and universities, along with charter towns, for building new forms of trust beyond kin.

books.thesis: Mimetic desire, applied to modern life and work.
books.summary:
Luke Burgis asks where our wants come from, and he draws on the thinker René Girard to say that they come mostly from other people. Wanting applies mimetic theory, the idea that desire is copied, to ordinary life in business, relationships, careers and social media.

Burgis argues that we rarely pick our desires on our own. We watch models, people we admire or compete with, and take on what they want, often without knowing it. He distinguishes thin desires, which are driven by imitation and tend to leave us unsatisfied, from thick ones, which are more durable and tied to what we really value. He also describes how rivalry grows when we copy those close to us, and how groups can turn on a scapegoat. The book is a popularisation, and Girard's theory has few experimental tests behind it. Burgis suggests that noticing the pattern gives us some freedom from it.
ideas: Girard's central claim, which Burgis builds on, is that people learn what to want by watching what others want, so desire is social, not spontaneous.
We tend to deny that we imitate. Burgis argues that this denial keeps the copying hidden and makes it more powerful.
Models can stand at a distance, like celebrities, or close at hand, like colleagues, and closeness is what makes rivalry likely.
Thin desires come mostly from imitation and tend to leave us restless, while thick desires hold up over time and tie to deeper values.
Rivalry grows between people who want the same thing and who are close, and it can come to matter more than the object itself.
Groups in tension may settle their conflict by blaming a scapegoat, an idea Girard developed at length and Burgis applies to modern settings.
Girard's theory has little experimental support, but Burgis argues that seeing where a want came from can make it easier to choose whether to follow it.
Burgis points to Peter Thiel, who studied with Girard and became an early investor in Facebook, as an example of how the theory moves from the seminar into business.
Girard's metaphysical desire means that we want not only the object but the being of the model, as if having what they have would make us who they are.
Social media increases the number of models we see and shows their reactions in real time, which Burgis suggests speeds up mimetic rivalry.

books.t: The Hero with a Thousand Faces
books.thesis: The hero's journey, argued as a universal pattern in myth.
books.summary:
Joseph Campbell asks whether the stories told by different cultures share a single underlying shape. In The Hero with a Thousand Faces he argues that they do, and that myths from around the world follow one pattern, which he calls the monomyth, drawing on Jung and Freud and on comparative study of myth and religion.

The pattern runs in three parts: the hero leaves the ordinary world, passes through a series of trials and revelations, and returns with something that benefits others. Campbell fills it in with stages such as the call to adventure, the refusal, helpers and guardians, the lowest point and the return. He treats these as expressions of inner psychological change, with myths serving as maps for growing up. Critics say the pattern is so general that it fits nearly anything, that Campbell selects his examples to suit it, and that his hero is mostly male. The book has been hugely influential on storytellers all the same.
ideas: Campbell's monomyth is the claim that hero stories everywhere share one structure with three parts: departure, initiation and return.
The hero's story typically begins with a call to adventure, which the hero may at first refuse, and then comes aid from a helper.
Crossing the threshold means entering a strange world, guarded by figures that test whether the hero is ready to go on.
The middle of the story is a series of trials that lead to a crisis, a kind of symbolic death or descent, followed by a gain.
Campbell reads these stages as images of inner psychological change, drawing on Jung's archetypes and Freud's analysis of dreams, and treats myth as a kind of shared dreaming.
The return brings something back for the community, and Campbell treats this as the point, since the hero's gain is meant to be shared.
Critics say the pattern is too loose, fits almost any story and was built from selected examples, and that the hero in his account is nearly always male.
The belly of the whale is Campbell's image for the threshold passage, in which the hero seems to vanish, as Jonah does, and is reborn after a symbolic death.
Atonement with the father is a central crisis in which the hero faces the power that rules his world, and comes through to a new understanding.
The hero who returns is called the master of two worlds, one who can move between the everyday and the sacred without being trapped in either.

books.thesis: Conversations on why myths still speak to us.
books.summary:
The Power of Myth grew out of a long series of conversations between the mythologist Joseph Campbell and the journalist Bill Moyers, filmed in the late 1980s. It asks why old stories still matter in a modern world that no longer believes them literally, and what they do for the people who live by them.

Because it is a conversation, the book moves loosely. Campbell argues that myths are metaphors for the experience of being alive and for stages of life, and that trouble comes when they are read as facts. He talks about heroes, rites of passage, marriage and the loss of shared stories in modern societies, and he urges people to follow what makes them feel alive. Critics say he generalises across traditions, flattens real differences between them and slips in his own tastes. The book is warm and accessible, and many readers met Campbell's ideas here first, so it carries more charm than rigour.
ideas: Campbell says myths are metaphors for the experience of being alive, and that reading them as literal history misses what they are for.
He suggests people are looking not for the meaning of life but for the experience of being alive, which myths help them feel.
Rites of passage once marked the move from childhood to adulthood, and Campbell worries that modern societies have lost these shared ceremonies.
Marriage is discussed as a union that asks two people to give up their separate selves, with the shared relationship as the thing to serve.
He advises people to follow their bliss, meaning the activity that makes them feel most alive, and trust that doors will open.
Campbell argues that the old myths no longer fit the modern world and that a new set of stories, drawing on the whole planet, is needed.
Critics say he treats very different traditions as one, and that his easy blending of them in conversation covers over real disagreements.
Campbell lists four functions of mythology, the mystical, the cosmological, the sociological and the pedagogical, and says modern life has lost the first.
The talks include discussion of Star Wars, whose creator George Lucas said he had drawn on Campbell's work, and Campbell treats the film as a modern myth.
He advises people to participate joyfully in the sorrows of the world, and says one needs a sacred place where one can find oneself.

books.thesis: Wrestling and soap ads carry hidden ideology, like the rest of everyday culture.
books.summary:
Roland Barthes asks what is hidden in the things a society treats as natural and harmless. Mythologies collects short essays he wrote for a French magazine in the 1950s, on subjects such as wrestling, soap powder, a car, wine and a magazine cover, and ends with a longer theoretical essay.

His argument is that everyday objects and images carry a second layer of meaning. A picture or a phrase signifies something plain, and then it is used to signify an idea, often a conservative or bourgeois one, in a way that makes history look like nature. He calls this layer myth. The essays are brisk and witty, and they ask readers to notice what has been made to seem obvious. Critics say his readings can be arbitrary, sure of themselves, and driven by his politics, since the same image could be read another way. The book has still taught several generations how to read advertising and popular culture with suspicion.
ideas: Barthes defines myth as a second layer of meaning added to a sign, so an ordinary image comes to carry an idea without seeming to.
Myth turns history into nature. What is made by particular people at a particular time is presented as simply how things are.
He reads professional wrestling as a spectacle of moral display, in which gestures show suffering and justice clearly for the crowd.
A magazine cover showing a young Black soldier saluting the French flag is read as a way of presenting empire as natural and welcome.
Wine, as he describes it, is made into a national symbol of Frenchness, which hides how particular and unevenly shared the habit is.
The essay on soap powders and detergents shows how advertising turns cleaning products into stories about depth and action.
The closing essay, Myth Today, gives the theory, and critics say his readings can be playful, political and not easy to check.
In the closing essay, Barthes defines myth as depoliticised speech, which removes the history and the human making from things and presents them as natural.
The bourgeoisie is ex-nominated, meaning it is never named and appears as the universal norm, which is why its values pass as common sense.
In the essay on toys, French playthings are shown to prepare children to be users and not makers, and the essay on the brain of Einstein shows how the scientist is turned into a myth of genius.

books.thesis: Play came before culture and runs all through it.
books.summary:
Johan Huizinga, a Dutch historian, asks what play is and what it has to do with culture. In Homo Ludens he argues that play is not a side activity of civilisation but one of its roots, older than culture itself, since animals play before humans have anything we would call culture.

He describes play as voluntary, set apart from ordinary life, bounded in time and space and ruled by agreed limits. He follows that spirit through law, war, poetry, ritual, philosophy and art, claiming that each began as a contest or a game. Critics say he stretches the idea of play until it covers too much, and that he is selective about his evidence. He ends on a worried note, arguing that in the twentieth century the real play spirit had weakened and been replaced by a shallow childishness. Whatever its faults, the book shaped how games and culture are studied.
ideas: Huizinga argues that play is older than culture, since animals play and do not need humans to teach them how.
Play is free. A person who is forced to play is no longer playing, which marks it off from work and duty.
It takes place within a boundary of time and space, a kind of magic circle in which the ordinary rules are replaced by those of the game.
Every game has rules, and Huizinga notes that someone who breaks them destroys the game, while someone who cheats still respects them.
He traces the play element in law, war, poetry and ritual, claiming that all of these began as contests of skill, courage or wit.
Contest, in the sense of a struggle for honour and reputation, is treated as one of the main ways play shapes social life.
In the last chapters he laments what he calls puerilism, a mix of childishness and propaganda that he thinks replaced real play, though many critics find that section dated.
The subtitle describes it as a study of the play element in culture, and the name Homo ludens is offered as a rival to Homo sapiens and Homo faber.
Huizinga says ritual and play overlap, since sacred performances take place in a marked-off ground where participants hold the play to be real and also know it as play.
He notes that play has aesthetic qualities such as rhythm, harmony and tension, and surveys words for play in many languages to show how differently the idea is divided.

books.thesis: Modern people turned "other-directed", steering by what their peers approve of.
books.summary:
David Riesman, with Nathan Glazer and Reuel Denney, asks how the American character was changing in the middle of the twentieth century. The Lonely Crowd proposes that societies produce characteristic personality types, and that a new one, steered by the approval of peers, was becoming dominant among the urban middle class.

The book describes three types. Tradition-directed people follow custom, inner-directed people follow values laid down early in life, and other-directed people steer by the signals of those around them. Riesman links these to stages of population and economic change, and compares the inner-directed person's inner gyroscope with the other-directed person's radar. He is wary but not hostile, noting gains in flexibility and costs in anxiety and conformity. Critics said that he drew on thin evidence and that the types were too loose. The book was still a surprise bestseller and gave the public a vocabulary for talking about conformity and consumer society.
ideas: Riesman proposes three social characters: tradition-directed, inner-directed and other-directed, each linked with a stage of economic and population change.
Tradition-directed people follow inherited custom and rank, and in such societies deviation brings shame from the group.
Inner-directed people take their goals from early parental teaching and hold to them through life, guided, as Riesman puts it, by an inner gyroscope.
Other-directed people look to their peers and to media for cues about what to want and how to act, and he compares them to radar.
The shift to the other-directed type is tied to the growth of cities, offices and consumer society, where getting on with people becomes the main skill.
He argues that other-directed people gain in warmth and flexibility but pay for it with anxiety about approval and a thinner sense of their own aims.
Critics said the evidence was thin and the types too loose, though the book was a bestseller and its terms entered everyday talk.
Riesman wrote the book with Nathan Glazer and Reuel Denney, and it began as a study of the American middle class that grew into a general theory of character.
He ties the three types to a population curve, with high growth potential, transitional growth and incipient decline, each producing its own typical character.
The autonomous type is the ideal, a person who can conform to norms but is free to choose not to, and Riesman contrasts this with the anomic person, who is simply cut off.

books.thesis: Consumer culture breeds fragile, approval-hungry selves.
books.summary:
Christopher Lasch asks what has happened to American character in the age of consumerism, therapy and celebrity. The Culture of Narcissism argues that social change has produced a new kind of person who is anxious, dependent on admiration and short on a stable sense of self, and he uses the language of clinical narcissism to describe it.

His claim is that this is a social pattern as well as a personal one. He points to the decline of family authority, the growth of bureaucracy and experts, mass media and the cult of celebrity, and a therapeutic outlook that replaced older moral and political frames. In this world people look for personal growth and approval while distrusting lasting commitments. The book draws on psychoanalytic writers and on cultural criticism more than on data. Critics say Lasch was nostalgic and moralistic, that he stretched the clinical term, and that he cherry-picked. It remains a much-quoted warning about self-absorption.
ideas: Lasch uses narcissism as a cultural diagnosis. In his account it describes a social pattern that produces anxious people who depend on others' admiration.
Consumer culture, he argues, feeds this by selling images of a better self and keeping people dissatisfied with what they have.
The therapeutic outlook, with its focus on personal feeling and growth, has taken the place of religion and politics as a way of finding meaning.
Experts and bureaucracies have taken over tasks once handled by families and communities, leaving parents less sure of their own authority.
Mass media and celebrity encourage people to see life as a performance, judged by an audience, so that being seen matters more than doing.
He describes a survival mentality, in which people cope day by day, avoid long commitments and treat relationships as things to be used.
Critics say Lasch was nostalgic and stretched a clinical term to cover a whole society, and that his evidence is mostly anecdote and cultural reading.
Lasch draws on the clinical work of Otto Kernberg and Heinz Kohut, and describes the narcissist as having a fragile self, a need for an audience and a fear of dependence.
