The chapter on sport argues that games have been turned from play into spectacle, with commercialism and the cult of winning replacing the joy of taking part.
He criticises what he calls pseudo-self-awareness, a habit of constant self-observation that he says leads to detachment from feeling and not to insight.

books.thesis: Empathy is biased and narrow. Rational compassion is a better guide.
books.summary:
Paul Bloom asks whether empathy, usually praised as the root of kindness, is actually a good guide to moral choices. In Against Empathy he argues that it is not. He separates two things people often mix: understanding what another person is thinking, which he accepts is useful, and feeling what they feel, which he thinks misleads us.

The case is that emotional empathy works like a spotlight. It favours people who are near, similar and identifiable, it responds poorly to large numbers, and it can push us toward cruelty against whoever we think threatens the one we feel for. He also cites research suggesting that taking on others' pain can lead to burnout, and he proposes rational compassion in its place, a concern for others' wellbeing that does not require sharing their feelings. Critics say that he defines empathy narrowly and that human care needs more feeling than he allows.
ideas: Bloom distinguishes cognitive empathy, understanding what someone feels, from emotional empathy, feeling it yourself, and his target is the second kind.
Empathy acts like a spotlight, strongest for people who are close to us, look like us or whose suffering we can picture clearly.
It is poor at numbers. People respond more to one named victim than to thousands, which skews decisions about charity and policy.
Empathy can lead to cruelty, because feeling for one victim may spur anger and harsh punishment toward whoever caused the harm.
Caregivers who take on their patients' pain can burn out, while those who respond with compassion cope better, and Bloom cites such research to support the contrast.
He proposes rational compassion, a concern for others' wellbeing that rests on thought and values and does not depend on sharing their feelings.
Critics say he defines empathy so narrowly that it becomes easy to attack, and that many kinds of care do depend on feeling with another person.
Bloom points to cases like the girl trapped in a well, who drew great public attention and money, while larger disasters receive far less, as a sign of how empathy chases vivid individuals.
He argues that empathy divides in politics, since it flows toward our own side and can turn into hostility toward the people who seem to have hurt them.
He concedes that empathy has value in private life, bringing pleasure, closeness and enjoyment of fiction, and aims his criticism at its role in moral and policy decisions.

books.thesis: Religious experience studied from the inside and judged by its fruits. Origins are beside the point.
books.summary:
William James, the philosopher and psychologist, gave these lectures in 1901 and 1902 and asked what religious experience is like for the people who have it, and how much it should count. He chose to look at the intense personal cases, the conversions, visions and saintly lives, since he thought the extremes reveal the nature of the thing.

The book collects first-person accounts and sorts them: the healthy-minded who see mostly good, the sick soul who feels evil and despair, the divided self and its sudden conversion, the habits of saints, and the states of mystics. James then judges them by their fruits, by what they do for a life, and not by their roots, whether they might be traced to nerves or biology. He dismissed explaining them away as medical materialism. His conclusion is cautious. Such experiences are real and often valuable, but they bind only those who have them.
ideas: James studies the personal side of religion, the feelings and experiences of individuals in their solitude, and sets institutions and doctrine aside.
He divides temperaments into the healthy-minded, who focus on good, and the sick soul, who cannot ignore evil, and argues that both are real ways of seeing.
The divided self is a person at war within, and James describes conversion as the sudden or gradual unification of that division.
He criticises medical materialism, the habit of dismissing a religious state because it can be linked to the body, noting that all states have bodily causes.
His test is practical. Experiences are to be judged by their fruits, by whether they make a person more charitable, steady and alive, not by where they came from.
Mystical states, he suggests, share four marks: they are hard to put into words, they feel like knowledge, they pass quickly and they feel as though they happen to you.
James concludes that mystical experiences carry authority for those who have them but give others no obligation to accept them, a view critics find both modest and evasive.
The book began as the Gifford Lectures at Edinburgh in 1901 and 1902, and its case studies come mostly from first-person accounts in letters and memoirs.
James describes saintliness as a set of traits including charity, purity and asceticism, and judges it by whether it makes a person better to live with.
He suggests religious experiences come from a subliminal region of the self that opens onto something more, and he holds that people then add overbeliefs beyond what the experience shows.

books.thesis: What we find in the world depends on how we attend to it. The right hemisphere's way of attending deserves its place back.
books.summary:
Iain McGilchrist, a psychiatrist and former literary scholar, asks how the way we pay attention shapes what we find in the world. The Matter with Things is a very long two volume work that continues his earlier book on the two brain hemispheres and argues that modern culture has come to favour one way of attending at the cost of the other.

His claim is that the left hemisphere attends narrowly, to what can be grasped and used, while the right attends broadly, to context, living things and what is new. He says the left has taken over, and that this has flattened our view of the world into a mechanism. He then pushes beyond neuroscience into physics, time, consciousness and value, arguing that truth, beauty and goodness are real parts of the world. Neuroscientists dispute his account of the hemispheres as too sharp a split, and some readers find the later philosophy loose.
ideas: McGilchrist argues that attention is not neutral. How we attend to the world decides what we find in it and what we miss.
He says the two hemispheres attend differently: the left narrowly and for use, the right widely, to context and to living, changing things.
His earlier thesis holds that the right hemisphere is the master and the left its emissary, and that the emissary has taken over modern culture.
The left's way of seeing, he claims, turns the world into a machine of separable parts, which suits manipulation but loses what is whole and alive.
He argues against the view that consciousness is a by-product of matter, and suggests that mind and matter are more entangled than materialism allows.
Truth, beauty and goodness are treated as real features of the world that we discover, not preferences we project onto it.
Neuroscientists object that the hemisphere split is overstated, and some readers find the philosophical chapters more assertion than demonstration.

McGilchrist holds that there are four ways of knowing, which are science, reason, intuition and imagination, and that a sound view of the world needs all of them working together. He thinks modern thought leans too far on reason and measurement.
He points to the corpus callosum, the band joining the hemispheres, and argues that it works partly to inhibit one side so that two different ways of attending can stay distinct.
He argues that the world is better understood as made of processes and relationships than of isolated things, so that what lies between things is as real as the things themselves.

books.thesis: It is now easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism. That failure of imagination shapes how we suffer.
books.summary:
Mark Fisher begins with a remark, often attributed to Fredric Jameson and Slavoj Zizek, that it is easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism. Capitalist Realism asks what it does to a culture when no alternative seems thinkable, and how that shows up in everyday suffering, work and education.

Fisher argues that capitalist realism is more than a belief. It is an atmosphere that shapes what feels possible. He looks at the film Children of Men as a picture of this closed future, at the spread of bureaucracy and targets in public services, which he calls market Stalinism, and at the way students feel unable to act while knowing things are wrong. He also challenges the habit of treating depression and stress as private chemical problems. The book is short, polemical and drawn from his teaching and cultural criticism, and readers disagree on how far its diagnosis extends.
ideas: Fisher takes up the line that it is easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism, and treats it as a description of our mood.
Capitalist realism, in his account, is an atmosphere that limits thought and action, in which no alternative to the present system seems worth imagining.
He reads the film Children of Men as a picture of a world where the future has been cancelled and all that remains is management.
Bureaucracy has not disappeared under the market. Targets, audits and paperwork have spread through schools and services, which Fisher calls market Stalinism.
He describes reflexive impotence, the state of students who know the system is broken and also feel they can do nothing about it.
Fisher challenges the habit of treating depression and anxiety as private chemical faults, and argues that their social causes in work and precarity are ignored.
The book is short and combative, based on teaching and cultural criticism, and critics find its evidence thin and its alternatives vague.

Fisher uses the term business ontology for the assumption that every institution, including schools, hospitals and the arts, ought to be run as a business. The idea is treated as common sense and is hard to question.
He discusses the film Wall-E as an example of how critique is absorbed. The film criticises consumerism, yet it does so as a product sold by the system it describes.
Fisher notes that the 2008 bank bailouts exposed the market's dependence on the state, yet he argues that the sense that there is no alternative survived the crisis.

books.thesis: The self is a model the brain can't recognise as a model. We live inside it.
books.summary:
Thomas Metzinger, a German philosopher of mind, asks what the self is, and whether anything in us corresponds to the sense of being someone. The Ego Tunnel is a popular version of his longer academic work, and it gives a bold answer: there are no selves, only the process of the brain modelling itself.

His central idea is that the brain builds a model of the body and of the world, and that we cannot see it as a model, because it is transparent to us. We live inside it, a kind of tunnel, and take it for reality. He draws on out-of-body experiences, the rubber hand illusion, lucid dreaming and virtual reality to show how easily the model can be shifted. He then raises ethical questions about changing consciousness and creating artificial minds that might suffer. Critics say the claim that no self exists depends on how self is defined, and the science is still unsettled.
ideas: Metzinger claims that no such thing as a self exists. What we have is a continuous process in which the brain models itself.
The central notion is the phenomenal self-model, the brain's internal picture of the body that makes us feel like a single someone.
The model is transparent. We cannot see it as a model, so we look through it, take its content for the real world and think we are directly in touch with things.
The ego tunnel is the narrow, constructed space of experience in which each of us lives, a bit like a private virtual reality.
The rubber hand illusion and out-of-body experiences show that the felt boundary of the body can be shifted by simple tricks.
Dreams, and especially lucid dreams, are presented as natural examples of the brain running a self-model and a world without sensory input.
Metzinger raises ethical questions about enhancing minds and building artificial ones that might suffer, though critics say the claim that no self exists depends on definitions.
He treats agency, the feeling of being the author of one's own actions, as another part of the self-model, and he is doubtful about a free will that would stand apart from the brain.
Metzinger draws on clinical cases in which parts of the self-model fail, such as patients who deny that a paralysed limb belongs to them, to show how fragile the sense of self can be.
He has called for a pause on work that could produce artificial consciousness, on the ground that a suffering machine would be a new kind of victim.

books.thesis: We expect more from technology and less from each other. Being connected isn't the same as being close.
books.summary:
Sherry Turkle asks what technology is doing to our relationships, and why we can feel so lonely while constantly connected. She is a psychologist at MIT who spent years interviewing people about robots and about networked life, and the book is organised in two halves around those themes.

The first half looks at social robots, from toy pets to machines designed as companions for the old, and notes how readily people attach to something that only seems to care. The second looks at phones, texting and social media, where people curate themselves and often prefer messages to calls. Turkle argues that we have come to expect more from technology and less from each other, and that being always connected can crowd out solitude and real conversation. Her evidence is largely interviews and observation, and critics say she worries too much and generalises from small samples. She is not against technology, and she hopes for a more reflective use of it.
ideas: Turkle's central claim is that we expect more from technology and less from each other, and that connection is not the same as closeness.
She describes the robotic moment, in which people are ready to accept machines as companions even when they know the machines feel nothing.
Simulated care raises a question for her about authenticity, since a robot that seems to listen may stand in for the harder work of human company.
Children and older people she interviewed formed real attachments to robot pets, which she took as a sign of unmet need and not just a curiosity.
Many people prefer texting to calling, because it lets them control what they say and when, and Turkle thinks this costs the give and take of conversation.
Online we present edited versions of ourselves, and the pressure to be seen turns life into material for sharing, so some feel they exist only when posted.
Critics say Turkle generalises from interviews and leans toward alarm. She herself says she is not against technology and hopes for more reflective use.

Turkle uses the phrase alive enough for the way children treat robot toys such as Furbys and Tamagotchis. Because the toys need care, children come to feel that they are living things, even if not quite animals.
She describes the tethered self, a person who is always connected, reaches for a phone to fill any gap, and finds it hard to be alone with their own thoughts.
She writes about MIT robots such as Kismet, built to respond to faces and voices, and notes that people feel recognised by them even when they know the responses are programmed.

books.t: On Kissing, Tickling and Being Bored
books.thesis: Grand theory tells us less about the psyche than the small things we do and feel.
books.summary:
Adam Phillips, a British psychoanalyst, suggests that grand theories of the mind explain less than the small things people feel and do. On Kissing, Tickling and Being Bored is a collection of essays that start from trifles and use them to approach questions about desire, childhood and the strange things that psychoanalysis tries to describe.

The essays do not build one argument. Phillips writes in a short, playful, aphoristic way, taking up a subject, turning it over and leaving it open. Boredom, for instance, is treated not as something empty but as a state in which a child waits for desire to appear. Tickling and kissing are considered as ordinary pleasures that are mixed up with fear and control. Freud and Winnicott are in the background, and Phillips treats their theories as stories to be used, not as settled fact. Readers who want conclusions may be frustrated, because he prefers questions.
ideas: Phillips doubts that large theories capture the mind, and prefers to start from small experiences, such as a kiss or a bad afternoon, that theories tend to skip.
Boredom is described as a waiting state in which a child searches for what to want, so rushing to fill it may get in the way of finding a desire.
Tickling mixes pleasure with helplessness and alarm, and Phillips uses it to show how closely enjoyment and loss of control can sit together.
Kissing is treated as a small, everyday act that holds a lot of the ambiguity about wanting and being wanted.
Freud's ideas are read as stories that are useful to think with, not as proven facts, and Phillips is playful about psychoanalysis even as he draws on it.
The essays are brief and aphoristic. Phillips raises a subject, turns it over and often ends on an open question.
Winnicott's thinking, with its emphasis on play and on being able to be alone, runs under several essays, though Phillips uses it freely.
The book's subtitle refers to the unexamined life, and Phillips treats it as a quiet answer to Socrates, suggesting that not every part of a life is improved by being analysed.
Phillips suggests that being tickled depends on trust, since the same helplessness that is fun with a friend would feel like a threat from a stranger.
A recurring move is to reverse the usual view, so that a symptom, a habit or a mood is read as an attempt at something and not simply as a fault to be removed.

books.thesis: We spend our lives fantasising about the lives we aren't living. That shapes the one we've got.
books.summary:
Adam Phillips asks why we spend so much of our lives thinking about the lives we are not living. Missing Out, subtitled In Praise of the Unlived Life, argues that these imagined alternatives matter. We compare our real lives with the ones we wanted, feared or missed, and that comparison shapes the life we have.

Phillips draws on Freud, on literature and on clinical experience in his usual essayistic way. He suggests that frustration is an unavoidable part of desire, since wanting means not having, and that people often handle this by imagining a better version of themselves that lives elsewhere. He treats envy and regret as signs of this habit. The book is more suggestive than systematic, and it does not offer a method for living better. It leaves open how far we should give up the fantasies, and he seems to hold that some are necessary. Readers who like a firm thesis may find it slippery.
ideas: Phillips says each of us lives alongside the lives we did not lead, and that these imagined lives affect how we feel about the real one.
Frustration is treated as part of wanting. To desire something is to lack it, and so a life of wanting is always a life of some missing out.
We often imagine a version of ourselves who made other choices and is happier, and Phillips suggests this fantasy can make the actual life seem thin.
Envy is read as a sign of the unlived life, a response to someone who seems to have what we gave up or never had.
Regret and the idea that we missed our chance can become a way of avoiding the risks of the present.
Fantasy is not simply an escape. Phillips holds that we need imagined lives to know what we want and to sense what is possible.
The book is an essay in the loose sense, drawing on Freud and writers, and it offers no method, which some readers find slippery.
He contrasts the modern promise that we can have it all with the fact of limits, and suggests that the promise makes ordinary satisfactions feel like losses.
Phillips reads the Oedipus story as a tale of what a child must give up, so that missing out is built into growing up.
He suggests that parents can pass their own unlived lives on to their children, who are then asked to live out what the parent missed.

books.thesis: Domination begins where mutual recognition fails. Love needs two people who can each be a subject.
books.summary:
Jessica Benjamin, a psychoanalyst and feminist thinker, asks why relations of domination and submission recur in love and in society, and what it would take for two people to meet as equals. The Bonds of Love uses psychoanalysis to argue that domination begins where mutual recognition fails.

Her central idea is that each person needs to be recognised by another, but recognition only counts if the other is truly independent, so the need contains a built-in tension. When people cannot hold it, one may try to control the other, and the relationship turns into one of master and servant. She reads this in the work of Freud and Hegel, in the way children separate from their mothers, in gender roles and in erotic submission, including the novel The Story of O. Critics have pressed her on how far her account depends on psychoanalytic assumptions, and on its application to politics.
ideas: Benjamin starts from the paradox of recognition: we need another person to confirm us, but only a separate person can do so in a way that counts.
When mutual recognition breaks down, each person may try to control the other, and the relationship hardens into domination and submission.
She reads Hegel's master and slave story as a picture of this failure, where one party's independence is bought at the cost of the other's.
In her account, the child must be recognised by the mother as a separate person, while the mother also needs to be seen as a person with a life of her own.
Gender roles come out of this history: the mother is often cast as an object, the father as the model of independence, and both split what should be shared.
She treats erotic domination as a way of acting out the failure of recognition, and discusses The Story of O as an example.
She presents mutual recognition as an ideal that is never fully reached, and critics question how far her psychoanalytic picture explains politics.
Benjamin draws on infant research, including the work of Daniel Stern, to argue that babies take part in exchange with others from very early, which replaces the picture of a passive infant.

Using Winnicott, she argues that the child needs to test the other with aggression and find that the other survives. That survival is how the other comes to seem real and separate and not just a projection.
She links the ideal of the independent, rational self in Western thought to domination, arguing that the ideal hides the dependence and care it relies on.

books.thesis: Modern life speeds up just to stay in place, and the price is no time left for anything to matter.
books.summary:
Hartmut Rosa, a German sociologist, asks why people in modern societies feel they never have enough time, even though technology saves time. Social Acceleration proposes that the speed of life has been increasing in three ways at once, and that this has become a kind of structural pressure that shapes the modern experience.

Rosa distinguishes technological acceleration, such as faster transport and communication, acceleration of social change, as jobs, families and knowledge go out of date more quickly, and acceleration of the pace of life, as more actions are crammed into each hour. He argues that these feed one another and are driven by competition and a cultural promise of more. People are forced to run just to stay in place, and he calls the result a frenetic standstill. His worry is that the present shrinks, so people lose any stable ground for lasting commitments. Critics say it generalises about a diverse world from one view of modern life.
ideas: Rosa identifies three kinds of acceleration: technological, social change and the pace of life, and argues that they reinforce one another.
Technology saves time on each task, yet we have less time overall, because the freed time is filled with more tasks and rising expectations.
Social change speeds up, so knowledge, jobs and relationships go stale faster, and what was reliable for one generation no longer holds for the next.
The shrinking of the present is his phrase for the way that stable ground shortens, so people can make fewer assumptions about what will last.
He argues that competition and a cultural promise that faster is better push the acceleration forward, and that individuals can hardly step out of it.
He calls the result a frenetic standstill: lots of motion, and a feeling that nothing really changes or leads anywhere.
Rosa suggests acceleration produces a new alienation from time, from places and from ourselves, and critics say his theory is dense and generalises from one view.
Rosa describes desynchronisation, in which different spheres speed up at different rates. Politics and law, for example, move more slowly than the economy, so democratic decisions fall behind events.

He lists forms of slowness, including natural limits, islands of deceleration, side effects such as traffic jams and burnout, and deliberate resistance, and argues that none of them reverses the overall trend.
Identity becomes situational. Instead of building a life around a lasting project, people adjust themselves from one moment to the next to changing demands.

books.thesis: What makes a life good? Resonance: the moments the world answers back.
books.summary:
Hartmut Rosa asks what makes a life good, and his answer in Resonance is that a good life depends on the quality of our relationship to the world. He proposes resonance as the central concept, a kind of responsive relation in which something outside us touches us and we answer in turn, and which he contrasts with alienation.

He argues that resonance cannot be forced or bought. It happens in moments when a piece of music, a landscape, a person, a task or a belief speaks to us and changes us a little, and it needs an openness that can be neither controlled nor guaranteed. He describes three kinds of axes along which it occurs: with other people, with things such as work and school, and with larger frames such as nature, art and religion. Modern society, driven by growth and speed, tends to turn the world into something to be mastered, and so resonance is under threat.
ideas: Rosa defines resonance as a responsive relation to the world, in which we are touched by something and answer back, and we change in the process.
Its opposite is alienation, the sense that the world is mute, indifferent or hostile, and that we can only use it or endure it.
Resonance cannot be commanded or purchased. It is, he says, always partly out of our control, and trying to engineer it tends to kill it.
He describes horizontal resonance with other people, such as family and friends, and diagonal resonance with things such as work, school and objects.
Vertical resonance concerns the larger frames of life, such as religion, nature and art, and Rosa argues that modern life has weakened many of them.
Modern society is driven by growth and speed, which he says treats the world as something to be mastered and so shuts out resonance.
Critics find the concept vague and hard to test, and say it is hard to tell what would count as a failure to resonate.

Resonance is different from an echo. An echo returns only my own voice, while resonance needs a counterpart with a voice of its own, so it can include friction and disagreement and is not the same as harmony.
Rosa argues that a good life is measured by the quality of our relation to the world and not by resources, options or money, which he treats as means and not ends.
He applies the idea to schooling, arguing that teaching works when teacher, pupil and subject respond to one another and fails when it is organised around performance targets alone.

books.thesis: Pain wrecks language and the world of the person in it. That is why it can be used to unmake people.
books.summary:
Elaine Scarry starts from a plain observation. Physical pain is nearly impossible to describe, and a person in agony loses the ability to speak in sentences. The book asks what that silence does to the sufferer, to the people around them, and to the world they live in.

She argues in two movements. The first looks at how pain shrinks a person's world to the size of a body and takes language with it, and how torturers exploit this by turning the prisoner's surroundings and voice against him. The second half turns to making. Tools, buildings, poems and beliefs are the human answer to pain, ways of extending the body and its feeling into a shared world. Scarry draws on Amnesty reports, the Bible and Marx. Some readers find the second half more speculative than the first, and she leaves open how far imagining can really repair what pain undoes.
ideas: Physical pain has no object. Fear and desire are about something, but pain is about nothing outside itself, which is part of why it is so hard to put into words.
Pain resists language and, at its extreme, destroys it. The person in agony is pushed back toward the cries and groans that come before speech.
For the person in pain, the pain is certain. For everyone else it is easy to doubt. Scarry builds her account of suffering around this gap between certainty and doubt.
Torture is built around interrogation, yet Scarry argues the questions are beside the point. The real work is staging the prisoner's own voice as something that can be broken and used.
In the torture room, ordinary objects such as a chair, a bed or a door become instruments of pain. The shelter a room normally gives is made to attack the person inside.
War, like torture, rests on injuring bodies. Scarry argues that the wounded and dead bodies are used to settle which side's contested beliefs will count as real.
Making and imagining run in the opposite direction from pain. A chair, a poem or a law carries human feeling outward into the world and gives it a shape others can share.
In severe pain the world shrinks to the size of the body, and the sufferer loses the usual sense of a wider world beyond it.
Scarry notes that when people try to describe pain they borrow the language of an injuring weapon, as in a stabbing or burning pain, and so speak of an agent that is not there.
She argues that torture produces a display of power for a regime whose authority is in doubt, turning the prisoner's pain into a show of strength that the regime does not truly have.

books.thesis: Modern identities, jobs and bonds won't hold their shape any more. Freedom comes with unease.
books.summary:
Zygmunt Bauman begins with a metaphor. Solids keep their shape and liquids do not, and he thinks that is a fair picture of life since the late twentieth century. Jobs, institutions, neighbourhoods and personal identities used to be built to last. Now they are expected to change, and the book asks what it feels like to live without anything settled to lean on.

Bauman works through the idea in sections on emancipation, individuality, time and space, work and community. He argues that early modernity melted old traditions in order to cast firmer ones, while the present keeps melting without much rebuilding. People are freer to choose, yet they carry the whole burden of choosing, and the blame when things fail. Power belongs to those who can move, and capital moves faster than anyone. The book is a long essay and not an empirical study, so its sweeping claims are more suggestive than proven.
ideas: Solid modernity melted inherited orders so that better, sturdier ones could replace them. Liquid modernity keeps melting without promising a replacement, so nothing is expected to last.
Individuals are handed the task of building their own identities. When the larger system fails them, the failure tends to be read as a personal shortcoming.
Power has become light and mobile. Capital can move on quickly, while those tied to a place, such as workers and local communities, are left with whatever it leaves behind.
Work has stopped being a lifelong project. Short contracts and constant restructuring make it hard to plan a career or build lasting trust with colleagues.
With distance easy to cross, time becomes the scarce resource. Speed and the ability to move on quickly turn into marks of status.
Old supports such as class, neighbourhood and tradition loosen. People gain freedom and lose company, guidance and the comfort of knowing what is expected of them.
In response to this unease, people look for safety in groups defined by sameness. The search for security can harden into suspicion of strangers.
Bauman worries that the agora, the space where private troubles can be turned into public issues, is emptying out, so people are left to deal with shared problems alone.
He separates individuals de jure from individuals de facto. People are formally free to choose their lives but often lack the means to do so, and this gap is a mark of the liquid age.

He uses the Fordist factory and Bentham's panopticon as images of solid-era power, built on fixed routines and the mutual dependence of capital and labour, in contrast to the present ease of moving on.

books.thesis: We try relationships out without committing, and still can't quite leave them.
books.summary:
Zygmunt Bauman turns his liquid modernity argument toward intimacy. People want close bonds, yet they keep an eye on the exit, and they stay anxious about being left or being stuck. The book asks why human relationships have become so frail and what that does to the people in them.

Bauman argues that consumer habits have seeped into love. A partner is weighed like a purchase, judged on satisfaction, and replaced if the return disappoints. Commitment looks like a risk that closes off other options, while a life without it feels lonely and unprotected. He notes how a market for advice, columns and guides thrives on this uncertainty, and he extends the worry to how we treat strangers and neighbours. The tone is that of an essayist and not a researcher, and Bauman offers no remedy. He suggests only that love needs a willingness to be vulnerable which the culture of keeping options open works against.
ideas: Bonds are entered with an exit in view. People want closeness and also want to stay free to leave, and the two wishes pull against each other.
Bauman contrasts relationships with connections. A connection is easy to make and easy to cut, and phones and online networks make it easier still.
Consumer habits seep into love. A partner gets judged like a product on satisfaction and is expected to be replaceable if the experience disappoints.
Commitment feels like a risk that closes off other options. Yet a life without it leaves people lonely and insecure, so they are stuck between two fears.
Advice columns and relationship experts do well because people distrust their own judgement. The advice often treats love as a skill to be bought and practised.
Sex is increasingly treated as a self-contained episode with no duty to continue afterwards, which fits a culture that prizes keeping options open.
Bauman takes up the old call to love your neighbour and asks how it holds up when strangers are mostly seen as a risk.
Bauman discusses semi-detached couples, who keep separate homes and lives, as a way of hedging against the risk of a bond that is hard to leave.
Virtual proximity, he suggests, makes contact easy and frequent but thin, and it may wear away the skills needed to sustain lasting ties.
He notes that, as other bonds feel fragile, a child can be treated as an object of emotional consumption, a dependable source of feeling, which places a heavy load on the child.

books.thesis: People seen as a category first and a person second have their inner lives deformed by it.
books.summary:
Frantz Fanon was a psychiatrist from Martinique, and this book is his attempt to describe what colonial racism does to the mind of a Black person. He asks why Black men and women in the Antilles and in France so often measure themselves against a white standard, and what it costs them to live in a world that sees skin first and a person second.

He looks at language, at desire and relationships across racial lines, and at the way a sense of inferiority is laid onto people from outside. He argues with psychoanalysts such as Octave Mannoni, and he borrows and bends Hegel's account of recognition. The prose moves between case analysis and personal testimony, and some of his claims about women and about homosexuality have been sharply criticised. The book ends without a programme. It asks for a person to be free of both history's weight and a fixed racial identity.
ideas: In the Antilles, speaking good French counts as a step toward being treated as fully human. Fanon shows how mastering the colonizer's language brings approval and also a loss of self.
Fanon argues that a sense of inferiority is produced by economic and social conditions. It gets laid onto the skin from outside and is no private trait of the individual.
On a train in France a child says, Look, a Negro. Fanon describes feeling reduced to an object fixed by another's gaze, no longer a person with his own body and view.
He reads the desire of some Black women for white men, and Black men for white women, as attempts to escape inferiority. Critics have found his treatment of women unfair.
Fanon rejects Octave Mannoni's claim that colonised peoples are dependent by temperament from the start. He argues that the colonial situation itself creates the dependence.
Using Hegel, Fanon argues that the Black man is denied real recognition. The slave's freedom was handed over by the master and never won, so reciprocal acknowledgement is missing.
The book closes by refusing to let either the weight of the past or a fixed racial essence define a person, and it asks for a life open to questioning.
Fanon argues that a full diagnosis needs sociogeny alongside ontogeny and phylogeny, meaning the social origin of the disorder, which he finds in colonial and racial relations.
He rejects Jung's idea of a collective unconscious as an inherited feature, saying that the Black person as a symbol of evil is learned from comics, stories and schooling.

Fanon describes reading Sartre's Black Orpheus, which treats negritude as a passing stage in a larger dialectic, and says it left him feeling that his own experience had been placed inside someone else's argument.

books.thesis: Colonial violence is psychological as well as political, and so is the violence of resistance.
books.summary:
Written while Frantz Fanon was dying of leukaemia and serving the Algerian independence movement, this book asks what colonialism does to people and what ending it will cost them. Fanon was a psychiatrist, and he treats colonial rule as a system that damages minds as well as economies. The question running through it is how a colonised people can become free without simply copying the order that ruled them.

Fanon argues that the colonial world is split into two zones kept apart by force, and that decolonisation is therefore a violent process. He describes violence as a way the colonised recover self-respect and unity. Critics including Hannah Arendt have disputed this, and how to read it remains debated. The national bourgeoisie, he says, tends to inherit the colonial machinery and use it for itself, and he warns about nationalism that lacks a social programme. The final chapter presents clinical cases from the Algerian war.
ideas: The colonial world is cut into two zones, the settler's town and the native quarter, kept apart by police and soldiers and described by Fanon as a world of opposites.
Fanon says decolonisation is always a violent process, since it replaces one order of people with another and no colonial power gives up its position out of politeness.
For the colonised, violence is described as freeing. It frees the native from a sense of inferiority and from passivity. Arendt and others have disputed this claim.
The national bourgeoisie, in Fanon's account, inherits the colonial machinery and imitates the old rulers. It lacks the means or will to build a new economy for everyone.
Fanon looks to the peasantry as the main revolutionary force. He thinks the urban workers have been partly bought off by a share in the colonial economy.
National consciousness without a social programme decays into narrow nationalism or tribalism. He warns of single-party rule and leaders who take the place of the people.
In the last chapter, Fanon presents clinical cases of Algerian fighters and French torturers whose disorders he links to the colonial war.

In the chapter On National Culture, Fanon warns that intellectuals who dig up pre-colonial traditions to restore pride risk freezing the past, and he says a living culture is made in the struggle for liberation.
He is wary of the spontaneity of rural revolt and argues that it needs political education, with leaders who explain and listen to the people instead of giving orders.
He ends by urging the Third World not to imitate Europe, and to work toward a new humanism and a new kind of person.

books.thesis: Patriarchy hurts men as well, because it teaches them to fear their own feelings.
books.summary:
bell hooks wrote this book to speak to men, and she begins from an uncomfortable observation. Many men say they want love and feel little of it, and many of the women around them find them emotionally closed. She asks why men are so often cut off from their own feelings, and she answers by looking at how boys are raised.

Hooks defines patriarchy as a system of domination that shapes men as well as women. Boys learn early to hide feeling, and that lesson is often taught by shaming or violence. In a series of short chapters on work, sex, violence and love, she argues that patriarchal masculinity ties a man's worth to power and provision and teaches him that vulnerability is weakness. She is also clear that women help sustain the system. Her proposal is that men can choose honesty and emotional openness, and that love offers a real alternative to dominance.
ideas: Hooks defines patriarchy as a system of domination that boys and men are socialised into, which makes it something men live inside and not simply benefit from.
Boys are taught early to bury what they feel. The lesson is often delivered through shaming, punishment or violence, sometimes by their own parents.
Many men want love, hooks argues, yet they have learned that needing it is weak. They settle for control, silence or distance instead.
Women help sustain patriarchy as well. Hooks says mothers and partners often teach and reward the same emotional restraint in boys and men.
She links male violence to the demand that men prove themselves through dominance, and suggests it often covers an unspoken pain.
Patriarchal ideas of work tie a man's worth to status and provision, leaving his sense of self fragile when that standing is lost.
Hooks argues that men can change by choosing honesty and emotional openness, and she presents love as a real alternative to the will to dominate.
Hooks criticises earlier feminist writing for leaving men out and treating them only as enemies, which gave men no picture of how they might change.
She argues that patriarchal men learn to treat sex as a performance or a conquest cut off from feeling, which leaves sex lonely and intimacy out of reach.
She discusses how images of Black men in popular culture tie manhood to dominance and violence, which she sees as an exaggeration of ideas held across society.

books.thesis: Gender is a performance repeated until it looks natural. It could be repeated differently.
books.summary:
Judith Butler wrote Gender Trouble to challenge a basic assumption in feminist thought, that there is a stable group called women whose interests politics should serve. She asks what produces that category, who it leaves out, and what the sense of an inner gender identity actually rests on.

Butler argues that the split between biological sex and cultural gender breaks down, because ideas about sex are already shaped by gender. She proposes that gender is performative, produced through repeated acts, gestures and speech that make it look natural, and she describes a heterosexual matrix that expects sex, gender and desire to line up. Drag is offered as an example of how imitation can expose the lack of an original. Performativity is often misread as choosing a gender each morning, and Butler denies that. The book is famously dense, and critics have argued over both its style and whether its politics can be put into practice.
ideas: Feminism often assumes a stable group called women. Butler argues that the category leaves people out and is itself made by the power it hopes to challenge.
The split between biological sex and cultural gender does not hold up for Butler, because our ideas about sex are already shaped by gender.
The heterosexual matrix is a framework that expects sex, gender and desire to line up, as in a male body, masculine behaviour and desire for women. Deviations get treated as failures.
Gender is performative. There is no doer behind the deed. Repeated acts, gestures and speech produce the appearance of an inner identity, and repetition makes it look natural.
Performativity is often misread as choosing a gender each morning. Butler says the acts are constrained by norms nobody picked, so freedom lies in how they are repeated.
Drag shows gender as imitation. It hints that the supposed original is itself an imitation, though critics dispute how subversive drag really is.
Change comes through subversive repetition, shifting the terms of gender from within. The book's difficult style has drawn complaints from readers who want the argument stated more plainly.

Drawing on Freud, Butler argues that gender identity is partly formed through gender melancholy, in which a lost same-sex attachment is taken in and not mourned, because the taboo on homosexuality forbids grieving it.
She reads Beauvoir's line that one is not born but becomes a woman, and asks whether that becoming is a matter of choice, concluding that it is shaped by norms.
Borrowing from Mary Douglas and Julia Kristeva, she argues that bodily boundaries are policed through the idea of the abject, so gender norms depend on excluded and disavowed bodies.

books.thesis: Science runs on imaginative pictures, and the picture of the lone rational mind is a myth.
books.summary:
Mary Midgley argues that human thinking runs on imaginative pictures, and that science is no exception. She uses the word myth for a deep, shared image that organises how people see things, and she does not mean that it must be false.

Midgley takes aim at several. One is the image of society as a pile of separate, self-interested individuals. Another is nature as a machine, and a third is progress as a steady climb. She is sharply critical of popular science that dresses opinions about human nature up as results, with the selfish gene as her chief example. Her philosopher's habit is to ask what a metaphor is quietly doing. The book also holds that no single science can describe everything, so different kinds of explanation have to live together. Some scientists found her too hostile to reductionism, and the book is more a collection of provocations than a system.
ideas: Myth in this book means a deep imaginative pattern, such as progress, that organises how people think. It is a way of seeing and need not be a falsehood.
Science runs on images such as nature as a machine. They are picked up early, shape which questions get asked, and are rarely checked.
The picture of society as built from separate, self-interested individuals is an old story, and Midgley argues it ignores how dependent humans are on one another from birth.
She criticises metaphors such as the selfish gene for slipping a view of human nature into what is presented as plain science.
Progress is another myth. The belief that history climbs steadily and that science will solve everything is something Midgley questions throughout the book.
Descartes's picture of mind as separate from the rest of nature feeds the fantasy of a detached, purely rational thinker, which Midgley treats as a myth about ourselves.
No single science covers everything, so different kinds of explanation, including those of the humanities, have to be allowed to coexist.
Midgley criticises the picture of evolution as a ladder or escalator leading up to humans, which she sees as a myth of progress dressed as biology.
She is wary of the claim that minds are computers and that brains can be copied, which she counts as another version of the machine myth.
She suggests that images such as Gaia, whatever their scientific standing, remind us that we belong to an interdependent whole, which the machine picture hides.

books.thesis: Capitalism has shaped how we feel and talk about intimacy, and made it cooler and more calculating.
books.summary:
Eva Illouz is a sociologist, and she begins with a puzzle. We talk about our feelings more than any earlier generation, in therapy, in offices, in relationships, and yet intimacy often feels calculated and thin. She asks how the economy and the language of emotion came to be so tangled together.

Her answer is a concept she calls emotional capitalism, in which economic life takes on the vocabulary of feeling and emotional life takes on the logic of the market. She traces how twentieth century managers drew on psychology to understand workers, how therapeutic language moved from the clinic into the home, and how skills such as communication became things to measure. Online dating serves as a late example, since partners appear as profiles ranked against criteria. The book is an argument about culture and not an experiment, and critics say it paints the past as warmer than it was.
ideas: Illouz coins the term emotional capitalism. Economic life takes on the vocabulary of feeling, and emotional life takes on the logic of calculation, so each shapes the other.
Managers in the early twentieth century used psychology to understand workers and raise productivity, which brought talk of emotion and communication into the workplace.
Therapeutic language spread from the clinic into the home. Words such as communication, needs and boundaries treat relationships as something to be worked on and negotiated.
Emotional skills came to be measured like job skills. Feeling is judged as competence, so a person can look emotionally better or worse equipped.
Online dating presents partners as profiles to be compared against criteria. Illouz uses it to show how people begin to evaluate each other like goods.
The ideal of the emotionally healthy person turns into a norm, so unhappiness can look like a personal failure to be fixed and not a shared problem.
She argues that feminism and therapy together promoted an ideal of equal, communicative marriage, which also made marriage easier to question and to leave.
Illouz reads the therapeutic narrative of the self, in which a person's past is told as an injury to be overcome, as a story now spread widely through self-help books and talk shows.
She looks at advice writers such as Dale Carnegie as teaching people to manage their feelings in order to get along and win cooperation, which links emotional skill to commercial success.

In her chapter on online dating she argues that the Internet favours imagination over bodily presence in early contact, so people form attachments to a textual self and are often let down at a first meeting.

books.thesis: Why does modern love hurt? Choice and self-worth are tangled together, and we compare endlessly.
books.summary:
Eva Illouz begins with a question that sounds almost too simple. Why does love hurt so much, and why does it seem to hurt more now that people choose their partners freely? Illouz, a sociologist, says a large share of the pain comes from the social conditions of choosing.

She argues that in earlier eras family, rank and moral character gave romantic choice firm footing. Today the choice rests on the self, so being chosen or rejected feels like a verdict on one's worth. The internet and the sexual marketplace add endless comparison, and Illouz speaks of uncertainty about what we want and feel. She also claims that men and women hold unequal power in that marketplace, a point critics dispute. The book offers a diagnosis and no cure. It does not suggest going back to constrained courtship, and it leaves open how people might love well under conditions that make love so exposed.
ideas: Illouz argues that much of love's pain comes from social arrangements. Psychology tends to treat it as individual damage, which she thinks misses the larger picture.
She uses Jane Austen's novels as a contrast case, where social rank and moral character gave romantic choice firmer footing than it has today.
Free choice ties romance to self-worth. Being chosen or rejected feels like a verdict on the person, so rejection hurts as recognition withheld.
Endless options and easy comparison, helped by the internet, lead people to measure each prospect against others. That makes commitment harder and keeps them browsing.
Illouz says people have become unsure what they want and what the other person wants, and that this uncertainty is built into how modern romantic choice works.
Sexual freedom, she argues, gives men and women unequal power in the sexual marketplace, because men can often delay commitment more easily. Critics say this is overstated.
The book offers a diagnosis and no cure. It does not argue for going back to arranged or tightly controlled courtship.
Illouz points to an asymmetry of time, in which age and the fertility timeline weigh on women far more than on men, and says this shapes who can afford to delay commitment.
She says psychology and self-help have rationalised romance, in the sense Max Weber gave the word, so that people learn to assess relationships by standards of fit, satisfaction and communication.
Idealising imagination plays a large part, she argues, since people build a picture of a partner in advance and suffer disappointment when the real person differs.

books.thesis: Be kind to yourself and you get more resilience than self-criticism ever gave you.
books.summary:
Kristin Neff, a psychologist, asks a practical question. When we fail or suffer, why are we so much harsher on ourselves than on a friend, and does that harshness help? Most of us half believe that an inner critic keeps us honest and driven. Neff sets out to test that belief against the research.

She breaks self-compassion into three parts. Self-kindness replaces harsh self-judgement, common humanity reminds us that failing is shared, and mindfulness means seeing painful feelings without burying them or being swept off by them. She separates it from self-esteem, which rises and falls with success and often depends on feeling above others. Drawing on studies, including some of her own, she reports links between self-compassion and lower anxiety and depression, and she argues it does not breed complacency. The book includes short exercises. Her roots in Buddhist practice shape the approach, and some critics think the research is still young.
ideas: Self-compassion means treating yourself the way you would treat a friend who is struggling, with warmth in place of the usual inner scolding.
Neff splits it into three parts, which are self-kindness, a sense of common humanity, and mindfulness. Each answers a different habit of harsh self-treatment.
Common humanity means seeing that failure and suffering are shared parts of life, which counters the feeling of being uniquely flawed or alone.
Self-esteem differs from self-compassion. Esteem rises and falls with success and often depends on comparison, while self-compassion stays available when things go badly.
Mindfulness here means noticing painful feelings as they are, without pushing them away or being carried off by them. One has to see suffering before one can be kind to it.
Neff cites research suggesting that self-criticism motivates less well than people think, and that people who treat themselves kindly tend to try again after failure.
The book offers short practices, such as a brief self-compassion break combining a calming phrase and a soothing touch, for building the habit.
Neff separates self-compassion from self-pity. Self-pity is absorbed in one's own troubles and forgets that others suffer too, while self-compassion keeps the shared human view in sight.
She argues that self-compassion is not self-indulgence. A person who cares about a friend wants them to grow, so a kind inner voice can still ask for change.

Drawing on emotion research, she describes self-criticism as triggering the body's threat response, while kindness engages a soothing system, which helps explain why harsh self-talk tends to backfire.

books.thesis: What does courage look like when a way of life ends? Hoping for a good that can't yet be imagined.
books.summary:
Jonathan Lear, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, takes up the story of Plenty Coups, the last great chief of the Crow nation. When the buffalo disappeared and the Crow were confined to a reservation, the activities that gave their lives shape, such as hunting and war, became impossible. Lear asks what courage can mean when the way of life that defined it comes to an end.

He argues that a culture can collapse in a way beyond physical loss. Plenty Coups, guided by a dream of the chickadee, led the Crow to adapt and hold on to a hope Lear calls radical. It is hope for a future good that the people cannot yet picture, since the concepts to describe it do not exist. The book offers a picture of hope at the edge of what a culture can understand, and does not offer a method.
ideas: Plenty Coups, the last great chief of the Crow, led his people through the end of the buffalo-hunting life and into reservation confinement. Lear uses his story as the book's main case.
A culture can collapse in a way beyond physical loss. When counting coup and warfare became impossible, the Crow lost the terms that made their lives intelligible.
As a boy Plenty Coups had a dream in which the chickadee, a small bird that survives by listening and learning, was held up as a model. Lear reads it as preparation.
Plenty Coups said that after the buffalo were gone, nothing happened. Lear reads this as a sign that the Crow could no longer tell events as stories with a point.
Radical hope is hope for a future good that exceeds our present ability to conceive it. It has no content yet, so it depends on trust that the world is basically good.
Courage is usually defined by a culture. Lear asks what it means when the culture that defines it is gone, and suggests that then courage is the hope itself.
Lear takes care to present this as a picture of hope under extreme conditions. He does not offer it as a recipe or claim that every choice of Plenty Coups was right.

Lear discusses the Crow decision to side with the United States against rival tribes, and reads Plenty Coups as judging that resistance would lead to the Crow's destruction, a choice made without being able to picture the future.
Lear speaks of the vulnerability of a culture. Every way of life rests on concepts that can cease to make sense, and its members may not be able to see this coming.
His main source is the life of Plenty Coups recorded by Frank Linderman, and Lear is aware that it is a recorded retelling and not a text in the chief's own hand.

books.t: Happiness, Death, and the Remainder of Life
books.thesis: Read together, Freud and Aristotle show what a good life asks of us once we know we will die.
books.summary:
Jonathan Lear sets two thinkers side by side who are rarely read together, Aristotle and Freud. Both are concerned with how a human being can live well, and both worked with a view of the mind in which reason and desire pull against each other. Lear asks what a good life demands from us once we take seriously that it will end.

He reads Aristotle's account of happiness as an activity carried out across a whole life. He notes the tension in Aristotle between a life of ethical action among others and a life of contemplation. Freud, in Lear's reading, adds that much of what moves us is unconscious, so a person may think he is living well while hiding conflict from himself. Lear is also a practising psychoanalyst, and he treats analysis as an ethical practice. It is better at framing the question of how to live in the time that remains than at settling it.
ideas: The book pairs Aristotle's ethics with Freud's psychoanalysis, on the assumption that both are trying to say what it takes for a human being to live well.
For Aristotle, happiness is an activity of living well across a whole life. It is no passing feeling, so it can only be judged over time.
Aristotle sketches two pictures of the best life, a life of virtuous action among other people and a life of contemplation, and Lear examines the strain between them.
Death presses on both thinkers. A good life must be one a person could stand behind while knowing that it will end.
Freud adds that much of what moves us is unconscious, so a person can believe he is living well while hiding a conflict from himself.
Lear is a practising analyst, and he treats psychoanalysis as an ethical practice aimed at living more honestly with one's own desires.
The remainder of life in the title points to the time left to a mortal creature. The book asks how that time can be lived well once death is taken seriously.
Lear draws on Aristotle's discussion of Solon's saying that no one can be called happy until death, which shows that the shape of a life is only fixed at its end.
He reads Freud's late idea of a death drive as an attempt to think about repetition and the pull toward ending, and he treats it as a serious question and not a settled doctrine.
He suggests that the analytic aim of making the unconscious conscious has an ethical side, since a person's character is shaped by what he can bear to know about himself.

books.thesis: Photographs make us feel we own the world, and quietly empty our experience of it.
books.summary:
Susan Sontag collected six essays on photography in this book, and she starts from an everyday fact. We live among photographs, and we tend to take for granted what they do to the way we see. The book asks what changes when experience becomes something a person can capture, keep and collect.

Sontag argues that photographing is a way of taking possession. It lets us feel that we own a place or a person while keeping a safe distance from them, and it turns the world into a stock of images. She compares our situation to Plato's cave and says that photographs seem to be pieces of the real, which gives them authority, though framing and choice shape what they show. She draws on surrealism, on Diane Arbus and on the habits of tourists. Some of her claims, particularly about Arbus, have been disputed, and she later revised her view that images simply numb us.
ideas: Sontag returns to Plato's cave. We live among images that tell us what the world is like, and we take them as a replacement for it.
Photographing is a way of taking possession. The traveller with a camera has a souvenir of the place and a protection from really meeting it.
The vocabulary of photography is borrowed from hunting and violence. People load, aim and shoot, and Sontag suggests that photographing people treats them as things.
A photograph seems like a piece of the real, a trace taken directly from the scene. That gives it authority, though framing and selection shape what it shows.
Every photograph is a reminder of mortality. It holds a moment from a life that has moved on, and old pictures of people long dead carry that quality.
Sontag links photography to surrealism and its taste for the overlooked and shabby. She reads Diane Arbus's pictures of outsiders as cold, a view critics have disputed.
As images multiply, shock wears off. A culture of images changes what counts as real and what we feel we need to look at.
Sontag notes that families use photographs to build a portrait chronicle, and that taking snapshots has become part of the ritual of family life, at weddings and on holidays.
She argues that the photographer's role is one of non-intervention. To record a scene of suffering is to stand outside it, and the camera can become a way of not acting.
She traces an American taste, from Whitman through Walker Evans to Arbus, for treating all things as equally worth seeing, and says this democratic vision can flatten moral distinctions.

books.thesis: The metaphors we wrap around disease add suffering and blame. Best to resist them.
books.summary:
Susan Sontag wrote this short book after her own treatment for cancer, though she keeps herself out of its pages. She noticed that diseases do more than make people sick. They attract meanings, and those meanings can cause their own suffering. She asks what is added when tuberculosis and cancer are described in terms of character, passion, repression and war.

Sontag compares the two diseases. TB was romanticised in the nineteenth century as a disease of sensitivity and passion that refined the sufferer. Cancer, in the twentieth, was cast as a shameful condition linked to repression and growth gone wild. In both cases the patient is hinted to be responsible. She also criticises military language, such as wars on cancer and invading cells, which makes death a defeat. Her answer is to resist metaphor and look at illness plainly, though she admits that this is hard.
ideas: Sontag argues that the healthiest way of being ill is the one most free of metaphor. The wish to see illness plainly drives the whole book.
In the nineteenth century, tuberculosis was romanticised as a disease of sensitivity and passion, and it lent the sufferer a refined, interesting look.
Cancer, in the twentieth century, was imagined as shameful and tied to repression and uncontrolled growth, which made it feel like a judgement on the person.
Both diseases get read as expressions of character. The patient is hinted to be partly responsible, which adds blame to the pain of being sick.
Military metaphors, such as the war on cancer or invading cells, turn the patient into a battlefield and make dying look like a defeat.
Diseases with unknown causes and no sure cure attract moral meaning. As understanding and treatment improve, the aura begins to fade.
Her remedy is to resist metaphor and speak about illness plainly. She admits that metaphor is hard to avoid and that people use it for understandable reasons.
Sontag wrote the essay while being treated for cancer, but she keeps her own case out of it and writes as a critic of language and ideas.
She notes that political language borrows illness, as when a society is said to be sick or a group is called a cancer, and says that this kind of metaphor can license harsh measures.
She observes that doctors in some countries used to withhold a cancer diagnosis from patients, because the word carried so much shame and dread.

books.thesis: Images of suffering don't guarantee compassion. They can numb as well as move.
books.summary:
Susan Sontag opens with a question from Virginia Woolf's Three Guineas. Woolf thought pictures of war's victims might unite people against war. Sontag asks whether that is true, and what we actually do when we look at images of other people's suffering. She is also revisiting her own earlier view, in On Photography, that a steady diet of such images numbs us.

She now argues that compassion is unstable. A picture can move a viewer, but the feeling fades or freezes if nothing can be done with it. She points out that the same image can serve opposite sides, depending on its caption and context, and that early war photographers sometimes arranged their scenes. She looks back to Goya's etchings and forward to the way memory increasingly works through pictures. A recurring warning is against assuming a shared us when we look at the pain of others, since safe viewers do not stand where the sufferers do.
ideas: Sontag begins with Virginia Woolf, who in Three Guineas thought pictures of war's victims might unite people against war. Sontag doubts the simple version of that hope.
She revises her earlier claim that images numb us. The problem, she says, is that compassion cannot last unless it turns into some kind of action.
The same picture of suffering can serve opposite sides. A caption and a context decide what it is taken to prove.
Early war photographers sometimes arranged their scenes, as Roger Fenton is said to have done in the Crimea, and a famous Capa photograph is still disputed. Photographs were never raw records.
Goya's etchings of war's cruelty show that the shock of images belongs to more than photography. Art made it hard to look away long before cameras did.
Sontag warns against assuming a shared we when looking at pictures of others' pain. Safe viewers do not stand where the sufferers do.
Memory increasingly works through pictures. A vivid image can stay with us while a narrative, which might help us understand, slips away.
Sontag notes that news pictures show the far-off dead of other peoples in ways seldom used for a nation's own dead, so that the dignity of being shown is unevenly given.
She suggests that an existing antiwar movement, and not the photographs alone, gave images of the Vietnam War their force.
She acknowledges that people feel an appetite to look at horror, and treats it as a fact to be faced and not only as a vice.

books.thesis: Crowds and rulers grow from one root: the wish to survive others.
books.summary:
Elias Canetti's book asks a blunt question. What are crowds, why do people join them, and how do they relate to the people who rule? Humans dislike being touched by strangers, and a crowd is the place where that fear is briefly reversed, as individuals feel themselves equal.

The first half is a taxonomy of crowds, including open and closed ones, baiting and flight crowds, and the images such as fire, sea and forest that societies attach to them. The second half turns to power. Canetti argues that commands leave a sting in whoever obeys, and that the root of power is the survivor, someone who stands among the dead and feels the satisfaction of having lived. He reads the memoirs of Daniel Paul Schreber as a portrait of paranoia as the illness of power. The book is a work of free association, not a proof, and many readers treat it as a meditation more than a theory.
ideas: People dread being touched by strangers. A crowd is where that fear reverses, and Canetti opens the book with this ordinary observation about how people guard their personal space.
Discharge is the moment a crowd forms, when differences of rank and status fall away and everyone feels equal.
Open crowds grow without limit but can vanish quickly, while closed crowds keep their boundaries and last longer. Canetti sorts many types of crowds in his taxonomy.
Societies attach symbols to crowds, such as fire, sea, rain, forest and grain. Canetti reads each as expressing a quality of the crowd it represents.
Every command leaves a sting in the person who obeys. People tend to pass that sting down to others beneath them, which creates chains of command.
The survivor sits at the root of power. Standing among the dead, he feels the satisfaction of having lived, and the ruler wants to be the one who survives everyone.
Canetti reads the memoirs of Daniel Paul Schreber as a portrait of paranoia, which he presents as the characteristic illness of power.

Canetti classifies crowds by their dominant feeling, including baiting crowds, flight crowds, prohibition crowds, reversal crowds and feast crowds, and he adds the double crowd, such as two armies or two sexes facing each other.
Crowd crystals are small, tight groups, such as armies or religious orders, that give a crowd its shape and keep it from dissolving.
He treats secrecy as central to power. The ruler conceals his intentions while demanding to know everything about others.

books.thesis: Intelligent people take up ideology to avoid the discomfort of being alone with the truth.
books.summary:
Czesław Miłosz, a Polish poet who left his country's diplomatic service in 1951, wrote this book to explain how intelligent writers and thinkers came to accept Stalinist rule. Why do educated people, who could see what was happening, choose to believe?

He uses two borrowed images. The Pill of Murti-Bing, taken from a novel by Witkiewicz, is a pill that makes its swallower serenely content with the new order. Ketman, a term Miłosz took from Gobineau's account of Persia, is the art of outward conformity while holding inward reservations. He offers four portraits of Polish writers, labelled with Greek letters, who each made peace with the regime for different reasons. He argues that a complete doctrine gives people certainty and a place in history, which is a relief after war. The book is a personal essay and not a study, and some of its sketches have been matched to real people by later readers.
ideas: The Pill of Murti-Bing comes from a novel by Witkiewicz. Swallowing it makes a person cheerfully content with the new order, and Miłosz uses it as an image for intellectual conversion.
Ketman is the art of outward conformity while holding inward reservations. Miłosz borrowed the word from Gobineau's account of Persia and describes several varieties of it.
A total doctrine offers answers, a place in history and relief from uncertainty. Miłosz suggests that this was especially tempting to minds exhausted by war.
He draws four portraits of Polish writers, named with Greek letters, who each reached an accommodation with the regime for different reasons.
Fear alone does not explain it. Miłosz insists that many intellectuals took up the new belief out of conviction and hunger for meaning.
He suggests that playing a role long enough can change the player. The mask of Ketman can harden into belief.
Miłosz writes as someone who felt the temptation himself, and the book unsettles because it does not treat those who gave in as fools.
The four portraits are labelled Alpha the Moralist, Beta the Disappointed Lover, Gamma the Slave of History and Delta the Troubadour, each showing a different route into accommodation.
Miłosz describes varieties of Ketman, such as national, professional and aesthetic, in which a person defends a compromise as serving the nation, his craft or beauty.
He describes how socialist realism required art to serve the doctrine, so that writers had to praise the order they lived under and were judged by their usefulness to the Party.

books.thesis: Aphorisms against hope, and strangely good company.
books.summary:
Emil Cioran was a Romanian writer who settled in Paris and wrote in French, and this collection of aphorisms is one of his late books. It circles a single idea, that being born is the original trouble, the one fact no argument can undo. The book is a run of short fragments, each in its own mood, on birth, sleeplessness, God, time and the thought of ending it all.

Cioran is hostile to hope, plans and progress, which he sees as ways of postponing a plain fact. He comes back often to suicide, as a thought that makes life bearable more than as an act. He is drawn to saints and mystics while having no faith, and he praises music, Bach especially, with something close to gratitude. The surprise is the tone. The despair arrives with wit, and many readers find the book consoling and good company.
ideas: Birth is treated as the original misfortune. The whole book circles the idea that having been born at all is a trouble that cannot be corrected.
Cioran returns often to the thought of suicide as something that makes life bearable, a resource he keeps in reserve, and he does not present it as a plan.
Insomnia is a recurring subject. Being awake at night, lucid and alone, sharpens his sense of existing as a burden.
Hope, plans and progress are targets of his scorn. He sees them as ways of postponing a plain fact that people would rather not look at.
Music, and Bach in particular, is among the few things he writes about with something close to gratitude.
Cioran writes about saints, mystics and Buddhists with envy, since he admires a faith he does not share.
The form is fragments, each a mood and not an argument, and the despair is delivered with wit. Many readers find that oddly consoling.
The French title, De l'inconvénient d'être né, speaks of an inconvenience, which gives the complaint a dry, understated tone that the English title only partly keeps.
Cioran returns to God and the idea of a flawed creator, using them to voice a complaint and not to set out a doctrine.
He treats writing as a way of getting through bad days, a means of managing despair and not a way of overcoming it.

books.thesis: Exhaustion and doubt, written about with unusual force.
books.summary:
A Short History of Decay was Emil Cioran's first book in French, published in 1949 after years of writing in Romanian. He is said to have rewritten it several times, and the prose has a formal, polished edge. The subject is exhaustion, doubt and the sense of coming at the end of something.

The book is a series of short essays and aphorisms, with no single argument. Cioran treats lucidity as a kind of illness, doubt as a habit that cannot even spare itself, and civilisations as organisms that tire and fall. He distrusts enthusiasm and system building, and he prefers failure and disillusion to the comfort of belief. Readers divide over whether this is nihilism or a perverse tonic, and the book gives no help in deciding. What is clear is the force of the sentences. Cioran makes weariness a subject with a style, and later books return to the same themes with less polish.
ideas: Cioran treats lucidity as a kind of ailment. In his telling, seeing the human situation clearly wears the observer down rather than freeing him.
Doubt is turned on everything, including itself. He points to exhaustion behind every system of belief that people offer him.
Civilisations are shown as organisms that age. Late cultures turn inward and tire, a theme that echoes Spengler.
The book was written in French, his adopted language, and the formal prose gives the despair a classical shape.
Weariness is treated as a kind of knowledge and not as a problem to be cured, and fatigue becomes a vantage point on modern life.
Cioran distrusts enthusiasm. He sees the energy of movements and causes as fanaticism waiting to happen, and he prefers disillusion.
The essays are bleak and ironic, and readers disagree about whether the effect is nihilism or a strange comfort.
He prefers the moralist, the mystic and the aphorist to the system builder, and treats philosophy as closer to temperament than to proof.
Time is cast as the real solvent, wearing away every conviction and giving all projects a sense of futility.
