Critics point to Cioran's early writing in Romania in the 1930s, which showed sympathy for the fascist Iron Guard, and ask how it bears on the later pessimism.

books.thesis: We become what we practise, and philosophy should be a kind of training.
books.summary:
Peter Sloterdijk takes his title from a line in a Rilke poem, in which a viewer standing before an ancient headless statue of Apollo feels the stone telling him to change. Sloterdijk's answer is that humans are creatures who practise, and that most of what we call character, belief and culture comes out of repeated exercise.

He calls the study of this anthropotechnics, and he reads religions, monastic orders, athletic regimes and artistic discipline as training systems. Religion, he suggests, has been misunderstood as a matter of belief when it is closer to a programme of exercises. He describes a vertical tension, the sense of being pulled between higher and lower ways of living. Toward the end he turns to global risks and asks what shared practice might be needed. Critics find the central claim stretched across too many cases, and its secular reading of religion is contested.
ideas: The title comes from a Rilke poem about a headless statue of Apollo that seems to demand change from the viewer. Sloterdijk takes the demand as his motto.
Humans are creatures who practise. Repetition and discipline make us what we are, and Sloterdijk calls the study of this anthropotechnics.
He suggests that what we call religions are better read as training programmes, collections of exercises, than as systems of belief.
Asceticism comes from the Greek word for exercise. Monks, athletes, philosophers and artists belong together as people who shaped themselves by practice.
Vertical tension is the sense that life is pulled between a higher and a lower way of being. Exercise is how people try to climb.
Modern culture has lost the language of practice. People are treated as producers and consumers, and Sloterdijk wants practice back, in a secular form.
Toward the end he turns to shared global risks and asks what common training a threatened world might need.
Sloterdijk builds on Pierre Hadot's reading of ancient philosophy as spiritual exercises, and extends it into a general theory of human self-formation.
He reads Nietzsche as a thinker of training, whose image of the overman stands for rising through practice and not for a biological type.
In the closing pages he proposes co-immunism, the idea of a shared protective system built through common practice, as a response to global risks.

books.thesis: Torture destroys trust in the world. Resentment, meanwhile, can be a moral stance.
books.summary:
Jean Améry was an Austrian-born essayist who was tortured by the Gestapo in Belgium, then sent to Auschwitz. He wrote these essays more than twenty years later. What can intellect do in a camp, what does torture destroy, and what do survivors owe to those who would prefer them to forgive?

The title essay argues that learning and culture gave very little protection in Auschwitz. In the essay on torture, Améry describes how the first blow shatters trust in the world, and how the victim is reduced to a body at another's mercy. Other essays deal with exile and the loss of home, with being made a Jew by one's persecutors, and with resentment. He insists that resentment can be a moral stance, since it refuses a forgiveness that would let the crime fade. The book is bleak and offers no reconciliation, and Primo Levi disagreed with him on several points.
ideas: In the title essay, Améry argues that learning and culture gave an intellectual little protection in Auschwitz, because the camp's reality outran any aesthetic or philosophical comfort.
In torture, the first blow shatters trust in the world. The victim learns that he cannot count on help from others and never fully regains that confidence.
Under torture the person is reduced to a body in the full power of another, and Améry describes the torturer as becoming sovereign over him.
He rejects the comfort that time heals. In his account, those who have been tortured stay tortured, and the experience does not turn into a lesson.
An essay on exile asks how much home a person needs, and shows how language, scenery and belonging stay with us after being lost.
Améry describes being made a Jew by his persecutors, who defined him that way though he had no religious tie. The label was given by the enemy.
Resentment, he argues, is a moral stance. Refusing to forgive keeps the crime in view when a world eager to move on would like it to fade.
The German title, Jenseits von Schuld und Sühne, means Beyond Guilt and Atonement, and points to the book's concern with guilt and to its German readers.
His essay on torture draws on his own arrest by the Gestapo in Belgium for resistance work, during which he was hung by his arms while being questioned.
He describes the camp figure called the Muselmann, the prisoner worn down past hope, as one for whom intellectual and moral life had stopped.

books.thesis: A chemist calmly records how Auschwitz tried to strip people of their personhood.
books.summary:
Primo Levi was a young Italian chemist and partisan when he was arrested in 1943 and sent to Auschwitz. The question in the title is addressed to the reader. If a person is stripped of name, clothes, hair and work worth doing, and forced to live at the edge of starvation, is that still a man?

He describes the arrival, the tattooed number, the bowl and spoon, the hunger, the camp economy of small trades, and the sickness ward. He is precise and calm, in the manner of a scientist taking notes, and the restraint is what makes the book hard to forget. He also records small moments that kept something human alive, such as a civilian who brought him bread and an attempt to recite Dante to a fellow prisoner. Levi insists he is a witness, and that the worst is known best by those who did not return.
ideas: The opening poem asks whether a person who works in mud, knows no peace and dies for a yes or a no is a man. That is the title question.
On arrival, prisoners are stripped of clothes, hair and names, and given tattooed numbers. Levi shows how the camp set out to erase the person before it killed him.
A guard tells Levi, who has reached for an icicle, that here there is no why. Levi takes it as the camp's refusal to give any reasons.
Survival depended on small things such as a bowl, a spoon, shoes and bread, and on a camp economy of trades and theft in which everything counted.
Levi describes the drowned, prisoners who gave up and went under, and the saved, who usually lived through luck, skill or compromise. He rejects any claim that the saved were the best.
A civilian Italian worker named Lorenzo brought him bread and food over months. Levi credits him with keeping alive a belief that goodness still existed.
On a walk for the soup, Levi tries to recite and translate Dante's canto of Ulysses to a fellow prisoner. For a moment the exchange feels like being human again.
A fellow prisoner, Steinlauf, insists on washing every day even without soap, arguing that prisoners must keep some form of dignity so as not to become beasts.
In the preface Levi says the book is not meant as a new accusation but as documentation for a calm study of certain aspects of the human mind.
His training as a chemist led to a place in the camp laboratory, which spared him outdoor work in winter, and scarlet fever left him in the infirmary when the camp was evacuated.

books.thesis: The grey zone, the shame of survivors, and where judgment runs out.
books.summary:
Primo Levi wrote this book near the end of his life, four decades after Auschwitz, and it reads as a stock-taking. Here he asks how it should be understood, and what has happened to the memory of it. The questions are hard ones, about how reliable memory is, why survivors feel shame, and where fair judgment of the people caught in the camps ends.

Levi warns that memory fades and reshapes itself, including that of survivors and of perpetrators. He describes the grey zone, the space between victim and oppressor where some prisoners were forced into cooperation, and he discusses the Jewish ghetto elder Rumkowski as an ambiguous figure. He writes of the shame of surviving, of the failure of communication, and of violence that served no purpose. Levi urges caution in judging, and the book closes with no verdict, only a sharper sense of what cannot be easily judged.
ideas: Memory is fallible. Levi warns that survivors' recollections fade and reshape themselves, and that perpetrators bend their own memories to fit what they can live with.
The grey zone is the space between victim and oppressor. Some prisoners were forced into collaboration, and Levi urges against hasty condemnation.
He discusses Rumkowski, the Jewish elder of the Łódź ghetto, as a figure who cannot be read simply as villain or victim.
Shame is common among survivors, who feel they lived by taking another's place. Levi also suggests, with pain, that on the whole the worst survived.
Communication failed in the camps. Prisoners who could not understand orders in a babel of languages were often punished or killed for it.
Violence in the camps often served no purpose beyond humiliation and cruelty. Levi gives it a chapter of its own.
In one chapter on the intellectual at Auschwitz, Levi disputes the idea that educated prisoners fared worse or better, and he disagrees with Améry's view in part.
Levi recalls that the SS told prisoners that none would live to tell the story and that no one would believe them if they did, which shaped the survivors' sense of a duty to testify.

He discusses the Sonderkommando, prisoners forced to work in the crematoria, and calls this the most demonic crime of the National Socialist state, while urging that no one has the right to judge them lightly.
In a chapter on letters from Germans, he reads responses from readers of his book, some sincere and some evasive, to show how a nation's memory of the camps was managed.

books.thesis: We build ourselves from scripts handed to us by others, and freedom works inside them.
books.summary:
Kwame Anthony Appiah asks how much of who we are is up to us. We think of identity as personal, yet the labels we live under, such as nation, race, gender and religion, come from other people.

Appiah starts from a liberal idea he takes from Mill, that people should be able to shape their lives by their own lights. He argues, though, that nobody builds a self from nothing. Language and social categories supply the scripts, and individuals work within them. Collective identities help people find company and meaning, but they come with demands, and they can become a tyranny. He doubts that a state should protect cultures against change when members choose differently, and he asks how far communities may shape children. The book is a work of philosophy that leaves many questions open, and critics ask how much room it leaves for group claims.
ideas: Everyone's life is shaped by social materials. Language, categories and roles supply the scripts we choose from, and no one writes a self from nothing.
Appiah draws on Mill's idea that people should shape their lives by their own lights, then asks how that works when we depend on others for the tools.
Collective identities such as gender, race, religion and nation give people company and meaning. They also come with demands, and Appiah warns they can turn into a tyranny.
A true self waiting to be discovered is a doubtful idea for Appiah. Making a self is a continuing conversation with others and with the labels on offer.
The state does not need to preserve cultures against change, Appiah argues, when the individuals inside them make other choices.
He asks how far parents and communities may shape children's identities, and where a liberal state may step in to protect a child's future choices.
Race is a label with social force and little biological support. Appiah uses it to show how labels shape the people who carry them.

Appiah criticises Charles Taylor's politics of recognition, warning that demanding public respect for group identities can push individuals into a script, such as how a Black person or a gay person should behave.
He draws on the idea of looping effects, associated with Ian Hacking, in which people who are classified change in response to the label, so that the category itself changes over time.
Examples such as being gay show how a label that began as medical or insulting can be taken up and given positive meaning, so that identities are made over time.

books.thesis: We can owe things to strangers without needing everyone to become alike.
books.summary:
Kwame Anthony Appiah wrote Cosmopolitanism for general readers. It asks how people can live together in a world of strangers who do not share our values, and what, if anything, we owe to people far away.

He pulls apart two strands of the cosmopolitan idea. One says that our obligations reach beyond family and nation. The other says that we should take the value of particular human lives seriously, including the different ways people live. Appiah argues that these two fit together, and that a cosmopolitan does not want everyone to become alike. He welcomes the mixing of cultures and finds the idea of a pure culture a fiction. He sees conversation as a better model than agreement. Moral change, he suggests, often comes through shifts in practice and honour. Critics say the book is optimistic and thin on structural injustice, and Appiah leaves open how much the duty to strangers should demand of us.
ideas: Cosmopolitanism has two strands. One says we have obligations beyond kin and nation, and the other says we should take seriously the value of particular human lives and ways of living.
A cosmopolitan does not want everyone to become alike. Appiah argues that many local ways of life should thrive, and he is wary of one homogenised global culture.
Cultures have always mixed, and the idea of a pure culture is a fiction. Appiah argues, in what he calls a case for contamination, that mixing is normal and often good.
Conversation is the model. People can live alongside each other without agreeing on values, if they talk and learn about each other's habits.
Moral change often comes through shifts in practice and honour. Appiah cites the end of foot-binding in China as an example.
He treats duties to distant strangers as real and asks how much they demand, taking a middle position short of giving up everything.
Who owns ancient objects? Appiah questions simple nationalist claims to cultural property and defends the idea of a shared human heritage.
Appiah calls fundamentalists counter-cosmopolitans, noting that they too live in a mixed world and often use its tools while resisting its variety.
He draws on his own family, a Ghanaian father and an English mother, as a living example of how a person can belong to more than one place.
He pairs universal concern with fallibilism, meaning that one can hold values firmly and still stay open to being wrong.

books.thesis: Character is an organised way of coping, and understanding it matters more than labelling it.
books.summary:
Nancy McWilliams wrote this book as a guide for therapists, and its question is practical. How can a clinician understand the person in front of her, so that treatment fits? Mainstream diagnostic manuals sort people by symptoms. McWilliams asks what lies underneath, which is a person's organised way of coping with anxiety and relating to others.

She uses two axes. One is the level of personality organisation, running from psychotic through borderline to neurotic. The other is character type, and she gives chapters to narcissistic, schizoid, paranoid, depressive, hysterical, obsessive-compulsive and other styles. She treats defences as protective ways of coping and does not treat them as defects. The therapist's own reactions count as diagnostic data. McWilliams is careful to say that people are mixtures, not boxes, and that the point of diagnosis is understanding. Critics from empirical psychology question how reliable psychoanalytic categories are, and the book's approach is rooted in a clinical tradition.
ideas: Diagnosis here is a way of understanding how a person organises experience in order to guide therapy, and labelling is secondary.
McWilliams uses two axes. One is personality level, running from psychotic to borderline to neurotic, and the other is character type, such as obsessive or hysterical.
Defences such as projection, denial, splitting and repression are protective ways of coping with anxiety. McWilliams treats them as expected features of character and not as defects.
She devotes chapters to personality styles including narcissistic, schizoid, paranoid, depressive, hysterical and obsessive-compulsive, each with its own typical fears and ways of relating.
The therapist's own emotional reactions to a patient, called countertransference, become diagnostic information about what the patient does to people.
She links patterns of character to early relationships, such as how a child handled dependence and loss, while avoiding simple claims about causes.
Symptom-based manuals group people by surface features. McWilliams argues that similar symptoms can come from different structures, which call for different treatment.

She separates primary defences, such as denial, projection and splitting, which are early and distort reality, from secondary defences, such as repression, rationalisation and sublimation, which are more mature.
Reality testing and a coherent sense of identity are the markers she uses, following Kernberg, to separate the psychotic, borderline and neurotic levels.
She stresses that most people mix several character styles, so the types work as lenses for understanding someone and not as boxes to put them in.

books.thesis: Babies think, imagine and experiment more than we assumed. So should the rest of us.
books.summary:
Alison Gopnik, a developmental psychologist, challenges the old assumption that babies are unfinished adults who do little but eat, sleep and cry. The question she asks is what babies and young children are actually doing with their minds, and what that tells us about thought, imagination, consciousness and love.

Gopnik argues that young children learn about the world much as scientists do. They form theories, test them, and revise, and experiments show that even small children can work out causes from patterns. Pretend play and imagining other possibilities, she suggests, are early forms of the capacity that later supports science and planning. She contrasts the lantern-like, wide awareness of children with the narrow spotlight of adult attention. A long childhood, in her account, evolved as a protected time for exploration, with adults supplying care. Some of her claims about babies' inner lives go beyond what the experiments can show.
ideas: Babies are no unfinished adults. Gopnik says they are learners running something close to experiments, nearer to scientists in their method than earlier views allowed.
Experiments suggest that young children can infer what causes what from patterns, using something like statistical reasoning to revise their theories.
Pretend play and imagining other possibilities are early forms of the capacity that later supports science and planning. Children are practising thinking about what might be.
Gopnik describes babies' awareness as lantern-like, wide and diffuse, in contrast to the narrow spotlight of adult attention. She compares it to vivid states such as travel or meditation.
Young children come to understand that other people want and believe different things from themselves, which Gopnik treats as an early stage of understanding other minds.
A long childhood evolved as a protected period for exploration. Children act as the species' research department while adults provide care.
Gopnik argues that caring for a child teaches something about love and moral life that philosophy often neglects.
Babies' brains have more connections than adults' and later prune them, a trade that gives up some flexibility for efficiency as a child grows.
Imaginary companions are treated as normal and not worrying, and as a sign of a child's skill at imagining other minds and other worlds.
She sets her view against the old picture of the baby as a blank slate, arguing that infants arrive with powerful ways of learning about the world.

books.thesis: Happiness acts like a promise, and it points people toward approved lives.
books.summary:
Sara Ahmed starts with a question that sounds contrary. What if happiness is something that tells us how to live, and is more than a feeling we hope to have? She asks what is going on when a culture treats happiness as the goal, and why some people are called unhappy when they refuse the way of life that is supposed to bring it.

Ahmed argues that happiness works as a promise. Certain things, such as marriage, family and a settled home, are marked as happy objects, and people are pointed toward them. Those who do not feel what they are supposed to feel become what she calls affect aliens. She follows the idea through figures, including the happy housewife, the unhappy queer, the melancholic migrant and the feminist killjoy, who is blamed for spoiling the mood when she points to a problem. The book questions the demand and considers what could come from declining it.
ideas: Happy objects are things that carry the expectation of happiness, such as family and marriage. People arrive at them already told what they should feel.
Happiness works as a promise that points people toward particular lives. Following the approved path earns the label happy, so the promise acts as instruction.
An affect alien is someone who does not feel what they are supposed to feel, such as being bored or sad at a wedding, and is often seen as spoiling the occasion.
The feminist killjoy is the person who points to a problem, such as sexism at a dinner table, and is blamed for causing unhappiness and not the problem itself.
The happy housewife is a figure Ahmed uses to show how the language of happiness can cover the constraints placed on women.
The unhappy queer is a figure for how queer lives are described as sad. Ahmed asks what happens when one refuses the promise.
The melancholic migrant is expected to be happy about integration and is seen as a problem if not. Ahmed asks what the demand says about belonging.
Ahmed traces the idea of happiness through philosophers such as Aristotle, Locke and Rousseau, and criticises modern happiness science for treating happiness as a goal that tells people how to live.
She notes that the word comes from hap, meaning chance, and suggests that this older sense points to what happens to us and not to what we are promised.
She suggests that unhappiness can be a source of insight, since those who feel bad about the world may see what the happy path hides.

books.thesis: Politics shapes desire, and we can criticise it without blaming individuals.
books.summary:
Amia Srinivasan, a philosopher at Oxford, grew this book out of an essay on whether anyone has a right to sex, written after attention fell on the online incel movement. The essays ask how political forces shape what we want, and what feminism can say about that without moralising at individuals.

She takes the pain of men who feel excluded from sex seriously, while rejecting the claim that anyone is owed it. She then argues that desire is not wholly private. Who we find attractive is shaped by racism, ableism and ideas of size and gender. Her answer is a politics of desire, in which we can question our tastes without being told that we are guilty for them. She is critical of carceral feminism, the reliance on policing and prison, and she takes up pornography and consent without settling for easy sides. Critics say she raises more than she resolves, which she mostly concedes.
ideas: Srinivasan takes seriously the pain of men who feel shut out of sex, as in the incel movement, and still rejects any claim that someone is owed sex.
No one has a right to sex, because sex requires another person's willing participation. An entitlement would give some people a claim on the bodies of others.
Desire is shaped by politics. Who people find attractive is influenced by race, size and disability, so personal taste is not wholly private.
She argues for a politics of desire. We can question what we want and why without being told we are guilty for it, and without dismissing it as simply natural.
Srinivasan is critical of carceral feminism, which relies on policing and prison, and points to how the criminal system treats people unequally by race.
In an essay on talking with students about pornography, she resists a simple pro or anti position and treats the questions as unsettled.
Consent is necessary but thin. Srinivasan suggests it leaves out whether sex is good, free and shaped by unequal pressures.
The title essay first appeared in the London Review of Books in 2018 and drew wide debate, partly because it was read as asking for sympathy toward people excluded from desire.
She examines how the credibility given to accusers and to the accused varies with race and class, showing that the same suspicion is not applied equally.
She argues that a feminism that speaks only of harm and consent leaves out pleasure, and that the aim should be a sexual life that is good as well as safe.

books.thesis: Before ethics, a simpler question: what is it to act on purpose?
books.summary:
Elizabeth Anscombe's short book of 1957 asks a question that looks too plain to need an answer. What is it to do something on purpose? Philosophers before her tended to say that an intentional act is one caused by a desire or mental state. Anscombe thought this missed what we actually do when we ask and answer questions about each other's actions, and she began from there.

She proposes that intentional actions are those to which a certain sense of the question Why? applies, where the answer gives a reason. She notes that a single event can be described in many ways, and that a person acts intentionally only under some descriptions. She argues that an agent usually knows what he is doing without observing it, and she contrasts this with prediction using her famous example of a shopping list. Anscombe thought that questions like this had to be settled before ethics could be done well.
ideas: Intentional actions are those to which a certain sense of the question Why? applies, meaning the answer gives a reason. Saying I did not know I was doing it rules it out.
One event can fall under many descriptions. A man moves his arm, pumps water, and poisons a household, and he acts intentionally only under some of those descriptions.
Reasons differ from causes. The question Why? asks for a reason, and a person may answer that he had none while some physical cause still operated.
An agent usually knows what he is doing without observing it. Anscombe calls this practical knowledge, and it differs from a prediction or an inference from evidence.
A shopping list guides a man's purchases, so the world has to match the list. A detective's list of what he buys describes the world, so the list has to match it.
A statement of what one is going to do can express an intention and not only forecast events, and the speaker is answerable to it in a way a forecaster is not.
Motives such as revenge or gratitude look backward at what has happened, while others look forward. Anscombe treats talk of motive as a fuller account of what someone is doing.
Answers to the question why form a chain of in order to replies, and the chain ends in something wanted for its own sake, which shows how actions are ordered by ends.
Intending is not a special inner event or feeling. Anscombe, working in Wittgenstein's shadow, holds that it shows in what a person does and says.
She discusses the practical syllogism, the Aristotelian pattern of reasoning from a want and a means to an action, and treats it as an account of how action is reasoned.

books.t: A Natural History of Human Morality
books.thesis: Morality evolved in two steps of cooperation. First people worked together, then they belonged to a group.
books.summary:
Michael Tomasello, a developmental and comparative psychologist, asks where human morality came from. His method is to compare what great apes and young children do, and to build an evolutionary story from the differences.

Tomasello offers a two-step story. In the first step, early humans faced conditions in which they could eat only by foraging together, and each partner became needed by the other. That interdependence, he argues, produced a sense of we, a feeling of deserving a share, and a face-to-face morality of mutual respect between partners. In the second step, larger groups competed with each other, and people came to see themselves as members of a culture with shared norms that apply to everyone. Those norms came to feel objective, and guilt and self-judgement followed. He presents this as a reasoned hypothesis. Critics ask how much we can really infer about ancestors, and he does not claim to explain every part of morality.
ideas: Tomasello compares great apes with young children. Apes sometimes help, but they rarely share fairly or hold one another accountable, as small children begin to do.
In the first step, early humans, in his reconstruction, increasingly depended on others to eat, so each partner in a joint hunt or forage became needed by the other.
Joint foraging gave rise to a sense of we, with partners treating each other as equals. It also gave rise to the idea that each deserves a share of the gains.
Second-personal morality is the face-to-face kind between equal partners. Each feels answerable to the other and can complain when treated unfairly.
In the second step, larger groups competed with one another. People began to identify with a whole culture and to take on its norms as their own.
Group norms came to feel objective, applying to anyone and not just to the people one cooperated with, and guilt and self-judgement grew from that.
Tomasello presents this as a reasoned evolutionary hypothesis. He does not claim it explains every part of morality, and critics ask how much can be inferred about ancestors.
The key idea is shared intentionality, the human ability to form joint goals and share attention, which he sees as what separates human cooperation from that of other apes.
In joint activity each partner sees roles as interchangeable, which Tomasello calls self-other equivalence, and he thinks this lays groundwork for a sense of impartiality.
As groups grew, reputation and partner choice came to matter, since people had to pick cooperative partners and be seen as cooperative themselves.

books.thesis: Life matters because it ends. We should care about this world and not an eternal one.
books.summary:
Martin Hägglund, a philosopher at Yale, asks what makes a life matter. Many traditions say that real meaning lies in eternity, a life with God or beyond death. Hägglund argues the reverse. If nothing could be lost, nothing would be at stake, and the things we care about matter because they can end.

He calls the right attitude secular faith. It means committing to people and projects that are fragile, with no guarantee, which gives urgency to how we spend our time. He reads Marx for a picture of freedom as time that is ours to use, and he argues that capitalism forces us to spend most of it making profit for others. He proposes a democratic socialist economy that would expand free time. Many readers find the step from metaphysics to economics abrupt, and religious readers dispute the claim that eternity would drain meaning.
ideas: Secular faith is a commitment to people and projects that can be lost, with no guarantee they will last. Hägglund says that this vulnerability is what gives life urgency.
Eternal life, he argues, would be worse than a finite one. If nothing could be lost, nothing would be at stake, and the things we love would lose their meaning.
Our attachments are sharp because those we love can die. Grief is the price of caring about something that can end.
Spiritual freedom is the capacity to ask what to do with the time we have. Religions saw it but placed its source in God.
Hägglund reads Augustine and Kierkegaard as thinkers who sensed the value of finite life and then turned toward eternity, and he argues this undercuts what they value.
He reads Marx for a picture of freedom as time of our own. Under capitalism most of our time goes to work that profits others.
He proposes a democratic socialist economy to widen free time. Many readers find the step from metaphysics to economics abrupt.
Hägglund criticises ideals of detachment, such as those found in Stoic and Buddhist thought, for asking us to care less about what can be lost, when he thinks that care is the point.
He reads Martin Luther King Jr. as an example of religious language put to work for a this-worldly cause, a faith in what people can do together and not in a promise of eternity.
Following Marx, he argues that under capitalism the value of things is set by the labour time society requires, which pushes everyone to treat time as something to be spent on work.

books.thesis: The self is experience in the first person, and it is already open to others.
books.summary:
Dan Zahavi, a phenomenologist in the tradition of Husserl, uses the subtitle Exploring Subjectivity, Empathy, and Shame, and the three words mark the book's route. He asks what a self is, and how a self relates to the other people whose minds it cannot enter.

He argues for a thin but real self, the first-person givenness of experience, in which each experience is given to me in a way it is given to nobody else. That minimal self does not need a soul or a life story, and he treats views that dissolve the self, as well as narrative views, as either too strong or building on something more basic. He then moves to other people and defends the idea that we perceive their feelings in their expressions and actions without inferring them. Shame serves as an example of how another's gaze can shape self-awareness.
ideas: The minimal self is the first-person givenness of experience. Each experience is given to me in a way it is given to no one else, and this belongs to experience itself.
Zahavi argues that views which deny the self often attack an inflated notion, while a thin sense of the self as experiential survives their criticism.
Narrative theories build the self out of life stories. Zahavi accepts that stories matter for identity, but he says they rest on a more basic experiential self.
The self is embodied. The lived body is both the point from which experience comes and something that other people can see from outside.
We can perceive others' feelings directly in their expressions and actions. Zahavi rejects the view that we must first infer them from outward behaviour.
Others are given as subjects whose experience I cannot have, and yet the shared world's objectivity depends on there being others, an idea he draws from Husserl.
Shame shows how self and other are bound together. In shame, my awareness of myself is shaped by the gaze of someone else.
He defends the Husserlian account of empathy as the experience of another's experience as theirs, which he distinguishes from emotional contagion and from simply sharing a feeling.
He criticises both theory theory and simulation theory, which treat understanding others as hidden mind reading, saying that much of it is direct and embodied.
He considers conditions such as schizophrenia, in which the sense of mineness of experience can be disturbed, to show that the minimal self is more than a belief.

books.thesis: Our experience is now raw material for predicting and steering behaviour.
books.summary:
Shoshana Zuboff, a Harvard professor, asks what has happened to the internet's promise of freedom. Her answer is that a new economic logic grew up inside the largest technology companies. They found that the traces we leave online could be collected, analysed and sold, and she asks what that does to privacy, autonomy and democracy.

Zuboff traces how Google found that data left over from use of its services, beyond what was needed to improve them, could predict what people would click on. She calls this behavioural surplus. Prediction products built from it are sold to advertisers in what she calls behavioural futures markets. She argues that the aim has widened from predicting behaviour to shaping it, which she calls instrumentarian power. She calls for new rights, including a right to the future tense and a right to sanctuary. Critics say she overstates how well advertising works.
ideas: Behavioural surplus is the data left over from using a service, beyond what is needed to improve it. Google found it could predict clicks, and it became raw material.
Prediction products built from that surplus are sold in behavioural futures markets. Advertisers are the customers, and users are the source of raw material.
Instrumentarian power aims at knowing and shaping behaviour through machines. Unlike totalitarian power, it shows no interest in belief or ideology.
The aim has moved from predicting behaviour to steering it. Zuboff points to tuning, herding and conditioning, and to games such as Pokémon Go that sent players to paying locations.
Companies claim private experience as free raw material, first by stealth and then by habit, and she describes a cycle in which regulators and users catch up too late.
Zuboff describes a radical indifference in these firms. They care little what a person's life contains and only that its traces can be turned into data.
She calls for new rights, such as a right to the future tense and a right to sanctuary. Critics say she overstates how well advertising works.
Big Other is her term for the networked institutional regime that turns behaviour into data and makes it computable, set against Orwell's Big Brother.
She frames power as the division of learning in society, meaning who knows, who decides who knows, and who decides who decides.
The extraction imperative pushes firms to gather more data from more areas of life, and she names economies of scope and economies of action, the second being the power to shape behaviour at scale.

books.t: Justice and the Politics of Difference
books.thesis: Injustice is built into social structures, and goes beyond distribution.
books.summary:
Iris Marion Young wrote this book to challenge the way many political philosophers had defined justice. The usual approach, she observed, treats justice as a matter of how goods, income and opportunities are shared out. She asks what that leaves out, and what it would mean to take seriously the fact that people belong to groups with different histories and experiences.

Young argues that the distributive model overlooks decision-making power, the division of labour and culture. She proposes that oppression is a structural matter, produced by ordinary people following the norms of institutions, so there may be no single tyrant to blame. She names five faces of oppression, which are exploitation, marginalisation, powerlessness, cultural imperialism and violence. She criticises the ideal of impartiality as hiding the standpoint of privileged groups, and she defends special representation in democratic bodies for oppressed groups. Against the ideal of community, she praises city life as the being together of strangers.
ideas: Young criticises theories that treat justice as sharing out goods and income. They overlook decision-making power, the division of labour and culture, which are not things to be divided.
She names five faces of oppression, which are exploitation, marginalisation, powerlessness, cultural imperialism and violence. Groups can suffer one or several of them.
Cultural imperialism happens when a dominant group's experience becomes the norm. Others are marked as different and deviant, while their own experience goes unseen.
Oppression is structural. It comes from ordinary people following the norms of institutions, so there may be no single tyrant to blame.
The ideal of impartiality claims a neutral, universal viewpoint. Young argues it tends to hide the standpoint of privileged groups and demands sameness from everyone else.
She defends group-differentiated representation, meaning special voice for oppressed groups in democratic bodies, as a way to bring their perspectives into decisions.
Against the ideal of face-to-face community, which can exclude, Young praises city life as the being together of strangers.
Young holds marginalisation to be perhaps the most dangerous face of oppression, since whole categories of people are expelled from useful participation in social life.
Her idea of a social group is defined by affinity and shared position and not by a shared essence, and she distinguishes it from a mere aggregate or a voluntary association.
She argues that standards of merit and qualification are less neutral than they appear, because dominant groups set them, and she defends affirmative action on that basis.

books.thesis: A clerk's fragmentary diary of an unlived life, watched so closely that the watching turns into the life.
books.summary:
The Book of Disquiet is a diary of fragments by Fernando Pessoa, written as the work of Bernardo Soares, an assistant bookkeeper in Lisbon. Pessoa left it unfinished in a trunk of papers when he died in 1935, and it was first published in 1982. The book follows a quiet man who sits in an office, walks through the city, and writes about the gap between the life he imagines and the one he lives.

He prefers his daydreams to the world, then notices what that preference costs him. He writes at length about small things, such as a street, a rainy day, a shop sign or his boss, and he treats the sentence as the one thing he can make. Pessoa called Soares a semi-heteronym, a version of himself with the volume turned down. Readers often take the book in small doses, and some find its stillness a kind of company.
ideas: The narrator is Bernardo Soares, an assistant bookkeeper in Lisbon. Pessoa described him as a semi-heteronym, a version of himself with the volume turned down.
The book is a set of fragments and not a story. It was found in a trunk after Pessoa died in 1935 and first published in 1982, and editions arrange it differently.
Soares prefers imagined lives to the one he lives. He is aware of what the preference costs him, and the book circles the gap between dream and ordinary life.
He looks at small things at length, such as streets, weather, rooms, the office and his employer, and finds that attention to them is a kind of life.
Soares watches himself so closely that he cannot act. The observer's own feelings become the whole content of his days.
Boredom and a feeling of unreality run through the book. Soares treats them as moods that come close to the truth of how he lives.
Writing is the one action open to him. The book records an unlived life, and the writing itself becomes a form of living.
Pessoa called the work a "factless autobiography". Soares has almost no events to report, so the record is of moods, thoughts and the look of the street.
Much of the book is set on the Rua dos Douradores in Lisbon, where Soares works and rents a room. The one street and one office stand in for the narrow world he never leaves.

Pessoa wrote under many heteronyms, including Alberto Caeiro, Ricardo Reis and Alvaro de Campos, who were poets with their own styles. Soares is the prose figure among them, which is why Pessoa called him only a semi-heteronym.

books.thesis: Moral reasoning has more than one mature form. Care and responsibility make up another.
books.summary:
Carol Gilligan, a psychologist who worked with Lawrence Kohlberg at Harvard, noticed a pattern in his studies of moral development. His stages placed abstract justice and individual rights at the top, and women often scored lower. She asked whether women were less developed, or whether the scale measured only one way of reasoning.

She compared two eleven-year-olds, Jake and Amy, who responded differently to a dilemma about a man stealing a drug for his dying wife. Jake treated it as a problem of competing rights to be solved by logic, while Amy asked about relationships and other ways out. Gilligan called this approach an ethic of care. She also interviewed women making decisions about abortion and described stages from caring for oneself to caring for others to holding both. Critics say her samples were small and that differences between men and women in moral reasoning are smaller than the book suggests.
ideas: Gilligan noticed that Kohlberg's stages of moral development put abstract justice and rights at the top, and that women often scored lower on them.

Gilligan compares two eleven-year-olds, Jake and Amy, on a dilemma about stealing a drug. Jake sees competing rights, Amy asks about relationships, and Gilligan reads her as thinking differently, not worse.
The ethic of care treats moral problems as conflicts of responsibility within relationships, resolved by attending to context and trying to keep connections intact.
She interviewed women facing abortion decisions and described a path from caring for oneself, to caring for others, to balancing both with honesty.
Gilligan challenges the idea that maturity means separation and detachment. She argues that mature adults also value attachment and responsibility.
Gilligan later stressed that the different voice is defined by theme and not by gender, since both men and women can speak in either.
Critics argue that her samples were small and that moral reasoning differs less between men and women than she suggested. Others value how she reframed moral psychology.

Gilligan points out that the major theories of development, including those of Freud, Piaget, Kohlberg and Erikson, were built mostly on studies of boys and men. Female development was then measured against a male standard.
She questions Erikson's sequence in which identity comes before intimacy. Women, she finds, often define themselves through relationships and care, so the order is reversed or merged.

The book rests on three interview studies: college students, women considering abortion, and a study of rights and responsibilities. Gilligan lets people's own words about conflict and choice carry the argument.

books.thesis: Who does the early caring shapes how people feel about self and other, and that reproduces social arrangements.
books.summary:
Nancy Chodorow, a sociologist and psychoanalytic thinker, begins with a question that many treat as settled. Why do women do most of the early caring for children, and why does the pattern keep repeating from one generation to the next?

Chodorow draws on object relations psychoanalysis, a tradition that focuses on a child's earliest bond with a caregiver, and not on Freud's emphasis on the father. She argues that because mothers do the early caring, daughters grow up identified with a mother and keep a more open, connected sense of self. Sons, to become masculine, must separate, and tend to build firmer boundaries and distance themselves from what is seen as feminine. In this way women are prepared emotionally for mothering and men for work outside the home. Her remedy is shared parenting by both sexes. Critics note that she writes mainly about white, middle-class families.
ideas: Chodorow asks why women do most of the early caring for children, generation after generation. She is not satisfied by explanations from biology or role training alone.
Because mothers do the early caring, daughters grow up identified with a mother and keep a more connected sense of self, which prepares them for mothering.
Sons, to become masculine, must separate from the mother. Chodorow argues this leads them to build firmer boundaries and to push away what is labelled feminine.
She draws on object relations psychoanalysts, who focus on the earliest bond between child and caregiver, in place of Freud's emphasis on the Oedipal father.
Women are prepared emotionally for mothering and men for work outside the home, so a division of public and private life keeps renewing itself.
Her remedy is shared parenting. If both men and women do the early caring, children of both sexes would have close primary caregivers of each, which could break the cycle.
Critics note she writes mainly about white, middle-class, heterosexual two-parent families and ask whether she treats developmental outcomes as more fixed than evidence supports.
Chodorow revises Freud's account of female development by giving the girl's early attachment to her mother much more weight than the Oedipal story does.

She separates personal identification with a real caregiver from positional identification with an abstract role. Boys, with an absent father, learn masculinity mostly through the second, which makes it more rigid and defensive.
Women, she argues, look to their children for the emotional closeness that relations with men often fail to give. This helps explain why the desire to mother is renewed in each generation.

books.thesis: Prison is as much a habit of mind as a necessity. Other answers to harm are worth imagining.
books.summary:
Angela Davis, a philosopher and longtime activist, asks a question most readers have never put to themselves: could a society do without prisons? The book is short and starts from the observation that prisons feel as natural as weather. Davis sets that feeling against history, since slavery once looked just as permanent to the people who lived beside it.

The argument moves through the history of the penitentiary, convict leasing and the growth of what she calls the prison industrial complex. Davis claims that reform tends to produce more prison, and she proposes abolition as a slow project of building other institutions in schooling, health care and ways of repairing harm. Critics say she is thin on what to do about serious violence. She mostly leaves that open, treating it as something to be worked out in practice rather than settled in advance.
ideas: Prison feels permanent because most people cannot picture life without it. Davis compares this to slavery, which also seemed a fixed part of the economy until it was abolished.

The Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery but kept an exception for punishment. Convict leasing in the South then moved many Black people from plantations into forced labor under the name of criminal justice.
The penitentiary began as a reform, an alternative to corporal punishment. Davis uses its history to show how each proposed fix, solitary confinement included, ended up extending the institution.
Davis points to the heavy over-representation of Black and Latino people in US prisons and reads it as a sign that race shapes who gets punished, beyond what crime rates explain.

She describes a prison industrial complex in which construction, supply and private management firms profit from incarceration, so that punishment gathers economic interests with reasons to want it to continue.
Women in prison, she argues, face strip searches and sexual abuse by staff. Imprisonment reproduces the gendered violence many of them already lived with outside.
Abolition, as Davis frames it, means building education, health care and restorative approaches until prisons are asked to do less. She admits that serious harm remains a hard question.

Davis borrows W. E. B. Du Bois's idea of abolition democracy. Ending slavery required building schools, land access and political rights, and abolishing prisons likewise requires building new institutions.
She ties the growth of imprisonment to the war on drugs and to mandatory sentencing. These policies, she argues, filled prisons without making communities safer.
Prison labor is paid pennies, and private firms use it for production. Davis sees this as a modern echo of convict leasing, with a profit motive for keeping beds full.

books.thesis: Creative work needs money and a door that locks. Talent without those conditions goes unseen.
books.summary:
Virginia Woolf was asked to lecture on women and fiction, and she turned the topic into a question about conditions. The book follows a narrator who wanders a fictional university town and a library, noticing who is let onto the lawn, who eats well, and who owns the books. Woolf's claim is plain: a woman needs money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.

A made-up sister for Shakespeare shows what happened to a gifted girl with no schooling and no privacy. Woolf then considers women writers who did get through, and what anger and poverty did to their prose. She ends by hoping for a mind not tied to one sex and for a future in which the poet who was never born might finally be. Some readers find her focus on the middle class limiting, a point later critics have pressed.
ideas: A woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction. Woolf says she can offer no grander conclusion than that.
The narrator is turned off the grass at a men's college and lunches well, then dines thinly at a women's college. Woolf ties that difference in comfort to a difference in thought.
Woolf invents Judith Shakespeare, a sister as gifted as William. With no school, no privacy and no way to earn, she is stopped before she can write anything.
Aphra Behn, who earned her living by writing in the seventeenth century, opened the way for women. Woolf says all women should lay flowers on her grave.
For centuries women served as looking glasses that reflected men at twice their natural size. Woolf says this flattering role depended on women staying narrow and unlearned.
Anger bends the work of even gifted writers such as Charlotte Brontë. Woolf thinks the best writing is free of resentment and does not write with a grievance in mind.
Drawing on Coleridge, Woolf proposes that a great mind is androgynous, able to draw on both the masculine and the feminine without being fixed to one.
The book grew from two talks given in 1928 at the women's colleges Newnham and Girton at Cambridge, on the topic of women and fiction.
The narrator inherits five hundred pounds a year from an aunt. She says this mattered more to her than the vote, because it freed her from bitterness toward men and let her think clearly.

Woolf imagines a novel by Mary Carmichael with the line "Chloe liked Olivia". Her point is that friendship between women had barely been shown in fiction, and that the lack had shaped what women could write.

books.thesis: A single London day told from inside several minds, with consciousness as a moving stream.
books.summary:
Mrs Dalloway follows one June day in London a few years after the First World War. Clarissa Dalloway, a society hostess in her fifties, walks out to buy flowers for a party she will give that evening. Around her, an old suitor returns from India, a shell-shocked veteran named Septimus Smith sits in a park with his wife, and Big Ben keeps striking the hours. The book asks what a life feels like from inside, and how much of a person never reaches anyone else.

Woolf tells it by sliding from one mind to another, often mid-sentence, so that thought runs on like a current while the clock keeps time outside. Clarissa and Septimus never meet, yet the novel sets them in quiet parallel, and news of his death reaches her at the party. Woolf leaves open whether Clarissa's life is shallow or quietly brave.
ideas: The whole novel takes place in one day in June, so the plot is small. What fills the pages is memory and perception moving through each character.
Woolf moves between minds without clear markers, sometimes within a sentence. A stranger noticed by one character becomes the thought of another, linking people who never speak.
Big Ben's chimes recur throughout, marking public time. Against them, the characters live a private time of recollection that can stretch a moment or fold years into it.
Septimus Smith came back from the war with what the doctors treat as nothing serious. His visions and grief are met with advice about rest and proportion rather than listening.
Clarissa thinks back to Sally Seton and a kiss at Bourton, and to why she refused Peter Walsh. The book keeps asking what she gave up for a safe marriage.
Clarissa's party is a gift she gives to hold people together, though she suspects it is also vanity. Woolf leaves both readings open and does not choose.
When Clarissa hears at her party that Septimus has killed himself, she feels a kinship with him. The book never fully spells out what she takes from his death.

The novel grew out of a short story, "Mrs Dalloway in Bond Street", and Woolf first planned for Clarissa herself to die at the party. In her later introduction she says Septimus was added, and he became a kind of double for Clarissa.
Septimus's doctors are Holmes and Sir William Bradshaw. Woolf makes Bradshaw's cult of proportion and conversion a quiet portrait of how authority crushes a person in pain.

Miss Kilman, the tutor of Clarissa's daughter Elizabeth, is poor, bitter and fiercely religious. Woolf shows her resentment of Clarissa's comfort, and also how Clarissa's dislike of her is partly unfair.

books.thesis: Abjection is the revulsion we feel at whatever threatens the boundary between self and not-self.
books.summary:
Julia Kristeva starts from something small and bodily, the reaction a person has to the skin on warm milk, a corpse, or a wound. She calls it abjection and asks why such things disturb us. Her answer is that the abject sits on the border of self and not-self. It is neither object nor subject, and it reminds us of the matter and the mother we had to push away to become someone.

Kristeva moves from Freud and Lacan to the biblical abominations of Leviticus and then to the twentieth century writer Louis-Ferdinand Céline. She argues that cultures and writers keep rebuilding the line between clean and unclean, and that literature in particular goes back to the abject to work on it. Her style is dense and associative, and some readers find the claims hard to test. She is clearer on how disgust marks a boundary than on whether the process can ever be finished.
ideas: Abjection is the reaction to what is neither object nor subject. A corpse, a wound or the skin on milk unsettles us because it blurs the line of the self.
Food loathing may be the oldest form of abjection. Kristeva describes the retching at a skin on milk as a refusal of whatever feeds us but also ties us to someone.
The abject lingers in ordinary life. It is the thing we expel, such as waste, to keep a body and a self clean enough to go on.
The mother's body is close to this early separation. Kristeva links abjection to the effort to break from her, an effort never fully completed.
She reads the abominations of Leviticus as a way of separating the pure from the impure, building on Mary Douglas, and sees purification rites as an answer to abjection.
In Christian thought sin and the body get reworked, and Kristeva follows how the abject is both condemned and taken in, as sin is named and then forgiven.
She analyses Céline's writing and its anti-Semitism as an attempt to write from inside the abject, and says literature can both expose and give shape to horror.

Kristeva says the abject is what "disturbs identity, system, order". The traitor, the liar and the criminal who acts with a clear conscience are abject because they ignore borders and rules, not because they are dirty.
She discusses phobia, using Freud's case of Little Hans, as another place where the border of the self is threatened and a feared object stands in for it.

Kristeva argues that religion once purified the abject and that literature now takes over part of that task. Writers such as Dostoevsky, Proust and Artaud are read as ones who go into the abject and give it form.

books.thesis: Ideas of dirt and pollution are really about order. What is out of place marks a society’s limits.
books.summary:
Mary Douglas, an anthropologist, begins with an ordinary thought: dirt is matter out of place. A shoe is fine on the floor and disgusting on the table. From there she asks why so many societies have rules about pollution, taboo and ritual cleanliness, and why those rules look so odd to outsiders. Her reply is that ideas of impurity are less about hygiene than about order. What a culture treats as dangerous shows where its categories are shaky.

She argues through cases, among them the dietary rules of Leviticus, the Lele of the Congo and their pangolin cult, and the way bodily margins are watched in many societies. Anything that fits no category can be avoided, condemned, or in some rituals made sacred. Douglas also insists that modern people are not exempt, since our own cleanliness codes carry meaning. The central link between disorder, classification and fear has stayed useful for many readers.
ideas: Dirt is matter out of place. It follows that dirt is relative, because nothing is dirty in itself and everything depends on the system of order it breaks.
Douglas rejects the view that primitive taboos were crude hygiene. She says our own rules of cleanliness also carry symbolic meaning and are not simply scientific.
Anomalies are awkward for any classification, so societies handle them in set ways. They may ignore them, label them, avoid them, control them, or turn them into something sacred.
She reads the Levitical dietary laws as a symbolic order of creatures, in which animals that fit no clear category are the ones called abominable. She later revised this reading.
Among the Lele, the pangolin is an odd creature that fits no ordinary category. Douglas describes how it becomes the center of a ritual instead of an object of avoidance.
The body is a model of society. Concerns about what crosses its edges, such as food, blood and waste, reflect a group's concern about its own limits.
Pollution beliefs can police behavior. Those who break social rules are described as dangerous and contaminating, which gives moral order a physical shape.

Douglas treats people in transition as dangerous because they fit no category. Drawing on van Gennep's rites of passage, she notes that initiates and others in a marginal state are often treated as both powerful and contaminating.

She criticizes earlier writers on religion, such as Frazer and Robertson Smith, for treating so-called primitive thought as a different kind of mind. Her view is that the difference lies in the classifications used, not in the quality of thinking.
Douglas says that when we clean and tidy we are not mainly escaping disease. We are positively reordering the environment to fit our ideas, and this holds for modern societies as much as for others.

books.thesis: Once feeling is part of the job, emotion becomes labor, and the worker pays for it.
books.summary:
Arlie Russell Hochschild noticed that some jobs ask workers to produce a feeling in themselves and in other people. Her main case is the flight attendant, whose smile and calm are part of the product, and she also looks at bill collectors, who are asked for something close to the opposite. The book asks what happens to a person when feeling is bought and sold, and who gets to decide how one ought to feel at work.

She names the practice emotional labor and separates it from the private emotion work people do at home. Drawing on training sessions, interviews and the sociology of Erving Goffman, she describes workers doing surface acting and deep acting, following feeling rules set by the employer. She argues that this can leave workers estranged from their own emotions, and that women, who do more of it, carry more of the cost.
ideas: Hochschild defines emotional labor as the management of feeling to create a visible display that is sold for a wage. Emotion work is the same effort made in private life.
Flight attendants at Delta Airlines were trained to produce the cabin's mood. Their smile was part of the product the company sold alongside the seat.
Surface acting changes only the outward display. Deep acting tries to summon the feeling itself, for instance by picturing the cabin as a living room and the passenger as a guest.
Feeling rules are social expectations about what one ought to feel and for how long. Employers can write them into training and supervise them, and workers may follow them without noticing.
Doing this work for years can leave a person unsure what they actually feel. Hochschild describes workers who feel numb or false and who withdraw to protect themselves.
Bill collectors are trained to be suspicious and stern. Hochschild uses them as the opposite case to the flight attendant, showing that jobs can require harshness as well as warmth.
Women are more often in emotional labor jobs, and they have less status to push back against rude customers. The cost of managing feeling falls unevenly along gender lines.
Hochschild uses the term emotive dissonance, a strain like cognitive dissonance, for the gap between what a worker feels and what the job requires them to show.
She notes a speedup in flight attendants' work. As airlines added passengers and cut staff, workers were told to keep smiling while doing more, so the display of warmth was stretched thin.
The ideas of surface and deep acting come from Goffman's dramaturgy and Stanislavski's acting method. Hochschild applies them to ordinary jobs, where the performance is a condition of pay.

books.thesis: A study built on listening to the felt story behind a political view, and what it says about status.
books.summary:
Arlie Russell Hochschild spent five years in southwest Louisiana, a region of bayous and petrochemical plants, talking with supporters of the Tea Party. She had a puzzle. Many of these people live next to heavy pollution, yet they favor less regulation and a smaller federal government. The book asks what feelings sit under that political view, and whether people who disagree can get close enough to find out. Hochschild calls the obstacle an empathy wall.

She answers with what she calls a deep story, a feels-as-if account of life in which people wait patiently in a long line toward the American Dream and watch others step ahead of them. It describes how it feels to be passed over and mocked. Hochschild argues that politics is partly about honor and standing. Critics say she gives too little weight to race and to the way industry shapes local opinion, and she leaves that debate open.
ideas: Hochschild describes the great paradox of the people she met. Many suffer the effects of pollution, yet they back politicians who want to loosen environmental rules.
The empathy wall is the barrier to understanding someone on the other side of a political divide. Hochschild tries to climb it by listening to people as people before judging their views.
A deep story is the feels-as-if account of life that underlies political belief. It sets facts aside and describes how things seem to those who hold it.
In her deep story, people wait in a long line for the American Dream. Others, such as minorities, women and immigrants, seem to cut ahead, and the government seems to help them.
Hochschild uses the Bayou Corne sinkhole, which forced a community to evacuate, as one example of local damage from industry in a state where distrust of government runs deep.
Louisiana relies on jobs from the oil and chemical industries, and many residents link their livelihoods to them. This makes pollution a trade people feel they have to accept.
Hochschild suggests that politics is partly a contest over honor and the feeling of being respected, so that economic arguments fail to move people whose pride is at stake.
The research took about five years, mostly around Lake Charles in southwest Louisiana. Hochschild spent time with Tea Party supporters, listened to their stories and returned several times.
She proposes that people follow an emotional self-interest more than an economic one. They choose the politics that lets them feel proud, hopeful and respected, even when it costs them materially.

Church, hunting, fishing and close family give the people she met a strong sense of belonging. Damage to the bayou and the land therefore feels like a personal loss, and also makes outside criticism feel like an insult.

books.thesis: Memory is reconstructed. Suggestion can alter it without the person remembering ever knowing.
books.summary:
Elizabeth Loftus, a psychologist, set out to test how reliable eyewitness memory is, and the book gathers a decade of her experiments. People watched staged accidents or film clips, then answered questions about what they saw. The small details of those questions kept changing the answers. The book asks what a memory is if the way you are asked about it can alter it, and what that means in a courtroom where a witness's word can decide a case.

Her central finding is that memory is rebuilt at recall from pieces, and information gained after an event can merge with the original. She shows this with leading questions, with false details planted in later questions, and with witnesses who stay confident in memories that are wrong. Loftus argues that jurors trust confident witnesses more than they should. Whether the original memory is overwritten or only hidden has been debated since.
ideas: Memory is rebuilt each time it is recalled, using fragments and later knowledge, so it works less like a recording than like a reconstruction.
In studies with films of car accidents, changing one word in a question altered estimates. Asking how fast cars were going when they smashed gave higher speeds than asking about hit.
Witnesses asked about smashed cars were more likely to say later that they had seen broken glass, though none appeared in the film. A leading word had added a false detail.
Misleading information introduced after an event can become part of the memory. In one set of studies, people shown a stop sign later reported a yield sign after a suggestive question.
Witnesses often cannot tell which details came from the event and which from later questions or conversation. The source of a memory is easily lost.
A witness's confidence does not reliably track accuracy, yet juries tend to find confident witnesses convincing. This is a main worry for courtroom use of testimony.
Whether suggestion overwrites the original memory or simply sits beside it has been debated. Some critics argue the original trace may survive and be hard to retrieve.
Loftus describes unconscious transference, in which a witness picks out a person who was seen elsewhere, such as a bystander at the scene, as the offender.

Lineups and photo spreads can push a witness toward a choice. The makeup of the lineup and the instructions given can lead a witness to pick the person who looks most like the culprit even when the culprit is absent.

Loftus argues that psychologists should be allowed to explain the limits of memory to juries. She notes that courts were reluctant, and that jurors tend to hold more trust in witnesses than the research supports.

books.thesis: Some of what we cling to for the good life is exactly what blocks it.
books.summary:
Lauren Berlant asks about a common kind of attachment: wanting something that stands in the way of what you want. A job, a relationship, a dream of upward mobility or a food can all promise a good life and wear a person down. The book is set in the decades after the postwar promise of secure work and lasting intimacy began to fade, and it asks why people keep returning to scenes that no longer deliver.

Berlant reads novels, films, essays and news stories, building the argument from close readings rather than from a single thesis. She describes the present as an impasse, a stretch of time in which one adjusts to a situation that keeps going without resolving. She also discusses slow death, the wearing out of populations through ordinary life. The prose is dense and the terms are her own, which some readers find hard going. She does not offer a cure.
ideas: An attachment is cruel when the thing desired is an obstacle to flourishing. The person cannot simply let go, since the object also gives some hope that keeps them going.

Berlant names the good life fantasy, a bundle of promises that includes upward mobility, job security, political equality and durable intimacy. After the postwar decades these promises lost much of their grip.
Optimism is not always happy. It can mean a steady inclination to return to a scene of fantasy, even when the scene is damaging or has stopped working.
Berlant's impasse is a stretch of time in which people adjust to a situation that neither ends nor changes. It is lived as waiting and getting by.
Crisis, Berlant argues, is often ordinary. What looks like an event becomes a condition of life, so that people live inside a continuing crisis with no clear turning point.
Slow death is the wearing out of a population through everyday life. Berlant treats eating and obesity as one example of people worn down while seeking relief.
Berlant reads films, novels and other texts as ways of registering feelings that politics fails to name, so culture becomes a place where people rehearse how to live in the present.
Berlant calls an object of desire a cluster of promises. A job, a romance or a political idea carries many hopes at once, which is why giving it up feels like losing the whole cluster.
She uses Raymond Williams's structure of feeling to describe how a historical present is sensed in the body and mood before it can be explained.

Her chapters read specific works, among them Mary Gaitskill's story of two girls, fat and thin, and the Dardenne brothers' films La Promesse and Rosetta. The latter are taken as portraits of post-Fordist work, where survival takes the place of a career.

books.thesis: Caste is a graded ranking of people. It has to be dismantled, and reforming it from inside won't do.
books.summary:
B. R. Ambedkar wrote this text as a speech for a Hindu reform group in Lahore in 1936. The organizers read it beforehand, asked him to remove passages, and he refused, so it was never delivered. It was written by a man who had himself been treated as untouchable.

Ambedkar argues that caste divides laborers into a graded ranking, with no way out. He criticizes social reformers and socialists who ignored it, and he says the real obstacle is the religious authority given to scriptures that sanction it. His proposed remedies include inter-dining and inter-marriage, but the deeper step is to reject the shastras that give caste its sanction. Gandhi replied in print and defended a version of varna. Their disagreement still shapes arguments about whether caste can be reformed from within or has to be ended.
ideas: The speech was invited and then rejected. The Lahore group withdrew the invitation after reading it, and Ambedkar printed the text himself instead of changing it.
Caste, Ambedkar says, is a division of laborers and not of labor. People are sorted at birth into fixed occupations regardless of talent or choice.
He describes caste as a graded inequality, with an ascending scale of reverence and a descending scale of contempt, so that almost everyone has someone to look down on.
Because the system is graded, those just above and below share no common grievance. This is a main reason, he argues, that there is no unified movement against it.
Ambedkar argued that socialists who thought economic change would be enough were mistaken. In India, he said, caste had to be tackled first or alongside class.
Inter-dining and inter-marriage are useful steps, but the real remedy is to destroy the belief in the sacredness of the shastras, the texts that justify caste.
Gandhi answered in his paper Harijan, defending a form of varna. Ambedkar rejected the distinction, and the disagreement over whether caste can be reformed from within continues.

Ambedkar contrasts a religion of rules with a religion of principles. He argues that what is called Hinduism is mostly a code of rules, and that rules enforce caste without any room for moral reasoning.
He rejects the claim that caste protects racial purity. Indians, he says, are already a mixed people, and caste is a social device and not a biological fact.
Caste, he says, kills public spirit. Charity, public opinion and virtue all become bound to one's own caste, so that people feel no duty to those outside it.

books.thesis: Tagore warns that a nation run like a machine makes people efficient and morally smaller.
books.summary:
Rabindranath Tagore delivered these lectures in Japan and the United States in 1916 and 1917, during the First World War. He had a reputation as a poet and some expected a celebration of India's coming nationhood. Instead he warned against the idea of the nation itself. The book asks what happens to people when a society organizes itself as a machine for power and profit, and why a country with Indian traditions should hesitate to copy it.

Tagore argues that the modern nation is an organization of politics and commerce that turns people into parts. It makes them efficient and shrinks their moral sense, since each person learns to ask what is good for the nation and not what is right. For India he sees the central trouble as social, with caste and division, rather than political. Critics call his view idealized and note that he was addressing a world already shaped by nations.
ideas: The lectures were given in Japan and America in 1916 and 1917, as Europe was at war. Tagore used the moment to question the nation as a form of life.
A nation, in Tagore's sense, is the organized power of a people used for political and commercial purposes. It is a machine for efficiency, and a machine has no heart.
He argues that the nation shrinks moral life. People trained to serve the nation's aims tend to treat conscience as secondary to national advantage.
In his lecture on Japan, Tagore admired how quickly the country had modernized. He worried that it was taking on the aggressive spirit of Western nationalism along with the technology.
For India, he saw the real problem as social, a matter of caste and division. Political independence alone, he thought, would not address it and might even reproduce Europe's mistakes.
Tagore contrasts the nation with society, which he describes as a natural human relation. He suggests that societies can be generous and varied while the nation tends toward uniformity.
Critics say Tagore's view is idealized and gives too little weight to the way colonized peoples used nationalism to resist empire. The tension between his warnings and that need remains.

Tagore calls the idea of the Nation one of the most powerful anesthetics men have invented. Under its influence a whole people can carry out a program of ruthless self-seeking without feeling its moral ugliness.

He describes British rule in India as government by a machine, an impersonal administration in which no person takes responsibility. The harm lies as much in this coldness as in any single act of cruelty.
His lectures in Japan were met coldly and drew criticism there. Tagore's warning about borrowing Western nationalism was not what many of his hosts wanted to hear.

books.thesis: Development means widening people's real freedoms, and income is only one means among others.
books.summary:
Amartya Sen asks what development is for. The usual answer is that countries should grow richer, and Sen replies that wealth is a means to something else: the freedom of people to live lives they have reason to value.
