Illness, hunger, illiteracy, political repression and the lack of any say in decisions are all unfreedoms. The book asks how development looks when measured by what people are able to do and be, and not only by income per head.

Sen supports the claim with cases, among them famines, the gap in survival between women and men, and the contrast between countries with similar incomes and very different health. He also holds that democracy and a free press matter for basic needs, since governments that must face criticism tend to prevent famine. Economists have asked how to measure capabilities in practice, and Sen leaves some of that work to others.
ideas: Sen defines development as the expansion of the real freedoms people enjoy. Income and growth count only to the extent that they help widen those freedoms.
He lists unfreedoms such as famine, undernourishment, lack of health care, lack of schooling, political repression and poor economic opportunity. Development, on his view, is the removal of them.

Five instrumental freedoms are named: political freedoms, economic facilities, social opportunities, transparency guarantees and protective security. Each helps the others, so progress in one often supports progress elsewhere.
Sen notes that famines have not occurred in functioning democracies with a free press. Rulers who must face voters and criticism have a strong incentive to prevent them.
Income is a poor guide to wellbeing. He compares groups with higher incomes but lower life expectancy, so the money available does not tell us what people can actually do.
The capability approach asks what a person is actually able to do and be. Two people with equal incomes can differ widely in real freedom, because of disability or illness for instance.
Sen argues against the claim that Asian values are hostile to freedom, saying that traditions of tolerance and argument exist across cultures, and that political rights are not a luxury for later.
Sen separates the constitutive role of freedom, as part of what development is, from its instrumental role, as a means to other ends. Both are needed to make sense of what a society is aiming at.
He gives special weight to women's agency. Education and paid work for women are linked to lower fertility and lower child mortality, so their freedom benefits wider society.
Sen defends the market as part of the basic freedom to exchange and to trade, while arguing that markets need public education, health care and rules to work for the poor.

books.thesis: We can spot injustices and reduce them without first agreeing on a perfectly just society.
books.summary:
Amartya Sen asks how people should go about pursuing justice. The dominant tradition in political philosophy, from Hobbes to Rawls, tries first to describe a perfectly just society and its institutions. He notes that we often agree that a wrong is a wrong without agreeing on what a perfect world looks like. The book is dedicated to Rawls's memory and treats him with respect while disputing the method.

Sen proposes a comparative approach that looks at actual lives and asks which of the available options reduces injustice. He illustrates the problem with three children and a flute, each with a reasonable claim to it. He draws on Adam Smith's impartial spectator, on Indian ideas of niti and nyaya, and on the practice of public reasoning. Critics say that without some idea of the ideal it is hard to rank anything, and Sen answers that rankings can be made without one.
ideas: Sen separates two approaches. One is transcendental institutionalism, which tries to identify perfectly just institutions. The other is realization focused comparison, which asks how to make things less unjust.
The three children and the flute show that reasonable people can disagree. One child made it, one plays it, and one has no toys, and each has a fair argument.
We can often agree that something is an injustice, such as slavery or famine, without agreeing on a complete theory of justice. Action does not have to wait for theory.
Sen takes from Adam Smith the idea of the impartial spectator, which asks us to consider views from outside our own group, even distant ones, when judging what is fair.
He draws a distinction between niti, justice as rules and institutions, and nyaya, justice as the realized outcomes in people's lives. He gives priority to the second.
Public reasoning matters because justice needs scrutiny from many viewpoints. Sen links this to democracy, which he understands as government by discussion, with open debate across borders.
Justice should be judged by the capabilities people have, meaning the real freedom to live as they have reason to value, in preference to resources or happiness alone.

Sen contrasts closed impartiality, in which only members of a given group are heard, with open impartiality, which brings in outside voices. Rawls's original position is his chief example of the closed kind.

He sets the social contract tradition of Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau and Rawls against a comparative line that includes Smith, Condorcet, Wollstonecraft, Marx and Mill. The second line is his preferred ancestry.
Sen argues that the power to help creates a reason to act. If we can reduce an injustice, we have a duty to consider doing so, even when the obligation is imperfect and no institution requires it.

books.thesis: People have many identities. Treat them as one, and that is how conflicts get made.
books.summary:
Amartya Sen starts from a worry about how people are sorted in the news and in politics: as Hindu or Muslim, Western or Islamic, Hutu or Tutsi. Everyone belongs to many groups at once, through nationality, profession, language, politics, class and faith, and Sen argues that the idea of a single defining identity is both false and dangerous.

The book calls the habit of reducing people to one category solitarism, and says it makes violence easier by shrinking people to a single label. He critiques Samuel Huntington's thesis of civilizations clashing and a multiculturalism that treats communities as fixed blocks, which he calls plural monoculturalism. He points to figures such as the emperor Akbar and the philosopher Maimonides as examples of tolerance within traditions that are often called intolerant. Sen insists that identity involves reasoning and choice, though critics say he underestimates how much people are born into a group's claims on them.
ideas: Every person has many identities at once, including nationality, class, language, profession and religion. Sen says no one of these has to dominate unless people are pushed to treat it that way.
Solitarism is the assumption that people can be understood through one affiliation. Sen holds that this view reduces and distorts people, and it is promoted by those who benefit from division.
Violence is often cultivated by teaching people that a single identity is the one that counts. Sen cites the Hutu and Tutsi division in Rwanda as a case of such a narrowing.
He rejects Huntington's picture of a clash of civilizations. Dividing the world by religion or civilization ignores the many other ways in which people identify and the variety within each group.
Plural monoculturalism, in Sen's term, is a multiculturalism that sees a society as a federation of separate communities, which neglects the choices of individuals within them and their wider ties.
Sen points to Akbar's tolerance in Mughal India and to Maimonides finding refuge in a Muslim ruler's court as examples that traditions are not uniformly intolerant.
Identity involves choice and reasoning. People decide how much weight to give each of their affiliations, and Sen argues that this capacity should be acknowledged and strengthened.
Sen recalls seeing as a boy a Muslim day laborer, Kader Mia, stabbed during a riot in Dhaka. He uses the memory to show how a man known to himself as a poor worker was killed for a religious label.

He argues that the 1940s communal violence in India turned neighbors and fellow workers into Hindus and Muslims within months. Agitators pressed a single identity forward until it overrode all others.
Sen criticizes faith-based schooling, which fixes a religious identity on children before they have a chance to reason about their other affiliations.

books.thesis: Colonialism damaged the rulers and the ruled alike, and it worked inside their ideas of themselves.
books.summary:
Ashis Nandy, a psychologist and social critic, argues that colonialism was more than conquest and taxes. It was also a state of mind that took root in both the rulers and the ruled. The book asks what colonial rule did to the way each side saw itself, and what a recovery of self could mean after it ended. Its title points to the odd closeness between the British and Indians, an intimacy that was also a conflict.

Nandy argues that colonial culture linked political domination to ideas about sex and age, so that the ruler appeared masculine and adult, and the ruled feminine or childlike. Indian responses sometimes copied the pattern, for example in cults of toughness. He reads Gandhi as a figure who resisted it by taking up traits the colonial scheme despised. Critics say Nandy leans on a romantic picture of traditional India, and that his psychological reading is more suggestive than proven.
ideas: Colonialism is a psychological process as well as an economic and political one. It reshapes the self-image of the ruler and the subject in ways that outlast the empire.
Nandy argues that the colonizers were also damaged. The ideology of dominance narrowed their sense of themselves and tied them to a view of progress that treated others as backward.
Colonial culture matched political hierarchy with sexual and age hierarchy. The ruler was adult and manly, and the ruled were childlike or effeminate, and this became a way of explaining rule.
Some Indian responses accepted this scheme and tried to prove manliness by copying the rulers. Nandy sees these hypermasculine reactions as another form of colonized thinking.
He reads Gandhi as a figure who rejected the scheme. By embracing qualities labeled feminine or childlike, Gandhi undercut the colonial categories that depended on contempt for them.
The title speaks of an intimate enemy. Ruler and ruled were bound in a relation that shaped each, and breaking it meant recovering a self not defined by the other.
Nandy suggests that the Western idea of progress, which ranks cultures by stages, is itself a legacy of colonialism, and that recovering other ways of seeing is part of ending it.
The second essay reads the killing of Gandhi by Nathuram Godse as a clash between Gandhi's tolerant, androgynous Hinduism and an aggressive, masculine Hindu nationalism.
Nandy treats Kipling and Orwell as British writers who both served the empire and were wounded by it. Their divided selves illustrate the damage he says colonialism did to the ruler.
He describes the British liking for martial races and the Indian cult of the Kshatriya, the warrior, as two sides of one idea. Both hold that the right to rule belongs to the manly and warlike.

books.thesis: Childhood and the self in India, read psychoanalytically.
books.summary:
Sudhir Kakar was a psychoanalyst trained in Europe who set out to describe childhood in India. The subtitle names the task, a psychoanalytic study of childhood and society, and the book asks how the early years of an Indian child differ from the pictures drawn by Freud and Erikson. It draws on case material, folk tales, myth and the daily life of the Hindu family, and it treats culture as part of how a self forms.

Kakar walks through infancy, childhood and adolescence, giving the mother and the wider household a central place. He suggests that in many Hindu families the baby is surrounded by closeness and care from several adults, which may leave a lasting wish for union and a ready trust in authority figures. Critics have objected that psychoanalytic categories fit India awkwardly and that a few families cannot stand for a whole society.
ideas: Kakar applies psychoanalysis to childhood in India but tries to adapt its categories to the family and culture he describes instead of applying European models unchanged.
The infant in a Hindu household is surrounded by many caregivers, with the mother central. Kakar thinks this early closeness leaves a strong wish for union and warm dependence.
The first years are marked by indulgence. Children are carried, fed and soothed on demand, and the later shift to expectations of obedience can be hard on the child.
The joint family offers a child many relationships, but it also asks for deference to elders. Kakar links this to the way authority is later accepted and sought.
Hindu myths and folk tales are used as evidence of the inner life of the culture. The stories of gods as children and lovers echo the wishes that shape ordinary development.
In early childhood the mother looms larger than the father, who tends to become important later, especially for sons. Kakar describes this as a common pattern, not a rule.
Critics have argued that psychoanalysis is a Western theory with limited fit to Indian experience, and that Kakar's sample is narrow. The book has been taken as a starting point for debate.
Kakar describes the Hindu samskaras, the rites of passage that mark a child's life such as the first feeding of solid food, and reads them for what they show about the family's wishes and fears.
He draws on Erik Erikson's stages of psychosocial development and tests how well they fit a Hindu life course.
Boys are welcomed and girls are treated as temporary members of the family who will leave at marriage. Kakar traces how this difference shapes a girl's early sense of herself.

books.thesis: Who gets heard? Who speaks for whom? And what does the history of reason leave out?
books.summary:
Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak's book asks who gets to speak and who is spoken for. Her main figure is the native informant, the person from whom Europeans take knowledge without giving that person a voice in the result.

She reads Kant, Hegel and Marx to show how their accounts of reason and history place colonized people outside the subject who knows. She returns to the question raised in her essay on the subaltern, revisiting the case of Bhuvaneswari Bhaduri, a young woman who took her own life in 1926 and whose act went unread by those around her. Spivak does not claim to give the subaltern a voice. She asks what it would take to listen, and the book leaves that question open, which some readers find evasive and others find honest.
ideas: The native informant is the figure from whom colonial knowledge was drawn but who is not permitted to speak as a thinker. Spivak finds traces of this figure in philosophy and literature.
She reads Kant, Hegel and Marx closely and shows how their central concepts of the subject, history or economy rely on a place outside it held by the colonized.
The subaltern is a person cut off from the routes through which a voice is heard. Spivak revisits her earlier claim that the subaltern cannot speak in that sense.
Bhuvaneswari Bhaduri, a young woman who killed herself in 1926, serves as an example of an act that was misread. Spivak argues that her message was not heard as she meant it.
Spivak reads a Mahasweta Devi story about a tribal community and an outsider trying to understand it, to ask how intellectuals approach people they cannot assume speak for themselves.
She is wary of the idea that an intellectual can simply give voice to the oppressed. Speaking on behalf of others can silence them, and she asks that this be examined.
The book's attention to the history of reason argues that postcolonial criticism needs to read the major texts of European thought carefully, not discard them.
Spivak borrows foreclosure from Lacan to describe how the native informant is written out of European texts. The figure is needed for the argument and then barred from it.

In the literature section she revisits Jane Eyre, Wide Sargasso Sea and Frankenstein. She argues that Bertha Mason is sacrificed so that Jane can complete her story as a heroine of feminist individualism.
Kant's account of the human subject relies on figures at the edge of humanity, such as the man in the raw state. Spivak reads these asides as signs of where the colonized are placed in philosophy.

books.thesis: Concepts that claim to be universal were made somewhere, and should be read that way.
books.summary:
Dipesh Chakrabarty asks about concepts such as citizen, modernity, science and capital, which present themselves as universal. Historians of India and other places cannot easily do without them, yet they do not fit cleanly. The book, with the subtitle postcolonial thought and historical difference, asks how to use these ideas while recognizing where they come from and where they strain.

He argues that the habit of historicism treats Europe as first and others as not yet, as if Indians and Africans were in a waiting room of history. He builds on Marx to describe two kinds of history, one that stands for the logic of capital and another made up of ways of life that do not fit it. He reads Bengali middle-class life, including the adda or talking circle, and the world of mill workers who dealt with gods.
ideas: Concepts such as citizen, modernity and the individual are presented as universal, but they were formed in European history. To provincialize Europe is to read them as local.
Chakrabarty calls European thought both indispensable and inadequate. Scholars outside Europe cannot do without it, but it does not capture their experience in full.
Historicism is the idea that societies go through stages, and it puts Europe at the front. Chakrabarty describes it as an imaginary waiting room, with others told to wait.
Drawing on Marx, he separates History 1, which presents the story of capital as universal, from History 2, the local ways of life that capital meets and cannot fully absorb.
He discusses adda, the Bengali habit of sustained and aimless conversation, as an example of a social form that Western categories of public sphere and civil society handle poorly.
Jute mill workers in Bengal lived among gods and spirits as well as among labor contracts. He asks how a historian can write about that without treating belief as error.
Provincializing Europe does not mean rejecting it or putting an Indian tradition in its place. Chakrabarty asks historians to use European ideas while attending to what they leave out.
Chakrabarty speaks of historicism's verdict of "not yet", the claim that colonized peoples are not yet ready for modernity. The delay is built into the structure of the story and not into the facts.
He writes from within the Subaltern Studies project, and he criticizes it for sometimes treating the religion of peasants as an early stage of consciousness waiting to mature.
He engages Heidegger as well as Marx, using Heidegger's idea of ways of being in the world to ask how gods and spirits can be real to those who live among them.

books.t: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World
books.thesis: Anticolonial nationalism did not simply copy the West. It claimed a domain of its own.
books.summary:
Partha Chatterjee asks whether anticolonial nationalism was only a copy of European ideas. The subtitle poses it as a question, a derivative discourse, and the book explores why the answer is no. Looking at Indian nationalism, Chatterjee shows that nationalists accepted much of the West's science and statecraft, while insisting on India's difference and on its own right to rule. The question is how a movement can borrow so much and still say something new.

He follows Indian nationalist thought through three stages, which he calls the moment of departure, the moment of maneuver and the moment of arrival. Bankim stands for the first, Gandhi for the second, and Nehru for the third. He uses Gramsci's idea of passive revolution to describe how the elite absorbed popular energy without giving up control. Critics have asked whether the three moments make too tidy a sequence, and whether the story describes mainly the educated elite.
ideas: Nationalism in the colonies is often judged as an imitation of European models. Chatterjee argues that this overlooks what anticolonial thinkers actually did with those models.

Chatterjee separates the problematic, the framework of knowledge a thinker works within, from the thematic, the claims made inside it. Nationalism shared colonial frameworks while arguing against colonial themes.
He suggests that this shared framework, shaped by ideas about the East, limited how far nationalism could depart from colonial thought even while it challenged colonial rule.
The moment of departure is when nationalist thought emerges from the encounter with colonial rule, and Chatterjee associates it with Bankim.
The moment of maneuver is when nationalism turns to the masses and uses their symbols. Gandhi stands here, drawing in peasants without giving them power.
The moment of arrival is when nationalist thought settles into the framework of the state and planning. Chatterjee connects this with Nehru and his ideas of order and progress.
Chatterjee uses Gramsci's concept of passive revolution to describe how the leading classes took in popular movements while preserving their own authority.
The book's subtitle is A Derivative Discourse, and it is posed as a question. Chatterjee's answer is that nationalism was derivative at the level of its framework but not at the level of its claims.

He reads Gandhi's Hind Swaraj as an attack on modern civilization itself and not just on British rule. This is why Gandhi could speak to peasants and why he fit awkwardly in the later nationalist state.
Chatterjee takes Said's Orientalism as a foil. He agrees that colonial knowledge worked as power, but asks why Said leaves little room for the colonized to answer back.

books.t: The Collected Essays of A. K. Ramanujan
books.thesis: Essays on folklore and translation, and on thinking that stays sensitive to context.
books.summary:
A. K. Ramanujan was a poet, translator and folklorist who wrote about India's stories and languages with a lightness that hid how much he knew. The collected essays gather his writing on folktales, classical poetry, translation and the idea of an Indian way of thinking. A common question runs under them: how do you describe a culture without flattening it into a few principles, and how do stories carry meaning from one setting to another?

In an essay on whether there is an Indian way of thinking, he proposes with caution that Indian thought and ethics are often context sensitive, where Western universals are context free. In an essay on the Ramayana, he follows how the story changes in many languages and traditions, with no single original. Some readers find his generalizations too tidy, and he said so himself with some humor.
ideas: Ramanujan asks whether there is an Indian way of thinking. He offers the idea, with caveats, that Indian thought is often context sensitive while Western thought leans toward context free universals.
He argues that rules of conduct in Indian traditions often depend on who a person is and what situation they are in, instead of applying one law to everyone.
His essay on the Ramayana describes many tellings in different languages and traditions, with changes in plot and attitude. He holds that no one version is the original.
Folktales travel across languages and regions, and each teller adapts them to a setting. Ramanujan treats this variation as part of the tale's life and not a corruption.
As a translator of classical Tamil and Kannada poetry, he wrote about the difficulty of carrying a poem into another language without turning it into something familiar.
He wrote in English and Kannada and translated from Tamil, so he lived among several languages. His essays treat that mix as an ordinary condition of Indian culture.
The Ramayana essay later became the subject of controversy when it was removed from a Delhi University reading list, which shows how contested the retelling of stories can be.
Ramanujan translated Kannada vachanas in Speaking of Siva, Tamil love and war poetry in The Interior Landscape, and Nammalvar's hymns in Hymns for the Drowning.
Classical Tamil poems are divided into akam, interior poems about love, and puram, exterior poems about war and public life. He uses the pair to show how a tradition maps feeling onto landscape.
In an essay on women's tales he describes a counter-system, in which women's oral stories in Kannada give a different view of marriage and family from the textual tradition.

books.thesis: Start with pure experience, before the world gets split into subject and object.
books.summary:
Nishida Kitaro's first book tries to start philosophy from the place before ideas harden into categories. He asks what experience is like before we split it into a self that sees and a world that is seen. His term is pure experience, a direct awareness that comes before judgment, such as the moment of hearing a melody or looking at a color without thinking about it.

The text moves in four parts, from pure experience to reality, the good and religion. Nishida argues that thinking, feeling and willing are all forms of this unified activity, and that the good lies in the full realization of the self. He ends by describing God as the unifying ground of reality, not as a being apart from it. Readers disagree about whether the book fits Western philosophy or a Zen outlook, and its terms are not easy to pin down.
ideas: Pure experience is the direct awareness that precedes the split between subject and object. Nishida describes it as experiencing facts just as they are, before any added judgment.
His examples include hearing a melody or seeing a color. In the moment of such experience there is no separate self reflecting on it, only the experience itself.
Experience does not belong to an individual who stands first. Nishida reverses the usual order, saying that the individual arises within experience and not the other way round.
Knowing, feeling and willing are not separate faculties. He treats them as different phases of one unifying activity of consciousness, which can be seen at work in attention and in thought.
The book is arranged in four parts that move from pure experience to reality, then to the good, and finally to religion. Each part builds on the idea of a single ground.
Nishida defines the good as the realization of the self. Acting well means becoming whole, and this is not the same as following rules or pursuing pleasure.
In his last section God is the unifying ground of the universe, not a being outside it. Critics have asked whether this stays close to a Zen view.
The phrase pure experience comes partly from William James. Nishida also drew on his Zen practice, which shaped how he treated direct experience.
Nishida says that love is the union of subject and object. To know something fully is to lose the gap between oneself and it.
It was his first book and is seen as the start of the Kyoto School. He later judged pure experience too psychological and moved toward the idea of basho, or place.

books.thesis: Ethics studies the human being as betweenness, individual and relation at once.
books.summary:
Watsuji Tetsuro wrote his major work on ethics in the 1930s and 1940s, and the title word, rinrigaku, names ethics as a study of rin, the relations between people. In Japanese, the word for human being, ningen, joins the characters for person and for between, and Watsuji reads this as a clue. A person is individual and relational at once, and ethics is the study of that twofold existence.

Watsuji argues that the individual and the community each arise by negating the other. A person separates from the group and then returns to it, and this movement is the structure of moral life. He criticizes Heidegger for describing human existence in terms of time and neglecting space, and he links his ethics to the study of climate and landscape in a companion work. Later critics note that Watsuji's emphasis on the whole fit uncomfortably with support for state authority in his time.
ideas: Ethics, in Watsuji's view, is the study of ningen, the human being understood as person and as the between. The word's characters themselves point to a being defined by relations.
He criticizes the starting point of much Western ethics, the isolated individual. For Watsuji, a person cut off from others is an abstraction, because human beings exist in relation from the first.
The individual arises by negating the community, and the community arises by negating the individual. Watsuji describes the movement back and forth as the basic structure of moral life.
He argues that ethics deals with relations such as family, neighborhood, economy and state. Each is a form of betweenness, a nested set of human connections within which people act.
Watsuji criticized Heidegger's Being and Time for treating human existence mainly through time. He thought the work gave too little place to space and to the shared world.
He links human existence to place and climate, a theme worked out in his book on climate, which asks how landscape shapes ways of living and of relating.
Critics note that his emphasis on the whole and on the state made his ethics compatible with the nationalism of his era. How far that is inherent remains debated.
Watsuji analyzes the word rinri. Rin means fellows or companions and ri means principle or order, so ethics is the order of human fellowship and not a rulebook for the lone will.
His book on climate, Fudo, sorts regions into monsoon, desert and meadow types. He links each to a characteristic temperament, such as a receptive, patient one for the monsoon lands.
He studied in Germany in 1927 and 1928 and read Being and Time there. His response to Heidegger shaped his view that human existence is spatial and social before it is temporal.

books.thesis: Iki is allure held at a distance, erotic tension kept alive by never quite closing.
books.summary:
Kuki Shuzo tried to explain a Japanese word that no European language seems to translate. Iki names a quality of style, in dress, manner and flirtation, associated with the pleasure quarters of Edo. It is stylish, a little cool, a little erotic and a little sad. Kuki had studied in Europe, and the book applies philosophy from Paris and Germany to a sensibility he missed while abroad.

Kuki says iki has three parts. One is bitai, a flirtatious attraction to another person that is kept alive by never being fulfilled. The second is a spirited pride, and the third is a calm resignation that refuses to cling. He then lists its forms in color, pattern and gesture, noting that vertical stripes and gray tones suit it. Some readers see the book as an elegant piece of cultural analysis, and others as a nationalist claim for Japanese uniqueness.
ideas: Iki names a style prized in Edo pleasure quarters, a way of dressing and bearing that is refined without being showy. Kuki treats it as a distinctive form of Japanese taste.
The first element, bitai, is flirtation, the attraction of one person to another. Kuki says iki depends on keeping it alive, without reaching its fulfillment.
The second element is ikiji, a spirited pride or backbone. It keeps allure from collapsing into dependence, and makes the person in iki seem self-possessed.
The third element is akirame, resignation, a calm that comes from knowing that attachments are fleeting. It gives iki a cool and slightly melancholy tone.
Kuki says that parallel lines, which approach each other but never meet, are an image of iki. He applies the idea to stripes in textiles.
He catalogs how iki shows in colors and objects, favoring muted blue gray tones and plain designs over bright ornament. Subdued surfaces suggest restrained feeling.
Critics debate whether the book is a philosophical study of an aesthetic or a case for Japanese uniqueness. Kuki himself treats the term as only partly translatable.
Kuki wrote the book after years in Europe, where he met Heidegger and studied phenomenology. He used European methods to describe a Japanese taste.
He maps iki against neighboring tastes such as shibui, which is astringent, hade, which is flashy, and yabo, which is boorish. Iki is defined in part by what it is not.
He treats iki as a way of being of a people and approaches it by interpretation, working out the meaning as it is lived and not defining it from outside.

books.thesis: Amae, the wish to be indulged, turns out to be a key to close relationships.
books.summary:
Takeo Doi was a Japanese psychiatrist who noticed, while working in the United States, that English had no good word for a feeling he knew well from home. The word is amae, which names the wish to be indulged, to lean on another person's goodwill and be forgiven for it. Doi asks whether this feeling explains a pattern of closeness in Japanese life, and whether it is more widely human than the language suggests.

He starts from the relation between mother and infant and follows the same wish into friendship, work and religion. He discusses the pair of inner and outer circles of obligation and the gap between public stance and private feeling. His book was widely read in Japan and abroad, and critics have said it makes Japanese uniqueness too neat. Others accept that amae is real but argue that it exists in many societies, which Doi himself half admits.
ideas: Amae comes from a verb meaning to depend on another's goodwill. Doi describes it as the wish to be indulged, usually first felt by an infant toward the mother.
Doi noticed the lack of an English word for amae while working in the United States. He took this gap as a sign that Japanese and Western cultures notice different feelings.
Amae continues into adulthood. Doi sees it in friendships, in relations between boss and employee and in the way Japanese people expect to be understood without saying everything.
He discusses the distinction between uchi, the inner circle, and soto, the outer one. Amae is easier within the intimate circle, while stiffer manners hold with outsiders.
Doi notes the contrast between public stance and private feeling. Amae thrives in the private sphere, though it is hard to express openly.
He argues that Western psychology tends to treat dependence as immaturity. Doi says that this may be an expression of a culture that prizes independence.
Critics suggest that amae is a universal feeling and not a mark of Japanese uniqueness. Doi's own work partly allows this, and the debate over how culture specific the concept is continues.

Doi shows how Japanese words for sulking and resentment, such as suneru, higamu and uramu, belong to a vocabulary of thwarted amae. The language records what happens when the wish for indulgence is refused.
He sets amae beside giri and ninjo, obligation and human feeling. Amae sits at the center of ninjo, which explains why obligation can feel both binding and warm.
Doi engages Ruth Benedict's The Chrysanthemum and the Sword. He argues that Japanese guilt and shame are shaped by fear of losing others' goodwill, which a plain shame culture label does not capture.

books.thesis: Chinese rural society pictured as ripples of obligation spreading out from each person.
books.summary:
Fei Xiaotong was a Chinese sociologist trained in anthropology, and these short essays, written in the 1940s, describe village China as he knew it. The book asks what holds people together in a society where most live close to the land and know everyone around them. Fei is interested in habits that Westerners might not notice, such as how people speak of the family, how they settle disputes, and why they trust those they have long known.

His best known image is the ripple. A person is like a stone dropped in water, and relations spread outward in circles of decreasing closeness. In a society of ripples, the family can stretch or shrink with the situation, and morals depend on how near someone stands. Fei also describes rural life as an acquaintance society, governed by custom and rites more than by law.
ideas: Fei describes rural China as a society of ripples. Each person stands at the center of circles of relations, with obligation weakening as the circles widen.
He contrasts this with the Western organizational mode, in which individuals belong to groups like sticks in a bundle of firewood, with clear edges and equal standing inside.
Because each person sits at the center of their own circle, the boundaries of the family are elastic. It can shrink to a household or expand to a wide kin network.
Moral standards in a society of ripples depend on closeness. What is owed to a relative differs from what is owed to a stranger, and public principles are harder to apply evenly.
Rural China is an acquaintance society, in Fei's phrase. People live among those they know from birth, and trust rests on long familiarity and not on written agreements.
Fei argues that such a society is ruled by ritual and custom learned in childhood, not by law enforced from outside, and that it works because everyone knows what is expected.
Fei's account is a sketch of a type of society as he saw it in the 1940s, and readers have asked how well it describes later or different parts of China.
The Chinese title uses xiangtu, the earthbound. Fei argues that rural people stay where their ancestors lived, and that this lack of movement is what makes trust through long familiarity possible.

Fei contrasts a Western relay model of inheritance, in which each generation hands the baton on, with a Chinese feedback model. In the feedback model the young are expected to repay their parents by supporting them.
In a society of acquaintances, he suggests, writing matters less because speech and shared habit carry most meaning. Fei uses this to explain why village life could run without written contracts.

books.thesis: Includes “Ah Q”, the story with its portrait of spiritual victory.
books.summary:
Lu Xun's first story collection, published in 1923, gathers short fictions about Chinese people at the end of the old order. In the preface he tells how he gave up medicine after seeing a slide of a Chinese man executed as a spy while other Chinese looked on, and decided that curing minds mattered more than bodies. He also describes an iron house with no windows, where people are asleep and will soon suffocate, and asks whether waking them only brings suffering.

In A Madman's Diary a man comes to believe that history and the people around him are devouring one another. Kong Yiji shows a failed scholar mocked in a tavern, and Medicine follows a family that buys a folk remedy for a dying son. The True Story of Ah Q gives the book's best known figure, a poor man who turns every humiliation into an imagined victory.
ideas: In the preface Lu Xun describes giving up medicine after seeing a slide of an execution in which Chinese onlookers stood watching. He turned to writing to change minds.
The preface imagines an iron house with no windows and sleepers about to suffocate. Lu Xun asks whether it is kind to wake them, and the book is his answer.
A Madman's Diary is narrated by a man who thinks the people around him are cannibals. Reading history, he sees the words eat people between the lines of benevolence.
Kong Yiji is a failed scholar in a tavern who wears a scholar's long gown and is laughed at by the customers. The story shows the cruelty of ordinary onlookers.
Medicine shows a family buying a roll dipped in the blood of an executed revolutionary, believing it will cure their son. Superstition and indifference both appear in the story.
Ah Q wins every defeat in his mind. When beaten, he tells himself it is like a son beating his father, and the story treats this spiritual victory as a national habit.
Lu Xun keeps hope slight. The collection ends with no promise that waking the sleepers will help, and readers still argue over whether the book is bitter or loving.
A Madman's Diary appeared in New Youth in 1918 and is counted as the first modern story in vernacular Chinese. The title is borrowed from Gogol.

In Hometown, the narrator returns to a village and finds it changed. The story ends with the thought that hope is like paths on the earth: there were none at first, but when many walk the same way, a path appears.
Ah Q is a village drifter without a home who is finally executed for a robbery he did not commit. The crowd watches the execution as a show, which repeats the image from the preface.

books.t: The Myth of the Lazy Native
books.thesis: Colonial writing built an image of idleness to justify rule. That image outlived empire.
books.summary:
Syed Hussein Alatas, a Malaysian sociologist, wrote about an image that European colonizers repeated for centuries: the native who prefers idleness to work. The book looks at accounts of Malays, Filipinos and Javanese from the time of early European contact through the nineteenth century. His answer is that it was an ideology, produced because the colonial economy wanted labor and the local people often did not want to give it on the terms offered.

Alatas reads the writings of administrators, travelers and scholars and shows how their picture of laziness was built from the colonial point of view, resting on their own needs and prejudices more than on observation. He argues that the image of the lazy native belonged to a larger set of ideas that excused rule and also shaped later local elites. He criticizes how the image survived the end of empire, even in the writing of some of the colonized themselves.
ideas: Alatas studies the image of the lazy native in colonial writing about the Malays, Filipinos and Javanese. He treats it as an ideology built for a purpose, not as a neutral observation.
Colonial plantations and mines needed cheap labor. People who refused harsh terms were called idle, and the label turned a political and economic quarrel into a fault of character.
He argues that the accounts rest on colonial assumptions about what counts as work, and overlook the labor local people actually did, such as farming, fishing and trade.
The image did not stand alone. Alatas places it among other stereotypes that justified rule, in which natives were childlike, backward or in need of supervision.
He compares attitudes toward groups seen as industrious, such as the Chinese migrants, and shows that the same economy judged different peoples by what they gave it.
The image survived the end of empire. Alatas shows local elites repeating it about their own people, and treats this as a sign of how thoroughly colonial ideas were absorbed.
His method is to analyze texts as a form of ideology. Critics say the book generalizes across diverse colonies, but its central claim that stereotypes can serve power is widely accepted.
Alatas draws on writings by colonial officials, travellers and missionaries from the sixteenth to the twentieth century. The pattern holds across Spanish, Dutch and British sources.
He discusses Jose Rizal's essay on the supposed indolence of the Filipino. Rizal traces whatever idleness existed to colonial conditions, such as forced labor and heavy taxes, and not to character.

Alatas is also known for the term captive mind, used for scholars in formerly colonized countries who take Western frameworks without question. The lazy native myth is a case study of what such a mind absorbs.

books.thesis: A nation is an imagined community, held together by shared print, language and time.
books.summary:
Benedict Anderson asks an awkward question about nationalism: why do people feel so strongly about a group of millions they will never meet? His answer begins with a definition. A nation is an imagined political community, imagined as limited and sovereign. It is imagined because no member will ever know most of the others, yet each carries an image of belonging. The book asks how that way of imagining became possible, and why it has spread to nearly every part of the world.

He points to the decline of religious communities and dynastic kingdoms, the rise of print capitalism and vernacular languages, and a new sense of time in which people share the same calendar moment. Novels and newspapers helped readers picture a society moving through that time. He traces the first nationalisms to Creole officials in the Americas, and later editions add chapters on the census, the map and the museum.
ideas: A nation is an imagined political community, imagined as both limited and sovereign. It is imagined because members will never meet most of their fellow members, yet feel a bond with them.
Before nations, people lived within religious communities and dynastic realms. Anderson argues that the decline of both made room for a new way of imagining belonging.
Print capitalism matters because publishers sold books and papers in the vernacular. Readers of the same language began to see themselves as part of a shared community.
Anderson borrows from Walter Benjamin the idea of homogeneous, empty time, in which many events happen at once across a society. The novel and the newspaper make that time visible.
The reading of a morning newspaper is a ceremony done by many people at once. Each reader knows that thousands of others are doing it too, which links strangers.
The first nationalisms, he argues, emerged among Creole elites in the Americas, who were born in the colonies and excluded from the highest posts by officials sent from the mother country.
Later editions added chapters on how colonial states used the census, the map and the museum to give nations their shapes. Critics say the book neglects oral culture.

The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is a symbol of the nation's imagining. Everyone knows what it stands for, yet no one knows whose remains lie inside, and the emptiness is what lets millions identify with it.

Anderson describes official nationalism as the answer of dynasties such as the Romanovs and the Habsburgs to popular nationalism. They adopted national language and identity from above to stay in power.
Nationalisms, he says, became modular. Once the Creole, linguistic and official models existed, later movements could copy and adapt them, so nationalism spread as a pattern.

books.thesis: Western description of the East, the book argues, worked as an instrument of power.
books.summary:
Edward Said noticed that European writing about the Middle East and Asia kept returning to the same few images: the sensual, despotic, unchanging East. Said was a literary critic born in Jerusalem, and he begins from the thought that the East of European writing is a made thing, something shaped and then taken for fact.

He argues that Orientalism, the study and description of the East, grew alongside European empire and became a way of managing it. He draws on Foucault to claim that knowledge and power work together and on Gramsci to describe how culture supports rule. He follows the pattern from Napoleon's expedition to Egypt through British officials like Cromer and Balfour and on to American experts after the Second World War. Critics have argued that he treats the West as a single block, ignores scholars who resisted the pattern, and says little about how the East should be described instead.
ideas: Said argues that the Orient is a European construction. It was produced through writing, scholarship and administration, and it says more about those who imagined it than about those it describes.
Orientalism, in his sense, is a style of thought that sets East against West. The East is cast as irrational, sensual and unchanging, the West as rational and capable of progress.
Said uses Foucault to argue that knowledge is tied to power. Describing a people is part of ruling them, and the scholar's authority serves the interests of empire.
He discusses Napoleon's expedition to Egypt as a moment when scholarship and conquest came together, with scholars attached to the army to study the country.
Said quotes British officials such as Balfour and Cromer, who explained why Britain should rule Egypt in terms of what Egyptians were said to be like.
He distinguishes latent Orientalism, a stable set of assumptions about the East, from manifest Orientalism, the particular statements made at different times by different authors.
Critics such as Bernard Lewis and Aijaz Ahmad argue that Said treats the West as one unit, overlooks scholars who did not fit, and offers no alternative way of describing the East.
Said distinguishes three meanings of Orientalism: an academic discipline, a style of thought based on a distinction between East and West, and a corporate institution for dealing with the Orient.

He traces modern Orientalism to philologists such as Silvestre de Sacy and Ernest Renan. Renan's treatment of Semitic languages as limited and primitive is his example of scholarship that passes judgment.

Flaubert's encounter with the Egyptian courtesan Kuchuk Hanem is used to show how the Orient was imagined as sensual and available. The last chapter follows these habits of thought into the American scholarship of the postwar era.

books.thesis: Education is political. People change their world when they can name it themselves.
books.summary:
Paulo Freire wrote this book in exile after the 1964 coup in Brazil, drawing on his work teaching adults to read in poor communities. He asks what education looks like when its aim is freedom instead of fitting people into the world as it is. It either helps people accept their situation or helps them question it, and it asks who gets to name the world and who is told what it contains.

Freire describes a banking model, in which a teacher deposits information into students, and sets against it problem-posing education, in which teacher and students investigate the world together through dialogue. He says that the oppressed can internalize the oppressor's image of them, so that freedom is also feared. Critics say his language is abstract and the proposals are hard to carry out in schools, and Freire invites that testing.
ideas: Freire describes the banking concept of education. The teacher deposits facts into students, who receive, memorize and repeat them. This trains people to adapt to the world as it is.
In problem-posing education, teacher and students learn together through dialogue. The teacher is also taught by the students, and the topic is drawn from the world they live in.

Conscientizacao is the process of becoming aware of the social conditions that shape one's life and of one's ability to change them. Freire thinks this awareness arises through reflection joined with action.
The oppressed can take in the oppressor's picture of themselves, so that they come to feel ignorant or unfit. For this reason freedom is also frightening to them.
Freire discusses a fear of freedom that affects the oppressed, who may prefer the security of a known place, and the oppressor, who may fear losing a position of advantage.
Praxis, in Freire's usage, is reflection and action together directed at changing the world. Action without reflection is activism, and reflection without action is empty talk.
Revolutionary leaders are warned not to manipulate the people they want to free or to treat them as an object. Freire says liberation has to be undertaken with them.
Freire's method begins with generative themes, drawn from the lives of the learners. Teachers and students investigate them together and codify them in pictures or situations to be discussed.
He lists anti-dialogical actions: conquest, divide and rule, manipulation and cultural invasion. Against them he sets dialogical ones: cooperation, unity, organization and cultural synthesis.

Dialogue, in his account, needs love, humility, faith in people, hope and critical thinking. He wrote the book in exile in Chile after the 1964 coup in Brazil, drawing on his literacy work with adults.

books.thesis: How group solidarity builds states, and how comfort wears them down.
books.summary:
Ibn Khaldun wrote the Muqaddimah in 1377 as the introduction to a larger history, and it became a book about how to read history at all. He lived in North Africa and Spain, held political posts and saw dynasties fall, and he asked why some groups rise to power and why states weaken after a few generations. The book treats society as something with its own regularities, which he calls the science of civilization.

His central idea is asabiyya, group feeling or solidarity, which gives a tribe the strength to take power. Once in power, a ruling group moves into city life, becomes accustomed to comfort, and loses the cohesion that made it strong, and a hardier group takes its place. He also criticizes historians who repeat reports without testing them against what is plausible. Modern readers argue about how far his cycle fits other places, and whether he foresaw economics and sociology.
ideas: Ibn Khaldun proposes a science of civilization, a study of the regular patterns in how human societies form, grow and decline. He sees this as a way to test historical reports.
Historians often repeat reports without checking them. Ibn Khaldun says that a claim should be tested against what is plausible about how societies work, and he criticizes careless chroniclers.
Asabiyya is the group feeling that binds people together, usually through kinship or shared life. It is the force that lets a group defend itself and take power.
Nomads and desert peoples, he argues, are tougher and more cohesive than city dwellers. They are able to conquer settled lands because their solidarity has not been softened by luxury.
Once a ruling group takes power it moves to city life and grows used to comfort. Its solidarity weakens, and the dynasty becomes vulnerable to a new group from outside.
A dynasty, in his view, lasts about three generations, or a hundred and twenty years. The first is hardy, and by the third the roots of its strength are forgotten.
Ibn Khaldun argues that heavy taxation can reduce a state's revenue by discouraging work and trade. Some modern economists cite this as an early version of an idea now well known.
The Muqaddimah is the introduction to a longer world history, the Kitab al-Ibar. Ibn Khaldun made the introduction into a separate science of society.
His term umran means civilization or social organization. He divides it into bedouin umran, the life of nomads and rural people, and sedentary umran, the life of towns.
Religion can add to group feeling. A call to a religious cause, he says, helps a dynasty gain power by joining the solidarity of its members to a larger purpose.

books.thesis: Living between cultures and languages, treated as a way of seeing.
books.summary:
Gloria Anzaldua grew up on the Texas side of the US border with Mexico. Her book, part essay, part poetry, shifts between English, Spanish and Nahuatl with no translation offered. It asks what it means to live in a place where cultures meet and rub, and to belong to none of them completely. She writes as a Chicana, a lesbian and a writer, and treats these positions as a place from which to see, as well as a place of pain.

Anzaldua introduces the mestiza consciousness, a way of thinking that tolerates ambiguity and holds contradictory parts together. She writes about the Aztec past, the Virgin of Guadalupe and the figure of Malinche, and about the policing of language, which she calls linguistic terrorism. Critics have asked how far her mythic history is accurate, and some find her mixed form hard to follow.
ideas: The border is described as an open wound, a place where one world grates against another and bleeds. Anzaldua treats it as both a physical line and a condition of life.
Anzaldua moves between English, Spanish, Tex-Mex and Nahuatl without translating. The shifting language mirrors the life she describes, and readers who lack one language are made to feel the border.

She describes the mestiza consciousness, a way of thinking developed by those who live between cultures. It involves tolerance for ambiguity and an ability to hold contradictions without choosing one.
Linguistic terrorism is her term for the shaming of people for how they speak. She says that being told your language is wrong is being told that you are wrong.
Anzaldua reaches back to the Aztec past and to the idea of Aztlan, claiming a long history for people of Mexican descent in the American Southwest. Critics debate the accuracy of this.
She examines the figures of the Virgin of Guadalupe, Malinche and La Llorona, women whose stories have been used to define what women may be in Mexican and Chicano culture.
As a queer woman in a culture that often condemned her, Anzaldua writes of standing outside more than one boundary. She presents that edge as a place to see from.
The first half of the book is prose essays and the second half is poetry. Both use the same mixed language, so the form of the book follows the border it describes.
Anzaldua describes the Coatlicue state, a stage of paralysis and crisis that she draws from the Aztec earth goddess. It is a necessary period of being stuck before a new consciousness emerges.

In How to Tame a Wild Tongue she opens with a dentist who tries to make her mouth behave, and then lists the several languages Chicanos speak. Chicano Spanish, she says, is a border tongue and not a corrupted one.

books.thesis: Reading a national character through its solitude, its masks and its festival.
books.summary:
Octavio Paz wrote this book of essays about Mexico in 1950, when he was a young poet and diplomat. He asks what it is to be Mexican, and he looks for the answer in behavior he thinks reveals it: the mask, the love of fiestas, the closed manner, the attitude toward death. He treats the national character as a way of being alone in the world that people of other countries may feel as well but do not live in quite the same way.

Paz begins with the pachuco, a young Mexican American in Los Angeles who lives between two cultures. He turns to the figure of the Mexican as son of the violated mother, linking national feeling to the Conquest, and to the festival as a release in which the mask comes off. Critics argue that he turns a diverse country into a single type, and that his picture of Mexican women is limited.
ideas: Paz opens with the pachuco, a young Mexican American in Los Angeles with a defiant style of dress and speech. He uses the figure to show life between two worlds.
The Mexican, in Paz's description, wears a mask. Politeness, irony and silence keep others at a distance, which he treats as a defense of a lonely and wounded self.
Paz reads the Conquest as a founding wound. The Mexican is the child of the violated mother, which he connects to the word chingada and to ambivalence toward origins.
The festival is a break from ordinary life. In the fiesta people spend heavily, shout and mix, and for a time the mask comes off and solitude is eased.
Mexicans, he suggests, have a particular relation to death. It is a familiar presence, joked about and celebrated instead of hidden, which shows an attitude to life as much as dying.
Paz discusses the Mexican Revolution as a search for a national face, an effort by the country to discover and affirm what it was, after years of imported forms.
Critics say that Paz makes a diverse country into a single type and that his account of women is thin. The book is an interpretation, and he offers it as one.
Paz contrasts Mexicans and North Americans. In his phrase, North Americans see the world as something to be perfected, while Mexicans see it as something to be redeemed.
A later postscript, Postdata, was added after the 1968 killings at Tlatelolco. Paz reads the massacre as a return of old sacrificial patterns in Mexican politics.
He argues that the nineteenth century imported liberal and positivist ideas that did not fit the country. The gap between the ideas and daily life, he says, added to the mask.

books.thesis: Essays on what it is to see yourself through the eyes of a society that despises you.
books.summary:
W. E. B. Du Bois published this collection of essays in 1903, when he was a young scholar at Atlanta University. He opens with a question put to him by white acquaintances, how it feels to be a problem, and a statement that the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color line. It asks what it is like to see yourself through the eyes of a society that despises you.

Du Bois describes double consciousness, the sense of always looking at yourself through the eyes of others, and the veil that separates Black and white Americans. He surveys the aftermath of emancipation, the work of the Freedmen's Bureau, life in the rural Black Belt of Georgia, and the sorrow songs that he treats as the nation's finest music. Some readers, then and now, have questioned his elitism, and he later revised parts of his thinking.
ideas: The central problem of the twentieth century, Du Bois writes, is the problem of the color line. He opens with the unspoken question white Americans put to him.
Double consciousness is the feeling of always looking at yourself through others' eyes. Du Bois describes a person both American and Black, with two warring ideals in one body.
The veil is his image for the barrier between Black and white worlds. Black people can see through it, though white Americans often cannot or will not.
He criticizes Booker T. Washington for accepting economic progress without political rights. Du Bois argues that giving up the vote and higher education would keep Black Americans in subordination.
Du Bois describes the Freedmen's Bureau, set up after emancipation, as a brief and incomplete effort to help formerly enslaved people with land, schools and justice.
In the Black Belt of Georgia, Du Bois travels through rural counties and shows the effects of debt and tenant farming on Black families after the war.
The sorrow songs, he writes, are the finest American music and a record of a people's grief and hope. Du Bois places them at the center of the book's closing pages.
The chapter Of the Passing of the First-Born is a lament for Du Bois's infant son, Burghardt. It is a plain and personal piece set among essays on politics and history.
The chapter Of the Meaning of Progress describes teaching in a rural school in Tennessee. Du Bois returns years later and sees how little has changed for the families he knew.
The story Of the Coming of John is fiction. A Black man comes home from his education and finds that he no longer fits, and the town's racism decides his fate.

books.thesis: The mind is split into id, ego and superego. The ego serves three harsh masters.
books.summary:
By 1923 Freud had found his early picture of the mind, built on conscious and unconscious, too crude for clinical facts such as unconscious guilt and resistance in patients who wanted to get well. The book asks how the mind is actually organized and why part of the self works against the person.

Freud proposes a structural model. The id holds drives, the ego develops from it as a surface that mediates with reality, and the superego forms from internalized parental authority. The ego must balance the three demands of id, reality and superego, which is a source of anxiety. The model is hard to test, and critics note that the three agencies read more like metaphors than measurable systems.
ideas: The id is the reservoir of instinctual drives. It operates by the pleasure principle and has no sense of time, logic or negation.
The ego develops from the id through contact with the outside world. It represents reason and caution, and works by the reality principle.
Freud compares the ego to a rider who must guide a stronger horse, and who often ends up steering it where it already wants to go.
The superego arises from the resolution of the Oedipus complex, when the child internalizes parental prohibitions as conscience and ideal.
Much of the ego is itself unconscious, so Freud drops the equation of the unconscious with the repressed alone.
A sense of guilt can be unconscious, and it explains why some patients cling to their symptoms and resist cure.
The ego is threatened from three sides, by the external world, the id's libido and the superego's severity, and anxiety signals each danger.
Freud writes that the ego is first and foremost a bodily ego. It is derived from bodily sensations, chiefly those from the surface of the body, and is a projection of that surface.
The word id comes from Georg Groddeck, who used das Es, the It, for the forces by which we are lived. Freud adopts it for the unknown and uncontrollable part of the mind.
Freud reduces the instincts to two classes, Eros and the death instinct. He says the harsh superego can become a pure culture of the death instinct.

books.t: Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality
books.thesis: Sexuality begins in infancy and develops in stages. Adult life is a product of that path.
books.summary:
Freud's 1905 book takes on the question of what sexuality is and where it comes from. Common opinion held that it appears at puberty with a fixed aim of reproduction. Freud asks how to explain perversions, childhood behavior and the wide range of adult desire within one account.

His answer is that the sexual drive is present from infancy, attaches to different bodily zones in turn, and only later organizes under genital primacy. Adult variation then reflects how development went, and no outcome is wholly natural or unnatural. The book was revised across several editions. Many of its claims about childhood and gender are now rejected, though its broad view that sexuality is shaped by development remains influential.
ideas: Sexual life does not begin at puberty. Infants show sexual activity such as thumb sucking, which Freud treats as pleasure independent of feeding.
The drive has a source, an aim and an object, and each can vary, which allows Freud to describe sexual variation without a single norm.
Development passes through oral, anal and genital phases, with a latency period before puberty in which the drive is held back.
Freud calls the child's disposition polymorphously perverse, meaning it can find satisfaction in many ways before it is organized.
Adult perversions are explained as fixations or regressions to earlier stages, and not as signs of a degenerate constitution.
Neuroses are described as the negative of perversions, because the repressed wishes appear in disguised symptoms.
At puberty the finding of an object is a refinding, since the first sexual object was the mother's breast.
Freud introduces erotogenic zones, parts of the body such as the mouth and anus that give sexual pleasure, and component instincts, which only later come together under the genitals.

He refuses to treat inversion, or same-sex object choice, as degeneration. He notes it occurs in people of otherwise sound health, and says everyone has the capacity to choose an object of either sex.
Children conduct their own sexual researches, he says, driven by curiosity about where babies come from. Their theories are mistaken but are an important step in development.

books.thesis: Religion and morality arose from a primal crime. Guilt over a murdered father founded society.
books.summary:
Freud asks how the earliest human communities came to hold their taboos and totem animals, and whether the similarity between the customs of tribal peoples and the obsessions of neurotic patients points to a common source.

He answers with a speculative story. A tyrannical father who kept all the women was killed and eaten by his sons, who then felt remorse and created the totem and the incest prohibition. This is the origin of religion and moral law. Anthropologists criticized it at once, since there is no evidence for such an event and it depends on the idea that guilt is inherited. Most readers treat it as a myth that clarifies Freud's thinking more than as history.
ideas: Taboos resemble the prohibitions of obsessional neurosis, in that both attach to forbidden wishes that people are drawn to and also fear.
Totemism forbids killing the totem animal and marrying within the totem clan, which Freud connects to the two crimes of the Oedipus complex.
The primal horde was ruled by a violent father. The brothers banded together to kill him and then identified with him through a totem meal.
Guilt after the killing led the sons to obey the father's former prohibitions, which created the basis of social order.
Freud links animism, religion and science as three stages of human thought, running from belief in the power of thoughts to reliance on reason.
Ambivalence, the mixture of love and hate toward the same person, is central to the taboo and to feelings toward the dead.
He assumes a collective mind that carries the memory of the crime across generations, which is the weakest point of the argument.
The book has four essays. They treat incest horror, taboo and ambivalence, animism and magic, and the return of totemism in childhood.
Freud builds on Darwin's primal horde, Robertson Smith's totem meal and Frazer's anthropology. His own contribution is to join them with the Oedipus complex.
In the last essay he uses Little Hans and his fear of horses as a childhood version of totemism. The horse stands in for the feared father in the same way as the totem animal.

books.thesis: Religion is a comforting illusion rooted in childhood helplessness. Reason can replace it.
books.summary:
Freud asks what religious belief is and why it has such power over civilization, which needs restraint on the drives to survive. He wants to know whether people can hold together morally without religious faith.

His argument is that religious ideas are illusions, which means beliefs driven by wish and not by evidence. They answer the helplessness people feel before nature and fate by recalling the protective father of childhood. Freud hopes humanity will outgrow them through education and the slow voice of reason. Critics, including Freud's own imagined opponent in the text, say he underrates how deeply belief meets needs, and he does not claim that religion is false, only that it lacks proof.
ideas: Civilization rests on renunciation of instinct, and people resent it, so culture needs ways to make that burden bearable.
Religious ideas are illusions, defined by Freud as beliefs in which wish fulfillment is a prominent motive, whether or not they happen to be true.
The adult feeling of helplessness revives the child's need for a father, and God is a projected exalted father.
Religion offers consolation against nature, fate and death, and also gives moral rules with a divine sanction.
Freud compares religion to a universal obsessional neurosis of humanity, which people may grow out of as they do childhood neuroses.
He proposes that morality can be justified by its usefulness to civilized life and not by divine command.
Science is no illusion, he says, because it can correct itself, and the belief that it cannot supply what we need would be the real illusion.
Freud separates an illusion from a delusion. A delusion contradicts reality, while an illusion might turn out true, but is held because of a wish.
He proposes an education to reality, in which children are not raised on religious doctrine and are prepared to meet the world as it is.
Near the end he writes that the voice of the intellect is a soft one, but it does not rest until it has gained a hearing. He calls this a ground for modest hope.

books.t: Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego
books.thesis: Groups hold together through libidinal ties to a leader. Members swap their ego ideal for him.
books.summary:
Freud asks why individuals in a crowd think, feel and act differently than they do alone, and what binds a group together. Earlier crowd theorists like Le Bon had described the effects but offered little explanation.

Freud proposes that the answer lies in love, in the broad sense of libido. Members are tied to the leader and thereby to each other, and in the Church and the army the leader takes the place of the ego ideal. Identification explains the shared emotion. The account is built on a limited range of examples, and its picture of crowds as regressive has been questioned by later social psychologists who stress shared identity and rational behavior.
ideas: Le Bon described the group mind as suggestible, impulsive and unreflective. Freud keeps the description but asks what produces it.
Group cohesion rests on libidinal bonds, which are aim-inhibited love, tying members to a leader and to each other.
Church and army are his model groups. Each rests on an illusion that the leader loves all members equally.
Identification is the earliest form of emotional tie to another person, and it can replace the object choice by taking the object into the ego.
Being in love and hypnosis both show an object taking the place of the ego ideal, which explains the credulity of the hypnotized and of the crowd.
Panic occurs when the tie to the leader breaks, which frees each member's anxiety and leaves the group to dissolve.
Freud links the group back to the primal horde, treating the leader as a return of the primal father.
Freud argues that social feeling arises from a reversal of envy and rivalry. Members who would compete demand equal treatment, and this becomes group spirit.
Such groups are loving inside and intolerant of outsiders. He notes that churches, which preach love, have been harsh toward those who do not belong.
He uses the phrase narcissism of small differences for the hostility between close neighbours, such as the English and the Scots. Small differences, he says, can stir up more feeling than large ones.

books.thesis: Grief lets go of a lost object. Melancholia turns the loss into an attack on the self.
books.summary:
This 1917 paper asks why mourning is a normal response to loss while melancholia, a similar state, is pathological. Both involve painful dejection and loss of interest in the world, yet only melancholia includes a drop in self-regard.

Freud argues that in mourning the person slowly detaches libido from the lost object by testing reality, bit by bit. In melancholia the loss is often unconscious, the object is taken into the ego, and the hostility meant for it is directed against the self. The essay is short and speculative, and later work on grief, including attachment theory, has revised its picture of mourning as a task of detachment.
ideas: Mourning is a reaction to the loss of a loved person or an abstraction such as a country or an ideal, and it is not an illness.
The work of mourning requires reality to be tested again and again, and each memory of the lost object must be withdrawn from.
Melancholia adds a striking fall in self-esteem, with the patient reproaching and belittling himself.
The melancholic's reproaches often fit the lost person better than the patient, because the self-accusations are displaced anger.
The lost object is introjected, so that the shadow of the object falls upon the ego and the ego is judged as the object was.
The loss in melancholia may be unconscious, so the patient knows whom he lost but not what he lost in him.
Freud relates the condition to ambivalence and to a regression toward the oral stage, and notes that melancholia can swing into mania.
Freud writes that in mourning it is the world that has become poor and empty, while in melancholia it is the ego itself. This is his main contrast between the two.
He notes a critical agency in the ego that judges and punishes the rest of it. This is a forerunner of the superego, which he develops in The Ego and the Id.
Suicide, he says, becomes possible only when the ego treats itself as an object and turns the hostility meant for the lost person on itself.

books.thesis: The uncanny is the familiar made strange. It returns what was repressed or once believed.
books.summary:
Freud's 1919 essay takes up an unusual topic in aesthetics, the feeling of dread that comes from something that is both known and alien. He asks what makes certain things uncanny and why the feeling differs from simple fear.

He begins from the German word unheimlich, which includes its opposite heimlich, meaning homely and also hidden. He argues the feeling arises when repressed infantile complexes or surmounted primitive beliefs are revived by some event. His main example is Hoffmann's story The Sandman. The essay is loosely organized and the reading of the story has been disputed, as have the limits of the concept in fiction, where Freud admits the rules differ.
ideas: The German unheimlich ties the unfamiliar to the familiar, since heimlich means both homelike and concealed, so the two meanings meet.
Ernst Jentsch had linked the uncanny to intellectual uncertainty, such as whether a doll is alive. Freud finds this insufficient.
In The Sandman, fear of losing the eyes is read as a substitute for the fear of castration, tied to the father figure.
The double, an image of the self that appears elsewhere, was once a protection against death and later became a sign of death.
Repetition and coincidence feel uncanny because they recall the compulsion to repeat that Freud finds in the unconscious.
Two sources are separated, repressed complexes that return and primitive beliefs, such as animism and the power of thought, that seem confirmed again.
Fiction can create uncanny effects the real world cannot, but it can also remove them if it announces that its world follows different laws.
Freud quotes Schelling's definition: the uncanny is everything that ought to have remained secret and hidden but has come to light.
Dead bodies, ghosts, severed limbs and the return of the dead are among his examples. They feel uncanny, he says, because they revive an old belief in the dead returning.
He treats the fear of being buried alive as the reverse of a fantasy of life in the womb. The most uncanny places, in his account, are those that recall the first home.

books.thesis: Hysterical symptoms come from forgotten trauma. Talking it out can remove them.
books.summary:
Breuer and Freud ask what causes hysterical symptoms, such as paralyses and lost speech, that have no organic basis, and whether they can be treated. The book collects case histories, including Breuer's Anna O. and Freud's patients such as Emmy von N. and Elisabeth von R.

Their argument, laid out in the Preliminary Communication, is that symptoms derive from memories of events whose emotion was never discharged. Recalling the event and voicing the feeling relieves the symptom. Freud's later chapters shift from hypnosis toward free association and begin to stress resistance and repression. The cases are told selectively, and later scholars have questioned the claimed cures, notably in the case of Anna O.
ideas: Hysterics suffer mainly from reminiscences, as the authors put it, meaning memories of events that continue to act on them.
A trauma produces symptoms when the emotional reaction to it was suppressed, and abreaction, or discharge of the affect, can relieve them.
The cathartic method uses hypnosis to bring forgotten memories into awareness, and Anna O. called it her talking cure.
Freud finds that not all patients can be hypnotized and develops the concentration technique, which leads to free association.
Resistance appears as the patient's reluctance to recall, which Freud takes as evidence that a force has kept the memory out of mind.
Symptoms are often symbolically tied to the trauma, so that a painful memory can show up as pain in a particular part of the body.
Freud's cases suggest that the traumas are mostly of a sexual or conflict-laden kind, an idea he pursues after the book.
