Freud's own cases include Frau Emmy von N., Miss Lucy R., Katharina and Fraulein Elisabeth von R. Anna O., the case that started it, was Breuer's.
Freud used a pressure technique, placing his hand on the forehead of the patient and promising a memory would come. It was a step between hypnosis and free association.
Breuer explained hysteria through hypnoid states, while Freud argued for defense, the active pushing away of intolerable ideas. The disagreement foreshadowed their break.

books.thesis: Psychoanalysis explains slips, dreams and neuroses by one theory of unconscious conflict.
books.summary:
Delivered to a general audience at the University of Vienna during the First World War, these lectures ask how an educated layperson should understand psychoanalysis. Freud sets out to present its method and findings in one account, starting with everyday phenomena.

The lectures run in three parts, on parapraxes, on dreams, and on the general theory of the neuroses. Freud argues that all three show meaningful mental acts produced by repressed wishes in conflict with the censor. He is open that some claims are provisional and he answers objections as he goes. The work remains the best single entry to his thought, though the theory of libido and the dismissal of critics have aged less well.
ideas: Slips of the tongue and forgetting have meanings. Each can be traced to an interfering intention the speaker did not know he held.
Dreams are wish fulfillments. The manifest content is a disguised form of latent dream thoughts, made by dream work.
Dream work uses condensation, displacement and symbolic representation, and it avoids the censor by distorting the wish.
Neurotic symptoms are compromise formations that express a forbidden wish and the defense against it at once.
Repression and resistance are the basic tools. The analyst meets resistance in the patient's reluctance to bring up painful material.
Transference is the patient's turning of old feelings toward the analyst, and it is both an obstacle and the main means of cure.
Anxiety is treated as the central problem of neurosis, with Freud tying it to libido that has not been discharged.
Freud treats the Oedipus complex as a core part of childhood development, with the child's early desire for one parent and rivalry with the other leaving traces in adult life.
The lectures describe free association as the basic method, in which the patient reports whatever comes to mind without editing, and Freud calls this the fundamental rule.
Freud divides the mind into the conscious, the preconscious and the unconscious, and he argues that a censor guards the border between the last two.

books.thesis: The God of Job is not wholly good. Humanity's moral growth forces him to change.
books.summary:
Jung reads the Book of Job as a psychological drama. He asks why a just God would let Job suffer on a wager, and what this tells us about the image of God in the Western mind and the unconscious from which it comes.

Jung argues that Yahweh is shown as unconscious of his own dark side, and that Job, by holding to his integrity, becomes morally more conscious than his maker. God then answers by becoming man in Christ, and later by the Assumption of Mary in the 1950 dogma. Theologians and Jungians have both objected. Jung treats images of God as psychic facts and not metaphysical claims, which he says is the limit of his argument.
ideas: Jung reads God in the Old Testament as a mixture of opposites, with goodness and unreflective violence together, and unaware of his own contradictions.
Job is wronged and does not give up his moral standing, which makes him more conscious than Yahweh and calls for a divine response.
The Incarnation is God's answer to Job, a way for God to share human suffering and to atone for what he did.
Jung links the figure of Sophia, divine wisdom, to the feminine element that was long suppressed in the Christian God image.
Revelation shows the unresolved shadow of God, with its violent apocalypse, which Jung sees as the return of the dark side.
The 1950 dogma of the Assumption is seen as an advance in the symbol of the Trinity toward a fuller divine image.
Jung insists he writes of psychic reality, because archetypal images of God exist in the psyche whatever their ultimate source.
Jung says Job's faith in an advocate in heaven shows he knows Yahweh is divided against himself, and that this knowledge puts Job morally ahead of God.
The wager with Satan is read as a sign of Yahweh's suspicion and moral weakness, since he lets a faithful servant suffer on a whim.
Jung calls the book of Ezekiel and the title Son of Man a sign that God is turning toward humanity, since the prophet is addressed as a human being.

books.thesis: Mother, rebirth, spirit and trickster are inherited patterns. They shape dreams and myth.
books.summary:
This small volume collects four essays in which Jung asks how the archetypes of the collective unconscious show up in myth, religion and the lives of individuals. He wants to show that universal forms recur in widely different cultures.

Jung treats each archetype as an inherited tendency to form images, filled with different content in each setting. He traces the mother archetype and its positive and terrible aspects, rebirth in its several types, the spirit in fairy tales, and the trickster in Native American myth. Critics say his method of amplification by comparison is selective and hard to test, and that the idea of inherited images lacks biological support.
ideas: An archetype is a form without fixed content, a tendency in the unconscious to produce images that vary with culture and person.
The mother archetype has loving and devouring sides, and appears in figures from the Great Mother goddess to the witch.
Jung distinguishes the personal mother from the archetype, so that a person's feelings can be attached to a larger image than the real parent.
Rebirth takes forms such as transmigration, resurrection and transformation, and is tied to the process of individuation.
In fairy tales the spirit appears as an old wise man who gives counsel when the hero is in need, representing a moment of insight.
The trickster, in Winnebago myth, is an early undeveloped figure who is both creator and fool, and a shadow of the collective.
The trickster's gradual change into a more civilized figure is read as a record of growing consciousness.
The collective unconscious is a layer of the psyche shared by all people, in contrast with the personal unconscious, which holds forgotten and repressed individual material.
Jung argues that archetypes are known only through their images, so we infer them from dreams, myths and fairy tales and cannot observe them directly.
The trickster appears in later figures such as the medieval carnival fool and the alchemical Mercurius, and Jung reads these as echoes of the same early pattern.

books.thesis: Meaningful coincidences may be real. Jung calls them an acausal connecting principle.
books.summary:
Jung takes on the question of events that coincide in time with a shared meaning but have no causal link, such as a dream matched by an outer event. He asks whether such coincidences are chance or point to a principle beyond cause and effect.

He proposes synchronicity, an acausal principle linking inner psychic states with outer events through meaning, usually when an archetype is activated. He draws on his clinical cases, the I Ching, astrology and J. B. Rhine's ESP experiments, and discussed the ideas with the physicist Wolfgang Pauli. Most scientists reject it, since the statistical evidence is weak and selective perception can account for the cases he offers.
ideas: Synchronicity means the occurrence of two or more events that coincide in time and are linked by meaning without a causal connection.
The standard example is a patient's dream of a golden scarab, while a scarab beetle tapped at the window during her session.
Jung proposes that synchronicities happen when an archetype is constellated, usually at moments of emotional intensity or transition.
He argues that causality is a statistical truth and not an absolute law, which leaves room for acausal events.
The I Ching and astrology are treated as methods that rely on the meaningful moment, and he ran an astrological marriage experiment.
Rhine's card-guessing results are cited as evidence that psyche can work independently of space and time.
Space, time and causality are joined by a fourth principle, which he suggests could be added to the physicists' framework.
Jung says the scarab case worked because the patient was stuck in an overly rational outlook, and the coincidence helped break it open.
He gives the term acausal connecting principle for meaning that links inner state and outer event, and he separates it from a cause that works across a distance.
The astrological marriage experiment compared the charts of many married couples and found, in Jung's reading, results that depended on the expectations of those running it.

books.thesis: Jung's inner visions were the raw material of his psychology. He staged them as a sacred book.
books.summary:
The Red Book is the record of the self-experiment Jung began in 1913, when he allowed fantasies and figures to appear in waking imagination after his break with Freud. The question it takes on is what lies behind the surface of the mind and how one can meet it without being overwhelmed.

Written in calligraphy and illustrated with paintings, the text follows Jung in dialogue with figures such as Elijah, Salome and Philemon, and describes a descent into the underworld and a search for his soul. He later said it held the source of all his work. It was published only in 2009. Readers disagree about whether it is a mystical text, a case record or a psychological experiment, and its style is deliberately strange.
ideas: Jung began deliberately entering fantasies in late 1913, which he called active imagination, and recorded them in the Black Books before the Red Book.
He meets inner figures such as Elijah, Salome and Philemon, and treats them as autonomous beings that speak back to him.
The book begins with the spirit of the depths and the spirit of this time, two conflicting claims on his soul.
Recovering the soul requires a journey downward, away from rational control, and the book treats this as a necessary loss of ordinary certainty.
Jung gives the images a lengthy commentary, which shows how concepts like the shadow, the anima and the self began as personal experiences.
The book depicts a mandala-like painting near the end, which he came to see as a map of psychic wholeness.
Jung held that he spent the rest of his life working out in scientific form what he had first seen in these visions.
The book is written in the style of a medieval illuminated manuscript, with calligraphic script and large painted images, which makes it as much a work of art as a record.
Jung describes a period in which he feared he was losing his mind, and he chose to follow the images instead of resisting them.
The book was kept private during Jung's life and published only in 2009 by the Philemon Foundation and his heirs, with Sonu Shamdasani as editor.

books.thesis: Neurosis comes from basic anxiety. People cope by moving toward, against or away from others.
books.summary:
Horney asks what drives neurotic conflict and why people hold contradictory needs that tear at their lives. She wants a theory that rests less on instinct and more on the person's relations with others, and on culture.

She argues that a child who feels isolated and helpless develops basic anxiety and adopts one of three strategies, moving toward people, against them or away from them. In a healthy person they can be balanced, but the neurotic is rigid and divided, and tries to solve the conflict through an idealized image of the self. Her view is clinical and drawn from her patients. It has been criticized for lacking empirical testing, though the three trends influenced later personality work.
ideas: Basic anxiety is the child's feeling of being isolated and helpless in a potentially hostile world.
The compliant type moves toward people. It needs affection and approval, and fears conflict and self-assertion.
The aggressive type moves against people. It needs to win, to control and to be admired, and sees others as threats.
The detached type moves away from people. It values self-sufficiency, privacy and freedom from obligation.
In neurosis the three trends become compulsive and cannot be balanced, so the person feels torn between them.
The neurotic builds an idealized self-image to escape the conflicts, and the gap between it and the real self creates self-hatred.
Cure means giving up the idealized image and accepting the real self, which Horney connects with a person's capacity for wholeheartedness.
Horney names the tyranny of the should, a set of rigid inner demands that the neurotic person tries to meet in order to match the idealized self.
She describes the search for glory as a drive toward absolute perfection, mastery and recognition that grows out of the need to escape inner conflict.
Resignation is the stance of a person who tries to settle conflict by giving up on striving, and Horney sees it as a way of withdrawing from life.

books.thesis: Social exchanges often hide scripts. People play games with ulterior motives and repeat them.
books.summary:
Berne's 1964 bestseller asks what actually goes on when people interact, and why the same painful patterns repeat in relationships, families and work. He wants a plain language that laypeople could use to understand it.

Drawing on transactional analysis, Berne divides the personality into Parent, Adult and Child ego states and analyzes the transactions between them. Games are repeating sequences with a hidden payoff, played out with set roles, and are distinct from honest intimacy. The catalogue of named games is vivid and readable. Critics regard the framework as more descriptive than rigorously tested, and its popular uptake went well beyond Berne's clinical aims.
ideas: Each person has ego states, Parent, Adult and Child, and communication works well when the states respond as expected.
A transaction is a unit of social exchange, and a crossed transaction produces conflict or breaks off communication.
A game is a series of complementary transactions with an ulterior motive, ending in a predictable payoff.
Games have named roles in the drama triangle of Persecutor, Rescuer and Victim, and players switch among them.
Examples include Why Don't You, Yes But, Now I've Got You, You Son of a Bitch, and Kick Me, each with a set pattern.
Berne separates games from rituals, pastimes and activities, and from intimacy, which is a candid game-free relationship.
Escape requires awareness, spontaneity and the capacity for intimacy, since these let a person drop the script.
Berne uses the term strokes for units of recognition, and he argues that people crave them so strongly that they will accept negative ones over none.
Games are classed by degree: a first degree game is socially acceptable, a second degree game is one the player would hide, and a third degree game ends in serious harm.
Berne defines a script as an unconscious life plan formed in childhood, and the later work on scripts grew out of the study of games.

books.thesis: Freedom and dignity are myths that block social design. Behavior is shaped by consequences.
books.summary:
Skinner asks why humanity, facing problems like war, overpopulation and pollution, still resists applying a science of behavior. His answer is that the ideas of autonomous man, freedom and dignity stand in the way of such a science.

He argues that behavior is controlled by its environment and its reinforcement history, not by inner choice. Because control is unavoidable, he says, we should design cultures deliberately so that useful behavior is reinforced. Critics, including Chomsky, objected that this ignores the mind, invites authoritarian control, and treats rhetoric about freedom as merely a fiction. Skinner holds that the real danger is control that goes unexamined.
ideas: Autonomous man, the inner agent who originates actions, is a pre-scientific explanation that survives in our talk of freedom and merit.
Behavior is shaped by operant conditioning, in which actions followed by reinforcement become more likely.
Punishment, which most societies rely on, is a poor way to control behavior, because it produces avoidance and resentment.
The literature of freedom mostly fights aversive control, and Skinner says that is worth doing but wrongly assumes freedom is a general goal.
Dignity and credit are given when we cannot see the causes of an act, and shrink as the causes come into view.
Control cannot be removed, only changed, so the question is who designs it and with what ends in view.
A culture survives when its practices help the group, so designing practices for survival is the aim of a technology of behavior.
Skinner argues that the idea of autonomous man leads us to praise and blame and to ignore the environment that actually produces behavior.
He sees the use of positive reinforcement as less harmful than punishment, and he says the best control is one the controlled hardly notice because it feels like choice.
Skinner says that what is called a feeling or state of mind should be explained by the history of reinforcement, and that mentalistic terms give the appearance of an explanation.

books.thesis: Psychedelics may treat mental illness and deepen ordinary consciousness. Pollan found both plausible.
books.summary:
Pollan takes up the revival of research on psychedelics after decades of prohibition. He asks what these substances do to the mind, whether they can help in depression, addiction and the fear of death, and what they might tell us about consciousness.

He combines history, interviews with researchers and underground guides, and his own journeys with psilocybin, LSD and 5-MeO-DMT. The central scientific idea is that psychedelics quiet the default mode network, which loosens the ego and may let people see their thinking afresh. Pollan is cautious about the evidence, which came from small trials, and acknowledges that personal experience is not proof.
ideas: Psychedelic research in the 1950s and 60s was promising, and then shut down amid the backlash against the counterculture and its political fallout.
Modern trials at Johns Hopkins and NYU found that guided psilocybin sessions eased anxiety in patients facing terminal illness.
Robin Carhart-Harris proposes that psychedelics reduce activity in the default mode network, which is tied to the sense of self.
A mystical experience, with a sense of unity and meaning, seems to predict lasting benefit, and the setting and set shape what happens.
Pollan suggests that the ego can be like a reducing valve, a filter that psychedelics temporarily open, following Aldous Huxley.
The book raises the idea that depression and addiction involve rigid patterns of thought, which a psychedelic experience may break.
Pollan reports that his own trips changed his sense of mortality and of his self, though he is wary of overclaiming from them.
Pollan tells how Albert Hofmann first synthesized LSD in 1938 and discovered its effects by accident in 1943.
The book covers the Beckley Foundation and the work of the Imperial College group, and it reports brain imaging that showed reduced blood flow in parts of the default mode network.
Pollan visits guides in underground therapy settings, and he points out that legal and cultural barriers keep these treatments outside of regular medicine.

books.thesis: Craving drives habits from sugar to smartphones. Curiosity about the feeling can loosen its grip.
books.summary:
Brewer, a psychiatrist and addiction researcher, asks why people stay caught in habits they know are harmful, and why willpower so often fails. He seeks a view of addiction that covers smoking, eating, worry and screens in one account.

He argues that habits run on a reward loop of trigger, behavior and reward, and that craving is its engine. Mindfulness works, he says, by making the actual reward of the behavior visible and by replacing the urge with curiosity. His evidence comes from his lab's trials on smoking and eating, which are promising but modest in size. The book is aimed at a general reader and draws on Buddhist ideas, which he treats as practical.
ideas: Habit formation follows a loop of trigger, behavior and reward, and the brain learns by reward-based learning.
Craving is the sense of wanting that makes the loop run, and it arises from the brain's pursuit of a reward, with dopamine involved.
Willpower is a weak tool, because the prefrontal cortex that supports it goes offline under stress, exactly when cravings hit hardest.
Mindfulness lets a person notice what the behavior actually feels like, and the real reward often disappoints.
Brewer teaches the acronym RAIN, which stands for recognize, allow, investigate and note, as a way of handling urges.
Curiosity about a craving feels better than the craving and works as a replacement, so it can be used in place of suppression.
The same loop applies to thinking habits, and Brewer discusses craving for approval and the self-image as drivers of unhappiness.
Brewer links craving to the idea of a dopamine-driven positive reinforcement loop first seen in animals, which he says also helps explain smoking and overeating.
He describes a clinical trial in which mindfulness training for smoking cessation outperformed a standard program, and he uses this as evidence for the method.
The book discusses the concept of the self as a habit, with the mind forming a story about who we are that is also rewarded by approval and then craved.

books.thesis: Pleasure and pain share one balance. Modern abundance tips us into compulsion and pain.
books.summary:
Lembke, a psychiatrist who runs an addiction clinic, asks why people in an age of abundance feel more anxious and depressed, and why compulsive use of drugs, phones, food and gambling has spread so widely.

She argues that the brain processes pleasure and pain on the same balance, like a seesaw, so that heavy pleasure is followed by a pain that pulls users back. Her remedy includes a period of abstinence to reset the balance, and a deliberate use of discomfort. She builds the account from patient stories. Some neuroscientists say the pleasure-pain seesaw is a simplification of dopamine's role, which is tied to wanting more than to pleasure.
ideas: The brain balances pleasure and pain like a seesaw, and each push toward pleasure is met by an opposite push toward pain.
Repeated use leads to neuroadaptation, so the baseline falls and the person needs more of the substance to feel normal.
Dopamine signals reward and motivation, and modern products deliver it in high doses with little effort.
A month of abstinence from the problem substance or behavior can let the seesaw level out and restore sensitivity to small pleasures.
Lembke advises self-binding, such as physical, time and category limits, to make compulsive use harder.
Deliberate hardship, such as cold showers or exercise, can set off a balancing pleasure response without the cost of a drug.
Radical honesty about one's behavior, shared with others, helps break the shame and the lies that sustain addiction.
Lembke names the case of patients who use a drug or habit to escape pain, and she argues that this makes the pain worse once the effect fades.
The book uses the term pleasure-pain balance and illustrates it with patients, including some she treats for compulsive overuse of media, sex and gambling.
Lembke warns that recovery often fails through relapse and that patients should plan ahead for triggers, since cues in the environment can revive craving long after use stops.

books.t: Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking
books.thesis: Good thinking uses tools. Thought experiments are devices that show what we cannot see.
books.summary:
Dennett offers a toolkit for thinking about hard topics such as evolution, meaning, consciousness and free will. He asks what makes a thought experiment useful and how to avoid being misled by intuitions that feel compelling but may be wrong.

The book presents around seventy tools, which he calls intuition pumps, with some general rules of thumb for criticism. He applies them to defend his own positions, including a naturalist view of evolution as a process that builds competence without comprehension, and a view of consciousness as no inner theater. Critics argue some pumps are rigged to produce his conclusions, and he concedes that an intuition pump is only as good as its fit with the facts.
ideas: An intuition pump is a thought experiment designed to pump intuitions, and it should be tested by varying its details.
Rapoport's rules ask a critic to restate the target's position so well that the target would say thanks, before offering any criticism.
Sturgeon's law holds that ninety percent of everything is crud, so judge a field by its best work, not its worst.
Evolution shows competence without comprehension, since natural selection builds clever designs without understanding anything.
The intentional stance predicts behavior by treating a system as a rational agent with beliefs and desires.
Dennett criticizes the Cartesian theater, the picture of a place in the brain where consciousness comes together for an inner viewer.
Searle's Chinese Room is called a misleading pump, and he questions its claim that running a program could not yield understanding.
Dennett lists a set of tools for criticizing, including how to compose a successful critical commentary and the use of reductio ad absurdum.
The book includes the term deepity, a statement that seems profound because it is true on one reading and trivial on another, though false or empty on the one that sounds deep.
Dennett proposes the idea of the zombie as a pump, and he argues that a being that acts exactly like a conscious person cannot be coherently said to lack consciousness.

books.thesis: Having too little of anything narrows the mind. That narrowing explains many poor choices.
books.summary:
Why do people who are short of money, time or food so often make decisions that deepen their shortage? Mullainathan, an economist, and Shafir, a psychologist, argue that the usual answers about character or culture miss the point.

They propose that scarcity captures attention and leaves less mental capacity for everything else. The focus helps with the pressing problem, but it causes tunneling, neglect of the future and weaker self-control. Experiments with shoppers, sugarcane farmers and others support the claim. A caveat is that some of the lab findings on scarcity and cognition have been harder to replicate, and the book's policy suggestions are modest rather than proven.
ideas: Scarcity captures the mind. When we lack something, our attention goes to it automatically, which the authors call the scarcity mindset.
Focus brings a benefit, since people under scarcity can be good at managing the pressing need, such as stretching a tight budget.
Tunneling is the cost of that focus. Things outside the urgent problem get neglected, including long-term plans and other tasks.
Scarcity creates a bandwidth tax. Worry about the shortage uses up mental capacity, which lowers measured fluid intelligence and self-control.
In a study of Indian sugarcane farmers, the same people scored lower on cognitive tests before harvest, when money was tight, than after it.
Poverty is explained by context and not by weak character. The authors argue that anyone placed in scarcity would show the same lapses.
Slack is valuable. Building in buffers, as with fewer deadlines or simple automatic defaults, helps people who have little spare capacity.
The authors describe the idea of juggling, where those with little must constantly trade off options, and they say this makes small mistakes more costly.
A study of shoppers at a mall found that thinking about a large car repair bill reduced reasoning scores in low income participants but not in the better off.
Payday loans and late fees are given as examples of how scarcity creates traps, where a short term fix leaves a person with even less to work with later.

books.thesis: People should bear the costs of their own decisions. Without that, systems drift toward fragility.
books.summary:
What keeps decision makers honest and systems robust? Taleb takes on the problem of advisers, experts and institutions who gain from being right but pay nothing when they are wrong.

His argument is that symmetry of risk is both an ethical rule and a practical filter. People with exposure to downside decide better, and those without it should be doubted. He also argues that small committed minorities can set the rules for a majority, and that survival of the whole matters more than the average outcome. The book is polemical and combative, and critics note that its sweeping claims and personal attacks are not always supported by evidence.
ideas: Skin in the game means having something to lose. Taleb treats it as a requirement for fairness and for reliable judgment.
The silver rule is a negative form of reciprocity. Do not do to others what you would not want done to you, which Taleb prefers to positive moral advice.
The intellectual yet idiot is a credentialed person who shapes policy and opinion without bearing the consequences of errors.
Ergodicity matters. The outcome for a group on average can differ from the outcome for one person who can be wiped out, so avoiding ruin comes before maximizing gain.
The minority rule says that an intransigent minority can impose its preferences on a flexible majority, using examples such as halal and kosher food labeling.
Antifragile systems depend on the failures of their parts. Entrepreneurs who fail teach the system, which only works if they actually pay for failure.
Taleb argues that soldiers, artisans and risk takers hold knowledge that pundits who bear no cost for being wrong tend to lack.
Taleb uses the Lindy effect, which says that the longer a non-perishable thing has lasted, the longer it is likely to last, to defend old ideas and traditions.
He criticizes the bureaucrat, who has no stake in outcomes, and contrasts the person who must live with the results of their choices.
Taleb argues that the payoff from risk should be tied to responsibility, and he cites the Code of Hammurabi, in which a builder was punished if a house fell and killed its owner.

books.thesis: Our mistakes in judgment are systematic, not random. That makes them predictable and sometimes usable.
books.summary:
Classical economics assumes that people weigh options rationally. Ariely asks what happens when behavior is tested directly, and why people err in the same direction again and again.

Through experiments, many run with students, he shows that choices depend heavily on relative comparisons, on the word free, on arousal and on social versus market norms. His conclusion is that irrationality has patterns, and understanding them can improve design and policy. A caveat is that several well-known results, including some on honesty and priming in his work, have faced replication problems, and Ariely himself has been involved in a data-integrity controversy, so the specific findings deserve care.
ideas: Relativity shapes choice. People judge options by comparison, so a decoy option that nobody picks can shift which of the other two they choose.
Free is a powerful emotional trigger. Zero price makes people take a worse deal, because it removes the sense of loss.
Social norms and market norms follow different rules. Paying a small amount for a favor can ruin willingness to help, while a gift keeps it.
Arousal changes judgment. In experiments with young men, sexual excitement shifted their stated preferences far beyond what they predicted for themselves while calm.
Procrastination and self-control fail in predictable ways, and commitment devices, which restrict future choices, can help.
Ownership raises value. People overvalue what they already have, and expectations shape experience, as in the beer experiment where a hidden ingredient changed ratings once it was named.
The dishonesty section argues that most people cheat a little but not a lot, and that reminders of morality reduce it.
Ariely describes the effect of anchoring, where an arbitrary number such as the last digits of a Social Security number can sway what people will pay.
The book tells of the Economist subscription case, where adding a decoy offer changed how many readers chose the print and web bundle.
Ariely describes coherent arbitrariness, in which an early arbitrary price shapes later choices, so that people stay consistent with the anchor without knowing it.

books.thesis: Boredom is a signal that we want to engage but cannot. It is neither laziness nor mere lack of stimulation.
books.summary:
Why does boredom feel so unpleasant, and what is it for? Danckert and Eastwood, both psychologists who study the topic, set out to treat boredom as a serious psychological state and not a trivial one.

They argue that boredom is the mind's way of telling us that our current activity does not meet our desire to be engaged, and that it pushes us to seek meaning. Chronic or poorly managed boredom is linked with risky behavior, poor mental health and a pull toward distraction. The book is a readable overview of a small research field, and some of its links between boredom and later outcomes are correlational, so causes remain open.
ideas: Boredom is the state of wanting to be engaged but being unable to. The authors define it by this mismatch, not by a lack of things to do.
Boredom works as a signal, like hunger or pain, that tells us our current situation is not satisfying a need to engage.
Three ingredients combine. A person is unable to focus, wants to do something, and finds nothing to satisfy that wish.
Boredom proneness differs between people. Those who score high are more likely to report depression, anxiety, risk taking and problems with attention.
Reaching for a phone or other quick stimulation relieves boredom briefly but does not fix the underlying lack of meaning.
The authors link boredom to agency. People who feel they have little control over what they do tend to feel bored more often, which also links to boredom in school and work.
Handled well, boredom can motivate people to find new goals and creative activity, so the authors advise using it as information and not escaping it.
The authors separate simple boredom from existential boredom, which is a deeper sense of meaninglessness that cannot be fixed by adding more activity.
They cite a study in which people chose to give themselves mild electric shocks rather than sit alone with their thoughts for a few minutes.
The book describes how boredom can be a sign that a person has lost a sense of purpose, and it argues that the cure lies in finding meaning, not in more entertainment.

books.thesis: Phone-based childhood has replaced play-based childhood. That shift is behind the rise in teen mental illness.
books.summary:
Why did rates of anxiety, depression and self-harm among adolescents climb sharply in the early 2010s in many wealthy countries? Haidt, a social psychologist, takes up the question for a general audience.

His argument is that children lost free play and independence in the real world while gaining smartphones and social media around 2010 to 2015, producing what he calls a great rewiring of childhood. He proposes four norms, including no smartphones before high school and no social media before 16. Critics, including some researchers in the field, say the evidence for causation is weaker than the book suggests, and that the data are mixed and the effect sizes small.
ideas: The great rewiring is Haidt's name for the shift from a play-based childhood to a phone-based one, which he dates to roughly 2010 to 2015.
Overprotection in the real world and underprotection online is the pattern he describes, with children kept from risk outdoors but exposed to harmful content online.
Four harms are named: social deprivation, sleep deprivation, attention fragmentation and addiction.
Girls are hit hardest by social media through comparison, relational aggression and perfectionism, while boys withdraw into video games and pornography.
Collective action problems explain why parents give in. A child without a phone is excluded when peers have them, so norms must change together.
The four proposed norms are no smartphone before high school, no social media before 16, phone-free schools and far more unsupervised play.
The book names anxious and depressed teenagers as a trend visible across the English-speaking world and parts of Europe, and he treats the timing as evidence for the cause.
Haidt describes four foundational harms of a phone-based childhood and he argues that they affect spiritual life as well, leading to what he calls spiritual degradation.
He defines the gap between the world of the screen and the real world as a loss of embodied experience, which includes play, touch and shared presence.
The book draws on the difference between a discover mode and a defend mode, and argues that children need risky play to move from fear to confidence.

books.thesis: Myth and religion encode how humans handle the unknown. Peterson argues they carry real psychological knowledge.
books.summary:
How do people build meaning, and why have ideologies caused so much atrocity in the twentieth century? Peterson begins from the question of how belief systems can drive people to such actions.

The book argues that myths across cultures share a structure of order, chaos and the hero who mediates between them, and that this structure reflects how the brain meets novelty. It draws on Jung, Piaget, neuroscience, Eliade and others. It is dense, sprawling and unusual in its method, and critics find its claims about universal archetypes and its use of evidence loosely argued. Readers should treat it as a speculative synthesis and not as established science.
ideas: The world is a place of explored territory and unexplored territory. Peterson describes these as order and chaos, often drawn as masculine and feminine in myth.
The hero is the figure who goes into the unknown, confronts chaos and brings back new order, a pattern he finds in stories across many cultures.
Anomalies, meaning events that violate expectations, trigger fear and exploration. Peterson links this to research on orienting responses in the brain.
Myth is a map of behavior, not a map of objects. It tells people how to act in a world that is full of significance.
The adversary is the force in myth that resists the hero. Peterson treats it as a figure of rigid belief or deliberate evil, depending on the story.
Totalitarian ideologies are described as attempts to deny anomaly. Peterson argues that believing one's own system is complete leads people to destroy those who disagree.
He draws on Jung's archetypes, for example the Great Mother and the Wise King, to argue that stories share recurring characters across cultures.
Peterson describes the known as explored territory, the unknown as unexplored territory and the knower as the process that moves between them.
He draws on the Babylonian creation myth, in which Marduk defeats the chaos dragon Tiamat, as an example of the hero confronting the unknown.
Peterson argues that the individual who takes responsibility and tells the truth is the figure that the hero myth sets as the ideal.

books.t: Women Who Run with the Wolves
books.thesis: Women carry an instinctive wild nature that society suppresses. Folk stories can help restore it.
books.summary:
What happens to a woman's creativity, intuition and sense of self when she is taught to be tame and compliant? Estés, a Jungian analyst and cantadora, a storyteller in the Latina tradition, takes up the question through myth and fairy tale.

She retells tales such as Bluebeard, The Ugly Duckling and Vasalisa the Wise, then interprets each as a map of psychic life, with the Wild Woman as an archetype of instinctive knowing. The book is poetic and has been influential and widely loved. Scholars note that its use of sources is loose and that the claim of a universal archetype is a matter of faith more than evidence, so it works best as inspiration and not as research.
ideas: The Wild Woman archetype stands for the instinctive, creative, intuitive self that Estés says is natural to women and often suppressed.
Stories work as medicine. Estés treats fairy tales as living guides that give psychological direction, not as entertainment.
In Bluebeard, the dangerous husband stands for a predatory force inside the psyche, and the heroine's intuition is her protection.
The Ugly Duckling is read as a story of a child who is in the wrong family and must find her own kind and her own nature.
Vasalisa the Wise shows trust in an inner knowing, symbolized by a small doll, that guides a girl through dangerous tasks.
Estés speaks of the la Loba figure, an old woman who gathers bones and sings them into life, as an image of creative restoration.
Reclaiming the instinctive self means setting boundaries, resting, making creative work and leaving relationships and roles that cage a woman.
Estés presents herself as a cantadora, a keeper of stories in the Latino tradition, and she draws on that heritage in retelling the tales.
The Handless Maiden is used to describe a woman whose creative power is given away through a bad bargain and who must regain it through a long journey.
The Red Shoes is read as a tale about a woman who loses touch with her instinctive life and whose compulsive dancing needs to be stopped.

books.t: Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds
books.thesis: Crowds go mad in a group, and they recover their senses one person at a time.
books.summary:
Why do whole societies pour money and belief into obviously foolish schemes? Mackay, a Scottish journalist, set out in 1841 to catalog episodes of collective folly across history.

His chapters cover financial manias such as tulip mania, the Mississippi Scheme and the South Sea Bubble, along with alchemy, witch hunts, prophecies, fashions in thinking and the Crusades. His thesis is that groups can be swept up in shared delusion. The book is anecdotal, the writing is moralizing, and historians have shown that parts of it, notably the tulip story, were exaggerated, so it is better as a source of patterns than as reliable history.
ideas: Men, it has been said, think in herds. Mackay holds that crowds fall into shared delusions and that individuals recover their judgment slowly.
Tulip mania in the Dutch Republic is his example of speculation driven by a belief that prices could only rise, although later historians dispute how severe it was.
The Mississippi Scheme in France, run by John Law, shows how a paper-money system and a promised colonial fortune turned into a bubble and collapse.
The South Sea Bubble in England shows speculation spreading through the public, including the educated, and shows how many companies with no real business were launched.
The book covers alchemy and fortune-telling to show that false authority attracts followers who want hidden knowledge.
Witch hunts and the Crusades serve as examples of moral and religious fervor turning into mass violence.
Mackay also writes about fashions, such as haunted houses and odd tastes in hair and beards, to show that folly appears even in light matters.
Mackay shows in the bubble chapters how early gains draw in new buyers, so that more people join just before the collapse.
The book includes chapters on slow poisoners and on the duel, which show how a fashion or a fear can spread through a society.
Mackay treats the Crusades as a long lasting popular frenzy that drew in whole nations.

books.thesis: Creating means facing the unknown. It takes courage, not only talent.
books.summary:
What does creativity demand of a person, and why does it often feel frightening? May, an existential psychotherapist, takes up the question of what happens when a person brings something new into the world.

He argues that creativity is an encounter between a person and the world, marked by intensity, commitment and risk, and that courage is the virtue required for it. He draws on art, myth and clinical work, with discussions of the daimonic, form and limits, and the role of the unconscious. The book is short and reflective, closer to philosophy than to experimental psychology, so its claims rest on interpretation and example.
ideas: Creativity requires courage, which May defines as moving ahead despite despair and not as the absence of fear.
Creative acts come from an encounter in which a person is absorbed in a task and the world meets them, giving the work its intensity.
Form and limits are essential. May holds that creativity works within constraints, such as the rules of a sonnet, and that limits give shape to freedom.
The daimonic is a drive, such as love or anger, that can take over the whole person. It can create or destroy, and creative people must engage with it.
Creativity operates partly through the unconscious, and breakthroughs often come in moments of insight after effort and rest.
May distinguishes creative work from mere talent or hobby, saying that real creation means entering a risk of losing one's former self.
Conformity is a threat to courage, since those who follow the crowd avoid the commitments that creative work requires.
May separates courage into physical, moral, social and creative kinds, and he says that creative courage is the discovery of new forms and symbols.
The book argues that the creative person must give up some personal certainty and enter a sense of being alone, and he calls this a kind of solitude necessary for work.
May discusses the role of encounter in creation, saying that the artist meets the world and gives it a form.

books.thesis: Self-actualization is not the top of a pyramid. Security and growth are both needed for a full life.
books.summary:
What did Maslow actually mean by self-actualization, and how can we apply it today? Kaufman, a psychologist, revisits Maslow's work and notes how his hierarchy of needs has often been misread as a rigid pyramid.

Kaufman proposes a revised model that he pictures as a sailboat, with security needs forming the hull and growth needs forming the sail, and he adds ten characteristics of a self-actualizing person. He draws on current research in personality and well-being. Some critics note that the original studies of Maslow's exemplars were small and subjective, and that Kaufman's update leans on his own selection of research.
ideas: The pyramid is a misreading. Maslow himself did not draw it, and Kaufman argues that needs can be pursued at the same time.
The sailboat model has a hull of security needs, which are safety, connection and self-esteem, and a sail of growth needs, which are exploration, love and purpose.
Security and growth work together. A person needs a sound hull to sail, and the sail is what takes them somewhere.
Kaufman lists characteristics of self-actualization, including a love of truth, openness to experience, a sense of purpose and creative engagement with life.
Transcendence is the final aim in Maslow's later thinking, which Kaufman describes as connecting to something larger than oneself.
Trauma and hardship can sit alongside growth, and Kaufman rejects the idea that only comfortable conditions allow self-actualization.
Stress and adversity can encourage posttraumatic growth, though Kaufman says this is not guaranteed and depends on support.
Kaufman describes the ten characteristics of self-actualization as overlapping and ongoing, and he says people move among them across a life instead of finishing them in order.
The book describes the idea of being a person who is whole by integrating different parts of oneself, as against growing by only one measure.
Kaufman notes that Maslow himself revised his model late in life and added a stage of transcendence beyond self-actualization.

books.thesis: Conflict eases when we state needs and feelings instead of judgments. Empathic listening then does the rest.
books.summary:
Why do conversations so often turn into blame, defensiveness and fights? Rosenberg, a clinical psychologist and mediator who worked in many conflict zones, takes up the question of how we can speak honestly without attacking.

He teaches a four-part process of observations, feelings, needs and requests, together with empathic listening to others. The idea is that behind every judgment lies an unmet need, and naming it opens connection. The method is practical and widely taught. Critics find it can sound formulaic or stilted in daily conversation, and it does not guarantee that the other person will cooperate.
ideas: The process has four parts: observe without evaluating, state a feeling, identify the need behind it and make a clear request.
Observations should be separated from evaluations. Saying what happened is different from calling someone lazy or rude.
Feelings differ from thoughts. Rosenberg asks people to name an emotion and not a judgment in disguise, such as feeling ignored.
Needs are universal, for example for respect, safety or autonomy, and understanding them avoids a focus on strategies.
Requests should be specific and doable, and they should not be demands. If a person cannot say no, it is a demand.
Empathy means listening for the feelings and needs of others without advice or reassurance, and this can calm anger.
Rosenberg calls evaluative, moralizing language life-alienating communication, and he calls his preferred style giraffe language for its large heart.
Rosenberg warns against the use of demands disguised as requests, and he suggests that the listener should hear a request as an offer from the heart.
He discusses the importance of expressing appreciation, by saying what the person did, the need it met and the feeling it brought.
The book describes how to use the protective use of force, which differs from punitive force because it aims to prevent harm and not to make the other person suffer.

books.thesis: Codependents lose themselves in controlling and rescuing others. Recovery means returning attention to oneself.
books.summary:
What happens to a person who organizes life around someone else's problems, such as an addicted partner or a troubled family? Beattie, writing from her own recovery in the 1980s, takes up that pattern and gives it a name.

She describes codependency as a set of habits, including caretaking, controlling, denial and low self-worth, and offers steps for detachment, setting boundaries and self-care, drawing on twelve-step ideas. The book was a bestseller and shaped popular language about relationships. Critics note that codependency is not a formal diagnosis, that the definition is broad enough to fit almost anyone, and that the book rests on personal experience more than research.
ideas: Codependency is defined as letting another person's behavior affect you and being obsessed with controlling that behavior.
Caretaking and rescuing are central habits. Codependents take on responsibility for others' feelings and problems, which can keep those problems going.
Denial and low self-worth are the roots, and codependents often do not recognize how much the other person's problem is shaping their life.
Detachment means separating yourself from the other person's problems with love, without hostility and without giving up care.
Boundaries are limits that say what you will and will not accept, and they require ending the pattern of rescuing.
Taking care of yourself is a practical step that includes naming your own feelings, needs and wants.
Recovery draws on twelve-step ideas, including accepting what you cannot control and finding support in groups such as Al-Anon.
Beattie argues that a person is not responsible for the choices of others and that letting go means allowing others to face the results.
She lists the common traits of codependents, including caretaking, low self-worth, repression of feelings and an urge to control.
The book encourages readers to say no without guilt and to ask for what they need directly.

books.thesis: Depression comes from distorted thinking. Changing thoughts changes mood.
books.summary:
Can depression be treated without relying only on drugs or long analysis? Burns, a psychiatrist who trained with Aaron Beck, presents cognitive therapy to a general audience as a self-help method.

He lists ten cognitive distortions, such as all-or-nothing thinking and mind reading, and teaches readers to record negative thoughts and replace them with more realistic ones, alongside activity scheduling. Controlled studies of the book as bibliotherapy have shown benefits for mild to moderate depression. Caveats are that it can seem to oversimplify, it is less suited to severe depression without professional care, and later cognitive therapy has added more than the book covers.
ideas: Cognitive therapy holds that feelings follow thoughts. A person who thinks in negative patterns feels depressed, and changing the pattern changes the mood.
The book lists ten distortions, including all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralization, mental filter, mind reading, fortune telling, emotional reasoning and should statements.
The triple-column technique has readers write the automatic thought, name the distortion and write a rational response.
Daily mood logs and activity schedules help people see patterns and notice pleasure and mastery in small tasks.
Perfectionism is treated as a source of misery, because it sets standards that cannot be met.
Burns addresses guilt, anger and low self-esteem as well as depression, with techniques for each.
The book includes a chapter on antidepressant medication, and Burns advises discussing severe symptoms with a professional.
Burns discusses the role of the 'no-lose' approach to procrastination, in which a person plans small steps and records the results.
He includes a self-test for depression so that readers can track the level of their mood from week to week.
Burns describes the technique of the 'externalization of voices', where a person argues back to the negative thought as if it were another speaker.

books.t: Complex PTSD: From Surviving to Thriving
books.thesis: Childhood abuse and neglect can leave lasting emotional wounds. Recovery is possible and takes particular tools.
books.summary:
What is different about the trauma left by chronic childhood abuse or neglect compared with a single frightening event? Walker, a psychotherapist who has worked with survivors and has his own history, writes a guide for people living with the effects.

He describes complex PTSD through four responses to threat, fight, flight, freeze and fawn, and shows how each shapes adult personality. He describes emotional flashbacks and the inner critic, then offers steps such as grieving, self-compassion and building safe relationships. The book is practical and widely read. It is based on clinical experience and not on controlled research, and C-PTSD as a diagnosis was added to the ICD-11 but not to the DSM-5.
ideas: Complex PTSD arises from prolonged relational trauma in childhood, and it differs from PTSD from a single event.
The four Fs are fight, flight, freeze and fawn. Each is a survival style that persists into adult life and relationships.
Emotional flashbacks are sudden regressions into the feelings of childhood, such as fear, shame or despair, without a visual memory.
The inner critic is the internalized voice of an abusive parent, and Walker describes steps for shrinking it.
Toxic shame is a core wound, a deep sense of being defective that came from abandonment and that drives many symptoms.
Recovery involves grieving what was lost, since crying and anger release old pain that was never allowed expression.
Healing happens in relationships, and Walker stresses that safe people and a good therapist are central to recovery.
Walker proposes that Complex PTSD be seen as a more accurate name than the diagnoses often given, as symptoms can look like depression, anxiety or personality disorders.
He describes the four Fs as adaptive types, such as the fight type who tends toward narcissism and the flight type who tends toward obsessive work.
Walker teaches the 13 steps for managing flashbacks, which begin with saying 'I am having a flashback' and reminding oneself that the danger is past.

books.thesis: Every part of us has a positive intent. Healing comes from leading with a calm Self instead of fighting parts.
books.summary:
Why do we feel pulled in different directions, and why do inner critics, addictions and anxieties seem so hard to dislodge? Schwartz, the founder of Internal Family Systems (IFS), offers the model to a general reader.

He holds that the mind is naturally multiple, made of parts that take on roles, some of them protective and some carrying pain. At the center is the Self, which has qualities such as curiosity and compassion, and therapy means helping the Self relate to the parts. IFS has growing clinical use but a limited research base, and claims that the Self is an inborn core go beyond what can be tested.
ideas: The mind is made of parts, which Schwartz treats as normal subpersonalities and not as a sign of disorder.
There are no bad parts. Even destructive behaviors come from parts trying to protect the person, though they use extreme methods.
Parts fall into roles: managers, who try to prevent pain, firefighters, who react when pain breaks through, and exiles, who carry the hurt of earlier events.
The Self is the core of a person, marked by the eight Cs, which include curiosity, calm, compassion and clarity.
Unburdening is the process by which a part releases the beliefs and emotions it took on from past hurt.
Burdens are extreme beliefs and feelings that parts carry, picked up in childhood or from the culture, and they are not the parts' true nature.
Schwartz applies the model to families and society, arguing that systems of parts exist in groups as well as in individuals.
Schwartz states that the Self cannot be damaged, though parts may block it, and he calls this the basis for healing without a need for the therapist to supply it.
The book describes the 'legacy burdens' that pass down through family lines and culture, such as beliefs about race, gender and worth.
Schwartz explains that a person can ask a part to step back and, with its trust, allow Self energy to reach the exile.

books.thesis: Therapy stories show how people avoid, defend and slowly face themselves.
books.summary:
What do people really bring to a therapist's room, and what happens as they change? Grosz, a psychoanalyst with decades of practice, answers with short case stories in place of a theory.

Each chapter follows a patient, with identifying details changed, and draws a lesson about loss, lying, change, love or the way we tell stories about ourselves. The recurring idea is that behavior is often an attempt to avoid pain that we do not know we feel. The book is humane and well written. As a collection of anecdotes from one clinician, it offers insight but not evidence, and the narrator naturally shapes the story to fit the lesson.
ideas: Behavior often serves to avoid a feeling. Patients repeat patterns that protect them from loss or fear, even when those patterns cause harm.
Lying to others and to ourselves is treated as a way to manage unbearable truths, and Grosz shows how honesty can slowly emerge in therapy.
Change is hard because even unwanted situations are familiar, and giving them up feels like another loss.
Praise can backfire with children, since empty compliments can make them avoid challenges for fear of not living up to them.
Grief takes forms that are not obvious, and an unexpressed loss can shape behavior for years.
The stories we tell about our past are edited, and therapy examines which parts we leave out.
Listening carefully to another person, without hurrying to fix, is itself a form of help.
Grosz describes a patient who could not hold on to money and shows how the habit expressed an unspoken belief about what she deserved.
The book gives the example of a child's refusal to speak of a lost parent and shows how silence can be a form of protection.
Grosz suggests that we often confuse what we want with what we think we should want, and therapy can help separate the two.

books.thesis: Attention is being eroded by many forces at once. Fixing it needs social change as well as personal discipline.
books.summary:
Why does it feel harder to concentrate than it used to? Hari, a journalist, sets out to understand the loss of focus across modern life and interviews researchers across many fields.

He names twelve causes, including technology designed to hold attention, constant switching, poor sleep, junk food, pollution, stress and the decline of mind-wandering and play. His claim is that the problem is partly structural, so individual willpower is not enough. The book is lively and wide ranging. Critics say it presents some contested findings, such as links to specific additives and the scale of tech's effect, with more confidence than the evidence allows.
ideas: Hari identifies twelve factors, including the speed-up of life, multitasking, sleep loss, poor diet, air pollution and children's lost freedom to play.
Technology companies design products to capture attention, using techniques such as variable rewards and endless feeds.
Switch-costing is the cost of moving between tasks. Hari argues that multitasking is mostly rapid task switching and leaves people worse at both tasks.
Mind-wandering is a needed state, and constant stimulation robs people of time for it and for deep thought.
Sleep loss harms attention, and he points to long-term studies showing that most people need more rest than they get.
Rising rates of an ADHD diagnosis are discussed, with Hari asking how much comes from the environment and not only from the individual.
Solutions include collective action, such as rules on the attention economy and a shorter working week, as well as personal habits.
Hari describes the work of Gloria Mark, who found that workers took on average about twenty three minutes to return to a task after an interruption.
He discusses the concept of cruel optimism in self help, which tells people to fix their own focus while the systems around them stay the same.
Hari tells of a visit to Tristan Harris and the idea that the design of phones and apps is a form of persuasion at scale.

books.thesis: ADD is a response to early stress and not a fixed defect. Understanding it can open the way to healing.
books.summary:
What is attention deficit disorder, and where does it come from? Maté, a physician who was diagnosed as an adult, examines the condition from his own history and from his years of practice.

He argues that ADD is not purely genetic and is shaped by early childhood environment, especially stress in the parent-child relationship, which affects how the brain develops. He describes ways to live with the traits and recover. This view is contested. Most researchers regard ADHD as strongly heritable, and the book's claim of environmental origin is stronger than the evidence supports, though its emphasis on compassion has been welcome to many readers.
ideas: Maté argues that ADD is a developmental condition shaped by the child's early environment as well as by temperament.
Early stress in the family, often passing from parent to child across generations, can lead the child to tune out as a way of coping.
He describes ADD as a way of coping with emotional pain, which includes a loss of connection with self.
The book rejects blame. Parents of children with ADD are usually stressed themselves, not bad people.
Maté draws on his own history, describing how he lost himself in work and music and neglected his family.
He notes that brain development depends on experience, so the brain can change with new relationships and practices.
Treatment means more than medication. He recommends structure, support, awareness and a compassionate relation to oneself.
Maté states that the inattention of ADD can be seen as a form of dissociation from distress, in which the child learns to tune out.
He says that ADD carries gifts as well as costs, such as creativity and sensitivity, though they are often hidden.
Maté describes the idea of attunement, where a parent's emotional presence in the first years helps set the pattern of the child's attention.

books.thesis: Modern culture produces illness. Many health problems are the cost of adapting to unhealthy conditions.
books.summary:
Why are chronic illness and mental distress so common in rich societies? Maté, writing with his son Daniel, takes up the question and argues that the usual medical focus on individual biology misses the context.

The book claims that trauma, defined as a wound that disconnects us from ourselves, together with social pressures such as inequality, isolation and consumer culture, lies behind much disease. It proposes compassionate inquiry and healing through authenticity. The ideas about the mind-body unity are widely discussed, but some critics say the book overstates the role of trauma in conditions like cancer and autoimmune disease and relies on selected research.
ideas: Maté defines trauma as the wound itself, not the event, so it is what happens inside a person as a result of hardship.
He argues that the mind and body are one system, and that suppressed emotions can contribute to illness such as autoimmune disease.
Normal is not the same as healthy. A culture that rewards overwork and disconnection can make illness a common result.
Two needs compete in a child, attachment and authenticity, and when forced to choose, a child gives up authenticity to keep the bond.
Compassionate inquiry is a method of asking questions that helps a person see how past experience shapes present behavior.
Social conditions such as poverty, racism and isolation affect health, and he argues that medicine should consider them.
Healing means returning to authenticity, through awareness, grief and connection, and not simply symptom control.
Maté describes the cultural myth of the separation of mind and body, and he says that modern medicine is built on it.
He introduces four A's of healing, which are authenticity, agency, anger and acceptance, and links them to the way the body responds to stress.
The book discusses the idea that the term normal is a statistical idea used to hide the fact that many common conditions reflect a sick society.

books.thesis: The mind is a system of computational organs. Natural selection shaped them to solve ancestral problems.
books.summary:
What is the mind, and how does it do what it does? Pinker, a cognitive scientist, tries to explain perception, reasoning, emotion, and social life in one framework.

His thesis combines the computational theory of mind with evolutionary psychology: the brain is a set of modules built by natural selection to solve problems faced by hunter-gatherers. He covers vision, intelligence, emotions, family, art and humor. The scope is impressive and the prose lively. Critics dispute how modular the mind is and say that evolutionary explanations for traits like music and humor are speculative and hard to test.
ideas: The mind is what the brain does, and Pinker describes thinking as a form of information processing, computation.
Natural selection explains the design of the mind, which was shaped to solve problems like finding food, avoiding danger and dealing with kin.
The mind is modular, with specialized systems for such tasks as vision, language and social reasoning, and not one general learning device.
Vision is a showcase. We see in three dimensions through inference, and optical illusions reveal the assumptions the system makes.
Emotions are adaptations that serve goals, such as fear for avoiding danger, and they act as commitments that make threats and promises credible.
The mind is not adapted to modern conditions. The mismatch between the environment of our ancestors and ours explains some of the problems of modern life.
Pinker treats art, music and humor as possible by-products of other adaptations, and he calls music auditory cheesecake.
Pinker discusses mentalese, a proposed language of thought beneath spoken language, as a way to explain how we think without words.
He argues that the mind is a product of reverse engineering, which asks what a trait was designed to do.
The book discusses kin selection and reciprocal altruism to explain family feeling and cooperation, and it treats these as part of the design of human nature.

books.thesis: Reason, science and humanism have improved human life, and the long-run data show it.
books.summary:
Pinker takes on the widespread belief that the modern world is sliding into decline. He asks whether the record of health, wealth, safety and knowledge supports that mood, and why intelligent people keep reading the news as a story of collapse.

He argues that life has improved on most measurable fronts over two centuries, and credits the Enlightenment ideals of reason, science and humanism. Progress is not automatic, he says, but a result of problem solving. Critics say he picks favorable indicators, plays down inequality, climate and catastrophic risks, and treats a trend as a promise.
ideas: The core Enlightenment ideals are reason, science, humanism and progress, and Pinker presents them as the source of modern gains rather than as an outdated creed.
Life expectancy has roughly doubled in developed countries since the 1800s, child mortality has collapsed, and the share of humanity in extreme poverty has fallen sharply.
Progress is not a law of nature. Entropy and the indifference of the universe mean things go wrong by default, so improvement requires knowledge and effort.
News coverage and the availability heuristic skew perception, because bad events are reported and gradual improvements are not, which feeds what Pinker calls progressophobia.
Violence, including war deaths, homicide and cruelty, has declined over the long run, extending the argument of his earlier book The Better Angels of Our Nature.
Existential threats such as nuclear war and climate change are treated as problems to be solved with institutions and technology, not as proof that doom is certain.
He defends science against the charge of scientism, arguing that scientific ways of thinking should inform the humanities and that moral progress depends on evidence.
Pinker invokes the second law of thermodynamics to explain that order is rare and must be created against a constant trend toward disorder.
He argues that the data on happiness, literacy, and leisure also show improvement, and he displays the data as graphs.
Pinker discusses tribal politics and motivated reasoning as threats to reason, and he argues that institutions such as science and open debate help correct them.

books.t: Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents
books.thesis: Parents who stay emotionally immature leave children lonely, and recovery starts with seeing it clearly.
books.summary:
Gibson, a clinical psychologist, takes on the problem of adults who feel unseen or drained by a parent who looked fine from outside. She asks how parents who were fed and housed but emotionally unavailable still shape a child's sense of self and relationships.

She describes four types of emotionally immature parent, namely emotional, driven, passive and rejecting, and shows how children adapt as internalizers or externalizers. The remedy is to stop hoping for change, set limits and build a truer self. The book rests on clinical experience rather than controlled research, and the labels can be applied too widely to ordinary imperfect parents.
ideas: Emotionally immature parents are self-focused, have low tolerance for stress, and are poor at empathy, so the child learns to manage the parent's feelings.
Gibson names four types: emotional parents who are driven by moods, driven parents who push and control, passive parents who avoid, and rejecting parents who withdraw.
Children adapt as internalizers, who take on blame and try to help, or externalizers, who act out and take risks. Both are survival strategies.
Emotional loneliness is the central wound, the sense of being unseen even in a family that looks intact.
Many adult children build a role-self to keep the relationship going and lose touch with their true self, which has to be rebuilt.
A fantasy that the parent will finally change keeps people stuck, and giving it up is part of healing.
Practical steps include observing the parent without taking the bait, limiting contact, setting boundaries and choosing relationships with emotionally mature people.
Gibson describes how emotionally immature parents use role reversal, where the child cares for the parent's needs in place of the other way around.
Gibson contrasts these parents with emotionally mature ones, who can reflect on their behavior, take responsibility and respond with empathy.
Gibson advises keeping interactions with such parents light and brief, and not expecting emotional closeness from them.

books.thesis: Chasing happiness and fighting bad feelings backfires. Valued action and acceptance work better.
books.summary:
Harris takes on the idea that a good life means feeling good, and that painful thoughts and feelings must be removed first. He asks why this approach leaves so many people anxious and stuck, and presents Acceptance and Commitment Therapy as an alternative for general readers.

His argument is that struggling against inner experience makes it worse, so people should accept thoughts and feelings, step back from them, and act on chosen values. Skills include defusion, mindfulness and committed action. ACT has good research support, but it is not clearly better than other therapies for every problem, and a self-help book does not replace treatment for severe conditions.
ideas: The trap rests on four myths: happiness is the natural state, unhappy people are defective, you must get rid of negative feelings to live well, and you should be able to control your thoughts.
Experiential avoidance, meaning efforts to escape unpleasant inner states, tends to increase suffering and shrink a person's life.
Cognitive defusion teaches people to see thoughts as passing words and images, for example by noticing 'I am having the thought that' rather than treating a thought as fact.
Acceptance means making room for painful feelings instead of fighting them, which Harris calls expansion.
Mindfulness and the observing self give a stable perspective from which thoughts and feelings can be watched without being obeyed.
Values act as a chosen direction, distinct from goals, and committed action means doing what matters even when discomfort is present.
Dropping anchor is a short exercise for moments of strong emotion, in which a person acknowledges their feelings, connects with their body and engages with what is around them.
Harris describes the 'struggle switch', a mental device that, when on, makes anxiety about anxiety worse, and he suggests turning it off.
The book explains that thoughts such as 'I am worthless' can be treated as the mind's habit of storytelling, with the label 'the storyteller' and 'the thinking self'.
Harris covers the 'choice point', a moment of deciding whether to move toward values or away from them, as a daily tool.

books.t: What Life Could Mean to You
books.thesis: A life is judged by how a person meets work, community and love. Social interest is the test of health.
books.summary:
Adler, the founder of Individual Psychology, takes on the question of what gives a human life meaning and why people end up with such different outlooks. He writes for the general reader and asks how each person's early circumstances shape the way they face the demands of living.

He argues that people feel inferior as children and strive for significance, and that healthy striving is joined to concern for others, which he calls social interest. Each person forms a style of life early, and it shows in how they handle three tasks. Many of his claims, such as those on birth order, are hard to test and later research on them is mixed.
ideas: Everyone starts with feelings of inferiority, and the drive to overcome them is the engine of development, which can be healthy or can turn into a superiority complex.
Social interest, or Gemeinschaftsgefuhl, is the capacity to feel connected to others and contribute, and Adler treats it as the measure of psychological health.
Life poses three main tasks: occupation, community or friendship, and love and marriage. Failure to meet them shows in a person's behavior.
A style of life is set in early childhood and acts as a private logic that guides later choices, so it can be read from early memories.
Birth position, whether eldest, second, youngest or only child, affects outlook, though Adler said it does not determine it.
Pampered and neglected children both develop faulty views of life, one expecting others to serve them and the other distrusting everyone.
Dreams and early recollections are used to reveal a person's style of life and goals, and the cure for maladjustment is to widen social interest.
Adler holds that the meaning of life is shaped by what each person makes of it, and that no one lives in a world of pure fact.
He discusses the inferiority complex as a person's use of feelings of weakness as an excuse to avoid the tasks of life.
Adler rejects the idea of a fixed fate from heredity and environment, saying that the person's interpretation of these matters more.

books.thesis: The good life is activity of the soul in line with virtue, and character is built by habit and judgment.
books.summary:
Aristotle takes on the question of what the highest human good is and how people can achieve it. He treats ethics as a practical inquiry into how to live, not a set of abstract rules, and asks what makes a life go well for a creature with our nature.

He argues that the good is eudaimonia, flourishing, which comes from exercising reason and the virtues over a whole life. Virtues are habits formed by practice and guided by practical wisdom. Interpreters dispute whether he ranks contemplation above civic life, the doctrine of the mean is vague in practice, and his views on slaves and women are plainly dated.
ideas: Every action aims at some good, and the highest good is eudaimonia, which is an activity over a complete life and not a feeling or a state.
The function argument holds that the human good lies in doing well what is distinctive of humans, namely activity of the rational soul.
Moral virtues such as courage and temperance are acquired by habituation, and they are a mean between excess and deficiency relative to the person and the situation.
Practical wisdom, or phronesis, is the capacity to see what to do in particular cases, and without it no virtue is complete.
Voluntary action requires that the agent knows what they do and that the source of action is in them, which is the basis for praise and blame.
Friendship is central to a good life, and Aristotle distinguishes friendships of utility, of pleasure and of character, with the last being the most lasting.
Contemplation is described as the highest and most self-sufficient activity, and pleasure is a completion of activity and not the goal of life.
Aristotle says that ethics is not an exact science, and he warns that one should look for only as much precision as the subject allows.
