He discusses the idea of akrasia, or weakness of will, in which a person knows what is best and yet acts against it.
Justice is treated as having a distributive and a corrective form, and Aristotle compares it to a kind of proportion.

books.thesis: A just city and a just soul are ordered by reason, and only philosophers should rule.
books.summary:
Plato takes on the question of what justice is and whether being just is better for a person than seeming just. Starting from a challenge by Glaucon and Thrasymachus, he builds an imagined city to see justice at large scale before looking for it in the individual.

He argues that justice is each part of city and soul doing its own work under the guidance of reason, and that rulers must be trained philosophers who know the Form of the Good. Readers dispute whether he means the ideal city as a program or as a model, and critics such as Popper read it as authoritarian, given the censorship, guardian class and noble lie.
ideas: The challenge of Glaucon, including the ring of Gyges, claims people are just only from fear of punishment, and the rest of the book answers it.
The ideal city has three classes, producers, auxiliaries and guardians, and is just when each class does its own work.
The soul has three parts, reason, spirit and appetite, and a just person is one in whom reason rules with the help of spirit.
Philosophers should rule because only they know the Good, and Plato proposes long education and shared property for the guardians.
The analogies of the sun, the divided line and the cave describe knowledge as an ascent from images and opinion to understanding of the Forms.
Poetry and music are regulated because they shape character, and Plato admits a founding falsehood, the noble lie, to bind the city together.
Existing regimes decline in order from aristocracy to timocracy, oligarchy, democracy and tyranny, and the tyrant is shown as the most wretched person.
Socrates defines justice in the soul as each part doing its own work, and this is why he says the just person is happier than the unjust.
The myth of Er closes the book with a story of the afterlife, in which souls choose their next lives and are responsible for their choice.
Plato argues that the guardians would have no private families, and that women could take part in guarding the city if they have the ability.

books.thesis: Love begins as desire for one body and can rise to the contemplation of beauty itself.
books.summary:
Plato takes on the nature of Eros, or erotic love, and what it is for. Set at a drinking party in Athens, the dialogue has a series of guests give speeches in praise of love and asks what love really wants and why it matters for a human life.

The speeches build to Socrates, who reports a lesson from the priestess Diotima. Love is a desire for the good to be one's own forever, and it can ascend from bodies to souls, laws and knowledge, ending with the Form of Beauty. Critics, notably Vlastos, argue that this ladder treats individuals as steps and not as people worth loving for themselves.
ideas: Phaedrus, Pausanias, Eryximachus and Agathon give speeches that treat love as a source of courage, a matter of two kinds of Aphrodite, a cosmic principle and a god.
Aristophanes tells a myth of humans once being double beings split by Zeus, so that love is the search for our lost other half.
Through Diotima, Socrates argues that Eros is not a god but a spirit between mortal and divine, born of Poverty and Resource, always needy and always seeking.
Love is desire to possess the good forever, which explains why people seek immortality through children, fame and works of the mind.
The ladder of love moves from loving one beautiful body to all bodies, then to souls, laws and knowledge, and finally to Beauty itself.
The Form of Beauty is unchanging and pure, unlike beautiful things that come and go, and seeing it is the goal of correct love.
The drunken entrance of Alcibiades, who describes Socrates as a man who resists his advances, shows philosophy in practice and complicates the neat theory.
Eryximachus, as a doctor, treats love as a force that governs the body and the cosmos, and he links it to harmony and health.
Agathon praises Love as the youngest, most beautiful and best of the gods, and Socrates then questions each of these claims.
The setting is a banquet held to celebrate Agathon's victory in a tragedy contest, and the guests decide to give speeches in praise of love instead of drinking heavily.

books.thesis: Socrates faces death on the belief that an examined life and obedience to justice matter more than survival.
books.summary:
This collection of four Platonic dialogues takes on the trial and death of Socrates in 399 BC. It asks what a philosopher owes to his city, to the gods and to his own principles when he is charged with impiety and corrupting the young.

Euthyphro tests definitions of piety, Apology gives his defense, Crito has him refuse to escape prison, and Phaedo gives his final conversation about the soul. Together they present him as a model of integrity. Plato is not a neutral reporter, the historical Socrates is hard to separate from Plato, and many readers find the Phaedo's arguments for immortality weak.
ideas: In Euthyphro, Socrates shows that each definition of piety fails, which illustrates his method of questioning and his claim that he knows he does not know.
In Apology, he explains that the oracle at Delphi led him to test those thought wise, and that his mission is to urge Athenians to care for the soul.
He says the unexamined life is not worth living and refuses to stop philosophizing even to save himself.
In Crito, he argues that one must never do wrong in return for wrong, and that escaping would break an agreement with the laws that raised him.
The personified Laws of Athens give an early argument for a kind of social contract, based on benefits received and continued residence.
In Phaedo, he offers arguments for the soul's survival, from opposites, recollection and affinity with the Forms, and says a philosopher practices dying.
The closing death scene, with the hemlock and his last words about owing a cock to Asclepius, presents his calm as the fruit of his philosophy.
At his trial, Socrates is charged with corrupting the young and not believing in the gods of the city, and he answers by describing his daimonion, a divine sign that holds him back.
The Phaedo describes the final conversation with friends such as Simmias and Cebes, in which they ask whether the soul might fade like the harmony of a lyre.
Socrates says that the convicted should not beg the jury for mercy, and he proposes that his fitting penalty would be free meals at public expense.

books.thesis: Freedom comes from caring only about what is up to you, namely your own judgments and choices.
books.summary:
Epictetus, a former slave who taught Stoicism in Nicopolis, takes on the question of how to live well when so much of life lies outside our power. The Discourses, written down by his student Arrian, are lectures and exchanges aimed at practice rather than theory.

His answer is that some things are up to us, our judgments, desires and choices, and others are not, such as body, reputation and property. Peace comes from focusing on the first and accepting the second. The text is mediated by Arrian, and critics argue the stance can drift into passivity, though Epictetus insists on duties to family and city.
ideas: The dichotomy of control divides things into those up to us, such as opinion, impulse, desire and aversion, and those not up to us, such as body, wealth and reputation.
Prohairesis, the faculty of choice, is the true self and cannot be compelled by anyone, not even a tyrant.
People are disturbed not by events but by their judgments about events, so training means examining impressions before assenting to them.
He teaches three disciplines, of desire, of action and of assent, which cover what to want, how to act towards others and how to think.
Roles and relationships such as son, citizen and brother carry duties, and one should act well in each regardless of how others behave.
Providence governs the world, so one should accept what happens as a good actor accepts the part given by the playwright.
The philosopher's school is compared to a hospital, and philosophy is described as a daily practice, not a body of doctrine to be recited.
Epictetus was born a slave and later became a teacher, and his Discourses were written down by his student Arrian.
He treats the use of impressions as the key task, and he suggests the practice of telling oneself 'you are an impression and not at all the thing you appear to be'.
Epictetus holds that the choice to be angry or calm belongs to us, and he asks students to meet insults by seeing that the injury lies in the judgment.

books.thesis: Reason can cure anger, fear and wasted time, and a good life is one in which we use our days well.
books.summary:
Seneca, Stoic philosopher and adviser to Nero, takes on the practical troubles of a Roman life: anger, grief, busyness, insecurity and the fear of death. This collection of dialogues and essays offers advice on how to meet them with reason.

His argument is that virtue is the only good, that most distress comes from false judgments, and that time is the thing we waste most. The essays blend Stoic doctrine with Roman moral rhetoric. Seneca's own wealth and political compromises have long been used against him, and his sharpest advice sometimes sits uneasily beside his life.
ideas: On Anger describes anger as a brief madness, arguing that it should be prevented by checking the first impulse and delaying a response, not merely restrained once it has arisen.
On the Shortness of Life says life is long enough if used well, and that people waste it on busyness, pleasure and the pursuit of other people's approval.
On the Happy Life holds that happiness lies in virtue and that wealth is a preferred but indifferent thing, which he defends against charges of hypocrisy.
On Tranquility of Mind advises a measured level of public involvement, simple living and acceptance of change as ways to reduce restlessness.
On Providence asks why good people suffer and answers that hardship is a training given by a rational universe.
The consolations to Marcia, Helvia and Polybius address grief with the Stoic view that loss is part of nature and with a recommendation to remember the dead with gratitude.
Premeditation of evils, imagining losses and misfortunes in advance, reduces their shock, and the wise person holds all external goods lightly.
Seneca writes of the examination of the day, in which he reviews his own faults each night, and he cites it as a habit he took from the philosopher Sextius.
On the Constancy of the Wise Man argues that the sage cannot be truly injured, since insults and losses touch only what is external.
On Leisure explains that a person may serve the public through study and thought when active public life is closed to them.

books.thesis: Fortune cannot give or take true happiness, which lies in the highest good that no one can remove.
books.summary:
Boethius, a Roman statesman imprisoned and awaiting execution around 524, takes on the problem of how a just person can fall so low and what, if anything, can console him. The work is a conversation between the prisoner and Lady Philosophy, written in alternating prose and verse.

She argues that fortune is changeable by nature, that worldly goods cannot satisfy, and that true happiness is the supreme good, which she identifies with God. Evil is powerless and providence orders all. Scholars note that the book is explicitly philosophical and hardly mentions Christianity, and many find its reconciliation of divine foreknowledge with free will unconvincing.
ideas: Lady Philosophy diagnoses the prisoner as having forgotten his own nature, and her treatment is gentle at first and then more rigorous.
Fortune's wheel illustrates that rising and falling are her nature, so complaining about reversals mistakes what she gave.
Wealth, honors, power and fame cannot make a person truly happy, since each is partial, unstable or dependent on others.
True happiness is the highest good, which is one with God, and people seek it in mistaken forms.
Evil people are in a sense powerless, because they fail to reach the good that every will aims at, and wrongdoing is its own punishment.
Providence is the divine plan seen as a whole, and fate is its unfolding in time, so apparent injustice has a place within a larger order.
Eternity is not endless time but the complete and simultaneous possession of unending life, and God's knowledge of future events does not remove human freedom.
The book is written as a mix of prose and verse, and Boethius wrote it while held in prison and awaiting execution on charges of treason.
Philosophy argues that the supreme good is also the source of all being, and she presents it as that which people seek whenever they seek anything.
Boethius takes up the problem of free will against divine foreknowledge, and Philosophy replies that God sees all at once and does not foresee as we do.

books.thesis: Fixed views and fixed names narrow us, and freedom comes from following the Way and letting things change.
books.summary:
The Zhuangzi, a Daoist text attributed to Zhuang Zhou, takes on the question of how to live when human values, judgments and categories look partial and shifting. It uses stories, jokes and paradoxes instead of systematic argument.

Its central claim is that every perspective is limited, that right and wrong depend on where one stands, and that a person who responds spontaneously to the Way finds ease and freedom. Death is treated as one more transformation. The book is a composite, only the inner chapters are usually credited to Zhuang Zhou, and readers disagree on whether it teaches skepticism, mysticism or a practical skill.
ideas: Free and easy wandering is the ideal of moving through life without being tied to fame, usefulness or fixed goals.
The Qiwulun chapter argues that 'this' and 'that' depend on each other and that disputes cannot be settled from within any single standpoint.
The butterfly dream, in which Zhuang Zhou cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamed a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming a man, illustrates the instability of our categories.
Cook Ding carving an ox shows skill as following natural patterns with no strain, a model for acting in line with the Way.
The useless tree survives because carpenters ignore it, which shows that apparent uselessness can protect and free a person.
When his wife dies, Zhuangzi drums and sings after first grieving, accepting death as part of the cycle of change and not as something to resist.
Fasting of the mind is a practice of emptying oneself of fixed ideas so that one can respond to things as they arise.
The Inner Chapters are traditionally credited to Zhuangzi himself, while the outer and miscellaneous chapters are thought to have been added by later followers.
The text opens with the giant fish Kun, which becomes the bird Peng, and the small creatures who laugh at it show how limited perspectives mistake their own range for the whole.
Zhuangzi uses the idea of the pipes of heaven, in which the wind blows through hollows and makes different sounds, to show that each voice speaks for itself.

books.thesis: A ruler who wants to keep power must learn to act by what works, not by what is conventionally good.
books.summary:
Machiavelli takes on how new rulers gain and hold power, and why they so often lose it. Writing in 1513 for the Medici after the fall of the Florentine republic, he sets aside imagined ideal states and looks at what actually happens in politics.

He argues that a prince needs virtu, skill and force of character, to cope with fortuna, the unpredictable element of events, and that he must be ready to act against conventional morality when the state requires. Readers dispute his purpose: some see a manual for tyrants, others a satire or a republican in disguise, given his Discourses on Livy.
ideas: Machiavelli promises to follow the effectual truth of things, which means judging politics by outcomes rather than by how rulers ought to behave in theory.
Virtu is a mix of boldness, skill and adaptability, and fortuna is the force of chance, which he compares to a river that can be channeled by preparation but not stopped.
New principalities are harder to hold than hereditary ones, and the new ruler must secure the support of the people and eliminate rivals decisively.
Cruelty can be well used if committed at once and for security, and badly used if repeated, and a prince should keep his promises only when it serves him.
It is better to be feared than loved if one cannot be both, but a prince must avoid being hated, especially by taking property or women.
Mercenary and auxiliary armies are unreliable, and a state needs its own citizen soldiers to be secure.
Cesare Borgia is offered as a model of skill, and the final chapter urges the liberation of Italy from foreign rule.
Machiavelli distinguishes between ruling by the lion and by the fox, saying a prince must have the strength to scare wolves and the cunning to avoid traps.
He gives advice on the role of advisers, saying that a prince should choose wise ministers and let them speak freely only when asked.
Chapter 18 argues that a prince must seem to have the good qualities, because the public judges by appearances and results.

books.thesis: Without a sovereign power to keep the peace, life reverts to war, so people rationally submit to authority.
books.summary:
Hobbes, writing during the English Civil War, takes on the question of why people should obey political authority and what makes a commonwealth stable. He builds his answer from a materialist account of human nature and a thought experiment about life without government.

He argues that in the state of nature, people are roughly equal and driven by fear and desire, producing a war of all against all, so they covenant to give up their rights to an absolute sovereign. Critics doubt his bleak view of human nature, object that absolute power invites abuse, and note that his account of religion was controversial in his day.
ideas: In the state of nature there is no common power, so life is, in his famous phrase, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short.
Equality of ability produces equality of hope and therefore competition, diffidence and glory-seeking as three causes of quarrel.
The laws of nature are rational rules, such as seeking peace and keeping covenants, that follow from the desire for self-preservation.
Covenants without a sword are only words, so a sovereign with the power to enforce them is necessary to make them binding.
Sovereignty is established by a covenant among subjects to authorize one man or assembly, and the sovereign's authority is not subject to the subjects' judgment.
Subjects keep one right that cannot be given up, the right to resist force against their own life, though this does not amount to a right to rebel in general.
The later parts argue that the church must be subordinate to the sovereign, and attack what Hobbes saw as clerical claims that weaken civil peace.
Hobbes pictures the commonwealth as an artificial man, a 'mortal god', whose soul is sovereignty and whose body is made of its subjects.
He denies that there is any fixed highest good and describes human life as a 'perpetual and restless desire of power after power, that ceaseth only in death'.
Liberty means the absence of external impediments, so subjects remain free wherever the law is silent, and acting from fear is still free action.

books.thesis: Government is legitimate only when it rests on consent and protects natural rights to life, liberty and property.
books.summary:
Locke takes on the basis of political authority, challenging the claim that kings rule by divine, inherited right. Written in the context of the Exclusion Crisis and published in 1689, the work asks what gives anyone the right to rule over others.

The First Treatise attacks Filmer's patriarchalism. The Second argues that people in a state of nature have rights under natural law, form government by consent to protect them, and may resist when it breaks that trust. Critics point to his property theory's ties to colonial dispossession, his own involvement in slavery, and the vague role of tacit consent.
ideas: The First Treatise refutes Robert Filmer's view that kings inherit Adam's authority, arguing that scripture and reason do not support absolute monarchy.
The state of nature is governed by a law of nature, which holds that no one may harm another in life, health, liberty or possessions.
Property arises when a person mixes labor with something in common, subject to the limit that enough and as good be left for others and that nothing be wasted.
The introduction of money lets people hold more than they can use without spoilage, and Locke accepts the unequal holdings that result.
People leave the state of nature because there is no impartial judge, and they form a commonwealth by consent to gain a settled law and enforcement.
Power is a trust, so the legislative must be supreme but is limited by the ends of government, and is kept distinct from the executive.
When rulers act against the public good, the people retain the right to remove them, and Locke defends this as a safeguard against tyranny and not an invitation to disorder.
Locke separates political power from paternal and despotic power, and argues that a father's authority over children is temporary and ends when they reach reason.
Consent can be tacit as well as express, so simply living under a government and enjoying its protection implies consent, though only express consent makes one a full member.
Prerogative is the executive's discretion to act for the public good where the law is silent or even against its letter, and Locke says the people are the final judge of its abuse.

books.thesis: Human understanding rests on habit and feeling, not on reason alone, and we know less than we think.
books.summary:
Hume sets out to build a science of man on the model of Newton's natural philosophy. He asks what the mind can really know, how passions move us, and where moral distinctions come from, using experience and observation rather than speculation.

He argues that all ideas derive from impressions, that causation is a habit of expectation and not a perceived necessity, and that the self is a bundle of perceptions. In morals, reason serves the passions and virtue is based on sentiment. Hume was dissatisfied with parts of the book, especially on personal identity, and it attracted little notice on release.
ideas: Perceptions divide into vivid impressions and fainter ideas, and every simple idea comes from a prior impression, so ideas without such a source are empty.
Causation is constant conjunction plus a habit of mind, and we never observe a necessary connection between cause and effect.
Induction cannot be justified by reason, since expecting the future to resemble the past is itself an assumption drawn from past experience.
There is no impression of a self, so a person is a bundle of perceptions in perpetual flux, and our sense of identity is a fiction produced by memory and imagination.
Reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions, since reason alone cannot move us to act.
Moral distinctions are not derived from reason, because they come from feelings of approval and disapproval, and Hume remarks on the gap between 'is' and 'ought'.
Justice is an artificial virtue, invented through convention to meet the needs of society, while others such as benevolence are natural.
Ideas are linked by three principles of association, resemblance, contiguity and cause and effect, which Hume calls a kind of gentle force that works like attraction among ideas.
Sympathy is the mechanism by which we feel the passions of others, and Hume uses it to explain how moral approval can be shared across people.
At the end of Book One, skeptical doubt leaves him anxious and isolated, and he finds relief only in dinner, backgammon and company, which shows that nature overrides philosophical argument.

books.thesis: Our knowledge of the world rests on custom, not proof, and we should hold beliefs in proportion to evidence.
books.summary:
Hume's later, shorter statement of his theory of knowledge takes on how far human reason can reach. Written to reach a broader readership than the Treatise, it asks what we can know about causes, the future, freedom and the claims of religion.

He divides knowledge into relations of ideas and matters of fact, argues that reasoning about the latter depends on custom, and recommends a mitigated skepticism. The essays on miracles and design press against religious claims. Critics say the argument on miracles is weaker than it looks, and Kant and later Quine questioned the sharpness of his divide.
ideas: Hume's fork separates relations of ideas, known by reasoning alone, from matters of fact, which depend on experience and can always be otherwise.
The problem of induction holds that nothing in past experience can prove that the future will resemble it, so our expectations rest on custom.
The idea of necessary connection comes from a felt habit of expecting the effect after the cause, not from anything seen in objects.
Liberty and necessity are reconciled by defining liberty as acting according to the will, a compatibilist view that holds that human actions are as regular as natural events.
On miracles, a wise person proportions belief to evidence, and testimony for a violation of natural law will almost always be less likely than that the witness is mistaken or lying.
The design argument is treated with caution, because we have no experience of other universes to compare ours to, and so the inference to a designer is weak.
Mitigated skepticism recommends modest, limited inquiry into everyday matters and holds that extreme doubt cannot be sustained in practice.
Animals learn from experience and act on expectation, which Hume takes as evidence that inference from custom is not a product of reasoning.
The missing shade of blue is offered as a possible counterexample to the claim that every idea is copied from an impression, though he treats it as too small to overturn the rule.
Belief in an external world rests on instinct rather than argument, since we only ever have perceptions before the mind and cannot step outside them to check.

books.thesis: Everything follows from the nature of God or Nature, and freedom is understanding our place within it.
books.summary:
Spinoza takes on the questions of what reality is, what the human mind is, and how a person can live well without superstition. Presented in geometrical form with definitions, axioms and proofs, the Ethics tries to deduce the whole of human life from first principles.

He argues that there is only one substance, God or Nature, whose attributes include thought and extension, and that everything follows with necessity. Humans are in bondage to passions until adequate ideas free them. Many readers find the geometrical form opaque, the monism is contested, and in his time the work was condemned as atheism.
ideas: There is one infinite substance, God or Nature, and everything else is a mode of it, so there is no creator separate from the world.
Thought and extension are two attributes of the same substance, and the order of ideas is the same as the order of things, so mind and body are not two causes.
Everything happens by necessity, with no free will in the usual sense, and belief in free will comes from ignorance of causes.
Each thing strives to persevere in its being, which Spinoza calls conatus, and this striving is the essence of every individual.
Emotions are modifications of the body that increase or decrease our power to act, and desire, joy and sadness are the basic ones.
Human bondage is being governed by passive emotions, and freedom comes from forming adequate ideas and understanding the causes of our feelings.
The highest knowledge is intuitive, seeing things as following from God, and it brings the intellectual love of God and a lasting kind of blessedness.
The Ethics is set out in the geometric manner, with definitions, axioms, propositions and proofs, as if human emotions could be studied like lines and planes.
There are three kinds of knowledge: opinion or imagination, reason, and intuitive knowledge, and only the second and third give adequate ideas.
Good and evil are relative to what increases or decreases our power of acting, and the free person, guided by reason, thinks of death least of all things.

books.thesis: Moral judgment grows out of sympathy and the imagined view of an impartial spectator.
books.summary:
Smith, writing before The Wealth of Nations, takes on the origin of moral approval and disapproval. He asks how self-interested creatures come to judge conduct, feel for others and hold themselves to standards, and answers from observation of ordinary social life.

He argues that we judge by imagining how an impartial spectator would feel, and that conscience is that spectator internalized. Sympathy lets us share another's feelings, and we want to be praiseworthy, not merely praised. Scholars have long debated how this fits with the later book, and critics worry that the spectator mirrors social convention.
ideas: Sympathy is the imaginative sharing of another person's situation, and approval means that our feelings match those of the person concerned.
The impartial spectator is an imagined observer through whom we judge our own conduct, which Smith also calls the man within the breast.
Humans desire not just praise but praiseworthiness, the quality of deserving praise even if none is received.
Propriety concerns the fitness of an action to its cause, and merit and demerit concern the deserved reward or punishment for its effects.
Justice, which forbids harm to others, is the pillar of society and can be enforced, while beneficence is a grace that cannot be required.
Admiration of the rich and powerful corrupts moral sentiments, because people mistake wealth for happiness and pursue it beyond what satisfies them.
Self-command is the virtue that restrains our passions in line with the spectator's view, and Smith holds it to be essential to all the other virtues.
Moral luck matters to Smith, who notes that we judge actions by their results even though intentions should count, and he treats this as a flaw that nature built in for practical reasons.
The 'invisible hand' appears here in a passage on the rich, who in pursuing their own ends divide the necessaries of life with the poor almost as if the earth had been shared equally.
General rules of morality arise from repeated experience of what we approve and disapprove, and a sense of duty is respect for these rules when feeling alone would fall short.

books.thesis: Easy optimism fails against real suffering, and the only workable answer is modest, practical effort.
books.summary:
Voltaire's satirical tale takes on the philosophy of optimism, the idea that this is the best of all possible worlds. Written after the Lisbon earthquake of 1755 and the Seven Years' War, it asks how such a view survives war, disease, slavery and natural disaster.

Candide is taught optimism by Pangloss and is then thrown through a series of disasters across Europe and the Americas that refute it, ending with the advice to cultivate our garden. Voltaire caricatures Leibniz's actual position, and the ending is ambiguous, since it can be read as wisdom or as a retreat from larger questions.
ideas: Pangloss repeats that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds, a distorted version of Leibniz's optimism that Voltaire uses as a target.
Candide's expulsion from Westphalia is followed by war, shipwreck, the Lisbon earthquake and the Inquisition, so that each event tests the doctrine against experience.
Voltaire satirizes the cruelty and hypocrisy of the church, the military and the aristocracy, including clergy who preach morality while acting without it.
The slave in Surinam who has lost a leg and a hand shows that European prosperity is built on brutality, and Candide's reaction to him marks a turn from optimism.
Eldorado is a utopia of reason and tolerance that Candide leaves, which suggests that an ideal society is no remedy for human restlessness.
Martin the Manichean scholar holds a pessimistic view of the world, and the contrast with Pangloss shows that neither extreme fits the facts.
The closing line to cultivate our garden recommends useful work and modest aims in place of speculation about the world's ultimate design.
The Old Woman tells of the loss of half a buttock and years of misery, and observes that many wish to die yet still cling to life, which shows suffering as common to all ranks.
Candide ends up married to Cunegonde, who has grown ugly and sharp tempered, and he keeps his promise out of duty, a deflating end to a romantic quest.
The Turkish farmer tells Candide that work keeps away three great evils, boredom, vice and need, which prepares the closing call to cultivate the garden.

books.thesis: Legitimate authority rests on the general will of free citizens, not on force or birth.
books.summary:
Rousseau opens with the problem that people are born free yet everywhere live in chains. He asks what could make political rule legitimate, given that no one has a natural authority over others and force creates no right.

His answer is a contract in which each person gives themselves wholly to the community and so obeys only a law they share in making. The general will, aimed at the common good, is sovereign and cannot be represented. Critics, from Constant to Berlin, argue that the idea of being forced to be free can license tyranny over dissenters.
ideas: Rousseau starts from the claim that man is born free and that political chains need a justification, since neither force nor paternal power creates a right to rule.
In the social contract each individual alienates all rights to the community and receives them back as a citizen, so in obeying the law they obey themselves.
The general will concerns the common interest, and Rousseau distinguishes it from the will of all, which is only the sum of private wishes.
Sovereignty belongs to the people and cannot be alienated or represented, so he is suspicious of representative government and favors direct assembly in small states.
Whoever refuses to obey the general will may be compelled to do so, which Rousseau describes as forcing them to be free.
He separates sovereign from government: the sovereign makes law, while the government is a magistracy that executes it and can be changed by the people.
Because laws need a shared moral sentiment, he proposes a civil religion and a lawgiver figure, ideas later readers have found uncomfortably illiberal.
Rousseau holds that the general will is always right, but the judgment that guides it is not always enlightened, which is why a people needs good guidance.
He distinguishes natural liberty, which is limited only by force, from civil liberty, limited by the general will, and adds moral liberty, which is obeying a law one prescribes to oneself.
Democracy, aristocracy and monarchy are suited to states of different size and climate, and he thinks that pure democracy fits only a very small state.

books.thesis: A life told with unsparing candor, Rousseau claims, shows one man's inner nature and his wrongs.
books.summary:
Rousseau writes the first major modern autobiography and asks what it would mean to show a human being exactly as he is. He sets out to give a complete account of his character, including shameful acts, so that readers can judge him with the full truth in hand.

The book follows him from Geneva childhood through years of wandering, patronage, love affairs and literary fame, stressing feeling over reason as the source of his character. He presents himself as basically good yet damaged by society. Readers have long noted that his memory is selective and self-justifying, and that his claim to total honesty is hard to sustain.
ideas: Rousseau opens by declaring that he is undertaking something without precedent, showing a man in all the truth of nature, himself.
He confesses specific faults, such as stealing a ribbon and blaming a servant girl, and the abandonment of his five children to a foundling hospital.
He treats childhood experiences, such as a punishment by Mlle Lambercier, as formative of his later tastes and temperament.
Feeling and sentiment come before reasoning in his account of himself, and he presents his sensibility as the key to his character and his writing.
His relationship with Mme de Warens is portrayed as the warmest and most formative of his life, a mix of mother figure, patron and lover.
Later books describe quarrels with Diderot, Voltaire and Hume, and a growing belief that he is the target of a conspiracy.
The text invites the reader to judge him, yet its self-justifying tone and gaps in fact make it as much a work of self-fashioning as of record.
The book opens with Rousseau declaring that when the trumpet of the last judgment sounds he will present this book to the Sovereign Judge and say he was what he was.
He recounts the road to Vincennes, where reading a prize question led to a sudden illumination that produced his First Discourse and launched his fame.
He earns his living copying music and has success with his opera The Village Soothsayer, yet he refuses a royal pension in order to protect his independence.

books.thesis: Cut off from society, Rousseau finds a quiet happiness in the pure sense of existing.
books.summary:
Written near the end of his life, the Reveries asks what remains of a person once he is rejected by everyone and can no longer defend himself. Rousseau, convinced he has been cast out by his contemporaries, turns to examine himself without an audience.

Across ten walks he reflects on memory, botany, lying, charity and moral duty, and arrives at the experience of existing in the moment as a self-sufficient happiness, like floating on the Lake of Bienne. The work is unfinished and its serenity sits beside real bitterness and persecution fears, which readers have to weigh when judging its calm.
ideas: The first walk presents Rousseau as alone in the world, outcast by his contemporaries, and sets the book as a record of his own state of mind rather than a case for others.
Rousseau describes the experience of pure existence, when the mind rests in the present with no desire or fear and feels only the sentiment of being.
The fifth walk, at the island in Lake Bienne, is his picture of this happiness, with drifting in a boat, watching the water and idle reverie.
He examines lying in the fourth walk, separating harmful deceit from harmless fiction and holding that truthfulness is owed where someone is wronged.
Botany becomes a gentle pastime that takes him out of self-torment, a way of attending to nature without expecting anything.
The work revisits episodes from his life, such as his accident with a Great Dane in the second walk, to ask what they show about how he experiences pain and recovery.
The tone moves between serenity and resentment, and the book remains unfinished, so its peace is partial and sometimes undercut by his sense of persecution.
The sixth walk notes that good deeds can turn into burdens once habit and obligation attach to them, and Rousseau says he values freedom from constraint above benevolence on demand.
The eighth walk considers the advantages of adversity and suggests that persecution drove him inward and taught him to find contentment within himself.
The tenth walk is unfinished and recalls his first meeting with Mme de Warens on Palm Sunday, written shortly before his death.

books.thesis: The mind shapes experience through its own forms, so reason cannot know things beyond possible experience.
books.summary:
Kant asks whether metaphysics can be a science. He wants to know how we can have knowledge that is both necessary and informative, and what limits reason must accept when it tries to reach beyond experience to God, the soul and the world as a whole.

His answer is transcendental idealism: space, time and the categories are contributions of the knowing mind, so we know appearances, not things in themselves. Claims about the soul, the cosmos and God fall into illusion when pushed past experience. The thing in itself has been a lasting point of dispute, and critics doubt that Kant can say it exists yet is unknowable.
ideas: Kant asks how synthetic a priori judgments are possible, claims that add to our knowledge yet hold independently of experience, as in mathematics and the principles of physics.
Space and time are forms of intuition that the mind brings to experience, so geometry applies to everything we can perceive.

The categories, such as causality and substance, are concepts of the understanding that make experience of objects possible, and the Transcendental Deduction argues that they apply to all appearances.
He distinguishes phenomena, things as they appear to us, from noumena, things as they are in themselves, and holds that only the former can be known.
The Transcendental Dialectic shows how reason falls into illusion when it tries to prove the soul's nature, the world's beginning or God's existence from concepts alone.
The Antinomies set out four pairs of opposed arguments about the world as a whole, such as whether it has a beginning, to show that reason contradicts itself when it oversteps.
Kant calls this shift his Copernican revolution, since objects must conform to the structure of our cognition and not the other way around, and he leaves room for faith by limiting knowledge.
The unity of apperception holds that the 'I think' must be able to accompany all my representations, and it grounds the unity of experience in a single subject.
Kant rejects the ontological argument for God by claiming that existence is not a real predicate, so adding it to a concept does not enlarge the concept.
The slogan that thoughts without content are empty and intuitions without concepts are blind sums up his view that knowledge needs both sensibility and understanding.

books.t: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
books.thesis: Morality rests on a law that reason gives itself, the categorical imperative, not on outcomes or desires.
books.summary:
Kant asks what the supreme principle of morality is and whether duty can have a basis that does not depend on what people happen to want. He seeks a standard that holds for every rational being, whatever their inclinations or circumstances.

He argues that only a good will is good without qualification and that an action has moral worth when done from duty. The categorical imperative, in several formulations, tests maxims for universality and respect for persons, and autonomy grounds it. Critics ask whether the formulations really yield one test, and whether the view is too rigid when duties conflict.
ideas: Kant opens by saying that nothing is good without qualification except a good will, since talents and happiness can be misused.
An action has moral worth only when it is done from duty and not merely in line with duty or from inclination, as in his example of the shopkeeper who deals honestly out of self-interest.
A hypothetical imperative commands means to an end we want, while a categorical imperative commands unconditionally and is the form of moral requirement.
The Formula of Universal Law asks whether you can will your maxim to become a universal law, and Kant applies it to false promises and neglect of talents.
The Formula of Humanity says to treat humanity, in yourself and others, always as an end and never merely as a means.
Autonomy of the will is the idea that rational beings are bound by laws they give themselves, which makes dignity, not price, the mark of a person.
Kant also imagines a kingdom of ends, a community of rational beings legislating shared laws, as a picture of what moral life would look like.
Kant separates perfect duties, such as not making false promises, which admit no exceptions, from imperfect duties, such as helping others, which leave room for choice about when and how.
He insists that moral philosophy must be pure and rest on reason, not on empirical anthropology, because a law that binds all rational beings cannot come from observing human nature.
The third section argues that we must act under the idea of freedom, and he uses two standpoints, the sensible world and the intelligible world, to make room for morality.

books.thesis: Consciousness develops through contradiction toward absolute knowing, and self-awareness depends on recognition by others.
books.summary:
Hegel sets out to trace how consciousness moves from the simplest claim to know something to a complete understanding of itself and the world. He wants to show that knowledge, freedom and social life grow out of one historical process.

The book follows shapes of consciousness, each of which falls into contradiction and gives way to a richer one, from sense certainty through self-consciousness, reason, spirit and religion to absolute knowing. It is famously dense and its final stage is contested; readers dispute whether it describes history, an individual's education or a logical structure.
ideas: Hegel starts with sense certainty and shows that even the most basic claim to know a particular thing depends on universals, so it cannot hold up as immediate knowledge.
Each shape of consciousness tests itself against its own standard, finds a contradiction and gives way to a new shape, a process Hegel calls determinate negation.
The master and slave passage argues that self-consciousness needs recognition from another, and that the bondsman gains independence through labor while the master depends on him.
Stoicism, skepticism and the unhappy consciousness show self-awareness retreating inward and seeking a perfect, unreachable otherness.
The chapter on Reason and Spirit places individuals in ethical life, culture and history, so freedom is realized in shared institutions and not only in the private will.
The section on the Beautiful Soul and the Terror of the French Revolution criticizes pure inwardness and absolute freedom as forms that destroy themselves.
Absolute knowing is the point at which spirit recognizes itself in its own history, and interpreters dispute whether this closes the system or is a philosophical standpoint.
The Preface says that the true is the whole and mocks the Absolute of Schelling as a night in which all cows are black.
In the chapters on Perception and on Force and Understanding, consciousness looks behind appearances for laws, and this search turns back on itself and prepares the way for self-consciousness.
Before the master and slave relation comes a struggle in which each self-consciousness risks its life to be recognized, and the one who yields becomes the bondsman.

books.t: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
books.thesis: Women seem inferior because they are denied education, and reason should guide both sexes.
books.summary:
Wollstonecraft takes on the claim that women are naturally weaker in mind and fit mainly to please men. She asks whether the faults attributed to women come from nature or from the way they are raised.

She argues that poor education trains women to value beauty and manners over understanding, which makes them dependent and shapes them into frivolous companions. She calls for national, coeducational schooling and for women to be treated as rational beings and as better mothers and citizens. Later readers note that she still accepts some traditional roles for women and sharply criticizes the women of her day.
ideas: Wollstonecraft holds that reason is common to both sexes, so there is no basis for claiming that women are made for submission.
She argues that the apparent weakness of women is an effect of upbringing, which teaches them to cultivate charm and cunning at the expense of understanding.
Rousseau's Emile is a main target, since he gives Sophie an education aimed at pleasing Emile, and she rejects that picture.
She criticizes the idea that women should be valued for beauty and sensibility, which she calls a kind of slavery that corrupts both men and women.
She proposes a system of national, coeducational day schools, so boys and girls learn together and form habits of reason and companionship.
Marriage, she says, should be a friendship between equals, and women's rational virtue would make them better mothers and more useful citizens.
She links tyranny in the home to tyranny in the state, so reform of women's status is bound up with the wider cause of liberty and the critique of hereditary power.
The book is dedicated to Talleyrand and urges the French revolutionary government to include women in its plans for national education.
Wollstonecraft attacks the conduct books of writers such as Fordyce and Gregory, which tell women to value docility and appearances over understanding.
She compares women with soldiers, since both are taught obedience and surface polish, and so lose the habit of thinking for themselves.

books.thesis: Simplifying life and living deliberately free a person from the labor and conformity that crowd out what matters.
books.summary:
Thoreau asks how a person should live, and what it costs to spend life earning the means of living. He moves to a cabin by Walden Pond in 1845 to test how little a person needs and what he can learn from nature.

Drawing on two years at the pond, he describes the economy of necessities, the seasons, the pond itself, and the habit of attention. He argues that most people are driven by needless possessions and borrowed opinions. Critics note that he lived near town and relied on friends and family, and his stance can seem privileged or self-satisfied.
ideas: Thoreau holds that most people live lives of quiet desperation because they work to maintain possessions and a standard of living they do not need.
The chapter on Economy counts the cost of things in life, meaning the amount of life exchanged for them, and shows how little shelter, clothing and food are required.
He went to the woods to live deliberately, to face only the essential facts of life, and see whether he could learn what it had to teach.
Solitude is not loneliness for him, and he finds companionship in nature, in reading and in his own thoughts.
Careful attention to the pond and the seasons, as in the chapters on Sounds and The Ponds, shows a way to see the ordinary world closely.
He argues that new inventions, such as the railroad, are often improved means to unimproved ends, and he distrusts progress measured by speed or commerce.
The book ends with spring and the idea of renewal, and holds that the sun is but a morning star, a call to wake up and keep living in new ways.
In Economy Thoreau keeps exact accounts, saying his cabin cost a little over twenty-eight dollars, to show how cheaply a person can meet real needs.
The chapter on Reading urges the study of the ancient classics in the original and treats serious books as a deliberate effort to be awake.
In The Bean-Field he hoes rows of beans and calculates his profit, and the labor becomes a lesson about cultivating himself as well as the soil.

books.thesis: Society may restrict individual liberty only to prevent harm to others.
books.summary:
Mill asks what limits society may legitimately place on the individual. He worries less about government tyranny than about the pressure of majority opinion and custom, which can suppress dissent and individuality without any law.

He defends what is called the harm principle, then argues for freedom of thought and discussion because even false opinions help test truth, and for individuality as a condition of human progress. His utilitarian grounding is questioned, as is the line between self-regarding and other-regarding acts, which proves hard to draw in practice.
ideas: The harm principle states that the only purpose for which power may be exercised over a member of a civilized community against his will is to prevent harm to others.
Mill argues that silencing an opinion is wrong because it may be true, because a false opinion still helps clarify the truth, and because unchallenged truth becomes dead dogma.
He warns of the tyranny of the majority, which works through social stigma and custom as well as law.
Individuality is a part of well-being, and he thinks that people should be free to try experiments in living.
He separates self-regarding conduct, which is the individual's own business, from conduct that affects others, which society may regulate.
The principle applies to adults of developed faculties, and he excludes children and what he called backward societies governed by despotism for their improvement.
Mill also shows that the idea of liberty requires limits, such as a rule against selling oneself into slavery, which shows tension with his own principle.
Liberty has three spheres, the inward domain of conscience and opinion, the liberty of tastes and pursuits, and the freedom to unite with others for any purpose that does not harm them.
In the last chapter Mill applies his principle to cases, and holds that the state may require education but should not provide it, to avoid a single mold for all minds.
He warns that custom can become a despotism and cites China as a society that was once advanced and then frozen by conformity.

books.thesis: Cultivating experience as aesthetic game, Johannes treats a young woman as material for pleasure and shows its emptiness.
books.summary:
This work, presented as found papers, asks what an existence devoted to aesthetic pleasure looks like from the inside. Kierkegaard gives a voice to the aesthetic life, where interest and enjoyment outrank commitment and ethics.

Johannes plans and carries out the seduction of Cordelia, a young woman, through patient arrangement of her feelings and engagement, then loses interest once he has her. Kierkegaard published it within Either/Or as one side of a choice, and many read it as a critique, not an endorsement, of the aesthetic stance, though its elegance makes that reading debated.
ideas: The diary is framed as papers found by an editor, and Johannes is a pseudonymous voice that Kierkegaard keeps at a distance from his own view.
Johannes treats seduction as an art, valuing the interesting over the beautiful and the process of winning over the result.
He studies Cordelia and arranges meetings, letters and an engagement so that she comes to feel she freely chooses what he has planned.
The engagement is for him a means to make her break from convention, after which he ends it once he has what he wanted.
The account shows an aesthetic life in which feeling is cultivated for its own sake and others become objects of interest.
Within Either/Or the diary is set against Judge William's letters defending ethical commitment such as marriage, so the reader is asked to weigh the two ways of life.
Readers disagree about whether the text exposes the emptiness of aestheticism or invites admiration for Johannes's skill, and it also reflects Kierkegaard's broken engagement to Regine Olsen.
Johannes places a young suitor, Edward, near Cordelia as a foil, so that her attention is turned toward himself by contrast.
The diary begins when Johannes sees Cordelia in the street, follows her, and then arranges to enter her aunt's household as a harmless visitor.
Kierkegaard later sets the aesthetic life as only the first of three stages, followed by the ethical and the religious, so the diary shows what the aesthetic way of life lacks.

books.thesis: Happiness depends chiefly on what a person is, not on what he has or how others see him.
books.summary:
Schopenhauer takes up the old question of how to live well and asks what contributes most to a happy life. He weighs the claims of personality, possessions and reputation, in the spirit of a practical guide even though his wider philosophy is pessimistic.

He divides goods into what one is, what one has and what one represents in others' eyes, and ranks them in that order. Health, cheerfulness and a rich inner life matter most, and honor, rank and fame matter least. His advice leans toward solitude and moderation, and it reflects his temperament, so it may not suit those who find meaning in society.
ideas: Schopenhauer sorts life's goods into three classes: what a man is, what he has and what he represents, and he holds that the first matters most.
Personality, including health, temperament and intellect, shapes happiness more than outer circumstance, since each person experiences the world through his own mind.
Wealth is useful only as protection from want and boredom, and he advises against hoarding it or chasing more than needed.
He argues that people give too much weight to the opinions of others, and that honor, rank and fame are poor sources of contentment.
Boredom and suffering are the two enemies of human life, and a person with rich inner resources suffers less from both.
Solitude suits those with inner wealth, while sociable people tend to depend on company to fill an emptiness.
He recommends a mild, steady approach to life, avoiding great hopes and fears, and he treats the aim of life as freedom from pain more than the pursuit of pleasure.
Cheerfulness and health are worth more than wealth, and Schopenhauer remarks that a healthy beggar is happier than a sick king.
He draws on Epicurus to sort desires into natural and necessary, natural but unnecessary, and neither, and advises limiting desires to the first group.
The first forty years of life, he says, give the text and the next thirty the commentary, which shows how experience changes how we read our own earlier years.

books.t: On the Suffering of the World
books.thesis: Life is dominated by suffering and striving, so compassion, not optimism, is the fitting response.
books.summary:
Schopenhauer asks what the world is worth and whether the common belief that life is good holds up when we look at it honestly. This short collection draws on his larger work to argue that pain is the normal condition and pleasure only its temporary relief.

He holds that the world is driven by blind will, which produces endless wanting and conflict, and that existence is better understood as something to be endured. He proposes compassion, ascetic denial of will and aesthetic contemplation as partial relief. Critics find the pessimism one-sided and note it rests on his metaphysics of will, which many reject.
ideas: Schopenhauer argues that suffering is positive and pleasure merely the absence of pain, so happiness is a brief pause in want.
The will is a blind striving at the root of all things, and in human beings it appears as ceaseless desire that is never fully satisfied.
Life swings like a pendulum between pain and boredom, since as soon as want is met, boredom arrives.
He rejects optimism as a cruel mockery of human suffering and says the world is the worst of all possible worlds in the sense that it could not last were it worse.
Compassion follows from seeing that all beings are fellow sufferers, and it is the foundation of morality in his view.
Aesthetic experience, especially music, offers a temporary release as the will is quiet while one contemplates something without desire.
Lasting relief comes only through denial of the will to live, a path of asceticism he links to Indian and Christian thought, though he says it is rare.

The principle of individuation is the way the world divides into separate things in space and time, and Schopenhauer says that seeing through it reveals that individuals are appearances of a single will.
Death destroys the individual but not the will itself, which he calls the thing in itself, so he treats the fear of death as largely a confusion about what we are.
He observes that Dante took the material for hell from this world, and then had nothing left to build heaven from.

books.thesis: Greek tragedy arose from the union of Apollonian order and Dionysian ecstasy, and was killed by Socratic rationalism.
books.summary:
Nietzsche asks how Greek tragedy came to be and why it matters to modern culture. He wants to understand how a people so aware of suffering could produce such affirming art, and what has been lost since.

He argues that tragedy blends two drives, the Apollonian love of form and illusion and the Dionysian dissolution of the self in music and intoxication. Euripides and Socrates broke the balance with optimistic reason, and Nietzsche hopes Wagner might revive it. He later criticized the book, and it is often faulted for weak classical scholarship and its attachment to Wagner.
ideas: Nietzsche names two artistic forces, the Apollonian, tied to dream, form and individuation, and the Dionysian, tied to intoxication, music and the loss of self.
Tragedy arises from the union of these forces, with the chorus and music carrying the Dionysian and the stage action giving it visible shape.
The Greeks faced the terror of existence and responded by creating beauty, as in the Olympian gods, which made life worth living.
Tragedy lets the audience feel the unity of life and the joy of creation and destruction, which affirms existence in spite of suffering.
Euripides brought rational argument and ordinary characters onto the stage, and Socrates stands for the faith that knowledge can correct existence, which Nietzsche sees as the end of tragedy.
He famously says that existence is justified only as an aesthetic phenomenon, which ties his view of life to art.
In the closing sections he looks to Wagner's music drama for the rebirth of tragic culture, a hope he later dropped as he turned against Wagner.
Nietzsche retells the story of Silenus, who tells King Midas that the best thing is never to be born and the second best is to die soon.
He traces tragedy to the chorus of satyrs in Dionysian ritual, which he thinks gave the audience a sense of being part of a larger life.
In a later preface, 'Attempt at a Self-Criticism', he calls the book badly written and heavy with Schopenhauer and Wagner, though he still defends its central questions.

books.thesis: Many ideals thought to be pure, from morals to art, have humble and psychological origins.
books.summary:
Nietzsche asks what we find when we examine high ideals with the tools of history and psychology. Written after he broke from Wagner and Schopenhauer, the book tests the claim that morality, religion and art come from something beyond the human.

In aphorisms, he traces such ideals back to ordinary drives, habits and fear, and recommends a cooler, scientific approach and free spirits who think for themselves. The book marks a turn from romantic metaphysics to a more skeptical style. The method of aphorism means the argument is scattered, and some of its claims, such as on women or race, have not aged well.
ideas: Nietzsche proposes a historical philosophy that studies how values arose, and holds that there are no eternal facts or absolute truths.
Moral feelings, such as pity and conscience, can be traced to custom, utility and fear instead of to a higher source.
Metaphysical beliefs came from errors about dreams, language and cause, and we can see their origins now that we understand the history.
Art and religion offer consolation, but he suspects that the genius is a figure of myth, and that great works come from steady labor.
The free spirit is a person who breaks from inherited convictions and sees the world with detachment, and the book is dedicated to such readers.
He encourages a scientific, humble attitude toward knowledge, and values method over discovery.
The text is made of numbered aphorisms, which lets him try ideas from different angles but also leaves the argument open and sometimes inconsistent.
The book is dedicated to Voltaire and appeared in 1878, and it marks Nietzsche's break with Wagner and with Schopenhauer's metaphysics.
He argues that the will is not free and that guilt and punishment must be rethought in light of how actions have causes.
Later volumes, including Assorted Opinions and Maxims and The Wanderer and His Shadow, extend the book, and the whole was gathered into a second edition in 1886.

books.thesis: Long-standing idols of philosophy and morality sound hollow when struck, and should be tested and overturned.
books.summary:
Nietzsche's late short work sets out to summarize his philosophy and to ask which cherished beliefs can stand up to hard questioning. He uses the image of tapping idols with a hammer to see whether they ring true or hollow.

He attacks the Socratic equation of reason and virtue, the idea of a true world behind appearances, the notion of free will and guilt, and Christian morality as anti-life. He also gives a short history of how the true world became a fable. The tone is polemical and compressed, and his pronouncements on race, nationality and others have been criticized.
ideas: Nietzsche calls the book a way to sound out idols with a hammer, treating inherited beliefs as things to test and not to revere.
Socrates is a symptom of decline in his view, since equating reason with virtue and happiness reflects a need to master unruly instincts.
In How the True World Finally Became a Fable he traces the idea of a true world from Plato through Christianity and Kant to its collapse.
The four great errors include confusing cause and effect and imagining free will, and he holds that these serve to assign blame and guilt.
Morality as Anti-Nature argues that moralities that condemn the passions rather than spiritualize them are hostile to life.
Under Skirmishes of an Untimely Man he comments on artists, writers and thinkers, and on the aesthetic state of intoxication as a source of creativity.
He ends by mentioning the Dionysian affirmation of life and the idea that what does not kill me makes me stronger, a motto that reflects his emphasis on health and strength.
The book opens with a section of Maxims and Arrows, short barbed sayings that set the tone of mischief and attack.
In The Improvers of Mankind he argues that moral systems which claim to improve people by taming them, as in the priestly law of Manu, work by weakening them.
What the Germans Lack criticizes German culture and education, and he says that teaching to think, speak and write has been neglected.

books.thesis: Teaism turns the plain act of drinking tea into a way of seeing beauty in imperfection and simplicity.
books.summary:
Okakura, writing in English for a Western audience around 1906, asks what tea means in Asian life and why the West misreads it. He presents tea as a philosophy and a form of aesthetic discipline that shaped Japanese art, architecture and manners.

He traces tea from a medicine to a drink to an ideal, and describes how Taoism and Zen shaped the tea ceremony, the tea room and flower arrangement. The central theme is an appreciation of the imperfect and the incomplete. The book is also a polite argument against Western contempt for Asia, and some readers find its picture of Japanese culture idealized.
ideas: Okakura calls teaism a cult founded on the adoration of the beautiful among the sordid facts of everyday existence, a way to find harmony in small acts.
He traces the progression of tea from medicine to beverage to a way of life, from China through Song and Ming practice to Japan.
Taoism and Zen shaped the tea ideal, with emphasis on the relative, the empty and the spontaneous, as in the Taoist idea that usefulness lies in emptiness.
The tea room is a plain, small space meant to hold a few people in calm, with its beauty in simplicity and in the absence of ornament.
The text values imperfection and the unfinished, since the viewer completes the idea in the mind.
The chapter on flowers argues that the tea master uses them with restraint, and criticizes wasteful display of cut blooms.
He includes a plea for cultural understanding between East and West and a reflection on how the tea masters met death, with the story of Rikyu.
Okakura notes that Westerners called Japan barbarous while she practiced the quiet arts of peace but civilized once she fought on Manchurian battlefields.
He describes three stages in the preparation of tea, the boiled cake tea of the Tang, the whipped powdered tea of the Song and the steeped leaf tea of the Ming.
The chapter on art appreciation holds that true understanding needs sympathy between viewer and work, and he retells the Taoist tale of the harp that only the right player could tame.

books.thesis: Philosophy offers no final answers, but its questions enlarge the mind and free it from prejudice.
books.summary:
Russell asks whether there is any knowledge so certain that no reasonable person could doubt it, and what we can know about matter, truth and the world. He writes a short introduction for general readers rather than a technical treatise.

He begins with appearance and reality, defends the existence of matter as the best hypothesis, and distinguishes knowledge by acquaintance from knowledge by description. He argues for universals and a priori knowledge and ends with the value of philosophy. His specific positions, such as sense data and his theory of truth, have been revised by later philosophers, including Russell himself.
ideas: Russell starts from the way a table looks different from different angles and asks what, if anything, we know about the real table behind appearances.
He argues that the existence of matter is the simplest and best explanation of our sense data, though it cannot be proved with certainty.
Knowledge by acquaintance is direct awareness of things, such as sense data, while knowledge by description is knowledge of things through definite descriptions.
He defends a priori knowledge of logic and mathematics against empiricism, and against Kant's view of such knowledge as shaped by the mind.
Universals, such as whiteness or resemblance, exist apart from particular things and are needed to account for general terms.
Truth is a matter of correspondence between belief and fact, and he rejects the coherence theory as insufficient.
The last chapter says philosophy should be valued for its questions, which free the mind from narrow ideas and bring a kind of greatness of thought.
Russell argues that Berkeley's idealism rests on a confusion, since a thing being known by us does not imply that it exists only in a mind.

The principle of induction cannot be proved by experience, because experience supports it only if it is already assumed, and Russell uses the chicken that expects food until the day its neck is wrung.
Knowledge is more than true belief, since one may believe something true by luck or from a false premise, and Russell raises this in the chapter on knowledge, error and probable opinion.

books.thesis: Happiness comes from outward interest and sensible habits, not from self-absorption.
books.summary:
Russell asks why so many people in comfortable circumstances are unhappy and what an individual can do about it. He writes as a practical guide that sets out common causes of unhappiness and the conditions of a satisfying life.

In the first half he examines causes such as competition, boredom, fatigue, envy, a sense of sin and fear of public opinion, many of which come from self-focus. In the second half he recommends zest, affection, work and impersonal interests, and balanced effort and resignation. The advice is commonsensical and sometimes dated, and it reflects a comfortable social position.
ideas: Russell says that unhappiness is often caused by habits of thought, including self-absorption, that a person can recognize and change.
Competition as the central aim of life leads to anxiety, and he argues for more attention to enjoyment than to winning.
Boredom and excitement are linked, since a life that seeks constant stimulation leaves people unable to bear quiet.
Envy is a major cause of unhappiness, and he suggests comparing oneself less with others and finding pleasure in what one has.
Fear of public opinion and a sense of sin hold people back from their own lives, and he advises a more rational approach to morality.
Zest, a broad interest in things and people, is the best mark of happiness, and affection and work provide steady satisfaction.
He recommends balancing effort and resignation, working to improve what can be changed and accepting what cannot, and widening interests so that no single loss is devastating.
The Byronic unhappiness of the proud who think the world is against them is one of the first causes he names, and he treats it as a fashionable pose rather than a deep truth.
For worry, he advises thinking through the worst that could happen until it loses its terror, which he says brings calm and clears the mind.
The happy person lives objectively, with free affections and wide interests, and finds happiness through contact with the world and not through self-regard.

books.t: Why I Am Not a Christian
books.thesis: The arguments for God and for Christianity's moral standing do not withstand rational scrutiny.
books.summary:
Russell asks what it means to be a Christian and whether the beliefs and moral claims of the faith are justified. The title essay, a lecture from 1927, is joined by other writings on religion, morals and freedom of thought.

He reviews the classic arguments for God, such as the first cause, natural law and design, and finds each unconvincing. He then challenges the character of Christ, doctrines on hell, and the church's effect on moral progress, and argues that fear lies behind religion. His case is largely rational and polemical, and critics say it overlooks more sophisticated theology and the role of religion in lived experience.
ideas: Russell defines a Christian as someone who believes in God and immortality and in Christ as the best and wisest of men, and he questions each element.
The first cause argument fails because if everything needs a cause then God needs one, and the world may simply have no cause.
The argument from natural law confuses descriptions of regularities with commands, and the argument from design does not explain the imperfect nature of the world.
He argues that the moral argument for God is weak, since if right and wrong are God's commands then they are arbitrary, and if not, God is not the source of morals.
On Christ, Russell criticizes the teaching on hell and the cursing of the fig tree as marks of moral limits, and says that other historical figures were wiser or kinder.
He holds that the church has hindered moral progress, for example in its views on divorce, sex and birth control.
Religion, he says, rests on fear and the wish for a protector, and a good world needs knowledge, kindness and courage instead.
The argument for remedying injustice claims that the world's injustice proves a God who will set things right, and Russell replies that the universe as we see it gives no ground for that inference.
The collection also argues against personal immortality, because mind seems bound to the body and memory and character change with changes in the brain.
A good life, in his famous line, is one inspired by love and guided by knowledge.

books.thesis: Sudden awareness of the bare, contingent fact of existence strips away the meaning we assume things have.
books.summary:
Sartre's novel, in the form of Antoine Roquentin's diary, asks what happens when a person stops taking the world for granted. Roquentin, a historian living in a provincial town, starts to feel a strange disgust at objects and at his own existence.

The nausea he feels reveals that things exist without reason or necessity, and that human life has no given purpose. He tests escapes such as his research, other people and love, and finds them insufficient, then glimpses a modest way forward through creating something, perhaps a book. The novel dramatizes ideas later set out in Being and Nothingness, and some readers find its conclusion thin.
ideas: Roquentin records a growing sense that something has changed in him, and the first signs include a pebble by the sea and a door handle that feel uncanny to touch.
The nausea reveals the contingency of existence: things simply are there without necessity or reason, and he is superfluous like everything else.
The chestnut tree root scene is the key moment, when he sees that the root has no explanation and that words and categories do not reach its bare existence.
The Self-Taught Man and the townspeople in the portrait gallery represent the bad faith of those who hide their freedom behind roles, humanism or social rank.
His historical research on the Marquis de Rollebon fails, as he realizes that the past cannot be recovered or given the stable meaning he sought.
His relationship with Anny shows that the old idea of perfect moments cannot be revived and that adventure is only a story imposed on life.
A jazz song, Some of These Days, suggests an escape by creation, and he decides to write something that might justify his life to others, a hint of the existential idea that meaning is made.
The novel is framed as a diary found among Roquentin's papers, and it opens with a publisher's note and undated pages.
The Self-Taught Man is humiliated when he is caught in an incident with a boy in the library and is thrown out, which exposes the limits of his humanism.
Roquentin calls the respectable citizens in the portrait gallery 'salauds', people who hide their contingency behind rights and duties, and he leaves Bouville for Paris at the end.

books.thesis: Science advances by bold conjectures tested against refutation. Verification never settles a theory.
books.summary:
Popper takes on the problem of demarcation: what separates genuine science from metaphysics and pseudo-science. He also faces Hume's problem of induction, since no number of observations logically proves a universal law.

His answer is falsifiability. A theory is scientific if it forbids certain outcomes and so can be shown wrong by observation. Scientists should propose risky conjectures, try hard to refute them, and tentatively keep those that survive. The book is dense and technical, and critics such as Kuhn and Lakatos argue that real science does not follow strict falsification, since researchers often protect core theories from awkward data.
ideas: Induction cannot justify scientific laws, because finite observations never logically entail a universal statement. Popper holds that science does not actually rely on it.
The criterion of demarcation is falsifiability. A theory that no possible observation could contradict is not scientific, however well it seems to fit the facts.
Science proceeds by deductive testing. Consequences are derived from a hypothesis and checked against observation, and a failed prediction counts against the theory.
Good theories take risks. The more a theory prohibits, the more informative it is and the higher its empirical content.
Corroboration is not confirmation. A theory that has survived severe tests is provisionally accepted, but it is never shown to be true or even probable.
Basic statements, the observations used in tests, are accepted by convention and remain open to revision. Popper rejects the idea that science rests on a firm bedrock of experience.
Ad hoc rescues of a threatened theory lower its scientific standing, so Popper sets methodological rules against evasive moves that reduce testability.
Popper separates the context of discovery from the context of justification and says the logic of knowledge concerns only the second, not the psychology of invention.
